Topical Past Papers · Topic 3 Past Paper Questions: Stoichiometry 12 real Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 3.1 Formulae and Equations · 3.3 The Mole and Calculations 3.1 Formulae and Equations These questions test whether you can build correct formulae from ion charges and turn information given in words into a balanced equation; examiners give one mark for the right formulae in the right places and a second for balancing, so never change a formula to make it balance. What examiners keep seeing Examiner reports keep finding formulae copied wrongly even when the paper prints them (HgO written incorrectly, oxygen written as O instead of O 2 ) and equations left unbalanced once the formulae are right; ionic equations also lose marks for missing state symbols or for including spectator ions. 0620/41/M/J/24 Q6(d)(ii) · May/June 2024 · [1 mark] When zinc oxide neutralises aqueous sodium hydroxide, sodium zincate is formed. The formula of the zincate ion is ZnO 2 2– . Deduce the formula of sodium zincate. Na 2 ZnO 2 (Two Na + ions are needed to balance the 2− charge on one ZnO 2 2− ion.) Why this scores One mark for Na 2 ZnO 2 . Treat the zincate ion like any other 2− ion such as SO 4 2− : total positive charge must equal total negative charge. Writing NaZnO 2 (charges not balanced) is the usual slip. 0620/43/O/N/25 Q3(f) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Deduce the formula of: … gallium(III) bromide … gallium(III) sulfate. gallium(III) bromide: GaBr 3 (Ga 3+ needs three Br − ) gallium(III) sulfate: Ga 2 (SO 4 ) 3 (2 × 3+ = 6+ balances 3 × 2− = 6−) Why this scores One mark for each formula. The Roman numeral (III) tells you the ion is Ga 3+ , so it behaves exactly like Al 3+ . Brackets around SO 4 are essential: Ga 2 SO 43 or Ga 2 S 3 O 12 will not be credited. 0620/41/M/J/23 Q4(f) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Oxygen can also be produced by the decomposition of mercury(II) oxide, HgO. The only products of this decomposition are mercury and oxygen. Write a symbol equation for this decomposition. 2HgO → 2Hg + O 2 Why this scores One mark for the correct formulae (HgO, Hg, O 2 ) on the correct sides and one for balancing. The examiner report noted oxygen written as O, Hg 2 for mercury and HgO miscopied even though it was printed in the question; oxygen is always diatomic, O 2 . 0620/43/O/N/22 Q4(c) · October/November 2022 · [2 marks] Phosphorus oxychloride has the formula POCl 3 . Phosphorus oxychloride is the only product of the reaction between phosphorus(V) chloride, PCl 5 , and phosphorus(V) oxide, P 4 O 10 . Write a chemical equation for the reaction between phosphorus(V) chloride and phosphorus(V) oxide. 6PCl 5 + P 4 O 10 → 10POCl 3 Check: P 6 + 4 = 10; Cl 30 = 30; O 10 = 10. Why this scores One mark for all three formulae on the correct sides and one for the fully balanced equation. Balance oxygen first: P 4 O 10 gives 10 O, so you need 10POCl 3 , then 6PCl 5 supplies the 30 Cl. The examiner report says many candidates had the right formulae but did not balance. 0620/42/M/J/23 Q4(d) · May/June 2023 · [3 marks] Complete the word equation for the reaction of NaOH(aq) with ammonium chloride. sodium hydroxide + ammonium chloride → sodium chloride + ammonia + water Why this scores One mark for each product. This is the reaction of an ammonium salt with an alkali, which always gives a salt, ammonia gas and water. The examiner report flagged ‘ammonium’ written instead of ammonia and ‘hydrogen’ instead of water. 0620/43/M/J/24 Q5(a)(iii) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: Barium sulfate, BaSO 4 , is an insoluble salt and is made by precipitation. Write an ionic equation for the precipitation reaction which produces barium sulfate. Include state symbols. Ba 2+ (aq) + SO 4 2− (aq) → BaSO 4 (s) Why this scores One mark for BaSO 4 as the only product, one for Ba 2+ and SO 4 2− as the only reactants and one for the state symbols: ions in solution are (aq), the precipitate is (s). Leave out spectator ions such as Na + and Cl − . 3.3 The Mole and Calculations These questions test the mole chain: convert what you are given into moles, use the ratio from the equation, then convert into what is asked for; examiners give a mark for each step, so clear working earns credit even if the final number slips. What examiners keep seeing The commonest losses are ignoring the mole ratio (treating 2 : 1 as 1 : 1), forgetting to divide cm 3 by 1000, and in percentage-by-mass questions counting only one atom of an element (e.g. 56 instead of 112 for Fe in Fe 2 O 3 ). Examiners also refuse fractions as final answers and M r values left as an unworked sum. 0620/42/F/M/24 Q1(b)(i) · February/March 2024 · [2 marks] Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in iron(III) oxide, Fe 2 O 3 . M r of Fe 2 O 3 = (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 160 mass of iron in one formula = 2 × 56 = 112 percentage of iron = (112 ÷ 160) × 100 = 70.0% Why this scores One mark for M r = 160 and one for using 112 to reach 70%. The examiner report notes many candidates used 56 (one Fe) and got 35%, and some used the atomic number of iron instead of its A r . 0620/43/O/N/24 Q4(f)(i) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: 0.325 g of Zn is added to dilute sulfuric acid which contains 0.0100 moles of H 2 SO 4 . The equation for this reaction is shown. Zn + H 2 SO 4 → ZnSO 4 + H 2 Determine whether Zn or H 2 SO 4 is the limiting reactant. Explain your answer. moles of Zn = 0.325 ÷ 65 = 0.00500 mol Zn is the limiting reactant : Zn and H 2 SO 4 react in a 1 : 1 ratio, and there are fewer moles of Zn (0.00500) than of H 2 SO 4 (0.0100), so the zinc is used up first and the acid is in excess. Why this scores One mark for 0.00500 mol of Zn and one for concluding Zn is limiting with the reason: fewer moles and a 1 : 1 ratio. Comparing masses (0.325 g against 0.0100 mol) instead of moles earns nothing. 0620/43/O/N/25 Q6(a) · October/November 2025 · [3 marks] Organic compound Q has the following composition by mass. C, 50.00%; H, 5.56%; O, 44.44% Calculate the empirical formula of compound Q. C: 50.00 ÷ 12 = 4.17; H: 5.56 ÷ 1 = 5.56; O: 44.44 ÷ 16 = 2.78 divide by the smallest (2.78): C 1.5 : H 2 : O 1 multiply by 2 to get whole numbers: C 3 : H 4 : O 2 empirical formula = C 3 H 4 O 2 Why this scores One mark for dividing each percentage by its A r , one for the ratio 1.5 : 2 : 1 (or 3 : 4 : 2) and one for C 3 H 4 O 2 . Do not round 1.5 to 2; a ratio ending in .5 means multiply everything by 2. Examiners also see atomic numbers used instead of A r values. 0620/41/M/J/24 Q5(d)(ii) · May/June 2024 · [4 marks] In an experiment, 1.405 g of CoSO 4 •xH 2 O is heated until all the water is given off. The mass of CoSO 4 that remains is 0.775 g. [ M r : CoSO 4 , 155; H 2 O, 18] … Determine the value of x using the following steps. Calculate the number of moles of CoSO 4 that remains. Calculate the mass of H 2 O given off. Calculate the number of moles of H 2 O given off. Determine the value of x. moles of CoSO 4 = 0.775 ÷ 155 = 0.00500 mol mass of H 2 O = 1.405 − 0.775 = 0.630 g moles of H 2 O = 0.630 ÷ 18 = 0.0350 mol x = 0.0350 ÷ 0.00500 = 7 Why this scores One mark per step: 0.00500 mol, 0.630 g, 0.0350 mol and x = 7. x is the ratio of moles of water to moles of anhydrous salt, so divide water by CoSO 4 , not the other way round, and give a whole number. 0620/41/O/N/24 Q4(a)(iii) · October/November 2024 · [4 marks] Source material: When magnesium nitrate is heated strongly, magnesium oxide is formed. The equation for this reaction is shown. 2Mg(NO 3 ) 2 → 2MgO + 4NO 2 + O 2 Calculate the volume of NO 2 gas, at r.t.p., formed when 7.40 g of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 is heated. Use the following steps. Calculate the M r of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 . Calculate the number of moles of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 used. Determine the number of moles of NO 2 formed. Calculate the volume of NO 2 gas, in cm 3 , at r.t.p. M r of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 = 24 + 2 × (14 + 3 × 16) = 148 moles of Mg(NO 3 ) 2 = 7.40 ÷ 148 = 0.0500 mol mole ratio Mg(NO 3 ) 2 : NO 2 = 2 : 4, so moles of NO 2 = 0.0500 × 2 = 0.100 mol volume of NO 2 = 0.100 × 24 000 = 2400 cm 3 Why this scores One mark for each step: 148, 0.0500 mol, 0.100 mol and 2400 cm 3 . The answer is asked for in cm 3 , so use 24 000 cm 3 per mole (24 dm 3 would give 2.40, which needs the unit dm 3 ). Forgetting the 2 : 4 ratio halves the answer. 0620/42/M/J/23 Q4(g) · May/June 2023 · [5 marks] In a titration, 25.0 cm 3 of 0.0800 mol / dm 3 aqueous potassium hydroxide, KOH(aq), is neutralised by 20.0 cm 3 of dilute sulfuric acid, H 2 SO 4 (aq). 2KOH(aq) + H 2 SO 4 (aq) → K 2 SO 4 (aq) + 2H 2 O(l) … Calculate the concentration of H 2 SO 4 , in g / dm 3 using the following steps. Calculate the number of moles of KOH used. Determine the number of moles of H 2 SO 4 which react with the KOH. Calculate the concentration of H 2 SO 4 in mol / dm 3 . Calculate the concentration of H 2 SO 4 in g / dm 3 . moles of KOH = 0.0800 × (25.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.00200 mol mole ratio KOH : H 2 SO 4 = 2 : 1, so moles of H 2 SO 4 = 0.00200 ÷ 2 = 0.00100 mol concentration of H 2 SO 4 = 0.00100 ÷ (20.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.0500 mol/dm 3 M r of H 2 SO 4 = (2 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16) = 98 concentration = 0.0500 × 98 = 4.90 g/dm 3 Why this scores Five marks: 0.00200 mol KOH, 0.00100 mol H 2 SO 4 , 0.0500 mol/dm 3 , M r = 98 and 4.90 g/dm 3 . The examiner report warns that fractions (such as 1/20) are not accepted as answers and that an M r left as ‘2 + 32 + 64’ may lose the mark: work every value out. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 4.1 Electrolysis · 4.2 Hydrogen–Oxygen Fuel Cells 4.1 Electrolysis These questions test definitions, predicting the products and observations at each electrode, ionic half-equations and electroplating; examiners reward exact products (never ions), visible observations and balanced half-equations with electrons on the correct side. What examiners keep seeing Writing anode half-equations with electrons gained (2Br − + 2e − → Br 2 ) or giving the halogen as the anode product when the halide solution is dilute (oxygen forms instead). 0620/43/O/N/24 Q2(a) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] State the meaning of the term electrolysis. The breakdown (decomposition) of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution , by the passage of an electric current. Why this scores One mark for “breakdown by the passage of electricity” and one for “an ionic compound that is molten or aqueous”. Examiners do not credit “separation into ions” or “separating elements”, and many answers lose the second mark by leaving out the molten/aqueous condition. 0620/42/M/J/21 Q4(e)(ii) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: The student repeats the experiment using concentrated aqueous sodium chloride. The student added litmus to the solution after the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride. State the colour seen in the solution. Give a reason for your answer. Colour: blue. Reason: the solution left behind is sodium hydroxide, which is an alkali (H + and Cl − ions are removed as hydrogen and chlorine, leaving Na + and OH − ions). Why this scores One mark for blue and one for naming sodium hydroxide / an alkali as what remains. The reason must say what is left in the solution; just saying “chlorine forms” earns nothing. 0620/41/O/N/24 Q3(e)(vi) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate undergoes electrolysis using graphite electrodes. State two diﬀerences seen if the electrolysis is repeated using copper electrodes instead of graphite electrodes. 1. The blue colour of the solution stays the same instead of fading. 2. No bubbles of gas form at the anode; instead the copper anode gets smaller as it dissolves. Why this scores One mark each for two of: colour stays constant, no bubbles at the anode, anode dissolves. These must be things you could see , so “Cu 2+ ions are replaced” on its own is an explanation, not a difference seen. 0620/41/O/N/24 Q3(e)(v) · October/November 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate undergoes electrolysis using graphite electrodes. Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the anode. 4OH − → O 2 + 2H 2 O + 4e − Why this scores One mark for O 2 as a product, one for OH − on the left with electrons on the right, and one for the fully balanced equation. Check it: four O and four H on each side, and a total charge of 4− on each side. Electrons are lost at the anode, so they go on the right. 0620/43/M/J/23 Q5(c)(i) · May/June 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: Spoons can be electroplated with silver. Name the substances used as:
the anode (positive electrode) …
the cathode (negative electrode) …
the electrolyte. Anode: silver Cathode: the spoon Electrolyte: aqueous silver nitrate Why this scores One mark each. The object being plated is always the cathode, because positive Ag + ions are attracted to it and reduced to silver. The examiner report notes candidates who swapped the spoon and silver, used graphite electrodes, or gave an insoluble electrolyte such as silver chloride; the electrolyte must be a solution containing silver ions. 0620/42/F/M/25 Q2(d)(iii) · February/March 2025 · [5 marks] Source material: Ionic compounds can be decomposed by the passage of an electric current using inert electrodes. Name the products and state the observations at the negative and positive electrodes when dilute aqueous potassium bromide, KBr, is decomposed by the passage of an electric current. Product at the negative electrode: hydrogen Observation at the negative electrode: bubbles of gas Products at the positive electrode: oxygen and water Observation at the positive electrode: bubbles of gas Why this scores One mark each for hydrogen, bubbles, oxygen, water and bubbles. Potassium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen forms at the cathode; the solution is dilute , so OH − ions are discharged at the anode (4OH − → O 2 + 2H 2 O + 4e − ), giving oxygen and water rather than bromine. The examiner report says bromine was the commonest wrong answer, and ions such as K + or Br − are never products. 4.2 Hydrogen–Oxygen Fuel Cells Short questions on the reactants, the overall equation and how fuel cells compare with petrol engines; examiners want specific chemical points, not general statements about the environment. What examiners keep seeing Vague answers such as “no pollution” or “renewable”, and giving “hydrogen is flammable” as a disadvantage (petrol is flammable too); the credited disadvantage is storing hydrogen under high pressure. 0620/42/F/M/22 Q4(c)(i) · February/March 2022 · [1 mark] Source material: Fuel cells are used to generate electricity. Name the reactants in a fuel cell. Hydrogen and oxygen. Why this scores One mark for both gases. Name both; the only product is water. 0620/43/M/J/23 Q5(d)(ii) · May/June 2023 · [1 mark] Source material: Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells can be used to produce electricity to power cars. Petrol produces carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide when it powers cars. State one disadvantage, other than cost, of using hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells to power cars compared to using petrol. Hydrogen is a gas, so it is difficult to store in a car: it has to be kept in tanks at high pressure. Why this scores One mark for a storage problem (high-pressure tanks); having few hydrogen filling stations is also credited. The examiner report says “hydrogen is flammable” does not score (petrol is flammable too), nor does “less efficient”, and many candidates lost the mark by giving an advantage instead. 0620/41/M/J/23 Q5(c)(i) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells can be used to produce electricity in vehicles. Write the symbol equation for the overall reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell. 2H 2 + O 2 → 2H 2 O Why this scores One mark for the correct formulae and one for balancing. It is the same equation as burning hydrogen. The examiner report notes H and O written as single atoms instead of H 2 and O 2 . 0620/41/O/N/24 Q5(a)(ii) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Hydrogen is used in fuel cells to produce electricity in vehicles. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using fuel cells instead of gasoline in vehicle engines. Advantage: the only product is water, so no carbon dioxide is released from the vehicle. Disadvantage: hydrogen is hard to store because it must be kept under high pressure in heavy tanks. Why this scores One mark for each. Be specific: “no carbon dioxide” or “only water is produced” scores, but vague answers like “no pollution” or “environmentally friendly” do not. Topical Past Papers · Topic 5 Past Paper Questions: Chemical Energetics 5 real Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 5.1 Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions 5.1 Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions These questions test the key definitions (ΔH, activation energy), explaining energy changes using bond breaking and bond making, and bond-energy calculations; examiners reward the exact key words, every step of working, and the sign of ΔH. What examiners keep seeing Leaving out the comparison when explaining why a reaction is exothermic, and dropping the minus sign (or miscounting bonds) in bond-energy calculations. 0620/42/F/M/23 Q3(b)(i) · February/March 2023 · [1 mark] Source material: N 2 (g) + 3H 2 (g) … 2NH 3 (g) ∆H = –92 kJ / mol … The forward reaction is exothermic. State what is meant by the symbol ∆H. The enthalpy change of the reaction. Why this scores One mark for “enthalpy change”. It is the thermal energy transferred, in kJ/mol; the negative sign here shows energy is released. 0620/42/O/N/23 Q5(b)(iv) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Define the term activation energy. The minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react. Why this scores One mark for “minimum energy” and one for “colliding particles must have to react”. “The energy needed to start a reaction” misses both key words and scores nothing. 0620/42/O/N/21 Q4(a) · October/November 2021 · [3 marks] Source material: Chlorine reacts with carbon monoxide to produce phosgene gas … The reaction is exothermic. Explain why the reaction is exothermic in terms of the energy changes of bond breaking and bond making. Breaking the bonds in the chlorine and carbon monoxide molecules takes in energy. Making the new bonds in phosgene releases energy. More energy is released when the new bonds form than is taken in when the old bonds break, so overall energy is given out. Why this scores One mark for each statement. The examiner report says three simple statements are enough but very few candidates gave all three; the usual loss is the comparison (energy released by bond making is greater than energy taken in by bond breaking). 0620/41/M/J/22 Q7(e) · May/June 2022 · [3 marks] Source material: Br 2 (g) + Cl 2 (g) → 2BrCl (g) Bromine monochloride, BrCl, is made by the reaction between bromine and chlorine. The chemical equation is shown. … Calculate the overall energy change for the reaction using bond energies. Bond energies given (kJ/mol): Br–Br 190, Cl–Cl 242, Br–Cl 218. Energy to break bonds: 190 + 242 = 432 kJ Energy released making bonds: 2 × 218 = 436 kJ Energy change = 432 − 436 = −4 kJ/mol Why this scores One mark for 432, one for 436 and one for −4 with its sign. The examiner report notes two common slips: doubling the bond-breaking total to 864 (only one Br–Br and one Cl–Cl bond are broken) and writing 4 instead of −4. 0620/41/O/N/25 Q4(b) · October/November 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: Gaseous sulfur tetrafluoride … reacts with steam in a reversible reaction. … SF 4 (g) + 2H 2 O(g) … SO 2 (g) + 4HF(g) … ΔH = –54 kJ / mol The equation for the reaction can be represented as shown in Fig. 4.2. … Table 4.1 shows some bond energies. … Use the bond energies in Table 4.1 and the value of ΔH of the reaction to calculate the S=O bond energy in kJ / mol. Use the following steps.
• Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants.
• Calculate the energy released when the bonds in the products form.
• Calculate the S=O bond energy. Bond energies given (kJ/mol): S–F 330, O–H 460, H–F 570. SF 4 has 4 S–F bonds, 2H 2 O has 4 O–H bonds, SO 2 has 2 S=O bonds and 4HF has 4 H–F bonds. Bonds broken: (4 × 330) + (4 × 460) = 1320 + 1840 = 3160 kJ Bonds formed: ΔH = energy in − energy out −54 = 3160 − energy out energy out = 3160 + 54 = 3214 kJ S=O bond energy: (2 × S=O) + (4 × 570) = 3214 2 × S=O = 3214 − 2280 = 934 S=O = 934 ÷ 2 = 467 kJ/mol Why this scores One mark each for 3160, 3214, subtracting the 4 H–F bonds to get 934, and dividing by 2 to get 467. The key step is rearranging ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed: because ΔH is negative, the products’ bond energy must be larger than 3160. Remember to count both S=O bonds in SO 2 . Topical Past Papers · Topic 6 Past Paper Questions: Chemical Reactions 18 real Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 6.2 Rate of Reaction · 6.3 Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium · 6.4 Redox 6.2 Rate of Reaction Rate questions test whether you can explain each change in conditions with collision theory; examiners reward the exact phrases “particles per unit volume”, “frequency of collisions” and “proportion of collisions with energy ≥ the activation energy”. What examiners keep seeing Writing “more collisions” or “more chance of collisions” instead of “more frequent collisions”, and saying particles gain kinetic energy when the change was concentration or surface area rather than temperature (examiner reports, June 2025). 0620/42/O/N/24 Q3(e)(i) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Deﬁne the term activation energy. The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for them to react. Why this scores One mark for “minimum energy” linked to colliding particles reacting. “The energy needed to start a reaction” misses both the word minimum and the idea of a collision. 0620/43/O/N/24 Q5(c)(ii) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: A student investigates the rate of decomposition of aqueous hydrogen peroxide, H 2 O 2 , using manganese(IV) oxide as a catalyst. … The student uses the apparatus shown in Fig. 5.1. loosely fitting cotton wool … records the mass at regular time intervals. State how the mass of the catalyst has changed, if at all, at the end of the experiment. No change: the mass of manganese(IV) oxide at the end is the same as at the start. Why this scores One mark for “no change”: a catalyst is not used up, so its mass and chemical composition are unchanged. Do not confuse this with the reading on the balance, which falls because oxygen escapes through the cotton wool. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(d) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: The symbol equation for the industrial production of ammonia is shown. N 2 (g) + 3H 2 (g) … 2NH 3 (g) ∆H = –90 kJ / mol State two methods of increasing the rate of this reaction. 1 Increase the temperature. 2 Increase the pressure. Why this scores One mark for each method. Give the direction of the change (“increase the pressure”), not just the factor: “pressure” on its own does not score. 0620/41/M/J/25 Q3(c)(vi) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: step 1 Powdered copper(II) carbonate is added to dilute sulfuric acid. Step 1 is repeated using sulfuric acid of concentration 0.200 mol / dm 3 instead of 0.100 mol / dm 3 . All other conditions are the same. The rate of reaction increases. Explain why the rate of reaction increases. Give your answer in terms of particles. The more concentrated acid has more acid particles per unit volume. So collisions between acid particles and copper(II) carbonate particles are more frequent (the collision frequency increases). Why this scores One mark for “more particles per unit volume”, one for “increased collision frequency”. The examiner report notes that “more particles” with no “per unit volume”, “more collisions” with no reference to frequency, and claims that the particles move faster or gain energy all lost marks: concentration does not change particle energy. 0620/43/M/J/25 Q3(c)(v) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: step 1 An excess of powdered zinc carbonate is added to dilute sulfuric acid. Step 1 is repeated using large pieces of zinc carbonate instead of powdered zinc carbonate. All other conditions are the same. The rate of reaction decreases. Explain why the rate of reaction decreases. Give your answer in terms of particles. Large pieces have a smaller surface area, so fewer zinc carbonate particles are exposed to the acid. The frequency of collisions between acid particles and zinc carbonate particles decreases. Why this scores One mark for smaller surface area, one for decreased collision frequency between particles. The examiner report says only a minority gave the particle explanation; “fewer collisions” without reference to time, “less chance of collisions” and anything about kinetic energy or speed scored nothing. 0620/42/M/J/25 Q6(d)(ii) · May/June 2025 · [3 marks] Source material: C 2 H 4 reacts with steam to form ethanol. The conditions for this process are 300 °C and 60 atm pressure. Explain, in terms of collision theory, why the rate of the forward reaction increases if the temperature increases. At a higher temperature the particles have more kinetic energy, so they move faster. The frequency of collisions between ethene and steam particles increases. A greater proportion of the collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy, so there are more successful collisions per second. Why this scores One mark each for: kinetic energy of the particles increases; collision frequency increases; a higher proportion of particles/collisions have energy ≥ the activation energy. The examiner report flags “particles have energy greater than the activation energy” (which implies all of them do) and “kinetic energy increases” with no mention of particles. 6.3 Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium These questions test the features of a dynamic equilibrium, predicting how temperature, pressure and a catalyst affect its position, and the Haber process conditions; examiners want a direction (left or right) plus a reason based on exothermic/endothermic or moles of gas. What examiners keep seeing Saying that at equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are equal: it is the rates that are equal and the concentrations that stay constant. A catalyst never moves the position of equilibrium. 0620/41/O/N/24 Q3(d)(i) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: Crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate can be obtained from aqueous copper(II) sulfate by crystallisation. State what is meant by the term hydrated. A hydrated substance is chemically combined with water. Why this scores One mark for “chemically combined with water”. “Contains water” or “wet” is not enough: the water is bonded into the crystal, and heating drives it off to leave the anhydrous salt (blue CuSO 4 ·5H 2 O → white CuSO 4 ). 0620/41/M/J/25 Q5(b)(iii) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Methanol, CH 3 OH, is manufactured by the reaction between hydrogen and carbon monoxide. An equilibrium mixture is produced. If a temperature of more than 250 °C is used, the yield of methanol decreases. State what can be deduced about the forward reaction. The forward reaction is exothermic . Why this scores One mark for “exothermic”. A higher temperature moves the equilibrium in the endothermic direction; the yield of methanol falls, so the reverse reaction is endothermic and the forward reaction exothermic. The examiner report says “endothermic” was the commonest wrong answer. 0620/43/O/N/25 Q4(a)(i) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: The reaction is a reversible reaction. When the three gases are in a closed container the system reaches equilibrium. Describe a reversible reaction at equilibrium in terms of: … • the rate of the forward reaction and the rate of the reverse reaction … • the concentrations of reactants and products. The rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the reverse reaction. The concentrations of the reactants and products stay constant (they no longer change). Why this scores One mark for equal rates, one for constant concentrations. Examiner reports for this definition say “the concentrations of reactants and products are equal” and “the forward reaction is equal to the reverse reaction” (no mention of rate) gained no credit. 0620/42/O/N/24 Q3(d) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Chloride P has the formula S 2 Cl 2 . Chloride Q has the formula SCl 2 . S 2 Cl 2 (g) + Cl 2 (g) … 2SCl 2 (g) Chloride P is converted to chloride Q by reaction with chlorine in a closed system. The reversible reaction reaches an equilibrium. The forward reaction is exothermic. Suggest two changes to the conditions which will result in a decrease in the concentration of chloride Q at equilibrium. 1 Decrease the concentration of S 2 Cl 2 or Cl 2 (remove some of a reactant), so the equilibrium shifts to the left. 2 Increase the temperature, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic (reverse) direction, to the left. Why this scores One mark for each change. Count the moles of gas before suggesting pressure: there are 2 moles of gas on each side, so changing the pressure does not move this equilibrium, and a catalyst never does. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(c) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] State the typical conditions and name the catalyst used in the industrial production of ammonia. Temperature: 450 °C Pressure: 200 atm (20 000 kPa) Catalyst: iron Why this scores One mark each for 450 °C, 200 atm (or 20 000 kPa) and iron; the units are part of the mark. The examiner report lists missing or wrong units and naming vanadium(V) oxide (the Contact process catalyst) as the usual slips. 0620/41/O/N/25 Q4(c) · October/November 2025 · [5 marks] Source material: Gaseous sulfur tetrafluoride, SF 4 , reacts with steam in a reversible reaction. SF 4 (g) + 2H 2 O(g) … SO 2 (g) + 4HF(g) ΔH = –54 kJ / mol State the effect, if any, on the position of equilibrium when the following changes are made. Give a reason for each of your answers. • The temperature is increased. • The pressure is increased. • A catalyst is added. Temperature increased: the position of equilibrium moves to the left. The forward reaction is exothermic, so a higher temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction. Pressure increased: the position of equilibrium moves to the left, because there are fewer moles of gas on the left (3) than on the right (5). Catalyst added: no change, because a catalyst increases the rates of the forward and reverse reactions equally. Why this scores Two marks for temperature (left + exothermic forward reaction), two for pressure (left + fewer moles of gas on the left) and one for “no change” with a catalyst. Steam is a gas here, so it counts: 1 + 2 = 3 moles on the left, 1 + 4 = 5 on the right. 6.4 Redox Redox questions test the definitions of oxidation, reduction and oxidising/reducing agents in terms of electrons and oxidation numbers, and working out oxidation numbers; examiners reward the definition in exactly the terms the question asks for. What examiners keep seeing Ignoring “in terms of oxidation number” and writing about electrons or oxygen instead, and writing oxidation numbers without a sign or with the sign after the number (“3−” instead of “−3”) (examiner report, June 2025). 0620/43/O/N/25 Q3(b)(iv) · October/November 2025 · [1 mark] Define the term reduction in terms of oxidation number. Reduction is a decrease in oxidation number. Why this scores One mark for “decrease in oxidation number”. Answer in the terms the question asks for: gain of electrons or loss of oxygen are correct facts about reduction but do not score here. 0620/42/O/N/25 Q2(d)(ii) · October/November 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: An oxidising agent converts Fe 2+ ions to Fe 3+ ions. Explain why the conversion of Fe 2+ ions to Fe 3+ ions is described as oxidation. Each Fe 2+ ion loses an electron, and loss of electrons is oxidation. Why this scores One mark for loss of an electron. Saying that iron “gains a positive charge” describes the result but not the reason: name the electron loss (OIL RIG). 0620/42/O/N/25 Q2(d)(i) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: An oxidising agent converts Fe 2+ ions to Fe 3+ ions. Define the term oxidising agent. A substance that oxidises another substance and is itself reduced. Why this scores One mark for “oxidises another substance”, one for “is itself reduced”. A common slip is to swap the two, writing that the oxidising agent is oxidised. 0620/42/F/M/25 Q3(g)(ii) · February/March 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: Aqueous chlorine, Cl 2 , reacts with aqueous potassium iodide, KI. One of the products formed is iodine, I 2 . Explain why this reaction is defined as a redox reaction. Give your answer in terms of electron transfer. Iodide ions (I − ) lose electrons to form iodine, so they are oxidised. Chlorine (Cl 2 ) gains electrons to form chloride ions, so it is reduced. Oxidation and reduction happen at the same time, so the reaction is redox. Why this scores One mark for iodide ions losing electrons, one for chlorine gaining electrons. Name the particles correctly: it is the iodide ions that lose electrons, not “iodine” or “potassium”. 0620/42/O/N/25 Q4(b)(iv) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] The oxidation number of the O atoms in Al (NO 3 ) 3 is –2. The formula of the aluminium ion in Al (NO 3 ) 3 is Al 3+ . Determine the oxidation number of the N atoms in Al (NO 3 ) 3 . Show your working. The oxidation numbers in the compound add up to 0. Let the oxidation number of N be x : (+3) + 3 x + 9(−2) = 0 3 + 3 x − 18 = 0 3 x = +15 x = +5 Why this scores One mark for using the oxygen total of −18 (nine O atoms), one for +5. Write the sign in front of the number: the examiner report notes that answers such as “5” or “5+” lose credit. 0620/42/O/N/24 Q3(f) · October/November 2024 · [4 marks] Source material: Chloride P has the formula S 2 Cl 2 . Chloride Q has the formula SCl 2 . S 2 Cl 2 (g) + Cl 2 (g) … 2SCl 2 (g) The reaction of chloride P with chlorine is a redox reaction. The oxidation number of Cl in chloride P and chloride Q is –1. Use oxidation numbers to explain why: … ● sulfur is oxidised in the forward reaction … ● chlorine is oxidised in the reverse reaction. Sulfur (forward reaction): in S 2 Cl 2 , 2S + 2(−1) = 0, so S = +1. In SCl 2 , S + 2(−1) = 0, so S = +2. The oxidation number of sulfur increases from +1 to +2, so sulfur is oxidised. Chlorine (reverse reaction): SCl 2 turns back into S 2 Cl 2 and Cl 2 . Chlorine goes from −1 in SCl 2 to 0 in Cl 2 (an uncombined element), an increase in oxidation number, so chlorine is oxidised. Why this scores One mark each for S = +1 in P, S = +2 in Q, Cl going from −1 to 0 in Cl 2 , and stating that both oxidation numbers increase . Always finish by linking the change to the definition: oxidation is an increase in oxidation number. Jump to: 7.1 Acids, Bases and Oxides · 7.3 Preparation of Salts 7.1 Acids, Bases and Oxides These questions test the proton-transfer definitions, strong versus weak acids, neutralisation and the classes of oxide; examiners reward the exact syllabus wording and the right type of arrow. What examiners keep seeing Using a one-way arrow for a weak acid’s dissociation was the commonest error in the 2023 and 2024 reports; also keep “strong” (how fully it dissociates) separate from “concentrated” (how much acid per dm 3 ). 0620/42/O/N/22 Q2(c)(i) · October/November 2022 · [1 mark] Explain in terms of proton transfer what is meant by a base. A base is a proton acceptor : it accepts a hydrogen ion, H + , from an acid. Why this scores One mark for “proton acceptor”, the syllabus definition, which the examiner report says was well known. Talking about OH − ions or pH does not answer a question asked “in terms of proton transfer”. 0620/42/M/J/23 Q4(f)(iv) · May/June 2023 · [1 mark] Write the ionic equation for the reaction when an acid neutralises a soluble base. H + (aq) + OH − (aq) → H 2 O(l) Why this scores One mark for the equation. A soluble base is an alkali, so the only ions that react are H + from the acid and OH − from the alkali; the examiner report says only the stronger candidates recalled this newer syllabus point. 0620/43/O/N/24 Q3(b)(i) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: SnO 2 is an amphoteric oxide. State the meaning of the term amphoteric. An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and bases , forming a salt and water in each case. Why this scores One mark: the answer must say it reacts with both acids and bases (alkalis). “Neutral” or “reacts with acids” alone scores nothing; ending with “to form a salt and water” matches the mark scheme exactly. 0620/42/F/M/24 Q1(d)(i) · February/March 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Equations for some of the reactions in the blast furnace are shown. … equation 3 CaO + SiO 2 → CaSiO 3 Explain why the reaction in equation 3 can be described as an acid–base reaction. CaO is a metal oxide, so it is a basic oxide . SiO 2 is a non-metal oxide, so it is an acidic oxide . The basic oxide neutralises the acidic oxide to form a salt, calcium silicate. Why this scores One mark for CaO being basic and one for SiO 2 being acidic. The examiner report says weaker answers just wrote “neutralisation” without saying which oxide is the acid and which is the base. 0620/42/O/N/25 Q4(a)(ii) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: Ethanoic acid, CH 3 COOH, is a weak acid. One mole of each acid is added separately to 1000 cm 3 of distilled water to form a dilute solution. Explain, in terms of dissociation, why: • nitric acid is described as a strong acid … • ethanoic acid is described as a weak acid. Nitric acid is completely dissociated into ions in water: HNO 3 → H + + NO 3 − . Ethanoic acid is only partially dissociated : most molecules stay as CH 3 COOH, so an equilibrium forms, CH 3 COOH ⇌ CH 3 COO − + H + . Why this scores One mark for “completely dissociated” for the strong acid and one for “partially dissociated” for the weak acid. Answers about concentration or pH alone do not score, because strength is about how far the acid dissociates. 0620/42/F/M/24 Q3(e) · February/March 2024 · [3 marks] Complete the equation to show the dissociation of ethanoic acid, CH 3 COOH, in aqueous solution. CH 3 COOH(aq) ⇌ CH 3 COO − (aq) + H + (aq) The reversible arrow is needed because ethanoic acid is a weak acid: it only partially dissociates, so an equilibrium forms. Why this scores One mark each for H + , for CH 3 COO − and for the reversible arrow. The 2023 and 2024 examiner reports say the commonest error was a one-way arrow; some candidates also released 4H + , but only the H in the COOH group ionises. 7.3 Preparation of Salts These questions test the solubility rules and the three ways of making a salt; examiners reward a method that suits the salt, the key practical steps in order, and observations you can actually see. What examiners keep seeing Writing conclusions instead of observations (“no more gas is produced”, “the reaction stops”), and in precipitation questions mixing the two solids without dissolving them first or washing the residue without saying “with distilled water”. 0620/42/F/M/24 Q2(g)(i) · February/March 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: Aqueous lead(II) ions are added to aqueous chloride ions. A white precipitate of insoluble lead(II) chloride, PbCl 2 , is formed. Name a lead(II) compound which can be used in this reaction. Lead(II) nitrate (all nitrates are soluble, so it supplies Pb 2+ (aq) ions). Why this scores One mark for lead(II) nitrate: the compound must be soluble to give aqueous lead(II) ions. The examiner report says “lead bromide” was the commonest wrong answer, but lead(II) halides are insoluble. 0620/43/M/J/25 Q3(c)(i) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: Zinc sulfate crystals are made by the reaction between zinc carbonate and dilute sulfuric acid, using the following steps. step 1 An excess of powdered zinc carbonate is added to dilute sulfuric acid. Give two observations which show that the zinc carbonate is in excess in step 1. 1. Extra zinc carbonate stops dissolving : some white solid is left at the bottom of the beaker. 2. There is no more fizzing when more zinc carbonate is added. Why this scores One mark for each observation. The examiner report says these were the only two accepted: “no more gas is produced” and “the reaction stops” are not observations, and the leftover solid must not be called a precipitate. 0620/42/O/N/25 Q3(f) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: The student adds aqueous sodium sulfate, Na 2 SO 4 (aq), to aqueous barium chloride, BaCl 2 (aq). … step 3 Stir the mixture and then filter it. step 4 Dry the solid left in the filter paper. The actual mass of dry BaSO 4 collected in step 4 is greater than the expected mass. This is because the student should do an additional step between step 3 and step 4. Suggest what the student should do in this additional step, and explain why the actual mass collected is greater than the expected mass. The student should wash the residue in the filter paper with a little distilled water before drying it. Unwashed, the solid is still wet with the filtrate, which contains dissolved sodium chloride . When it dries, this NaCl is left on the barium sulfate and adds to its mass. Why this scores One mark for washing (rinsing) the residue with water and one for explaining that the extra mass is soluble sodium chloride left on the solid. 0620/42/O/N/25 Q3(h) · October/November 2025 · [3 marks] Source material: A student prepares a sample of the insoluble salt barium sulfate, BaSO 4 . The student adds aqueous sodium sulfate, Na 2 SO 4 (aq), to aqueous barium chloride, BaCl 2 (aq). State the name of a different: • barium salt that can be used in place of BaCl 2 … • sulfate salt that can be used in place of Na 2 SO 4 … • barium salt that can be made by this method. Instead of BaCl 2 : barium nitrate (soluble). Instead of Na 2 SO 4 : potassium sulfate (or ammonium sulfate), which is soluble. Another barium salt made this way: barium carbonate , which is insoluble (e.g. mix barium nitrate and sodium carbonate solutions). Why this scores One mark for each. The first two must be soluble (all nitrates, and all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts, are soluble); the third must be insoluble, because precipitation only works when the product is insoluble. 0620/41/M/J/21 Q5(a) · May/June 2021 · [5 marks] Source material: Lead(II) iodide, PbI 2 , is insoluble in water. … All sodium salts are soluble in water. Salts that are insoluble in water are made by precipitation. You are provided with solid lead(II) nitrate, Pb(NO 3 ) 2 , and solid sodium iodide, NaI. Describe how you would make a pure sample of lead(II) iodide by precipitation. Your answer should include: … practical details … a chemical equation for the precipitation reaction. Dissolve the lead(II) nitrate in distilled water in one beaker, and the sodium iodide in distilled water in another. Mix the two solutions and stir: a yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide forms. Filter the mixture; the lead(II) iodide stays in the filter paper as the residue. Wash the residue with distilled water to remove the soluble sodium nitrate. Dry the solid between filter papers or in a warm oven. Pb(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) + 2NaI(aq) → PbI 2 (s) + 2NaNO 3 (aq) Why this scores Marks for dissolving the solids in water, making the two solutions, filtering, washing with water and drying, plus the balanced equation (the ionic equation also scores). The examiner report says many mixed the two solids without dissolving them, said “wash” without saying with water, wrote PbI instead of PbI 2 , or wasted time crystallising the filtrate. 0620/43/O/N/21 Q5(b) · October/November 2021 · [5 marks] Source material: 20.0 cm 3 of dilute sulfuric acid neutralises 25.0 cm 3 of 1.00 mol / dm 3 aqueous sodium hydroxide. At the end of the titration the conical flask contains aqueous sodium sulfate with the dissolved indicator as an impurity. Describe how to prepare a pure sample of sodium sulfate crystals from the original solutions of dilute sulfuric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide of the same concentrations. You are not required to give details of how to carry out the titration. Mix 25.0 cm 3 of the sodium hydroxide with exactly 20.0 cm 3 of the sulfuric acid again, but without the indicator , so the sodium sulfate solution is pure. Pour the solution into an evaporating basin and heat it to evaporate some of the water. Stop heating at the saturation point (crystals form on a cold glass rod dipped into it); do not heat to dryness. Leave the solution to cool so that crystals form. Filter off the crystals and dry them between filter papers . Why this scores One mark each for: repeating with the same volumes but no indicator, heating, stopping at the saturation (crystallisation) point, cooling to crystallise, and describing how to dry. The examiner report says many described the titration anyway, did not say when to stop heating, left out crystallising, or wrote “dry” without saying how. x: Topical Past Papers · Topic 8 Past Paper Questions: The Periodic Table 17 real Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 8.1 Periodic Table, Group I and Noble Gases · 8.3 Group VII: the Halogens · 8.4 Transition Elements 8.1 Periodic Table, Group I and Noble Gases These questions test how the Periodic Table is arranged and the trends and reactions of Group I; examiners reward correct directions for trends, real observations and correct formulae. What examiners keep seeing Giving conclusions such as “hydrogen is given off” as observations, and writing wrong formulae: sodium oxide is Na 2 O, and a Group I metal with water gives the hydroxide (KOH), not the oxide. 0620/42/M/J/25 Q1(c) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Using numbers only, state the: number of metals in Period 3 of the Periodic Table 3 (Na, Mg and Al are metals; across the period the elements become non-metallic, and Si is not counted as a metal.) Why this scores One mark for 3. Across a period, elements change from metallic to non-metallic character. The question says “numbers only”, so write just the number on the answer line. 0620/43/O/N/20 Q5(a) · October/November 2020 · [1 mark] Describe the trend in the reactivity of Group I elements. Reactivity increases down the group (lithium is the least reactive). Why this scores One mark, but the direction is essential. The examiner report says “reactivity increases” with no direction, or “they are very reactive”, did not score. 0620/42/F/M/25 Q3(f) · February/March 2025 · [1 mark] Name the noble gas which has the same electronic configuration as a Br – ion. Krypton . A bromine atom gains one electron to form Br − , which then has 36 electrons, the same as krypton at the end of Period 4. Why this scores One mark for krypton. Use the Periodic Table printed in the paper: the examiner report says weaker candidates lost easy marks in this question by not using it. 0620/43/M/J/25 Q6(c)(i) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Give two observations when lithium is added to water. 1. Fizzing (bubbles). 2. The lithium floats on the water and slowly disappears . Why this scores One mark for each different observation (fizzing, floats, moves on the surface, solid disappears). The examiner report says “a gas is produced” is not an observation, and “fizzing” plus “bubbling” only scores once because they are the same thing. 0620/42/O/N/21 Q5(d)(v) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] Write the chemical equation for the reaction of sodium with oxygen. 4Na + O 2 → 2Na 2 O Why this scores One mark for the formula Na 2 O (two Na + ions balance one O 2− ion) and one for balancing. The examiner report says only a small proportion got the formula of sodium oxide right. 0620/43/M/J/22 Q6(a)(ii) · May/June 2022 · [5 marks] Source material: The Group I metals react with cold water. Transition elements do not react with cold water. Describe the observations when potassium is added to cold water. Write a balanced equation for the reaction. Include state symbols. Observations: the potassium floats and moves quickly around on the surface; it fizzes vigorously; it melts into a ball; the hydrogen catches fire with a lilac flame ; the potassium soon disappears. Equation: 2K(s) + 2H 2 O(l) → 2KOH(aq) + H 2 (g) Why this scores Two marks for any two observations, then one for KOH or H 2 as a product, one for the balanced equation and one for state symbols. The examiner report says K 2 O was a common wrong product and water was often wrongly given as (aq). 8.3 Group VII: the Halogens These questions test the trends down Group VII and displacement reactions; examiners reward correct colours, the halogen/halide distinction and correctly balanced (ionic) equations. What examiners keep seeing Mixing up the halogen and its halide ion (bromine and bromide), and not knowing that potassium halide solutions are colourless; both are flagged in the 2022 and 2024 examiner reports. 0620/41/M/J/22 Q7(c) · May/June 2022 · [1 mark] Group VII elements are known as the halogens. Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Predict the physical state of astatine at room temperature and pressure. Solid : melting and boiling points increase down Group VII, and iodine, above astatine, is already a solid. Why this scores One mark for solid. The examiner report says “gas” was the commonest wrong answer; the states go gas → liquid → solid down the group, so astatine continues the trend. 0620/42/M/J/23 Q2(b) · May/June 2023 · [1 mark] Explain why Group VII elements have similar chemical properties. Their atoms all have the same number of electrons in the outer shell (seven). Why this scores One mark. The examiner report says answers that left out the word “number” (“same electrons in the outer shell”) did not get credit. 0620/42/M/J/23 Q2(e)(ii) · May/June 2023 · [1 mark] Source material: Chlorine displaces bromine from aqueous potassium bromide but does not displace fluorine from aqueous sodium fluoride. State why chlorine does not displace fluorine from aqueous sodium fluoride. Chlorine is less reactive than fluorine . Why this scores One mark. A halogen can only displace a less reactive halogen from its halide, and reactivity decreases down Group VII. Compare the two elements; “chlorine is not reactive enough” does not say what it is compared with. 0620/43/M/J/22 Q6(c)(i) · May/June 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: When aqueous bromine is added to aqueous potassium iodide a reaction occurs. Describe the colour change of the solution. Original colour of potassium iodide solution: colourless . Final colour of reaction mixture: brown (iodine has been displaced). Why this scores One mark for each colour. The examiner report says most candidates did not know that potassium iodide solution is colourless; the brown colour is the iodine formed when bromine displaces it. 0620/41/M/J/22 Q7(d)(ii) · May/June 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: When aqueous chlorine is added to aqueous potassium bromide a reaction occurs. The ionic half-equations for the reaction are shown. Cl 2 (aq) + 2e – → 2Cl – (aq) 2Br – (aq) → Br 2 (aq) + 2e – Identify the species that is oxidised. Explain your decision. Species oxidised: bromide ions, Br − . Explanation: each bromide ion loses an electron , and oxidation is loss of electrons. Why this scores One mark for Br − and one for “loses electrons”. The examiner report says “bromine” was the commonest wrong species; bromine is the product, not the species that is oxidised. 0620/41/O/N/23 Q3(b)(ii) · October/November 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: A student bubbles chlorine gas into a test-tube containing aqueous potassium bromide. Complete the ionic equation for this reaction. Include state symbols. Cl 2 (g) + 2Br − (aq) → 2Cl − (aq) + Br 2 (aq) (K + ions are spectator ions, so they are left out.) Why this scores One mark for Br 2 and Cl − as products, one for the balanced equation and one for state symbols. Chlorine is (g) here because it is bubbled in as a gas. 8.4 Transition Elements These questions test the properties that set transition elements apart from Group I metals; examiners reward properties that are special to transition elements and comparisons that name both groups. What examiners keep seeing Giving properties shared by all metals (conducting electricity, forming positive ions or basic oxides) or only physical properties when chemical ones are asked for; the 2022 reports also warn against “it” or “they” when comparing two groups. 0620/42/F/M/23 Q4(c)(i) · February/March 2023 · [1 mark] Source material: Some physical and chemical properties of transition elements are shown. physical properties: … high density … high strength State one other physical property of transition elements. High melting point . Why this scores One mark. High density and high strength are already given, so repeating them scores nothing; the mark scheme looks for high melting point. 0620/43/O/N/24 Q5(c)(i) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Manganese(IV) oxide is the catalyst in this reaction. Explain the meaning of (IV) in manganese(IV) oxide. (IV) is the oxidation number of manganese in the compound: manganese is +4 . Manganese is a transition element with variable oxidation numbers, so the Roman numeral shows which one is present. Why this scores One mark for “oxidation number of manganese” and one for +4. “It has four of something” misses both the term and the positive sign. 0620/42/M/J/22 Q3(b)(ii) · May/June 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: One chemical property of transition elements is that they form coloured compounds. State two other chemical properties of transition elements. 1. They and their compounds act as catalysts . 2. They have variable oxidation numbers (e.g. iron forms Fe 2+ and Fe 3+ ). Why this scores One mark each. The examiner report says many gave physical properties, or chemical properties shared by all metals such as forming basic oxides or positive ions. 0620/43/M/J/20 Q7(e)(ii) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Source material: Iron is a transition element. Give two ways in which the properties of transition elements differ from the properties of Group I metals. 1. Transition elements have much higher melting points than Group I metals. 2. Transition elements and their compounds act as catalysts ; Group I metals do not. Why this scores One mark each from: higher melting point, higher density, harder, act as catalysts, variable oxidation numbers, coloured compounds. Each point is a comparison, so make clear which group has the property. 0620/43/M/J/25 Q5(b)(iii) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: Ethanoic acid is manufactured in the reaction between methanol and carbon monoxide. Suggest which element from the list is a suitable catalyst for the reaction. Give a reason for your answer. aluminium carbon cobalt magnesium sodium Catalyst: cobalt . Reason: cobalt is a transition element , and transition elements and their compounds often act as catalysts. Why this scores One mark for cobalt and one for the reason that it is a transition element. The examiner report says many did not use the Periodic Table to spot cobalt as the only transition element, and chose others for being “very reactive” or “unreactive”. Topical Past Papers · Topic 9 Past Paper Questions: Metals 18 real Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 9.1 Properties, Uses and Alloys of Metals · 9.4 Reactivity Series and Corrosion · 9.6 Extraction of Metals 9.1 Properties, Uses and Alloys of Metals These questions test what an alloy is, why alloys are harder than pure metals, and how a metal’s use follows from its properties; examiners reward exact property words (ductile, low density, good conductor, resists corrosion) and a particle explanation built on layers. What examiners keep seeing Calling an alloy a “compound” or a “combination of elements”, or forgetting that it must contain a metal. In the hardness explanation, saying the particles are “closer together” or the bonds are “stronger” instead of describing different-sized atoms that stop the layers sliding. 0620/43/M/J/25 Q3(b)(i) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Zinc is present in alloys such as brass. State the meaning of the term alloy. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (for example, brass is copper mixed with zinc). Why this scores One mark, and it needs two ideas: the word “mixture” and the presence of a metal. The examiner report says many candidates wrote “compound” or “combination of elements”, or left out the metal, and lost the mark. 0620/41/M/J/25 Q3(b)(i) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Copper is in alloys such as brass. State one reason why alloys are more useful than pure metals. Alloys are harder and stronger than the pure metals they are made from. Why this scores “Harder” or “stronger” earns the mark. Answers such as “better” or “more useful” only repeat the question; the examiner report advises learning the syllabus statement word for word. 0620/42/F/M/23 Q4(b)(i) · February/March 2023 · [1 mark] Source material: Copper can be stretched into wires. Copper wires conduct electricity. Name the property of metals which means that they can be stretched into wires. Ductility (metals are ductile). Why this scores One mark for ductile / ductility. Do not confuse it with “malleable”, which means it can be hammered into shape. 0620/42/O/N/24 Q2(e) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] State why aluminium is used in food containers. Aluminium resists corrosion : its protective oxide layer stops it reacting with the food or drink. Why this scores The mark is for resistance to corrosion. “Light” or “cheap” does not explain why it is safe to keep food in, so always link the use to the property that matters for that use. 0620/41/O/N/23 Q2(d) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] State two physical properties of aluminium that make it suitable for use in overhead electrical cables. 1 It is a good conductor of electricity . 2 It has a low density , so the long cables are light enough for the pylons to hold up. Why this scores One mark each for good electrical conductor and low density. The question asks for physical properties, so a chemical property such as resisting corrosion is not the answer it wants. 0620/41/O/N/20 Q2(c) · October/November 2020 · [3 marks] Brass is an alloy of zinc. Explain, in terms of particles, why brass is harder than pure zinc. In pure zinc the atoms are all the same size and are arranged in regular layers . Brass also contains copper atoms, which are a different size , and these disrupt the regular layers. So it is harder for the layers to slide over each other when a force is applied, which makes brass harder. Why this scores One mark each for: layers of atoms, different-sized atoms in the alloy, and layers less able to slide. The examiner report found this very difficult for candidates; common wrong ideas were particles “closer together”, “stronger bonds” or “stronger intermolecular forces”. 9.4 Reactivity Series and Corrosion These questions use the reactivity series to predict reactions with steam and displacement reactions, explain why aluminium seems unreactive, and explain how rusting is stopped; examiners reward comparisons made directly with iron and explanations in terms of electrons or oxidation. What examiners keep seeing In sacrificial protection, saying the magnesium or zinc “rusts” instead of the iron (only iron and steel rust), claiming it works as a barrier, or writing “sacrificial protection” without explaining that the more reactive metal loses electrons in preference to iron (examiner reports 2020 and 2021). 0620/41/M/J/21 Q6(d)(ii) · May/June 2021 · [1 mark] Source material: Steel consists mainly of iron. Iron forms rust when it reacts with water and oxygen. Magnesium blocks can be attached to the bottom of steel boats. Explain why replacing the magnesium blocks with copper blocks will not prevent the bottom of the boat from rusting. Copper is less reactive than iron , so the iron would still lose electrons (be oxidised) and rust instead of the copper. Why this scores The mark needs a comparison with iron. The examiner report says “copper is less reactive than magnesium” and “copper is unreactive” were common and did not score. 0620/43/M/J/20 Q7(e)(i) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Iron forms hydrated iron(III) oxide when it rusts. Write a word equation to represent the formation of rust. iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide Why this scores One mark for the reactants (iron with both oxygen and water) and one for the product. Leaving out water or oxygen loses a mark, because rusting needs both. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q2(c)(iii) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Most Group II metals form a gas when placed into cold water. An alkaline solution is also formed. One Group II metal reacts very slowly when placed in cold water. When heated, the metal reacts with steam to form a white solid. Identify this metal and name the white solid formed. Metal: magnesium White solid: magnesium oxide Why this scores One mark for magnesium and one for magnesium oxide. With steam a metal forms its oxide (plus hydrogen), not its hydroxide, so “magnesium hydroxide” does not score. 0620/41/M/J/21 Q6(d)(i) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: Steel consists mainly of iron. Iron forms rust when it reacts with water and oxygen. Magnesium blocks can be attached to the bottom of steel boats. Explain how the magnesium blocks prevent iron from rusting. Magnesium is more reactive than iron . So the magnesium loses electrons (is oxidised) in preference to the iron ; the magnesium corrodes away and the iron is not oxidised. Why this scores One mark for magnesium being more reactive than iron and one for magnesium being oxidised / losing electrons instead of iron. The examiner report says “sacrificial protection” with no explanation, “magnesium rusts instead” and “magnesium forms a barrier” were common answers that did not score. 0620/43/O/N/24 Q3(e)(ii) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Part of the reactivity series is shown. magnesium most reactive aluminium tin copper least reactive An aqueous solution of tin(II) sulfate contains Sn 2+ ions. Two experiments are carried out. Experiment 1 Copper is added to aqueous tin(II) sulfate. Experiment 2 Magnesium is added to aqueous tin(II) sulfate. Write an ionic equation for any reaction that occurs in each experiment. If no reaction occurs, write ‘no reaction’. Experiment 1: no reaction (copper is below tin, so it cannot displace it). Experiment 2: Mg + Sn 2+ → Mg 2+ + Sn Why this scores One mark for “no reaction” in Experiment 1 and one for the ionic equation in Experiment 2. Sulfate ions do not change, so they are spectator ions and must not appear in the ionic equation. 0620/41/O/N/23 Q2(e) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Explain the apparent unreactivity of aluminium. Aluminium is covered by a thin layer of aluminium oxide . This oxide layer is unreactive , so it stops water or acid from reaching the aluminium underneath. Why this scores One mark for the aluminium oxide layer and one for saying the layer is unreactive. On a similar question the examiner report said most answers missed out the word “unreactive” or did not name aluminium oxide. 9.6 Extraction of Metals These questions test the blast furnace (the job of each raw material, with equations), why aluminium needs electrolysis in molten cryolite and what happens at each electrode, and roasting zinc blende; examiners reward exact chemistry, such as naming silicon(IV) oxide and slag, rather than “removes impurities”. What examiners keep seeing Mixing up the jobs of the raw materials: giving “lowers the operating temperature” (cryolite’s job) as a reason for adding coke, calling cryolite a catalyst, or saying the carbon anodes “wear away” without stating that carbon reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide (examiner reports 2021 and 2022). 0620/43/M/J/20 Q7(c)(i) · May/June 2020 · [1 mark] Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted by reduction with carbon. Aluminium is more reactive than carbon (above carbon in the reactivity series), so carbon cannot remove the oxygen from aluminium oxide. Why this scores One mark for the comparison with carbon. “Aluminium is very reactive” on its own does not say why carbon fails. 0620/41/M/J/22 Q6(a)(ii) · May/June 2022 · [1 mark] Source material: Zinc is extracted from its ore which is mainly zinc sulfide, ZnS. The steps for this extraction are shown. … step 1 … Zinc sulfide is converted into zinc oxide. Describe how zinc sulfide is converted into zinc oxide in step 1. The zinc sulfide is heated strongly in air (roasted); it reacts with oxygen in the air to form zinc oxide and sulfur dioxide. Why this scores The mark needs both ideas: heat strongly / roast, and air. The examiner report says one of these was often missing, and “oxygen” was often written instead of air. 0620/43/O/N/23 Q5(b)(i) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Give two reasons why coke is added to the blast furnace. 1 Coke burns in the hot air, releasing heat that keeps the furnace hot. 2 Coke reacts with carbon dioxide to make carbon monoxide , which reduces the iron(III) oxide to iron. Why this scores Any two of: releases heat, reacts with carbon dioxide to form carbon monoxide, reduces iron(III) oxide. On a similar question the examiner report saw many answers confuse coke with cryolite (“lowers the operating temperature”) or call it a catalyst. 0620/43/O/N/22 Q3(c)(i) · October/November 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: Electrolysis is carried out on aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite. Give two reasons why the electrolysis is carried out on aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite instead of electrolysing molten aluminium oxide only. 1 The operating temperature is lower than the very high melting point of aluminium oxide, which saves energy and cost. 2 The molten mixture is a better conductor of electricity than molten aluminium oxide alone. Why this scores One mark each for a lower operating temperature and better conductivity. The examiner report lists answers that scored nothing: cryolite is a catalyst, it lowers the melting point of aluminium, or it lowers the boiling point; “it is a solvent” just repeats the question. 0620/43/M/J/24 Q6(a)(iv) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] Explain why limestone is added to the blast furnace. Give details of the chemical reactions that are involved. Limestone is added to remove the main impurity, silicon(IV) oxide (sand). In the furnace, limestone undergoes thermal decomposition : CaCO 3 → CaO + CO 2 The calcium oxide (a base) reacts with the acidic silicon(IV) oxide to form slag , which floats on the molten iron and is tapped off: CaO + SiO 2 → CaSiO 3 Why this scores Three marks: limestone thermally decomposes to calcium oxide; calcium oxide reacts with silicon(IV) oxide; slag is formed. “Removes impurities” on its own earns nothing because the question asks for the reactions. 0620/42/F/M/20 Q2(b)(iii) · February/March 2020 · [4 marks] Source material: Aluminium oxide has a melting point of about 2000 °C, but the electrolysis process operates at about 900 °C. Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction taking place at: … the negative electrode (cathode) … the positive electrode (anode) Cathode (−): Al 3+ + 3e − → Al Anode (+): 2O 2− → O 2 + 4e − Why this scores Two marks per electrode: one for the correct ion gaining (cathode) or losing (anode) electrons, and one for the correct, balanced equation. Examiner reports note the usual errors: electrons on the wrong side and 3Al on the right-hand side. x: Topical Past Papers · Topic 10 Past Paper Questions: Chemistry of the Environment 12 real Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 10.1 Water and Fertilisers · 10.3 Air Quality and Climate 10.1 Water and Fertilisers These questions test the chemical test for water and the physical test for purity, the stages of water treatment, and ammonium-salt fertilisers (their equations and percentage of nitrogen); examiners reward exact colours, exact temperatures and a precise purpose for each step. What examiners keep seeing Confusing a test for water with a test for pure water: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate only shows that water is present; purity needs a boiling point of exactly 100 °C (or a melting point of exactly 0 °C). The examiner report says many candidates suggested filtering, testing the pH or evaporating instead. 0620/42/M/J/21 Q5(d)(ii) · May/June 2021 · [1 mark] Source material: Ammonium nitrate, NH 4 NO 3 , is a compound of nitrogen. State a use of ammonium nitrate in agriculture. As a fertiliser (it supplies nitrogen for crop growth). Why this scores “Fertiliser” earns the mark. The examiner report says vague answers such as “to help plants grow” and ideas about changing the acidity of soil were not credited. 0620/42/O/N/23 Q2(c)(iii) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] State the colour change seen when a few drops of water are added to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. From white to blue . Why this scores One mark for each colour, in the right order. Do not mix it up with anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride, which goes from blue to pink. 0620/43/M/J/20 Q4(a) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Filtration and chlorination are two stages in water treatment. State the purpose of each stage. Filtration: removes insoluble solids (small particles) from the water. Chlorination: kills microbes (bacteria), so the water is safe to drink. Why this scores One mark for each purpose. Filtration does not remove bacteria or dissolved substances, and chlorine does not “clean” the water: it kills microbes. 0620/41/O/N/21 Q2(b)(iv) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is used to test for the presence of water. Describe a test for pure water. Measure its boiling point: pure water boils at exactly 100 °C (at atmospheric pressure). (Or: pure water melts / freezes at exactly 0 °C.) Why this scores One mark for using the boiling (or melting) point and one for the exact value. The examiner report says many candidates wanted to filter the water, test its pH or evaporate it, none of which scored; copper(II) sulfate only shows water is present. 0620/41/M/J/23 Q6(c) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] When sulfuric acid reacts with ammonia the salt produced is ammonium sulfate. Write the symbol equation for this reaction. 2NH 3 + H 2 SO 4 → (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 Why this scores One mark for (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 as the product and one for the balanced equation. The examiner report says few candidates wrote the right formula, and many added water or hydrogen as products: ammonia + acid gives the ammonium salt only. 0620/42/F/M/23 Q3(c)(iii) · February/March 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: Ammonia reacts with an acid to form ammonium sulfate, (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 . Calculate the percentage composition by mass of nitrogen in (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 . M r of (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 = (2 × 14) + (8 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16) = 132 mass of nitrogen = 2 × 14 = 28 % nitrogen = 28 ÷ 132 × 100 = 21.2% Why this scores One mark for M r = 132 and one for 21.2%. Remember there are two nitrogen atoms in the formula (28, not 14), and work out the M r as a number rather than leaving it as a sum. 10.3 Air Quality and Climate These questions test the composition of clean air, where each pollutant comes from and what it does, catalytic-converter equations, photosynthesis and the greenhouse effect; examiners reward linking each gas to its correct source and effect and, for global warming, a step-by-step account in terms of thermal energy. What examiners keep seeing Mixing up the pollutant stories: saying the nitrogen in nitrogen dioxide comes from the fuel (it comes from the air), calling nitrogen dioxide a greenhouse gas, or blaming carbon dioxide for damage to the ozone layer (examiner reports 2020 and 2022). 0620/43/O/N/23 Q3(a)(i) · October/November 2023 · [1 mark] Source material: Nitrogen is converted into ammonia, NH 3 , in the Haber process. Nitrogen is obtained from air. State the percentage of nitrogen in clean, dry air. 78% Why this scores One mark for 78%. Learn the oxygen figure (21%) as well: examiner reports note that it is much less well known than the nitrogen figure. 0620/42/F/M/22 Q3(a) · February/March 2022 · [2 marks] Explain how nitrogen dioxide is formed in car engines. Nitrogen and oxygen from the air taken into the engine react together. They react because of the very high temperature inside the engine when the fuel burns. Why this scores One mark for nitrogen and oxygen from the air reacting, one for the high temperature. The examiner report says a surprising number of candidates thought the nitrogen comes from the fuel. 0620/42/F/M/23 Q1(g) · February/March 2023 · [2 marks] Carbon dioxide, CO 2 , is a reactant in photosynthesis. Name the two products of photosynthesis. Glucose and oxygen . Why this scores One mark for each product. Water is the other reactant, not a product, and “sugar” is less safe than naming glucose. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q1(b) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Nitrogen dioxide, NO 2 , and carbon monoxide are removed from a car exhaust by a catalytic converter. Write the symbol equation for this reaction. 2NO 2 + 4CO → N 2 + 4CO 2 Why this scores One mark for nitrogen and carbon dioxide as the only products, one for balancing. Check the oxygen atoms: 4 from 2NO 2 plus 4 from 4CO gives the 8 in 4CO 2 . 0620/42/O/N/25 Q1(d) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Gaseous oxides of nitrogen are atmospheric pollutants. One adverse effect of oxides of nitrogen is the formation of acid rain. State two other adverse effects of oxides of nitrogen. 1 They cause photochemical smog . 2 They cause respiratory problems (they irritate the lungs and airways). Why this scores One mark each for photochemical smog and respiratory problems. Oxides of nitrogen are not the answer for global warming, so “greenhouse effect” does not score. 0620/41/O/N/23 Q5(c)(ii) · October/November 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: Methane is a greenhouse gas which contributes to global warming. Explain, in terms of thermal energy, how greenhouse gases cause global warming. Energy from the Sun is absorbed by the Earth’s surface, which then emits thermal (infrared) energy . Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb this thermal energy and re-emit some of it back towards the Earth, so less thermal energy escapes into space . As the amount of greenhouse gas increases, more thermal energy is kept in, so the average temperature of the atmosphere rises. Why this scores One mark for greenhouse gases absorbing thermal energy, plus two from: the Earth’s surface absorbs the Sun’s energy, the Earth emits thermal energy, less thermal energy is lost to space, more greenhouse gas means a higher temperature. Do not mention the ozone layer, which is a different problem.
