The model answers and commentary are original and are not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Topical Past Papers · Topic 11 Past Paper Questions: Organic Chemistry 23 real Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 11.1 Organic Formulae, Naming and Fuels · 11.4 Alkanes and Alkenes · 11.6 Alcohols and Carboxylic Acids · 11.8 Polymers 11.1 Organic Formulae, Naming and Fuels These questions test the vocabulary of organic chemistry (homologous series, structural isomers, general formulae) and the link between chain length and the properties of petroleum fractions; examiners reward the exact defining phrases. What examiners keep seeing Definitions lose marks when they are half-remembered: a structural isomer needs both “same molecular formula” and “different structural formula”, and a homologous series is about the same functional group and general formula, not just “similar compounds”. 0620/42/F/M/22 Q6(a)(ii) · February/March 2022 · [1 mark] Explain why members of a family of organic compounds have similar chemical properties. They all contain the same functional group , and it is the functional group that takes part in (and decides) the reactions. Why this scores One mark for “same functional group”. Answers such as “they have the same general formula” or “they are in the same family” do not explain the chemistry, so they score nothing. 0620/42/F/M/20 Q1(d)(i) · February/March 2020 · [2 marks] Source material: Gasoline and kerosene are both fuels. They have different properties. Describe the differences in the properties given. … viscosity of the fuel … flammability of the fuel Viscosity: kerosene is more viscous than gasoline (it is thicker and flows less easily). Flammability: gasoline is more flammable than kerosene (it catches fire more easily). Why this scores One mark for each comparison. Each answer names which fuel is more viscous or more flammable; writing “kerosene is viscous” on its own is not a comparison. The reason (kerosene has longer-chain molecules) was the next 1-mark part. 0620/42/O/N/23 Q6(a) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Give two characteristics that are the same for all members of a homologous series. 1 They have the same general formula . 2 They contain the same functional group (so they have similar chemical properties). Why this scores One mark for “same general formula” and one for “same functional group”. Avoid “same physical properties”: physical properties show a trend , they are not the same. 0620/41/O/N/22 Q6(d)(i) · October/November 2022 · [2 marks] Describe what is meant by the term structural isomer. Compounds with the same molecular formula but a different structural formula (the atoms are arranged differently). Why this scores Two marks: one for “same molecular formula” and one for “different structural formula”. “Same formula, different structure” is too vague to be safe; say molecular and structural . 0620/42/O/N/25 Q5(b)(ii) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: This question is about the homologous series of alkanes. Name one other physical property of alkanes that shows a trend, other than melting points and boiling points. Describe this trend as the carbon chain length of alkanes increases. Property: viscosity. Trend: viscosity increases as the carbon chain gets longer – longer-chain alkanes are thicker and flow less easily. Why this scores One mark for a physical property (viscosity, or volatility / flammability) and one for the correct direction of change as chain length increases. Do not give a chemical property such as “reactivity”, and make sure the trend matches the property named. 0620/41/O/N/24 Q5(d) · October/November 2024 · [4 marks] For each of the homologous series shown, name a member that contains six hydrogen atoms. … alkanes … alkenes … alcohols … carboxylic acids Alkanes: ethane, C 2 H 6 Alkenes: propene, C 3 H 6 Alcohols: ethanol, C 2 H 5 OH Carboxylic acids: propanoic acid, CH 3 CH 2 COOH Why this scores One mark per correct name. Use each general formula (C n H 2n+2 , C n H 2n , C n H 2n+1 OH, C n H 2n+1 COOH) and count every hydrogen, including the H in –OH and –COOH. The question asks for names , so give the name, not just a formula. 11.4 Alkanes and Alkenes These questions test the reactions of alkanes (combustion, substitution with chlorine in UV light) and alkenes (cracking, addition, the bromine water test); examiners reward precise reagents, conditions and balanced formulae. What examiners keep seeing Examiners report that many candidates leave out the reagent itself (writing only “nickel catalyst, heat” for hydrogenation, or “bromination” for the test) and describe bromine water going “clear” instead of colourless. 0620/41/O/N/20 Q6(d)(ii) · October/November 2020 · [1 mark] Explain, in terms of bonding, why there is no colour change when aqueous bromine is added to ethane. Ethane is saturated: it has only single C–C bonds and no C=C double bond, so bromine cannot add across it. Why this scores One mark for “only single bonds / no double bond”. The examiner report notes that “the bonds are weaker” or “alkanes are unreactive” did not score: the answer must be about the type of bond. 0620/42/F/M/21 Q5(b) · February/March 2021 · [2 marks] Describe the test for an unsaturated hydrocarbon. Test: add aqueous bromine (bromine water) and shake. Observation: the orange bromine water turns colourless . Why this scores One mark for the reagent and one for the result. The examiner report warns that “bromination” is not a description of the test, and “clear” is not accepted for colourless. 0620/42/O/N/24 Q5(b) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Alkenes are manufactured by cracking larger alkane molecules. State two conditions needed for cracking large alkane molecules. 1 A high temperature. 2 A catalyst. Why this scores One mark each for high temperature and a catalyst. “Heat” on its own is weaker than “high temperature”; do not add pressure or UV light, which belong to other reactions. 0620/42/O/N/24 Q5(c)(i) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: When one molecule of dodecane, C 12 H 26 , is cracked, three molecules of but-1-ene and one other product are formed. Use molecular formulae to complete the symbol equation for this reaction. C 12 H 26 → 3C 4 H 8 + H 2 (Three C 4 H 8 use all 12 carbon atoms and 24 hydrogen atoms, leaving 2 hydrogen atoms: H 2 .) Why this scores One mark for C 4 H 8 as the formula of but-1-ene and one for the fully balanced equation with H 2 . Cracking can make hydrogen as well as alkenes, so check the atoms balance before adding an alkane. 0620/42/M/J/22 Q5(d)(i) · May/June 2022 · [3 marks] Source material: Alkene A is converted into alkane B in reaction 4. State the reagent and conditions for reaction 4. Reagent: hydrogen, H 2 . Conditions: a nickel catalyst and heat (high temperature). Why this scores One mark each for hydrogen, a (nickel) catalyst and a high temperature. The examiner report says many candidates forgot to name hydrogen as the reagent and gave only the conditions. 0620/42/O/N/25 Q5(d)(ii) · October/November 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: Propane has the structural formula CH 3 CH 2 CH 3 . When propane undergoes a monosubstitution reaction with chlorine at room temperature, two organic products can be formed. Give the structural formula and state the name of each organic product formed. Product 1: CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 Cl, 1-chloropropane Product 2: CH 3 CHClCH 3 , 2-chloropropane Why this scores One mark for each structural formula and one for each matching name. The chlorine replaces one H either on an end carbon (1-) or on the middle carbon (2-); writing C 3 H 7 Cl twice does not show two different products. 11.6 Alcohols and Carboxylic Acids These questions test the two ways of making ethanol and their conditions, combustion and oxidation of ethanol, the acid reactions of carboxylic acids and how esters are named; examiners reward exact conditions and correctly balanced equations. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports say the advantage of fermentation is that it uses renewable raw materials, not that it is “cheaper” or “less harmful”, and that many ethanol combustion equations left out oxygen or gave the wrong products. 0620/42/O/N/21 Q6(d) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] Ethanol is a fuel. Write the chemical equation for the complete combustion of ethanol. C 2 H 5 OH + 3O 2 → 2CO 2 + 3H 2 O Why this scores One mark for the correct species (ethanol and oxygen giving carbon dioxide and water) and one for balancing. Count the O in ethanol: 1 + 6 = 7 oxygen atoms on each side. The examiner report notes many answers missed out oxygen as a reactant. 0620/41/O/N/21 Q5(d)(ii) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: Butanoic acid, CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 COOH, is a carboxylic acid. Complete the chemical equation for the reaction of butanoic acid and sodium carbonate, Na 2 CO 3 . 2CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 COOH + Na 2 CO 3 → 2CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 COONa + H 2 O + CO 2 Why this scores One mark for the salt, sodium butanoate (CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 COONa), and one for water and carbon dioxide completing the equation. Acid + carbonate always gives salt + water + carbon dioxide; the Na replaces the H of –COOH. 0620/41/O/N/23 Q6(d) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: Ethanol is manufactured by two methods: method 1 … fermentation of aqueous glucose method 2 catalytic addition of steam to an alkene. Give one advantage of each method of production of ethanol. Method 1: it uses a renewable raw material (sugar from crops). Method 2: the reaction is fast (high rate), and it can run continuously. Why this scores One mark for “renewable” for fermentation and one for “fast / high rate” (or purer product) for hydration. The examiner reports say “cheaper”, “less harmful” or “more ethanol” do not score. 0620/43/O/N/25 Q6(c)(iii) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: Carboxylic acids react with alcohols to form esters. Ester S has the structural formula CH 3 CH 2 COOCH 2 CH 2 CH 2 CH 3 . Name the carboxylic acid and the alcohol which react together to form ester S. Carboxylic acid: propanoic acid (CH 3 CH 2 COOH). Alcohol: butan-1-ol (CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 CH 2 OH). Why this scores One mark for each name. Split the formula at the –COO– link: the part ending in C=O (three carbons, CH 3 CH 2 CO–) comes from the acid, and the chain on the other oxygen (four carbons) from the alcohol, so the ester is butyl propanoate. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q6(c)(i) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: Ethanol is made by reacting ethene with steam in an industrial process. State the conditions and type of catalyst used in this industrial production of ethanol. Temperature: 300 °C Pressure: 6000 kPa (60 atm) Catalyst: an acid catalyst (phosphoric acid) Why this scores One mark each for the temperature with units, the pressure with units and “acid” as the type of catalyst. Units are required, and the catalyst must be an acid, not a metal such as nickel or iron. 0620/43/M/J/21 Q7(d) · May/June 2021 · [4 marks] Source material: step 1: decane to ethene … step 2: ethene to ethanol Ethanol can be produced from long chain alkanes such as decane, C 10 H 22 , in a two-step process. … name the type of chemical reaction that occurs … write a chemical equation. Step 1: type of reaction: cracking. C 10 H 22 → C 8 H 18 + C 2 H 4 Step 2: type of reaction: addition (hydration). C 2 H 4 + H 2 O → C 2 H 5 OH Why this scores One mark for each reaction type and one for each balanced equation. The examiner report says “combustion” was often wrongly given for step 1; cracking gives a shorter alkane plus ethene, and any balanced set of products containing C 2 H 4 is fine. 11.8 Polymers These questions test the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation, the monomers behind nylon, PET and proteins, and the problems of disposing of plastics; examiners reward precise names of functional groups and linkages. What examiners keep seeing The examiner report notes that many candidates wrote “amide” when the monomer functional group is an amine : the amide is the linkage formed, not the group in the monomer. 0620/42/F/M/20 Q5(b) · February/March 2020 · [1 mark] Polyamides are condensation polymers. What does the term condensation mean when used to describe this type of polymer? When the monomers join, a small molecule (water) is also produced as well as the polymer. Why this scores One mark for stating that water (a small molecule) is formed as well as the polymer. This is the key difference from addition polymerisation, where the polymer is the only product. 0620/43/M/J/20 Q8(b) · May/June 2020 · [1 mark] Items made from nylon are often disposed of by burying them in the ground. This is called landfill. Why is the disposal of nylon using landfill a problem? Nylon is non-biodegradable , so it stays in the ground for a very long time and landfill sites run out of space. Why this scores One mark for “non-biodegradable” (or that landfill space runs out). Saying “it is bad for the environment” is too vague to score. 0620/43/O/N/25 Q6(d)(ii) · October/November 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Fig. 6.1 shows part of a polymer structure. Suggest why it is not possible to write the molecular formula of this polymer. Polymer molecules have no fixed length: the number of repeat units (n) varies from one molecule to another and is very large, so there is no single molecular formula. Why this scores One mark for the idea that the chain length is indefinite or varies. The empirical formula of an addition polymer is the same as its monomer’s, but the molecular formula cannot be fixed. 0620/43/O/N/22 Q6(d)(ii) · October/November 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: Proteins are natural polymers. Proteins contain amide linkages. Synthetic polyamides also contain amide linkages. Identify the two functional groups present in the monomers used to produce synthetic polyamides. 1 Carboxylic acid group, –COOH (in a dicarboxylic acid). 2 Amine group, –NH 2 (in a diamine). Why this scores One mark for carboxylic acid and one for amine. The examiner report says “amide” was often written instead of amine and did not score; alcohol and alkene were also common wrong answers. 0620/42/O/N/24 Q6(b)(i) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: PET is a polyester. Name the two types of monomer molecules needed to make polyesters. 1 A dicarboxylic acid (two –COOH groups). 2 A diol (two –OH groups). Why this scores One mark each for dicarboxylic acid and diol. Each monomer needs a functional group at both ends to make a chain, so “carboxylic acid and alcohol” is not enough on its own. Topical Past Papers · Topic 12 Past Paper Questions: Experimental Techniques and Chemical Analysis 18 real Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0620/42/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 12.1 Experimental Design and Titrations · 12.3 Chromatography, Separation and Purification · 12.5 Identification of Ions and Gases 12.1 Experimental Design and Titrations Short questions on choosing the right apparatus and running a titration; examiners reward the exact name of the apparatus and exact indicator colours in the right order. What examiners keep seeing Writing “measuring cylinder” for a volume given to 0.1 cm 3 (it must be a pipette or burette), and getting the methyl orange start colour wrong (yellow in alkali, not orange). 0620/41/M/J/22 Q3(c)(i) · May/June 2022 · [1 mark] Source material: A student determines the concentration of a solution of dilute sulfuric acid, H 2 SO 4 , by titration with aqueous sodium hydroxide, NaOH. … 25.0 cm 3 of 0.200 mol / dm 3 NaOH is transferred into a conical flask. Name the piece of apparatus used to measure exactly 25.0 cm 3 of 0.200 mol / dm 3 NaOH in step 1. (Volumetric) pipette . Why this scores One mark for pipette. The examiner report says “measuring cylinder” was the commonest wrong answer: the volume is given to one decimal place (25.0 cm 3 ), which only a pipette measures accurately enough. 0620/41/M/J/22 Q3(c)(iii) · May/June 2022 · [1 mark] Source material: The titration is repeated several times until a suitable number of results is obtained. State how the student decides that a suitable number of results have been obtained. When at least two titres are concordant : they agree to within 0.10 cm 3 of each other. Why this scores One mark for two results within 0.2 cm 3 (or less) of each other, so a number is essential. The examiner report did not credit vague words such as “similar” or “close”, or “take the average”. 0620/42/M/J/22 Q2(d)(iii) · May/June 2022 · [1 mark] Source material: A 25.0 cm 3 sample of limewater is placed in a conical flask. The concentration of Ca(OH) 2 in the limewater is determined by titration with dilute hydrochloric acid, HCl. As well as limewater and dilute hydrochloric acid, state what other type of substance must be added to the conical flask. An indicator (e.g. a few drops of methyl orange). Why this scores The question asks for the type of substance, so “indicator” is the mark; a named indicator is only credited if the word indicator is there. The examiner report notes universal indicator was wrongly given by weaker candidates. 0620/43/O/N/24 Q4(a)(ii) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: Dilute sulfuric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide can be used to prepare sodium sulfate crystals using a method that involves titration. … Thymolphthalein is used as an indicator for this titration. Suggest why universal indicator is not used for this titration. Universal indicator changes through many colours gradually as the pH changes, so there is no single sharp colour change to show the end-point. Why this scores One mark for the idea of too many colour changes (no sharp end-point). Saying it “is not accurate” without the reason does not score. 0620/43/O/N/24 Q4(a)(i) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Dilute sulfuric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide can be used to prepare sodium sulfate crystals using a method that involves titration. … Thymolphthalein is used as an indicator for this titration. State the colour change of thymolphthalein at the end-point of this titration. From blue to colourless . Why this scores One mark for each colour, in the right order: the alkali starts in the conical flask, so the indicator starts blue and turns colourless when the acid neutralises it. Write “colourless”, never “clear”. 0620/41/O/N/25 Q3(f) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: The student adds a few drops of methyl orange indicator to the NaOH(aq) in the conical flask. step 3 The student adds 0.200 mol / dm 3 H 2 SO 4 (aq) to the flask until the end-point is reached. State the colour change observed in step 3. From yellow to orange . Why this scores One mark for yellow (methyl orange in alkali) and one for orange (the end-point). Red is the colour in excess acid, so it is not the end-point colour; a similar question in 2022 found most students wrongly started with orange. 12.3 Chromatography, Separation and Purification These questions test whether you can name and describe separation methods step by step; marks go to the key verbs (filter, wash, dry, heat to saturation, cool) and key terms (locating agent, fractional distillation). What examiners keep seeing Mixing up the residue and the filtrate: to get an insoluble solid you wash and dry the residue, while crystallising the filtrate is for a soluble salt. Heating a solution to dryness also loses marks. 0620/43/M/J/20 Q4(c)(iii) · May/June 2020 · [1 mark] Source material: Chromatography can be used to test the purity of substances. State how a colourless substance can be made visible on a chromatogram. Spray the dried chromatogram with a locating agent , which makes the spots show up. Why this scores One mark for “locating agent”; the key term is what is credited, so use it rather than a vague “spray a chemical on it”. 0620/43/M/J/24 Q1(f) · May/June 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: Name the process used to: separate a mixture of several liquids with different boiling points Fractional distillation . Why this scores One mark for fractional distillation. “Distillation” alone is simple distillation, which only separates a solvent from a solution. 0620/41/O/N/24 Q6(e) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] A mixture of the three amino acids, A, B and C, can be separated and the amino acids identiﬁed using paper chromatography. Complete the equation for R f . R f = distance travelled by the substance (spot) ÷ distance travelled by the solvent (solvent front), both measured from the baseline. Why this scores One mark for the distance moved by the substance on top and one for the distance moved by the solvent underneath. Writing it upside down gives R f values above 1, which is impossible. 0620/42/M/J/22 Q2(c)(iii) · May/June 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: Limewater is a saturated solution of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH) 2 (aq). Describe how you would make a sample of limewater starting with solid calcium hydroxide. Add excess solid calcium hydroxide to distilled water and stir until no more dissolves (so the solution is saturated). Filter off the undissolved solid; the filtrate is limewater. Why this scores One mark for adding excess solid to water, one for filtering. The examiner report called this the hardest question on the paper: many left out filtration, and weaker answers used excess water, which does not give a saturated solution. 0620/41/O/N/24 Q3(d)(iii) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate can be obtained from aqueous copper(II) sulfate by crystallisation. Describe how this crystallisation is done. Heat the solution in an evaporating basin to evaporate some of the water until it is saturated (a drop on a cold glass rod forms crystals). Then leave it to cool so that crystals form. Why this scores One mark for heating, one for heating only to the saturation (crystallisation) point and then cooling. Heating to dryness does not score, because it drives off the water of crystallisation. 0620/41/M/J/23 Q6(d)(iii) · May/June 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: Lead(II) sulfate is an insoluble salt. The precipitate of lead(II) sulfate forms in an aqueous solution. Describe how pure lead(II) sulfate can be obtained from the mixture. Filter the mixture; lead(II) sulfate stays on the filter paper as the residue. Wash the residue with a little distilled water to remove the soluble ions left on it. Dry it between sheets of filter paper (or in a warm oven). Why this scores One mark each for filter, wash with distilled water and a way of drying. The examiner report says many students crystallised the filtrate instead: the product is the insoluble residue, not the solution. 12.5 Identification of Ions and Gases Recall questions on tests for ions and gases; every test needs the reagent and the exact observation (colour, precipitate, whether it dissolves in excess). What examiners keep seeing Giving the wrong precipitate colour (white for iodide instead of yellow) or a non-test such as “pungent smell” for ammonia; the examiner reports also note students forgetting to add sodium hydroxide in excess. 0620/42/M/J/21 Q2(c)(i) · May/June 2021 · [1 mark] Source material: Aqueous silver nitrate is a colourless solution containing Ag + (aq) ions. Describe what is seen when aqueous silver nitrate is added to aqueous sodium iodide, NaI(aq). A yellow precipitate forms. Why this scores One mark for yellow precipitate (silver iodide). The examiner report says the commonest error was “white precipitate”, which is chloride. 0620/42/F/M/25 Q5(d)(ii) · February/March 2025 · [1 mark] Describe a test for chlorine gas. Test: hold damp litmus paper in the gas. Observation: the litmus paper is bleached (turns white). Why this scores The single mark needs both the test and the result. The examiner report notes some students confused chlorine with chloride ions and described a silver nitrate test. 0620/42/F/M/22 Q3(c)(iii) · February/March 2022 · [2 marks] State the test for ammonia. Test: hold damp red litmus paper in the gas. Observation: the litmus paper turns blue . Why this scores One mark for damp red litmus, one for it turning blue. The examiner report warns that “pungent smell” is not a valid test. 0620/42/O/N/25 Q2(c)(ii) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: Iron can form two different ions, Fe 2+ and Fe 3+ . Describe a test for aqueous Fe 2+ ions. Test: add aqueous sodium hydroxide (or aqueous ammonia). Observation: a green precipitate forms, which is insoluble in excess (and turns brown near the surface on standing). Why this scores One mark for the reagent, one for green precipitate. Red-brown is Fe 3+ , so the colour must be exact. 0620/42/M/J/22 Q2(c)(iv) · May/June 2022 · [3 marks] Source material: Limewater is a saturated solution of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH) 2 (aq). Describe how you would test for the presence of calcium ions in a sample of limewater. Test: add aqueous sodium hydroxide drop by drop, then in excess. Observations: a white precipitate forms, which is insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide. Why this scores One mark for the reagent, one for white precipitate and one for insoluble in excess. The examiner report says some lost the third mark by not adding the alkali in excess; a flame test (orange-red) was also credited. 0620/43/O/N/24 Q4(e)(ii) · October/November 2024 · [5 marks] Source material: Potassium hydrogen sulfate, KHSO 4 , dissolves in water to form solution X. Solution X contains K + , H + and SO 4 2– ions. State the observations when the following tests are done.
  • A flame test is carried out on X.
  • Solid copper(II) carbonate is added to X.
  • Aqueous barium nitrate acidified with dilute nitric acid is added to X.
Flame test: a lilac flame (K + ). Copper(II) carbonate: bubbles (fizzing) as CO 2 is given off; the green solid dissolves ; a blue solution forms (H + reacts like an acid). Acidified barium nitrate: a white precipitate (SO 4 2− ). Why this scores Five marks for lilac flame, bubbles, solid dissolves, blue solution and white precipitate. These are observations, so write what you see (“bubbles”), not “carbon dioxide is made”.
