t: Past Paper Questions: Motion, Forces and Energy
x: Topical Past Papers · Topic 1 Past Paper Questions: Motion, Forces and Energy 58 real Cambridge IGCSE Physics Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0625/42/M/J/24 Q2(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 1.1 Physical Quantities and Measurement · 1.2 Motion · 1.3 Mass and Weight · 1.4 Density · 1.5.1 Effects of Forces · 1.5.2 Turning Effect and Centre of Gravity · 1.6 Momentum · 1.7.1 Energy, Work and Power · 1.7.3 Energy Resources · 1.8 Pressure 1.1 Physical Quantities and Measurement These questions test the scalar/vector distinction, careful timing technique and combining two vectors; examiners reward the words “magnitude” and “direction”, a clear method, and a resultant given with both its size and its direction. What examiners keep seeing Re-using a quantity named in the question (speed, velocity, force) earns nothing, and in vector questions many candidates give the angle to the wrong line or subtract the two values instead of using Pythagoras. 0625/43/O/N/24 Q1(a)(i) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] State the difference between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity. A scalar has magnitude (size) only, but a vector has both magnitude and direction . Why this scores One mark for the idea that a vector has direction and a scalar does not. Saying only “a vector has direction” is enough, but stating both sides makes the comparison clear. 0625/41/O/N/22 Q2(a)(i) · October/November 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: A force is a vector quantity. State two features of a vector quantity. 1. It has a magnitude (size). 2. It has a direction . Why this scores One mark each for magnitude and direction. Keep the two features separate on the two answer lines. 0625/42/F/M/21 Q2(b)(ii) · February/March 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: Speed is a scalar quantity and velocity is a vector quantity. Write down one other scalar quantity and one other vector quantity. Scalar quantity: mass (or distance, time, energy, temperature). Vector quantity: weight (or force, acceleration, momentum, displacement). Why this scores One mark for any correct scalar and one for any correct vector. The examiner report notes that speed and velocity earn nothing because they are already in the question. 0625/42/O/N/22 Q2(a) · October/November 2022 · [3 marks] A pendulum swings with a time period of approximately one second. Describe how to use a stop-watch to determine the time period of the pendulum. Place a fixed marker (fiducial mark) at the centre of the swing, so that each complete oscillation (there and back) can be judged from when the bob passes the marker in the same direction. Use the stop-watch to time 10 complete oscillations . Divide the total time by 10 to get the time period; repeat and take an average. Why this scores One mark each for timing oscillations with the stop-watch, using a reference mark to judge a complete oscillation, and timing several oscillations then dividing. The examiner report says very few mentioned a fiducial mark, and that a “swing” must clearly mean there and back. 0625/42/F/M/23 Q1(a) · February/March 2023 · [4 marks] A boat crosses a river. The boat points at right angles to the river bank and it travels at a speed of 3.5 m / s relative to the water. A river current acts at right angles to the direction the boat points. The river current has a speed of 2.5 m / s. By drawing a scale diagram or by calculation, determine the speed and direction of the boat relative to the river bank. The two velocities are at right angles, so use Pythagoras: speed 2 = 3.5 2 + 2.5 2 = 18.5 speed = √18.5 = 4.3 m/s tan θ = 3.5 ÷ 2.5 = 1.4 θ = 54° to the river bank , pointing downstream (in the direction of the current). Figure: tip-to-tail vector triangle for the boat. The resultant joins the start of the first arrow to the tip of the last. Why this scores Two marks for the speed (Pythagoras or a correct vector triangle) and two for the angle (trigonometry or a correctly drawn resultant with arrows). The examiner report says the angle was often given to the river flow line rather than the bank, or the two speeds were simply subtracted. 1.2 Motion These questions test acceleration as rate of change of velocity, distance from a speed–time graph, and the motion of falling objects; examiners reward precise definitions, equations written before substitution and force explanations that link air resistance to speed. What examiners keep seeing Defining acceleration as “change in velocity over time per second” or as the equation alone loses the mark, and in falling-object answers candidates contradict themselves by saying the object “decelerates” before reaching terminal velocity. 0625/42/O/N/23 Q1(a)(ii) · October/November 2023 · [1 mark] Source material: A car accelerates uniformly in a straight line from rest at time t = 0. Explain in words what is meant by the term acceleration. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (the change in velocity per unit time). Why this scores One mark for “rate of change of velocity” or “change in velocity per unit time”. The examiner report says quoting the equation, or writing “rate of change of velocity over time”, was not precise enough. 0625/42/F/M/20 Q1(a) · February/March 2020 · [2 marks] Source material: A rocket is launched vertically upwards from the ground. The rocket travels with uniform acceleration from rest. After 8.0 s, the speed of the rocket is 120 m / s. Calculate the acceleration of the rocket. a = Δ v ÷ Δ t = (120 − 0) ÷ 8.0 a = 15 m/s 2 Why this scores One mark for the equation a = Δ v /Δ t with the numbers, one for 15 m/s 2 . Watch the unit: m/s 2 , not m/s. 0625/41/M/J/21 Q1(c) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: A skydiver of mass 76 kg is falling vertically in still air. At time t = 0, the skydiver opens his parachute. Explain why opening the parachute cannot reduce the speed of the skydiver to zero. Air resistance depends on speed, so as he slows down the air resistance decreases until it equals his weight. The forces are then balanced at a speed above zero, so there is no resultant force and he stops decelerating; he falls at a new, lower terminal velocity. Why this scores Two marks for the idea that the forces balance at a speed greater than zero, and that once they balance there is no further deceleration (or: at zero speed there would be no air resistance but the weight would still act). The examiner report says many just repeated their answer to the previous part. 0625/43/M/J/24 Q1(c) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: A ball of mass 130 g is launched from the ground at an initial velocity of 14 m / s vertically upwards. It decelerates until it is at rest momentarily at a height h above the ground. … the time taken for the ball to reach height h is 1.4 s. Calculate h. Ignore the effect of air resistance. The deceleration is uniform, so distance = average speed × time. average speed = (14 + 0) ÷ 2 = 7.0 m/s h = 7.0 × 1.4 = 9.8 m ≈ 10 m Why this scores Full marks for any valid method: average speed × time, the area under the speed–time graph, or equating kinetic energy lost to gravitational potential energy gained (½ mv 2 = mgh gives 10 m). The examiner report warns against using the starting speed 14 m/s as if it were the average. 0625/43/M/J/24 Q1(d) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] The ball is dropped from the top of a tall building. Describe and explain the motion of the ball as it falls. Consider the effect of air resistance in your answer. At first the ball accelerates downwards at 9.8 m/s 2 , because its weight is the only force acting on it. As its speed increases, the air resistance (upwards) increases, so the resultant downward force decreases and the acceleration decreases. When the air resistance equals the weight, the resultant force is zero, the acceleration is zero and the ball falls at a constant speed: its terminal velocity. Why this scores One mark each, up to three, for: the ball accelerates (at 9.8 m/s 2 at first, due to its weight); air resistance increases with speed; resultant force and acceleration decrease; terminal velocity when the resultant force is zero. The examiner report warns against contradictions such as saying the ball “decelerates” or that its acceleration increases. 0625/42/O/N/20 Q1(b) · October/November 2020 · [4 marks] Source material: A sky-diver jumps out of a hot-air balloon, which is 4000 m above the ground. At time = 30 s, she opens her parachute. Describe, in terms of the forces acting on the sky-diver, her motion between leaving the balloon and opening her parachute. Her weight acts downwards and air resistance acts upwards, opposing her motion. At first her weight is much bigger than the air resistance, so the resultant force is downwards and she accelerates downwards. As her speed increases the air resistance increases, so the resultant force gets smaller and her acceleration decreases. When the air resistance equals her weight the resultant force is zero, so her acceleration is zero and she falls at a constant speed (terminal velocity) until the parachute opens. Why this scores Marks for the forces (weight down, air resistance up, resultant force down causes acceleration, air resistance increases with speed) and for the motion (accelerates, acceleration decreases, terminal velocity when forces balance). The examiner report says weaker answers gave no directions for the forces or described what happened after the parachute opened. 1.3 Mass and Weight These short questions test the definitions of weight and gravitational field strength and the equation W = mg ; examiners reward word-perfect definitions and answers with the correct unit (N for weight, kg for mass). What examiners keep seeing Giving weight in kilograms, or multiplying when you should divide in W = mg , are the commonest errors; on another planet, find the mass first because mass does not change. 0625/42/O/N/24 Q1(a)(ii) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Define, in words, the term weight. Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object that has mass (the effect of a gravitational field on a mass). Why this scores One mark for “gravitational force on a mass/object”. Avoid “the force of gravity” alone or answers that mix weight up with mass. 0625/41/O/N/25 Q2(a) · October/November 2025 · [1 mark] Define gravitational field strength. Gravitational field strength is the force per unit mass acting on an object in a gravitational field. Why this scores One mark for “force per unit mass”. Writing g = W / m as symbols only is risky in a “define” question; say it in words. 0625/42/O/N/24 Q1(a)(i) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: A rocket has an initial mass of 7.4 × 10 6 kg. Calculate the initial weight of the rocket. W = mg = 7.4 × 10 6 × 9.8 W = 7.3 × 10 7 N Why this scores One mark for 7.3 × 10 7 N, using g = 9.8 N/kg as given on the front of the paper. The unit must be N, not kg. 0625/42/O/N/21 Q2(c) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] The weight of an object is 4.0 N on a planet where the acceleration of free fall is 8.7 m / s 2 . Calculate the mass of the object. W = mg , so m = W ÷ g = 4.0 ÷ 8.7 m = 0.46 kg Why this scores One mark for W = mg rearranged, one for 0.46 kg. The examiner report lists a missing or wrong unit and multiplying 4.0 by 8.7 as the common errors. 0625/41/O/N/25 Q2(b)(i) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: Table 2.1 contains information about the planet Mars. … gravitational field strength 3.7 N / kg An object has a weight of 42 N at the surface of the Earth. Calculate the weight of the object at the surface of Mars. Mass is the same everywhere. On Earth: m = W ÷ g = 42 ÷ 9.8 = 4.3 kg On Mars: W = mg = 4.3 × 3.7 W = 16 N Why this scores One mark for finding the mass with W = mg (4.3 kg), one for 16 N. Keep the unrounded mass (4.29 kg) in your calculator to avoid rounding errors. 1.4 Density These questions test ρ = m / V , measuring the volume of an irregular solid and floating; examiners reward correct unit conversions (cm to m before cubing), a clear displacement method and comparisons of density. What examiners keep seeing Forgetting to convert cm to m (2.0 cm = 0.020 m) or forgetting to change mass into weight with W = mg ; in floating questions, comparing the density of steel with water instead of the average density of the whole ship. 0625/43/O/N/25 Q4(a)(i) · October/November 2025 · [1 mark] A rectangular glass tank contains 3.0 m 3 of liquid. The mass of the liquid is 2800 kg. Calculate the density of the liquid. ρ = m ÷ V = 2800 ÷ 3.0 = 930 kg/m 3 Why this scores One mark for 930 kg/m 3 (933 is fine) with the unit. 0625/43/O/N/23 Q1(a) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Oil of density 0.80 g / cm 3 is poured gently onto the surface of water of density 1.0 g / cm 3 . The oil and the water do not mix. Describe and explain the final position of the oil relative to the water. Description: the oil floats as a layer on top of the water. Explanation: the oil has a lower density than the water, and a less dense liquid floats on a denser one. Why this scores One mark for the position (on top) and one for the reason (oil is less dense than water). Use the comparative “lower density than water”, not just “oil is light”. 0625/42/F/M/23 Q2(a) · February/March 2023 · [2 marks] The ship is made of steel. The density of steel is 7800 kg / m 3 and the density of water is 1000 kg / m 3 . Explain why the ship floats in the water. The ship is hollow: it is not solid steel but contains a large volume of air. So the average density of the ship (steel plus air) is less than the density of the water , and it floats. Why this scores One mark for the air spaces/hollow ship, one for comparing the average density of the ship with that of water. The examiner report says many wrongly claimed denser objects float or argued about the area of the base. 0625/43/O/N/23 Q1(b)(i) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: An irregularly shaped solid object has a density of 2.7 g / cm 3 . Describe a method to measure the volume of the irregularly shaped solid object. Partly fill a measuring cylinder with water and read the volume. Lower the object in on a thread until it is fully submerged and read the new volume. Volume of object = new volume − starting volume. Why this scores One mark for measuring the water volume then immersing the object, one for subtracting the readings. The examiner report says “find the difference in the level” was too vague: refer to the volume read from a measuring cylinder. 0625/43/M/J/20 Q2(a) · May/June 2020 · [3 marks] Source material: A scientist fills a container with sea water. The container has dimensions 30 cm × 30 cm × 40 cm. The density of sea water is 1020 kg / m 3 . Calculate the mass of the sea water in the container. V = 0.30 × 0.30 × 0.40 = 0.036 m 3 ρ = m ÷ V , so m = ρ V = 1020 × 0.036 m = 37 kg Why this scores One mark for the volume in m 3 , one for m = ρ V , one for 37 kg. Convert each length to metres before multiplying: 30 × 30 × 40 cm 3 is not 0.036 m 3 unless you divide by 10 6 . 0625/42/F/M/21 Q1(a) · February/March 2021 · [3 marks] Source material: Fig. 1.1 shows a piece of glass of thickness 2.0 cm and area 0.15 m 2 . The density of the glass is 2.6 × 10 3 kg / m 3 . Take the weight of 1.0 kg to be 10 N (acceleration of free fall = 10 m / s 2 ). Calculate the weight of the piece of glass. V = area × thickness = 0.15 × 0.020 = 0.0030 m 3 m = ρ V = 2.6 × 10 3 × 0.0030 = 7.8 kg W = mg = 7.8 × 10 = 78 N Why this scores One mark for using ρ = m / V , one for W = mg , one for 78 N. The examiner report names stopping at the mass (7.8 kg) and not converting 2.0 cm to 0.020 m as the common errors. 1.5.1 Effects of Forces These questions test Hooke’s law, the limit of proportionality, F = ma and why circular motion needs a resultant force; examiners reward a written equation, correct units and precise vocabulary such as “directly proportional” and “perpendicular to the motion”. What examiners keep seeing Confusing the limit of proportionality with the elastic limit, and forgetting that weight acts too: when a spring pulls on a hanging mass, the resultant force is the tension minus the weight, not the tension alone. 0625/43/M/J/21 Q1(a) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: The value of the spring constant k of the spring is 0.20 N / cm. The spring reaches its limit of proportionality when the load is 15 N. Calculate the extension of the spring when the load is 3.0 N. F = kx , so x = F ÷ k x = 3.0 ÷ 0.20 = 15 cm Why this scores One mark for F = kx (or x = F/k) with the numbers in, one for 15 cm with its unit. k is in N / cm, so the extension comes out in cm: no conversion is needed, but a missing or wrong unit cost candidates the second mark. 0625/43/M/J/21 Q1(b) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: The value of the spring constant k of the spring is 0.20 N / cm. The spring reaches its limit of proportionality when the load is 15 N. Explain what is meant by the term limit of proportionality of the spring. Up to a certain load, the extension of the spring is directly proportional to the load (it obeys Hooke’s law). The limit of proportionality is the point (here a load of 15 N) beyond which the extension is no longer proportional to the load, so the extension–load graph stops being a straight line. Why this scores One mark for “extension proportional to load”, one for saying this only holds up to the limit. The examiner report says weaker answers described the elastic limit instead (the spring not returning to its original length), which is a different idea. 0625/41/M/J/25 Q2(a)(i) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: A resultant force is applied to an object moving with a velocity v in a straight line. State two different changes to the motion that the resultant force may cause. 1. A change in the speed of the object (it speeds up or slows down). 2. A change in the direction in which the object is moving. Why this scores One mark each for speed (or magnitude of velocity) and direction. The examiner report notes that some answers gave the same change twice in different words, e.g. “speeds up” and “accelerates”, which earns only one mark. 0625/41/M/J/23 Q2(b)(iii) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: At the end of the straight section, the track remains horizontal but bends to the right, as shown in Fig. 2.1. When the motorcyclist reaches the bend, she travels around the bend in a circular path at a constant speed. Explain why there must be a resultant force on the motorcyclist as she travels around the bend. Her direction of motion is changing all the time, so her velocity is changing even though her speed is constant. This means she is accelerating. An acceleration needs a resultant force ( F = ma ). The force acts perpendicular to her motion, towards the centre of the circular bend. Why this scores Two creditworthy points: the change in direction means a change in velocity (an acceleration), and the resultant force is perpendicular to the motion / towards the centre. The examiner report says simply restating that “a force is needed to go round the bend” earns nothing, and naming friction or air resistance as the resultant force is wrong. 0625/42/O/N/25 Q2(a)(i) · October/November 2025 · [3 marks] Source material: A truck moves with a constant acceleration. The speed of the truck increases from 13 m / s to 22 m / s. The time taken for this increase in speed is 4.5 s. The mass of the truck is 3700 kg. Calculate the resultant force acting on the truck. a = Δ v ÷ Δ t = (22 − 13) ÷ 4.5 = 2.0 m/s 2 F = ma = 3700 × 2.0 F = 7400 N Why this scores One mark for finding the acceleration (2.0 m/s 2 ), one for F = ma with the numbers substituted, and one for 7400 N. Use the change in speed (22 − 13), not the final speed, in the acceleration. 0625/41/O/N/24 Q1(c)(ii) · October/November 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: An object of mass 0.50 kg is attached to the spring. The object is pulled downwards until the tension in the spring is 6.5 N. The object is released. Calculate the acceleration of the object immediately after it is released. Weight W = mg = 0.50 × 9.8 = 4.9 N (downwards) Resultant force = 6.5 − 4.9 = 1.6 N (upwards) a = F ÷ m = 1.6 ÷ 0.50 a = 3.2 m/s 2 (upwards) Why this scores One mark for the resultant force (tension minus weight = 1.6 N), one for using F = ma, one for 3.2 m/s 2 . The trap is dividing the whole 6.5 N by the mass, which ignores the weight pulling the other way. 1.5.2 Turning Effect and Centre of Gravity These questions test the moment of a force, the principle of moments, the two conditions for equilibrium and how the position of the centre of gravity affects stability; examiners reward the word “perpendicular” and clear links between centre of gravity, base and toppling. What examiners keep seeing Leaving out “perpendicular” when defining the moment of a force, and giving only one condition for equilibrium (or writing “weight = lift” instead of “no resultant force”). The examiner reports also note candidates confusing moment with momentum. 0625/41/O/N/23 Q4(a)(i) · October/November 2023 · [1 mark] State what is meant by centre of gravity. The point through which the whole weight of an object can be taken to act. Why this scores One mark for “the point where all the weight seems to act”. Saying “the centre of the object” or “where the mass is” does not score. 0625/42/M/J/23 Q1(a)(i) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: Fig. 1.1 shows a helicopter which is stationary at a height of 1500 m above the ground. State the two conditions necessary for the helicopter to remain in equilibrium. 1. There is no resultant force on the helicopter. 2. There is no resultant moment on the helicopter (about any point). Why this scores One mark for each condition. The examiner report says “weight = lift” or “clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments” on their own were incomplete, and the no-resultant-moment condition was the one most often missed. 0625/43/M/J/20 Q3(b) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Source material: In a double-decker bus there are two passenger compartments, one above the other. There are 30 passengers in the upper compartment of the bus and 2 passengers in the bottom compartment of the bus. State how this affects the stability of the bus and the reason for this. The bus becomes less stable : it is more likely to topple over. Most of the passengers’ mass is high up, so the centre of gravity of the bus is raised. A smaller tilt is then enough for the line of action of the weight to fall outside the base, so the weight produces a moment that turns the bus over. Why this scores One mark for “less stable / more likely to topple”, one for the reason: the higher centre of gravity can more easily move outside the base. Saying only “it is top-heavy” does not explain the physics. 0625/41/O/N/22 Q3(c)(i) · October/November 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: A rock climber, of total mass 62 kg, holds herself in horizontal equilibrium against a vertical cliff. … The climber’s centre of mass is 0.90 m from the cliff. Calculate the moment about her feet due to her weight. Weight = mg = 62 × 10 = 620 N (this paper takes g = 10 N/kg) moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot = 620 × 0.90 moment = 560 N m Why this scores One mark for force × perpendicular distance with 620 × 0.90 substituted, one for 560 N m. Weight acts vertically and her feet are on the cliff, so the 0.90 m horizontal distance is the perpendicular distance. The examiner report notes some candidates used the wrong distance or unit (the unit is N m, not N/m or J). 0625/41/O/N/24 Q3(a) · October/November 2024 · [3 marks] Define the moment of a force and describe the effect that it measures. The moment of a force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point (pivot) to the line of action of the force. It measures the turning effect of the force about that point. Why this scores Two marks for force × perpendicular distance from the pivot (only one if “perpendicular” is missing) and one for “turning effect”. The examiner reports repeatedly say that “force × distance” without “perpendicular” loses a mark. 0625/41/M/J/25 Q2(b) · May/June 2025 · [4 marks] Describe how a uniform metre ruler, a pivot and a selection of masses can be used to demonstrate that there is no resultant moment on an object in equilibrium. You may include a labelled diagram in your answer. Balance the uniform metre ruler on the pivot at its centre (the 50 cm mark), so its weight acts through the pivot and has no moment. Hang a mass on one side of the pivot, then hang a different mass on the other side and slide it along until the ruler balances horizontally. Record each mass and its distance from the pivot. Calculate each moment as force (weight = mg ) × perpendicular distance from the pivot. Show that the sum of the clockwise moments equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments, so there is no resultant moment. Repeat with different masses and positions. Figure: masses hung either side of a pivot; distances measured from the pivot to each mass. Why this scores One mark each for: ruler balanced on the pivot (a labelled diagram can earn this), adding masses on both sides and adjusting until balanced, moment = force × perpendicular distance, and clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments. The examiner report says the strongest answers described the technique (moving the masses until balanced), not just the principle. 1.6 Momentum These questions test the definitions of momentum and impulse, conservation of momentum in collisions and explosions, and resultant force as rate of change of momentum; examiners reward a written equation, a clear sign convention for direction, and answers that link impulse, force, momentum and time. What examiners keep seeing Forgetting that momentum is a vector: when an object bounces back or two objects move towards each other, one velocity must be negative. The examiner reports show many candidates adding momenta that should be subtracted, or saying the impulse gets smaller on a soft surface. 0625/42/M/J/25 Q3(a) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Define momentum. Momentum = mass × velocity ( p = mv ). Why this scores One mark for mass × velocity. The examiner report says some answers wrote “speed” instead of velocity or gave the definition of impulse. 0625/42/O/N/23 Q3(a)(iii) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: The balloon is filled with air and then the air is released. As the air leaves the balloon, the balloon experiences a force. Explain how momentum is conserved as the balloon accelerates. Before the air is released the total momentum is zero. The air leaving the balloon moves in the opposite direction to the balloon. The momentum gained by the balloon is equal in size to the momentum of the escaping air but in the opposite direction, so the total momentum stays zero. Why this scores One mark for the air moving in the opposite direction to the balloon, one for the balloon’s momentum being equal in size to the air’s. The examiner report says many answers only stated the law of conservation of momentum, or only talked about the balloon. 0625/41/O/N/23 Q1(b)(ii) · October/November 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: The mass of the ball is 0.20 kg. … The speed of the ball immediately before it strikes the path is 14 m / s. The speed of the ball immediately after it strikes the path is 12 m / s. Show that the change in momentum of the ball when it bounces off the path is 5.2 kg m / s. Take upwards as positive. Momentum before = mv = 0.20 × (−14) = −2.8 kg m/s Momentum after = 0.20 × (+12) = +2.4 kg m/s Change in momentum = 2.4 − (−2.8) = 5.2 kg m/s Why this scores One mark for p = mv, one for the two momenta with opposite signs, one for the subtraction giving 5.2 kg m/s. The examiner report says candidates had to show that the velocities are in opposite directions; working back from the given answer without the signs did not earn full credit. 0625/43/M/J/24 Q3(b)(ii) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: The concrete floor under the seesaw is replaced with a rubber floor. A child falls from the seesaw and experiences an impulse when they hit the floor. Explain how the rubber floor reduces injury to the child. Use ideas about impulse, force, momentum and time in your answer. The child’s change in momentum (the impulse) is the same on both floors, because they hit the floor at the same speed and stop. The rubber floor deforms, so this change in momentum takes place over a longer time . Force = rate of change of momentum ( F = Δ p ÷ Δ t ), so a longer time means a smaller force on the child, which causes less injury. Why this scores Any three of: same impulse / change in momentum, over a longer time, F = change in momentum ÷ time, smaller force. The examiner report says a common misconception was that the rubber floor reduces the impulse; vague answers about “cushioning” scored nothing. 0625/43/O/N/25 Q2(b) · October/November 2025 · [3 marks] Source material: A cricket ball is travelling at a speed of 25 m / s horizontally through the air. The mass of the ball is 0.14 kg. A player catches the ball and the ball comes to rest. The player’s hands are in contact with the moving ball for 9.7 ms. Calculate the horizontal force exerted by her hands to bring the ball to rest. Change in momentum Δ p = mv = 0.14 × 25 = 3.5 kg m/s t = 9.7 ms = 9.7 × 10 −3 s F = Δ p ÷ t = 3.5 ÷ 0.0097 F = 360 N Why this scores One mark for converting 9.7 ms to seconds, one for F = change in momentum ÷ time, one for 360 N. Forgetting to convert milliseconds gives an answer 1000 times too small. 0625/42/M/J/25 Q3(b) · May/June 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: Fig. 3.1 shows two toy trains, A and B, on a track. The mass of train A is 0.45 kg and the mass of train B is 0.21 kg. The trains do not have motors. Train A travels towards train B and they collide. Immediately before the collision: • the velocity of train A is 0.34 m / s to the right … • the velocity of train B is 0.12 m / s to the left. The trains stick together when they collide. Calculate the velocity of the trains immediately after the collision. Take right as positive. Total momentum before = (0.45 × 0.34) + (0.21 × −0.12) = 0.153 − 0.0252 = 0.1278 kg m/s Total momentum after = (0.45 + 0.21) × v = 0.66 v Momentum is conserved: 0.66 v = 0.1278 v = 0.1278 ÷ 0.66 v = 0.19 m/s to the right Why this scores Marks for the momentum before (with B’s momentum negative), the momentum after using the combined mass, equating them, and 0.19 m/s with the direction. The examiner report says common errors were adding the two momenta, not combining the masses, and simply adding or subtracting velocities. 1.7.1 Energy, Work and Power These questions test the energy equations ( E k = ½ mv 2 , Δ E p = mg Δ h , W = Fd , P = W / t and efficiency) and describing energy transfers between stores; examiners reward the equation written first, a clear substitution and a final answer with the correct unit. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports keep listing the same slips: forgetting to square the speed in ½ mv 2 , leaving a mass in grams, writing efficiency as just “output ÷ input” without the words “useful energy (or power)”, and dropping the unit or the power of ten in the final answer. 0625/43/M/J/24 Q2(c)(i) · May/June 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: Fig. 2.1 shows solar-powered traffic warning lights. … The efficiency of the solar cell is 22%. State what is meant by 22% efficiency. 22% of the total energy (power) input to the solar cell is transferred as useful energy (power) output; the other 78% is wasted. Why this scores One mark for linking 22% to the useful output as a fraction of the total input. The examiner report notes that answers which just say “22% of the energy is used” are not precise enough: say useful output compared with total input. 0625/42/F/M/23 Q2(c) · February/March 2023 · [2 marks] A crane lifts a container 48 m vertically upwards. The mass of the container is 30 000 kg. Calculate the energy transferred to the gravitational potential energy stored in the container. Δ E p = mg Δ h Δ E p = 30 000 × 9.8 × 48 Δ E p = 14 112 000 J = 1.4 × 10 7 J Why this scores One mark for the equation with the values substituted and one for the answer with its unit. The examiner report says weaker answers lost the second mark through the wrong power of ten or no unit: 1.4 × 10 7 J (or 14 MJ) is fine, “1.4 × 10 7 ” alone is not. 0625/41/M/J/21 Q2(b) · May/June 2021 · [3 marks] Source material: Fig. 2.1 shows a wooden trolley of mass 1.2 kg at rest on the rough surface of a bench. … The trolley moves with an initial speed of 0.065 m / s. As the trolley moves across the rough surface, it slows down and stops. Explain, in terms of the work done, the energy change that takes place as the trolley slows down. Friction between the trolley and the rough bench acts against the motion, so work is done against friction as the trolley moves along. The energy for this work comes from the trolley’s kinetic energy store, so its kinetic energy decreases to zero. The work done against friction transfers this energy to the thermal (internal) energy store of the trolley, the bench and the surrounding air, which warm up very slightly. Why this scores One mark each for work done against friction, kinetic energy decreasing to zero, and thermal energy produced. The examiner report says many candidates described the energy change but never used the phrase “work done”, or only defined work done without linking it to friction: the question asks for it, so say it. 0625/42/O/N/22 Q3(b)(ii) · October/November 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: Fig. 3.1 shows a small water turbine driven by a tidal flow of water to generate electrical power. The mass of water passing through the turbine each second is 6.0 × 10 3 kg. The speed of the water is 2.0 m / s. 40% of the kinetic energy of the water is converted to electrical energy. Calculate the electrical power generated. Kinetic energy of the water passing through each second: E k = ½ mv 2 = ½ × 6.0 × 10 3 × 2.0 2 = 12 000 J This is transferred every second, so the input power is P = E ÷ t = 12 000 ÷ 1 = 12 000 W Electrical power = 40% of 12 000 W = 0.40 × 12 000 = 4800 W Why this scores Marks for ½ mv 2 , turning energy per second into power, taking 40% and the final 4800 W. The examiner report lists the usual slips: not squaring the speed, taking 60% instead of 40%, and giving the unit as J instead of W. 0625/43/O/N/21 Q2(a) · October/November 2021 · [4 marks] Source material: The load of 12 kg is raised to a height of 1.7 m above the ground. … The time taken for the load to fall to the ground is 1200 seconds. The load falls at constant speed. Calculate the rate of transfer of gravitational potential energy as the load falls to the ground. Step 1: energy transferred Δ E p = mg Δ h = 12 × 10 × 1.7 = 204 J (this paper takes g = 10 N/kg) Step 2: rate of transfer (power) P = Δ E ÷ t = 204 ÷ 1200 P = 0.17 W Why this scores Marks build up through mgh , the value of the energy (204 J), dividing by 1200 s and the final 0.17 W. “Rate of transfer” means energy per second, so the unit is W (J/s is also accepted); the examiner report says answers in J or m/s lost the final mark. 0625/42/O/N/23 Q1(c) · October/November 2023 · [4 marks] The car decelerates from 13.0 m / s to 0 m / s at a constant deceleration. The mass of the car is 1350 kg. The car travels 13 m in 2.0 s as it decelerates. Show that the work done by the car as it decelerates is approximately 1.1 × 10 5 J. Deceleration: a = Δ v ÷ t = (13.0 − 0) ÷ 2.0 = 6.5 m/s 2 Braking force: F = ma = 1350 × 6.5 = 8775 N Work done: W = Fd = 8775 × 13 = 114 075 J ≈ 1.1 × 10 5 J Check: the work done equals the kinetic energy lost, ½ mv 2 = ½ × 1350 × 13.0 2 = 114 075 J. ✓ Why this scores One mark each for W = Fd , F = ma , the force 8775 N and the unrounded work 114 075 J. In a “show that” question the examiner report rewards equations written in symbols and no early rounding; using g as the acceleration was a common error. The kinetic-energy route also scores, but only if you state that work done = change in kinetic energy. 1.7.3 Energy Resources These questions test how each energy resource is used to generate electricity, where its energy originally comes from (usually the Sun, through nuclear fusion), and its advantages and disadvantages; examiners reward a specific point followed by its consequence, not vague words such as “natural” or “eco-friendly”. What examiners keep seeing Examiners report that many candidates call a resource renewable because “it is natural” or “it comes from the Sun”, which earns nothing: say it is replaced and will not run out. When asked for resources that do not come from the Sun, wave, hydroelectric, biomass and fossil fuels are common wrong answers: the right ones are geothermal, tidal and nuclear. 0625/42/O/N/24 Q3(c) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Tidal energy and wind energy are both renewable energy resources. Suggest one reason why tidal energy is a more useful energy resource than wind energy. Ignore the costs of construction and maintenance. Tides are predictable and reliable: they come in and go out at known times every day, whereas the wind can drop or stop without warning, so the output of a wind turbine cannot be relied on. Why this scores One mark for the idea that tides are regular, predictable or reliable (or the reverse point about wind). Comparing the two directly, as here, makes the reason clear. 0625/41/M/J/21 Q9(c) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Nuclear fusion in the Sun is the source of most but not all of the resources that are used to generate electrical energy on Earth. State two resources for which nuclear fusion in the Sun is not the source. 1. Geothermal energy 2. Tidal energy Why this scores One mark for each correct resource; nuclear (fission) energy would also be accepted. The examiner report notes that wave energy was a common wrong answer: waves are caused by winds, which come from the Sun heating the Earth. Do not write “tidal wave”, which means a tsunami. 0625/42/O/N/21 Q4(a) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] A power station uses wind energy to generate electricity. State and explain whether this method of generating electricity is renewable. Statement: renewable. Explanation: the wind is constantly replaced (the Sun keeps heating the atmosphere), so using it to turn turbines does not use it up and it will not run out. Why this scores One mark for “renewable” and one for the idea that the resource is replaced or will not run out. The examiner report says answers such as “it is natural”, “it comes from the Sun” or just repeating “renewable” did not earn the explanation mark. 0625/43/O/N/25 Q3(b) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Describe how useful energy may be obtained from geothermal resources. Cold water is pumped deep underground, where it is heated by hot rocks and turns into steam. The steam returns to the surface and turns a turbine that drives a generator to produce electricity (or it is used directly to heat buildings). Why this scores One mark for water being heated by hot rocks underground and one for how the steam is used (turning a turbine and generator, or heating buildings). Name the hot rocks: “heat from the Earth” on its own is too vague. 0625/41/O/N/23 Q5(a) · October/November 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: Many methods of generating electrical power involve the use of water. Describe one method of generating electrical power from energy stored in water. Hydroelectric power: water is held behind a dam in a high reservoir, where it has a store of gravitational potential energy. When the water is released it flows downhill through pipes, and its gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy. The fast-moving water turns a turbine, and the turbine drives a generator, which generates electricity. Why this scores The mark scheme gives one mark each (up to three) for naming the method, how the water’s energy is released, the transfer between energy stores, the water turning a turbine, and the turbine driving a generator. This answer makes five creditworthy points, so it is safe even if one is judged too brief. 0625/42/M/J/20 Q3(b) · May/June 2020 · [4 marks] State and explain one advantage and one disadvantage of heating the water in a solar panel compared with heating the water in a coal-burning boiler. Advantage: a solar panel burns no fuel. Explanation: no carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas) or other polluting gases are released, so it does not add to global warming or air pollution, unlike burning coal. Disadvantage: it does not work at night and heats much less water on cloudy days. Explanation: the panel only works when sunlight falls on it, so hot water may not be available when it is needed, whereas a coal boiler can be used at any time. Why this scores One mark for each valid point and one for an explanation that follows from it. Each explanation must give the consequence, compared with the coal boiler; stating “renewable” on its own, without saying why that matters, is too vague to earn the explanation mark. 1.8 Pressure These questions test p = F/A and the liquid-pressure equation Δp = ρgΔh; examiners reward the equation written first, weight (not mass) used as the force, and careful handling of atmospheric pressure. What examiners keep seeing Mixing up total pressure and pressure due to the liquid: to find a depth you must subtract atmospheric pressure first (the examiner report says many candidates added it instead). Using mass instead of weight in p = F/A is the other common slip. 0625/43/M/J/23 Q2(a)(i) · May/June 2023 · [1 mark] Define pressure. Pressure is the force per unit area ( p = F ÷ A ). Why this scores One mark for force per unit area. The examiner report says “force on a certain area” or “force acting on an object” does not score: say unit area, or write the equation. 0625/43/M/J/23 Q2(a)(ii) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Describe how pressure in a liquid varies with its depth and with its density. Depth: the pressure increases as the depth increases (it is proportional to depth). Density: at the same depth, a denser liquid gives a greater pressure (Δ p = ρ g Δ h ). Why this scores One mark for each correct variation. The examiner report says weaker answers thought pressure decreases as density increases; learning Δp = ρgΔh avoids this. 0625/41/M/J/21 Q3(b)(ii) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: Fig. 3.1 shows a device that uses liquid pressure to lift heavy boxes. … The boxes are lifted by pumping oil into the cylinder. As the boxes are lifted, the depth of the oil increases. Explain why the pump must exert an increasing pressure on the oil as the depth of the oil increases. Pressure in a liquid increases with depth (Δ p = ρ g Δ h ), so the deeper column of oil adds extra pressure at the bottom, where the pump pushes the oil in. The pump must overcome this extra pressure from the weight of the oil to keep the upward force on the piston constant and keep lifting the boxes. Why this scores One mark for linking the greater depth of oil to a greater pressure, one for the pump having to overcome it to keep the force constant. The examiner report says many candidates gave the first point but did not explain why the pump has to push harder. 0625/43/M/J/20 Q2(b)(ii) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Source material: Fig. 2.1 shows a submarine. The submarine is fully submerged in the sea. … The atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa and the total pressure on the top surface of the submarine is 500 kPa. A hatch (an opening door) on the top surface of the submarine has an area of 0.62 m2. Calculate the downward force on the hatch due to the total pressure on the top surface of the submarine. p = F ÷ A , so F = pA F = 500 × 10 3 × 0.62 F = 3.1 × 10 5 N Why this scores One mark for F = pA with the numbers in, one for 3.1 × 10 5 N. The question asks for the total pressure, so use 500 kPa (not 400 kPa) and convert kPa to Pa. 0625/43/M/J/21 Q2(b) · May/June 2021 · [3 marks] A diver dives to a depth below the surface of the sea where the total pressure is 3.0 × 10 5 Pa. The atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10 5 Pa. The density of the sea water is 1030 kg / m 3 . Calculate the depth of the diver below the surface of the sea. Pressure due to the water = 3.0 × 10 5 − 1.0 × 10 5 = 2.0 × 10 5 Pa Δ p = ρ g Δ h , so Δ h = Δ p ÷ (ρ g ) Δ h = 2.0 × 10 5 ÷ (1030 × 10) (this paper takes g = 10 N/kg) depth = 19 m Why this scores One mark for p = ρgh, one for subtracting atmospheric pressure before rearranging, one for 19 m. The examiner report says the most common mistake was adding the atmospheric pressure instead of subtracting it. 0625/42/M/J/23 Q3(b) · May/June 2023 · [4 marks] Source material: Fig. 3.2 shows a side view of the pond with a layer of ice floating freely on the water. The surface area of the pond is 5.0 m 2 . The mass of the ice is 690 kg. The density of water is 1000 kg / m 3 . Point X is 0.45 m below the ice. Calculate the pressure at point X due to the ice and the water. Weight of ice = mg = 690 × 9.8 = 6762 N Pressure due to ice = F ÷ A = 6762 ÷ 5.0 = 1352 Pa Pressure due to water = ρ g h = 1000 × 9.8 × 0.45 = 4410 Pa Total = 1352 + 4410 = 5762 Pa pressure at X = 5.8 × 10 3 Pa Why this scores Marks for the pressure due to the water, the weight of the ice, adding the two pressures, and 5.8 × 10 3 Pa. The examiner report says weaker answers found only the water pressure, subtracted the two, or used the mass of the ice instead of its weight. Topical Past Papers · Topic 2 Past Paper Questions: Thermal Physics 18 real Cambridge IGCSE Physics Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0625/42/M/J/24 Q2(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 2.1 Kinetic Particle Model of Matter · 2.2 Thermal Properties and Temperature · 2.3 Transfer of Thermal Energy 2.1 Kinetic Particle Model of Matter These questions test the particle model: arrangement and motion in solids, liquids and gases, Brownian motion, how gas particles cause pressure, absolute zero and pV = constant; examiners reward answers that mention particles (or molecules) explicitly and use precise phrases such as “more frequent collisions with the walls”. What examiners keep seeing “More collisions” does not score: examiners want collisions that are more frequent and (for a temperature rise) harder , with a larger change in momentum. The examiner reports also note that many candidates write a learnt answer about heating a gas when the question asks something else, such as simply how a gas exerts pressure. 0625/42/M/J/23 Q4(b)(ii) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Explain what is meant by the term absolute zero. Refer to particles in your answer. Absolute zero (0 K, −273 °C) is the lowest possible temperature. At absolute zero the particles have the least possible kinetic energy, so they cannot be slowed down any further and nothing can be cooled below this temperature. Why this scores One mark for the particles having the least kinetic energy and one for “lowest possible temperature”. The examiner report says stronger answers gave both; a common wrong answer was that absolute zero is the temperature at which water freezes. 0625/43/M/J/23 Q3(a)(ii) · May/June 2023 · [3 marks] Describe, in terms of the motion and arrangement of particles, the structures of solids and gases. Solids: the particles are packed closely together in a regular pattern, in fixed positions. They vibrate about these fixed positions. Gases: the particles are far apart and randomly arranged. They move quickly and freely in random directions. Why this scores Any three of the mark-scheme points score: solid particles vibrate, are in fixed and close positions; gas particles move freely and quickly, are random and widely separated. The examiner report says weaker answers did not mention particles at all; cover both motion and arrangement for each state. 0625/42/O/N/25 Q4(a)(i) · October/November 2025 · [3 marks] Source material: Fig. 4.1 shows gas trapped in a cylinder by a piston. … The volume of gas is 240 cm 3 . The piston is pushed to the left and is held in its new position. The pressure of the gas increases from 1.0 × 10 5 Pa to 1.4 × 10 5 Pa. The temperature of the gas remains constant. Calculate the volume of the gas when the piston is in its new position. p 1 V 1 = p 2 V 2 (fixed mass of gas at constant temperature) 1.0 × 10 5 × 240 = 1.4 × 10 5 × V 2 V 2 = (1.0 × 10 5 × 240) ÷ (1.4 × 10 5 ) = 171 cm 3 = 170 cm 3 Why this scores One mark for pV = constant with the values substituted, one for the rearrangement and one for 170 cm 3 . Quick check: the pressure went up, so the volume must go down. Keeping the volume in cm 3 is fine because both sides use the same units. 0625/43/M/J/22 Q4(a)(ii) · May/June 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: Fig. 4.1 shows apparatus used to observe the motion of smoke particles (Brownian motion). … The smoke particles are seen as bright specks of light when looking through the microscope. Explain, in terms of forces and the motion of air molecules, the cause of the motion of the smoke particles. The air molecules are very small and light compared with the smoke particles, and they move very fast in random directions. Each smoke particle is bombarded by air molecules from all sides. At any instant, more molecules hit one side of a smoke particle than the other, so the collisions exert an unbalanced (resultant) force on it and it moves. The direction of this resultant force keeps changing at random, so the smoke particle moves in a jerky, random path. Why this scores Four marks for: air molecules bombard the smoke particles; they are small (low mass); they move very fast; they move randomly; the collisions give an unbalanced force. The examiner report warns against mixing up the two: keep “air molecules” for the invisible particles doing the hitting and “smoke particles” for the specks you can see. 0625/42/F/M/21 Q4(a) · February/March 2021 · [4 marks] In terms of the momentum of molecules, explain how a gas exerts pressure on the walls of its container. The gas molecules move randomly at high speed and keep colliding with the walls of the container. When a molecule hits a wall and bounces back, its velocity reverses, so its momentum ( mv ) changes. Force is the rate of change of momentum, so each collision means the wall exerts a force on the molecule, and the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. Many collisions every second add up to a total force on the wall; pressure is this total force divided by the area of the wall ( p = F / A ). Why this scores One mark each for: molecules hit the walls; their momentum changes; force = rate of change of momentum; pressure = force ÷ area. The examiner report says many candidates explained why pressure rises when a gas is heated instead, a learnt answer to a different question that scores little here. 0625/43/O/N/23 Q4(b) · October/November 2023 · [4 marks] The temperature of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume changes from 300 K to 400 K. State and explain, in terms of particles, the effect on the pressure of the gas. Statement: the pressure of the gas increases. Explanation: at the higher temperature the gas particles have more kinetic energy, so they move faster. The particles therefore collide with the walls more frequently, and each collision has a larger change in momentum, so it exerts a larger force on the wall. A larger total force acts on the same area of wall, so the pressure (force ÷ area) increases. Why this scores One mark for “increases”, one for faster particles (more kinetic energy) and two from: more frequent collisions, harder collisions (larger force or momentum change), pressure = force ÷ area. The examiner report says “more collisions” on its own was not credited: it must be more frequent collisions with the walls. 2.2 Thermal Properties and Temperature These questions test particle explanations of expansion and evaporation, the definitions of specific heat capacity and latent heat, and multi-stage energy calculations; examiners reward precise particle language and an equation written before the numbers. What examiners keep seeing In multi-stage calculations, candidates leave out the change-of-state energy or use one temperature change for the whole process: split it into stages and add them. In definitions, write “by 1 °C”, not “to 1 °C”, and include “per kg”. 0625/42/F/M/24 Q4(a) · February/March 2024 · [2 marks] Define specific heat capacity. The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (the energy transferred per unit mass per unit rise in temperature). Why this scores Both marks need the energy to be per unit mass (1 kg) and per unit temperature change (1 °C); leaving out the mass describes thermal capacity and scores only one mark. The examiner report notes answers that wrote “to 1 °C” instead of “by 1 °C”. 0625/41/M/J/21 Q5(b) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Explain, in terms of molecules, why a liquid expands more than a solid when heated. The attractive forces between the molecules of a liquid are weaker than the forces between the molecules of a solid. So for the same energy supplied, less work has to be done to pull the liquid molecules apart, and they move further apart than the molecules in the solid. Why this scores One mark for weaker intermolecular forces in the liquid, one for linking this to a greater separation for the same energy input. The examiner report says arguments based only on liquids already having larger spacings were less successful, and never say the molecules themselves get bigger. 0625/42/M/J/24 Q4(a) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] State two ways that evaporation differs from boiling. 1 Evaporation happens only at the surface of the liquid; boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles of vapour forming inside it. 2 Evaporation happens at any temperature; boiling happens only at one temperature, the boiling point. Why this scores One mark per difference. The examiner report warns that “only at the surface” and “no bubbles” are the same idea, so giving both as your two differences scores only one mark: the second point should be about temperature. 0625/43/O/N/22 Q5(a) · October/November 2022 · [4 marks] Three identical dishes, A, B and C, contain an equal volume of water. Dish A is outside in sunlight and experiences no wind during the day. Dish B is outside in sunlight and experiences a strong wind during the day. Dish C is in a dark room. Water evaporates from each dish. After 12 hours, a student measures the volume of water in each dish. Dish C contains the largest volume of water and dish B contains the smallest volume of water. Explain, in terms of particles, why the three dishes have different volumes of water. Evaporation happens when the most energetic (fastest) water molecules at the surface escape from the liquid. In dishes A and B, energy from the Sun is absorbed by the water molecules, so their kinetic energy increases and more of them have enough energy to escape. Dish C gets no sunlight, so it has the lowest rate of evaporation and keeps the most water. In dish B the wind carries molecules away once they have left the surface, so they cannot fall back into the water. So dish B has the highest rate of evaporation and loses the most water. Why this scores Four marks: Sun’s energy absorbed by the molecules (more kinetic energy); faster molecules escape from the surface; the wind removes molecules after they leave so they do not re-enter; a correct comparison of evaporation rates. The examiner report says the wind does not give molecules energy or “blow off the top layer”, and “no water evaporates from C” is wrong: its rate is just lower. 0625/41/O/N/24 Q4(a) · October/November 2024 · [4 marks] Describe an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of aluminium. You may draw a diagram. Include in your answer: • the measurements made • any equations needed. Take an aluminium block with two holes. Put an electric heater in one hole and a thermometer in the other, and wrap the block in insulation. Measure the mass m of the block on a balance and its starting temperature. Switch on the heater for a measured time t (stopwatch), recording the heater power P (or the voltmeter reading V and ammeter reading I ). Record the highest temperature reached and work out the temperature rise Δθ. Energy supplied: E = Pt (or E = IVt ) Specific heat capacity: c = E ÷ ( m Δθ) Why this scores Marks go for a workable way of heating the aluminium, a matching way of finding the energy supplied ( E = Pt or E = IVt ), at least one correct measurement (mass, temperature change or time) and the equation c = E /( m Δθ). Make sure the energy equation fits your method: an electric heater pairs with E = Pt . 0625/43/M/J/22 Q5(b)(ii) · May/June 2022 · [5 marks] Source material: A bowl contains 500 cm 3 of water at a temperature of 5.0 °C. … When the bowl is removed from the freezer, it contains ice at a temperature of –18.0 °C. The density of water is 1000 kg / m 3 . The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J / (kg °C). The specific heat capacity of ice is 2100 J / (kg °C). The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 3.3 × 10 5 J / kg. Calculate the energy given out as the water cools from 5.0 °C to ice at –18.0 °C. Mass of water: m = ρ V = 1000 × 500 × 10 −6 = 0.50 kg Water cooling 5.0 °C → 0 °C: E 1 = mc Δθ = 0.50 × 4200 × 5.0 = 10 500 J Water freezing at 0 °C: E 2 = mL = 0.50 × 3.3 × 10 5 = 165 000 J Ice cooling 0 °C → −18.0 °C: E 3 = mc Δθ = 0.50 × 2100 × 18.0 = 18 900 J Total energy given out = 10 500 + 165 000 + 18 900 = 194 400 J = 1.9 × 10 5 J Why this scores One mark each for E = mc Δθ, E = mL , using 4200 with Δθ = 5, using 2100 with Δθ = 18, and the final answer. The examiner report says weaker answers left out the freezing stage, subtracted it instead of adding, or used one Δθ of 23 °C for the whole change. 2.3 Transfer of Thermal Energy These questions test whether you can name the right transfer process and explain it with particles, electrons, density changes or infrared; examiners reward naming the process first, then the mechanism. What examiners keep seeing Answers drift into the wrong mechanism: lattice vibrations when the question asks about electrons, “heat rises” instead of “less dense air rises”, or a second process added when only the main one is asked for. 0625/42/O/N/24 Q5(c) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: On a sunny day, the temperatures of a black tarmac road and the air above the road increase. State the main method of thermal energy transfer from the air immediately above the road to the rest of the air. Convection . Why this scores One mark for convection. Conduction is the answer for the layer of air touching the tarmac (the previous part); after that it is the moving, less dense warm air that carries the energy upwards. 0625/43/O/N/25 Q5(d) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] The Earth’s surface absorbs incoming radiation from the Sun and also emits thermal radiation from its surface. Over the past 50 years, scientists estimate that the average temperature of the Earth’s surface has increased by approximately 0.75 °C. Explain what is causing this average temperature rise. The amount of greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide and methane, in the atmosphere has increased (mainly from burning fossil fuels). These gases absorb infrared emitted by the Earth’s surface and re-emit some of it back towards the surface, so less radiation escapes into space. The Earth now absorbs energy faster than it loses it, so its average temperature rises. Why this scores One mark for more greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane or water vapour) in the atmosphere, one for less radiation escaping or more being re-emitted back to the surface. Vague answers such as “pollution” do not name the cause. 0625/43/M/J/24 Q5(a) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: Fig. 5.1 shows two containers, each filled with hot water. The outer surface of the metal container is hot. Explain how electrons transfer thermal energy through the metal of the container. Metals contain free (delocalised) electrons. Electrons next to the hot water gain kinetic energy and move quickly through the metal lattice. They collide with ions far away from the hot water, transferring energy to them, so energy reaches the outer surface. Why this scores Any three of: free/delocalised electrons; they gain energy at the hot side; they move through the metal; they collide with distant ions or atoms and pass on energy. The examiner report says lattice vibrations earn nothing here, and weaker answers had the electrons “vibrating” instead of moving through the metal. 0625/41/M/J/22 Q6(c)(ii) · May/June 2022 · [3 marks] Source material: Fig. 6.1 shows a road next to the sea. The air above the road is heated by the warm road. A cyclist travelling along the road notices that a cool breeze is blowing from the sea to the land. Explain how convection produces this breeze. You may include a diagram if it helps your answer. The air above the warm road expands, so its density decreases. This warmer, less dense air rises. Cooler, denser air from above the sea moves in low down to replace it: this is the breeze the cyclist feels. Figure: the convection current that produces a sea breeze. Why this scores One mark each: the heated air’s density decreases; the warm air rises; cooler air from over the sea moves in to replace it. “Heat rises” earns nothing, and the examiner report notes many candidates struggled to apply convection to this setting. 0625/42/O/N/22 Q5(b) · October/November 2022 · [3 marks] Source material: Fig. 5.1 shows an aluminium block after leaving a furnace in a factory. Fig. 5.1 shows a factory worker standing 3 m from the block. State and explain the main process by which thermal energy is transferred to the worker. Radiation (thermal radiation). The hot block emits infrared, which is electromagnetic radiation, in all directions. The infrared travels to the worker without needing a medium and is absorbed by the worker’s skin and clothes. Why this scores M1 for radiation, then one mark for infrared/electromagnetic and one for it travelling to and being absorbed by the worker. The examiner report says adding a second process cost credit, and answers that just repeated “thermal energy is transferred to the worker” scored nothing. 0625/41/O/N/25 Q4(b) · October/November 2025 · [4 marks] The immersion heater is removed from the beaker. One metal rod and one plastic rod are placed in the beaker of hot water as shown in Fig. 4.1. The rods are at room temperature (20 °C) before they are placed into the beaker. Describe how the temperature of point X on each rod changes after the rods are placed in the beaker. Explain your answer. The temperature at X rises on both rods, but it rises much faster on the metal rod than on the plastic rod. Thermal energy travels along each rod from the hot water by conduction. The metal contains free (delocalised) electrons that move quickly along the rod and carry energy to X. The plastic has no free electrons and conducts only by slow lattice vibrations, so it is a poor conductor. Why this scores Two marks for the description (X gets hotter on both, faster on the metal rod), one for naming conduction and one for linking the metal’s faster rise to its free electrons. Just writing “metal is a good conductor” describes but does not explain.
