Topical Past Papers · Topic 3 Past Paper Questions: Waves 28 real Cambridge IGCSE Physics Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0625/42/M/J/24 Q2(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 3.1 General Properties of Waves · 3.2.1 Reflection and Refraction of Light · 3.2.3 Thin Lenses and Dispersion · 3.3 Electromagnetic Spectrum · 3.4 Sound 3.1 General Properties of Waves These questions test wave vocabulary, v = f λ and how wavelength controls diffraction; examiners reward vibrations described relative to the direction of energy travel and calculations with converted units. What examiners keep seeing In v = f λ questions candidates rearrange wrongly or forget to convert km, kHz or MHz; in diffraction questions many describe transverse/longitudinal differences instead of comparing wavelength with gap size. 0625/42/F/M/25 Q7(a)(i) · February/March 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Fig. 7.1 is a scale drawing of light waves approaching a narrow slit. Name the wave effect produced by the narrow slit. Diffraction . Why this scores One mark for diffraction. The examiner report lists refraction and dispersion as the usual wrong answers: refraction needs a change of medium, but here the waves simply spread out after the gap. 0625/43/O/N/21 Q6(b) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] Sound waves from a television are diffracted through doorways. Light waves from a television are not diffracted through doorways. Suggest why light waves and sound waves behave differently in this situation. The wavelength of sound is similar to the width of a doorway (around a metre), so sound diffracts (spreads out) a lot as it passes through. The wavelength of light is far smaller than the width of the doorway, so light diffracts by a negligible amount. Why this scores One mark for light’s wavelength being much smaller than the doorway, one for sound’s wavelength being similar to the gap so it diffracts more. The examiner report says few answers scored because many listed transverse/longitudinal differences with no link to diffraction. 0625/41/M/J/20 Q6(b) · May/June 2020 · [3 marks] Sound waves are longitudinal waves. Describe how a longitudinal wave differs from a transverse wave. In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction the wave travels (the direction of energy transfer). In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction the wave travels. A longitudinal wave is made up of compressions and rarefactions; a transverse wave has crests and troughs. Why this scores One mark each: longitudinal vibrations parallel to the direction of energy travel; transverse vibrations perpendicular to it; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions. Always say what vibrates relative to what: “it moves up and down” on its own is too vague. 0625/42/M/J/23 Q6(b) · May/June 2023 · [3 marks] The velocity of a P-wave in the Earth’s solid crust is 7.2 km / s and its frequency is 4.5 Hz. Calculate the wavelength of this P-wave. v = f λ, so λ = v ÷ f λ = 7200 m/s ÷ 4.5 Hz λ = 1600 m (1.6 km) Why this scores C1 for the equation, C1 for the substitution (7.2 km/s = 7200 m/s), A1 for 1600 m with a length unit. The examiner report lists writing λ = fv , rearranging wrongly and leaving out the unit as the usual losses. 0625/41/M/J/21 Q6(c) · May/June 2021 · [3 marks] Source material: Fig. 6.1 is a full-scale diagram that represents a sound wave travelling in air. The wave reaches a barrier. Fig. 6.2 shows the wave passing through a gap in the barrier. The frequency of the wave is increased to a value many times greater than the value obtained in (b). Describe and explain two ways in which a diagram representing the wave with the greater frequency differs from Fig. 6.2. 1 The compressions and rarefactions would be drawn much closer together, because the speed of sound in air is unchanged, so a higher frequency gives a shorter wavelength (λ = v ÷ f ). 2 The wave would spread out much less after passing through the gap (less diffraction), because its wavelength is now much smaller than the gap width. Why this scores One mark for compressions/rarefactions closer together, one for less diffraction, one for explaining with the smaller wavelength (or smaller wavelength-to-gap ratio). The examiner report notes many saw that the wavelength decreases, but few answers were complete. 3.2.1 Reflection and Refraction of Light These questions test the three refractive index equations (n = sin i ÷ sin r, n = c ÷ v, n = 1 ÷ sin c) and total internal reflection; examiners reward an equation written in symbols before the numbers, and both conditions for total internal reflection. What examiners keep seeing Defining refractive index vaguely (“how much light bends”, or leaving out the word sine), and dividing by n when you should multiply, or the other way round: write n = c ÷ v first and rearrange it. 0625/43/M/J/25 Q5(a) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Define, in words, refractive index for a ray of light travelling from air to water. The refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in air to the speed of light in water. Why this scores One mark for the ratio of the two speeds in words. The examiner report notes that students who tried “sin i over sin r” often left out the word sine or which angle, and lost the mark. 0625/41/M/J/24 Q4(b)(i) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: The refractive index of the glass used to make the lens is 1.5. The speed of light in air is 3.0 × 10 8 m / s. Calculate the speed of light in the glass. n = c ÷ v , so v = c ÷ n v = 3.0 × 10 8 ÷ 1.5 v = 2.0 × 10 8 m/s Why this scores One mark for the equation rearranged correctly and one for the answer with its unit, to 2 s.f. like the data. The examiner report says weaker students multiplied by n (light is slower in glass, so the answer must be smaller) or used sin i ÷ sin r. 0625/42/O/N/25 Q6(b)(i) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Light can be totally internally reflected when striking the boundary between two different regions. State two conditions that are necessary for total internal reflection to occur. 1. The light must be travelling in the region where it is slower (the optically denser one, e.g. glass) towards the region where it is faster (e.g. air). 2. The angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle. Why this scores One mark for each condition. Saying only “the angle must be large” is not enough: compare it with the critical angle. 0625/41/O/N/25 Q6(b)(i) · October/November 2025 · [3 marks] Source material: Fig. 6.1 shows part of an optical fibre used in high-speed broadband communication. The optical fibre is made of glass with a refractive index of 1.4. Calculate the critical angle c. n = 1 ÷ sin c , so sin c = 1 ÷ n sin c = 1 ÷ 1.4 = 0.714 c = sin −1 (0.714) = 46° Why this scores One mark for n = 1 ÷ sin c (the mark scheme accepts the equation in this form only), one for sin −1 (1 ÷ 1.4) and one for 46°. Using sin c = n gives an impossible value above 1. 0625/41/O/N/20 Q9(b) · October/November 2020 · [3 marks] Describe and explain the action of optical fibres in communication technology. You may draw a diagram in your answer. The signal (e.g. telephone or internet data) is coded as pulses of light or infrared, which are sent into one end of a thin glass fibre. Each time the light hits the inside surface of the fibre, its angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected and stays inside the fibre, even round bends. The pulses reach the far end with very little loss and are decoded back into the information. Figure: each time the light hits the inside wall, i is greater than the critical angle c, so it is totally internally reflected and the light or infrared pulses stay inside the fibre. Why this scores One mark each for light or infrared travelling along the fibre, total internal reflection at the inner surface, and the light carrying coded information. The examiner report says many answers explained the physics but never linked it to carrying a signal, which lost the third mark. 0625/41/O/N/22 Q6(b)(ii) · October/November 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: The red light travels through the plastic and hits the straight edge of the block at its midpoint M. Fig. 6.1 shows that some of the light is reflected and that some light travels in the air along the straight edge of the plastic block. The speed of light in air is 3.0 × 10 8 m / s. At M, the angle between the red light in the plastic and the normal is 37°. Calculate the speed of the red light in the plastic. The light leaves along the edge, so the angle of refraction is 90° and 37° is the critical angle. n = 1 ÷ sin c = 1 ÷ sin 37° = 1.66 n = c ÷ v , so v = c ÷ n v = 3.0 × 10 8 ÷ 1.66 v = 1.8 × 10 8 m/s Why this scores Marks for n = 1 ÷ sin c, for n ≈ 1.7, for v = c ÷ n, and for the final answer with unit. The key step is spotting that light grazing along the edge means 37° is the critical angle; the examiner report says students who found n usually went on to full marks. 3.2.3 Thin Lenses and Dispersion These questions test exact definitions (principal focus, focal length, monochromatic, virtual image) and how a converging lens corrects long sight; examiners reward precise wording about what the rays of light do. What examiners keep seeing Defining monochromatic as “one colour” (not credited: say single frequency), and thinking long-sighted people cannot see distant objects (they cannot focus on near objects). 0625/41/M/J/25 Q5(c)(i) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: The ray of light is monochromatic red light with a wavelength of 680 nm in air. Define monochromatic. Light of a single frequency. Why this scores One mark for “single frequency” (single wavelength is also accepted). The examiner report says “light of a single colour” was the common answer that did not score. 0625/41/O/N/23 Q6(b) · October/November 2023 · [1 mark] Converging lenses can be used as magnifying glasses. State whether the image produced when a lens is used as a magnifying glass is real or virtual. Explain why. Virtual: the rays of light leaving the lens never actually meet; they only appear to come from the image, so it cannot be formed on a screen. Why this scores The single mark needs “virtual” and a reason. Saying “it is upright” or “it is enlarged” describes the image but does not explain why it is virtual. 0625/41/O/N/21 Q5(b) · October/November 2021 · [1 mark] State what is meant by focal length. The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus. Why this scores One mark for a distance between the two correct points. The examiner report says some students gave the distance from the focus to the principal axis, which makes no sense. 0625/41/O/N/21 Q5(a) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] Explain, in terms of the behaviour of light rays, what is meant by principal focus for a thin converging lens. Rays of light that travel parallel to the principal axis are refracted by the lens and all converge to one point on the axis on the other side of the lens. That point is the principal focus. Why this scores Full marks need the rays to be parallel (to the principal axis) and to meet at a point after passing through the lens . The examiner report says most answers were too vague, often describing where an image forms instead. 0625/41/M/J/24 Q4(c) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] Converging lenses are used in spectacles (glasses) to correct one problem with vision. State the name of the problem and explain how a converging lens is used to correct it. You may draw a diagram. Name of problem: long-sightedness . In a long-sighted eye, light from a near object is not bent enough, so it would focus behind the retina. The converging spectacle lens starts bending the rays inwards before they enter the eye, which shortens the overall focal length of the spectacle lens and eye lens together. The rays now meet on the retina, so a sharp image is formed. Figure: the converging spectacle lens starts bending the rays from a near object O inwards, so together with the eye lens they focus on the retina instead of behind it. Why this scores One mark for long-sightedness, one for the lens moving the image forward (shorter combined focal length) and one for the image focused on the retina. The examiner report says diagrams helped students gain credit, and the common error was thinking long sight means distant objects are blurred. 3.3 Electromagnetic Spectrum These questions test the uses and dangers of each region, why particular waves are chosen for communication, and v = fλ with EM waves at 3.0 × 10 8 m/s; examiners reward specific reasons, not properties every EM wave shares. What examiners keep seeing Giving a general property (“travels fast”, “uses total internal reflection”) as the reason a wave is chosen, and not converting GHz to Hz (× 10 9 ) in calculations. 0625/42/M/J/25 Q5(b)(i) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Bluetooth is used to connect a mobile (cell) phone to headphones. State the name of the region of the electromagnetic spectrum used by Bluetooth. Radio waves. Why this scores One mark. The examiner report lists ultraviolet, infrared and ultrasound as the wrong answers seen; ultrasound is not part of the EM spectrum at all. 0625/43/O/N/20 Q7(a) · October/November 2020 · [2 marks] State two uses for infrared radiation. 1. Thermal imaging cameras. 2. Remote controls for televisions. Why this scores One mark per correct use, with no extra detail needed. The examiner report says medical uses were wrong here because students mixed infrared up with X-rays or gamma rays. 0625/41/M/J/23 Q6(b) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: A mobile phone (cell phone) network uses microwaves of frequency 1.9 × 10 9 Hz to transmit and receive signals. State two reasons why microwaves are used for mobile phone (cell phone) signals. 1. Microwaves can pass through the walls of buildings, so phones work indoors. 2. Their short wavelength means only a short aerial is needed, so it fits inside a small phone. Why this scores These are the two reasons the syllabus names, one mark each. The examiner report says “long wavelength, low frequency” or general EM properties did not score, because they do not explain why microwaves are chosen over other waves. 0625/43/M/J/23 Q5(a)(ii) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: Two types of electromagnetic radiation are used in glass optical fibres for high-speed broadband. Give two reasons why these two types of electromagnetic radiation are used in glass optical fibres for high-speed broadband. (The two types are visible light and infrared.) 1. Glass is transparent to visible light and infrared, so very little of the signal is absorbed along the fibre. 2. They can carry data at a very high rate, which high-speed broadband needs. Why this scores One mark for transparency of glass to these waves, one for carrying a high rate of data. The examiner report says “they travel quickly” and “they are totally internally reflected” were not credited. 0625/42/O/N/23 Q7(c)(i) · October/November 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: A Bluetooth headset can be used to listen to music on a mobile (cell) phone without the need for wires to connect the headset to the phone. The headset uses frequencies in the range 2.40–2.48 GHz. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves when the frequency is in the middle of the frequency range. Middle frequency = (2.40 + 2.48) ÷ 2 = 2.44 GHz = 2.44 × 10 9 Hz v = f λ, so λ = v ÷ f λ = 3.0 × 10 8 ÷ 2.44 × 10 9 λ = 0.12 m Why this scores Marks for the mid-point 2.44 GHz, for λ = v ÷ f with the right numbers, and for 0.12 m. The examiner report says many lost the last mark by not converting GHz to Hz or leaving out the unit. 0625/43/O/N/20 Q7(b) · October/November 2020 · [3 marks] X-rays are used in hospitals to help treat patients. Suggest and explain three precautions for the safe use of X-rays. 1. The radiographer stands behind a lead screen or leaves the room, because lead absorbs X-rays and staff would otherwise receive a dose every day. 2. Parts of the patient’s body that are not being treated are covered with a lead apron, which absorbs the X-rays so healthy cells are not exposed. 3. The exposure time is kept as short as possible and the number of X-rays limited, to keep the patient’s total dose, and so the risk of cell damage and cancer, low. Why this scores Each mark needs a precaution and its reason (absorbs radiation, reduces intensity or limits dose). The examiner report says many students listed sensible precautions but gave no explanation, or described precautions for handling radioactive samples instead. 3.4 Sound These questions test definitions (ultrasound, compression, rarefaction), v = fλ and echo timing, and describing a practical method; examiners reward 20 kHz stated as a number, the doubled distance in echo questions and named measuring instruments. What examiners keep seeing Forgetting that an echo travels there and back, and describing a speed-of-sound experiment without saying how the distance is measured (a metre rule is not suitable for a long distance). 0625/43/M/J/25 Q6(a) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Define the term ultrasound. Sound with a frequency higher than 20 kHz. Why this scores One mark, and the number is needed. The examiner report says “high-frequency sound” without 20 kHz, or giving a use of ultrasound, did not score. 0625/41/M/J/20 Q6(a) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Source material: The speed of sound in air is 340 m / s. Calculate the range of wavelengths for sounds that are audible by a healthy human ear. Human hearing: 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. λ = v ÷ f Highest frequency: λ = 340 ÷ 20 000 = 0.017 m Lowest frequency: λ = 340 ÷ 20 = 17 m Wavelengths range from 0.017 m to 17 m Why this scores One mark for using λ = v ÷ f with a hearing-range limit, one for both values. You must recall 20 Hz to 20 kHz yourself: it is not given. The highest frequency gives the shortest wavelength. 0625/43/O/N/20 Q6(a) · October/November 2020 · [3 marks] Sound waves consist of compressions and rarefactions. Explain the terms compression and rarefaction. Give your explanation in terms of the spacing of molecules and the pressure for sound waves in air. Compression: a region where the air molecules are closer together than normal, so the pressure is higher than normal. Rarefaction: a region where the air molecules are further apart than normal, so the pressure is lower than normal. Why this scores One mark for each spacing statement and one for the pair of pressure statements. The examiner report says vague wording (“more compact”, “more molecules”) or leaving out pressure lost marks. 0625/42/O/N/24 Q8(b) · October/November 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: A fisherman uses high frequency sound waves to locate fish in the sea. High frequency sound waves travel from the boat through the sea water. The speed of sound in water is 1500 m / s. The seabed is 22 m below the boat. Calculate the time taken for the boat to receive the reflected wave from the seabed after the sound is emitted. Distance travelled = there and back = 2 × 22 = 44 m v = s ÷ t , so t = s ÷ v t = 44 ÷ 1500 t = 0.029 s Why this scores One mark for doubling the distance to 44 m, one for t = s ÷ v and one for 0.029 s. Using 22 m gives 0.015 s, which loses the first and last marks. 0625/43/M/J/25 Q6(c)(i) · May/June 2025 · [3 marks] Source material: Ultrasound is used to locate objects below the surface of the sea. Describe how ultrasound is used to locate an object below the surface of the sea. You may draw a labelled diagram as part of your answer. A pulse of ultrasound is sent down into the water from a transmitter on a ship. It reflects off the object and the echo is picked up by a receiver on the ship. The time between sending the pulse and receiving the echo is measured. Depth of the object = speed of sound in water × time ÷ 2 (the pulse travels there and back). Figure: the pulse travels down to the object and the echo travels back up, so the distance to the object is speed × time ÷ 2. Why this scores One mark each for the reflection from the object, measuring the time for the pulse to go and return, and using speed × time to find the distance. The examiner report says the clearest answers used a labelled diagram, and weaker ones never mentioned reflection. 0625/43/O/N/21 Q6(a) · October/November 2021 · [5 marks] Describe an experiment to determine the speed of sound in air. State the apparatus you need, details of how to take measurements and how to calculate the speed of sound in air. You may use the space below to draw a labelled diagram as part of your answer. Apparatus: a starting pistol (or two wooden blocks to bang together), a trundle wheel or long tape measure, and a stopwatch. Distance: two students stand on a large open field. Measure the distance between them with the trundle wheel, e.g. 400 m. Time: student A fires the pistol (or bangs the blocks above their head). Student B starts the stopwatch on seeing the smoke (or the blocks hitting) and stops it on hearing the bang. Light arrives almost instantly, so this is the time for the sound. Repeat several times and take the mean time. Calculation: speed of sound = distance ÷ mean time, e.g. 400 m ÷ 1.2 s ≈ 330 m/s. Why this scores Five marks: how the sound is made, suitable apparatus (including a distance-measuring device), how the distance is measured, exactly when the stopwatch starts and stops, and speed = distance ÷ time. The examiner report says students often forgot to name a distance-measuring device; with an echo method, remember to double the distance. x: Topical Past Papers · Topic 4 Past Paper Questions: Electricity and Magnetism 46 real Cambridge IGCSE Physics Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0625/42/M/J/24 Q2(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 4.1 Simple Magnetism · 4.2.1 Charge, Current and Resistance · 4.2.5 Electrical Energy and Power · 4.3 Electric Circuits · 4.4 Electrical Safety · 4.5.1 Electromagnetic Induction and the a.c. Generator · 4.5.3 Magnetic Effect of a Current and the Motor Effect · 4.5.6 Transformers 4.1 Simple Magnetism These questions test precise definitions (magnetic field, field direction), the difference between magnetic and non-magnetic materials, and choosing iron or steel for a job; examiners reward exact wording such as “region”, “force on a north pole” and “repulsion”. What examiners keep seeing Defining a magnetic field as “the area around a magnet” with no mention of a force on a pole, and mixing up magnetic and electric fields (“force on a positive charge”). In material questions, many choose iron for a permanent magnet because it is “easy to magnetise”: permanent magnets need steel. 0625/42/O/N/25 Q8(a) · October/November 2025 · [1 mark] State what is meant by a magnetic field. A magnetic field is a region in which a magnetic pole (or magnetic material) experiences a force . Why this scores One mark for the full idea: a region and a force on a magnetic pole. The examiner report notes that “the area around a magnet” or “where an object feels a force” (object not described as magnetic) is not enough. 0625/42/M/J/23 Q8(a)(ii) · May/June 2023 · [1 mark] Define the direction of a magnetic field. The direction of a magnetic field at a point is the direction of the force on a north pole placed at that point. Why this scores One mark for “direction of the force on a N pole”. Common wrong answers were “the direction of the force on a positive charge” (that is an electric field) and “towards the N pole” (field lines point away from N, towards S). 0625/41/M/J/25 Q6(a) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Fig. 6.1 shows a person using a magnetic window cleaner. The part on the outside of the window is attracted to the inside part through the glass window. Glass is not a magnetic material. State the difference between magnetic and non-magnetic materials. A magnetic material (such as iron, steel, nickel or cobalt) is attracted by a magnet (it experiences a force in a magnetic field); a non-magnetic material such as glass is not attracted and feels no force. Why this scores One mark for linking magnetic materials to being attracted by a magnet / feeling a force in a magnetic field. The examiner report warns against confusing a magnetic material with a magnet , and against talking about delocalised electrons. 0625/41/M/J/25 Q6(b) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Each part of the window cleaner contains two magnets. Suggest a suitable material for the magnets in the window cleaner. Explain your answer. Steel , because it makes a permanent magnet : once magnetised it stays magnetised, so the two parts keep attracting each other through the glass. Why this scores One mark for steel with the reason that it stays magnetised. The examiner report says many chose iron (“easy to magnetise”), which misses that this needs a permanent magnet, and “steel is strong” earned nothing. 0625/41/M/J/20 Q7(a)(ii) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Source material: An electromagnet consists of a solenoid X that is made of copper wire. The solenoid contains an iron core. Explain why: iron is a suitable material for the core of an electromagnet. Iron is a magnetic material that is easily magnetised by the field of the solenoid, so it makes the magnetic field much stronger. It is a temporary (soft) magnetic material, so it loses its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off and the electromagnet can be turned off. Why this scores One mark for “magnetic / easily magnetised” and one for “temporary / easily demagnetised”. Both ideas are needed: a steel core would be magnetised too, but it would stay magnetised after the current stops. 0625/42/M/J/24 Q7(a) · May/June 2024 · [4 marks] Fig. 7.1 shows three bars of steel, A, B and C. A student is given the three pieces of steel. Two of the pieces are magnetised and one piece is unmagnetised. Describe and explain how the student determines which piece is unmagnetised using only the three pieces of steel. Bring one end of bar A close to one end of bar B, then turn one bar round and test the other end, watching each time for attraction or repulsion . Repeat the same tests with A and C, and with B and C. Only two magnets can repel each other, so the pair that repels at some point are the two magnetised bars. The bar that only ever attracts (at both of its ends, with both other bars) and never repels is the unmagnetised one, because a magnet attracts any magnetic material. Why this scores One mark for bringing ends together, one for looking for attraction/repulsion and testing different ends, and two for repeating with the other pairs and using “repulsion only happens between two magnets”. The examiner report says the key word is repulsion ; vague answers such as “see which one sticks” lost marks. 4.2.1 Charge, Current and Resistance These questions test definitions (electric field, e.m.f.), charging by friction in terms of electron transfer, and the equations Q = It , E = QV and R = V / I , including how resistance depends on length and cross-sectional area; examiners reward correct unit conversions (ns, minutes, MJ) and answers with units. What examiners keep seeing Describing charging by friction as a movement of positive charges or ions: only electrons move. In calculations, the most common slips are not converting prefixes (ns → s, MJ → J, minutes → s) and leaving out the unit. 0625/41/M/J/24 Q6(a)(i) · May/June 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: The sphere is negatively charged. The charge on the sphere produces an electric field in the surroundings. State what is meant by ‘electric field’. An electric field is a region in which an electric charge experiences a force . Why this scores One mark for a region where a charge feels a force. The examiner report says “a region where any object experiences a force” or “the region around a charged object” was not enough. 0625/41/O/N/20 Q8(a) · October/November 2020 · [2 marks] Explain what is meant by electromotive force (e.m.f.). The e.m.f. of a source (cell, battery or power supply) is the energy it supplies (the electrical work it does) per unit charge in driving the charge around a complete circuit . Why this scores One mark for linking e.m.f. to the source driving charge round the circuit, one for “energy (work done) per unit charge”. “The voltage of a battery” scores nothing; learn the syllabus definition word for word. 0625/42/M/J/25 Q7(b)(i) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: A plastic rod is rubbed with a cloth. The plastic rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth becomes positively charged. Explain why. Friction between the cloth and the rod makes electrons move from one material to the other. Electrons are transferred from the cloth to the rod , so the rod gains extra electrons (negative) and the cloth is left with fewer electrons than protons (positive). Why this scores Two marks: electrons move, and they move from the cloth to the rod. The examiner report says answers lost credit by talking about positive charges or ions moving: protons never move when you rub an insulator. 0625/42/M/J/20 Q9(c) · May/June 2020 · [3 marks] There is a current of 3.0 A in a copper wire. Calculate how many electrons pass through the copper wire every 60 s. The charge on an electron is 1.6 × 10 –19 C. Q = It = 3.0 × 60 = 180 C number of electrons = total charge ÷ charge on one electron = 180 ÷ (1.6 × 10 −19 ) = 1.1 × 10 21 electrons Why this scores One mark for Q = It , one for 180 C, one for dividing by the electron charge to get 1.1 × 10 21 . Two steps are needed: find the charge first, then count how many electron charges make it up. 0625/42/O/N/21 Q8(b) · October/November 2021 · [3 marks] There is a current in a wire of 0.65 mA for 2.2 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows. Q = It Q = 0.65 × 10 −3 A × (2.2 × 60) s = 0.65 × 10 −3 × 132 Q = 0.086 C Why this scores One mark for Q = It , one for substituting in amps and seconds, one for 0.086 C. Both conversions matter: mA → A (× 10 −3 ) and minutes → seconds (× 60); missing either gives an answer out by a factor of 60 or 1000. 0625/41/O/N/23 Q8(b) · October/November 2023 · [4 marks] Source material: Fig. 8.2 shows that the circuit also includes a battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 9.0 V and a resistor P. The resistance of P is 4.0 Ω. The current in P is 1.5 A. … the magnitude X of the charge that flows through P in 600 s The cylinder is removed from the circuit and replaced with a new cylinder made of the same modelling clay. The new cylinder is twice the length and has half the cross-sectional area of the first cylinder. Calculate the time that it now takes for a charge of magnitude X to flow through resistor P. First cylinder: total R = V ÷ I = 9.0 ÷ 1.5 = 6.0 Ω, so R cylinder = 6.0 − 4.0 = 2.0 Ω X = It = 1.5 × 600 = 900 C Resistance ∝ length, so twice the length doubles R ; resistance ∝ 1/area, so half the area doubles it again. New R cylinder = 4 × 2.0 = 8.0 Ω New total resistance = 8.0 + 4.0 = 12 Ω New current I = 9.0 ÷ 12 = 0.75 A t = Q ÷ I = 900 ÷ 0.75 = 1200 s Why this scores Marks for R ∝ length, R ∝ 1/area, the new cylinder resistance (4 × 2.0 = 8.0 Ω) and the final 1200 s. The examiner report says most found 8.0 Ω but forgot to add P’s 4.0 Ω before working out the new current. 4.2.5 Electrical Energy and Power These questions test P = IV , P = I 2 R and E = IVt = Pt , the kilowatt-hour and the cost of electricity; examiners reward matching units (kW with h for kWh, W with s for J) and clear working in “show that” questions. What examiners keep seeing Mixing units: multiplying watts by hours and calling it kWh, or forgetting that 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10 6 J. The examiner reports single out the missing W → kW conversion more than any other error. 0625/42/M/J/25 Q7(c)(i) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Define the kilowatt-hour (kW h) in words. One kilowatt-hour is the energy transferred by a device working at a power of 1 kW for one hour . Why this scores One mark for energy transferred at a rate of 1 kW for 1 hour. The examiner report says answers that left out energy , or just said “kilowatts times hours”, did not score. 0625/43/O/N/21 Q8(b)(i) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: An electric iron has a power of 2400 W. The potential difference (p.d.) of the mains supply is 220 V. Calculate the electric current in the iron. P = IV , so I = P ÷ V = 2400 ÷ 220 I = 11 A Why this scores One mark for P = IV rearranged, one for 11 A. Give 2 s.f. to match the data (10.9 rounds to 11). 0625/43/M/J/23 Q6(c) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] The 2500 W heater is used in a country where electricity costs 0.30 dollars per kilowatt-hour. Calculate the cost of using the heater continuously for two days. Energy E = Pt = 2.5 kW × (2 × 24 h) = 2.5 × 48 = 120 kWh Cost = 120 × 0.30 = 36 dollars Why this scores One mark for E = Pt with energy × price per kWh, one for $36. The examiner report says weaker answers lost the mark by not converting 2500 W to 2.5 kW (giving 36 000 dollars). 0625/43/M/J/25 Q9(b) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] The power lost in a cable is 1.25 × 10 –3 W. The resistance of the cable is 0.050 Ω. Calculate the current in the cable. P = I 2 R , so I 2 = P ÷ R = 1.25 × 10 −3 ÷ 0.050 = 0.025 I = √0.025 = 0.16 A Why this scores One mark for P = I 2 R , one for 0.16 A. The examiner report notes some candidates gave I 2 (0.025) as the answer: remember the square root. 0625/43/M/J/24 Q9(b)(ii) · May/June 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: The maximum energy stored in the battery of the mobile phone is 0.012 kW h. The charging plate in Fig. 9.1 has a useful output power of 15 W. The phone manufacturer claims that the battery can be charged to 50% capacity in less than 30 minutes. Show that this claim is true. Maximum energy = 0.012 kWh = 0.012 × 1000 W × 3600 s = 4.32 × 10 4 J Energy for 50% = 4.32 × 10 4 ÷ 2 = 2.16 × 10 4 J P = E ÷ t , so t = E ÷ P = 2.16 × 10 4 ÷ 15 = 1440 s ≈ 24 minutes 24 minutes is less than 30 minutes, so the claim is true. Why this scores One mark for the energy needed for 50%, one for using t = E / P , one for the comparison with 30 minutes. In “show that” questions the final comparison sentence is a mark in itself; the examiner report says many candidates did not attempt this part. 0625/41/M/J/20 Q8(b)(ii) · May/June 2020 · [3 marks] Source material: The power supply used in an electric vehicle contains 990 rechargeable cells each of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 1.2 V. When in use, each pack supplies a current of 3.5 A. The packs are connected in parallel to supply a large current to drive the electric vehicle. Explain why it is necessary to use thick wires to carry this current. A thicker wire has a larger cross-sectional area, so it has a smaller resistance . The power wasted in the wire is P = I 2 R , so with a large current a small resistance means less thermal energy is generated in the wires. This makes the system more efficient and stops the wires overheating, which could melt the insulation or start a fire . Why this scores One mark each for smaller resistance, less heating in the wires, and a consequence (more efficient / less fire risk). Each point builds on the one before, so write them in order. 4.3 Electric Circuits These questions test drawing circuits with correct symbols, series and parallel rules (combined resistance, why lights are wired in parallel) and how potential dividers with LDRs and thermistors respond to changes; examiners reward correct symbols and explanations that link resistance to the share of the p.d. What examiners keep seeing For parallel resistors, working out 1/ R and forgetting to take the reciprocal. In potential-divider explanations, stating the change without the reason: say that the fixed e.m.f. is shared in the ratio of the resistances. 0625/43/M/J/24 Q2(b) · May/June 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: Fig. 2.1 shows solar-powered traffic warning lights. The two lights in Fig. 2.1 are connected in parallel. State one advantage of a parallel connection in a lighting circuit. If one lamp breaks, the other lamp stays lit , because its own branch of the circuit is still complete. Why this scores One mark for one lamp still working if the other fails (each lamp getting the full p.d. was also accepted). The examiner report says “both lamps get the same voltage” is true but is not an advantage. 0625/42/O/N/25 Q7(a) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: A circuit consists of an a.c. supply and two lamps. The lamps are connected in parallel. Draw the circuit diagram. See the diagram: an a.c. supply symbol (circle with a wave) and two lamp symbols (circle with a cross), each lamp on its own branch between the same two junctions. Figure: an a.c. supply with two lamps in parallel. Each lamp has its own branch between the two junctions. Why this scores One mark for the correct a.c. supply and lamp symbols, one for the lamps clearly in parallel. Use a ruler, close every gap in the wires and do not use a d.c. cell symbol for an a.c. supply. 0625/42/M/J/22 Q9(b) · May/June 2022 · [3 marks] Two resistors of resistance 2.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate the combined resistance of the resistors in this arrangement. 1/ R = 1/ R 1 + 1/ R 2 = 1/2.0 + 1/3.0 = 5/6 R = 6/5 = 1.2 Ω Why this scores One mark for the parallel formula, one for the substitution, one for 1.2 Ω. The examiner report says some wrote R = 1/ R 1 + 1/ R 2 or forgot the final reciprocal. Check: the combined resistance must be less than the smallest resistor (2.0 Ω). 0625/41/O/N/24 Q6(c)(ii) · October/November 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: A potential divider is made by connecting a light-dependent resistor (LDR) and a thermistor in series. The voltmeter measures the potential difference (p.d.) across the LDR. The resistance of the LDR decreases and the resistance of the thermistor increases. Explain what happens to the reading on the voltmeter. The voltmeter reading decreases . The e.m.f. of the supply is constant and is shared between the LDR and the thermistor in the ratio of their resistances. The LDR’s resistance is now a smaller proportion of the total resistance , so it takes a smaller share of the p.d. Why this scores One mark for “decreases” and two for the reasoning: constant e.m.f., and the LDR having a smaller fraction of the total resistance and so a smaller fraction of the p.d. Saying only “its resistance falls so the voltage falls” misses the sharing idea. 0625/42/M/J/20 Q8(a) · May/June 2020 · [4 marks] A light-emitting diode (LED) is a diode that emits light when there is a current in it. Draw a circuit diagram showing an LED, connected so that it is lit, in series with a battery and a fixed resistor. Use standard electrical symbols. See the diagram: a battery, a fixed resistor (rectangle) and an LED (diode symbol with two arrows pointing outwards) in one loop. The LED is forward-biased : its triangle points in the direction of the conventional current, away from the positive (long) plate of the battery and round towards the negative terminal. Figure: battery, fixed resistor and LED in series. The LED triangle points the same way as the conventional current (from + round to −), so it is forward-biased and lights. Why this scores Marks for correct symbols for the LED, resistor and battery, all in one series loop, and one mark for the LED the right way round. A diode only conducts one way, so an LED drawn backwards will not light and loses that mark. 4.4 Electrical Safety These questions test exactly how fuses, circuit breakers and the earth wire protect people and wiring; examiners reward the full chain fault → large current → fuse melts or breaker trips → circuit broken, and a fuse rating just above the normal current. What examiners keep seeing Vague phrases such as “electricity goes to earth” or “the earth wire prevents shocks” earn nothing on their own: name the current, its path to earth and the fuse melting. Do not mix up the earth wire (protects the user) with the fuse (protects the wiring from overheating). 0625/42/F/M/25 Q3(c) · February/March 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Fig. 3.1 shows a mains electric heater used to heat a small room. The metal outer casing of the heater is earthed. State why this is an important safety feature. If a fault makes the live wire touch the metal casing, the current flows to earth through the earth wire instead of through a person, so the user does not get an electric shock. Why this scores One mark for linking the earth wire to preventing a shock when the casing becomes live. The examiner report notes many answers confused the earth wire with the fuse and wrote about overheating or fires. 0625/43/O/N/21 Q8(b)(iii) · October/November 2021 · [1 mark] Source material: An electric iron has a power of 2400 W. The potential difference (p.d.) of the mains supply is 220 V. Fuse ratings of 3 A, 5 A, 10 A, 13 A and 30 A are available. State which of these fuse ratings is suitable for use in the iron. I = P ÷ V = 2400 ÷ 220 = 10.9 A 13 A (the smallest rating above the normal current) Why this scores One mark for 13 A. A quick I = P / V check shows 10 A would melt in normal use, while 30 A would not protect the cable. 0625/42/O/N/20 Q8(b) · October/November 2020 · [2 marks] State and explain why fuses and circuit breakers are installed in electrical circuits connected to the mains supply. They protect the wiring and the user: a fault that causes too large a current could make the cables overheat and start a fire, or give someone a shock. When the current rises above the rating, the fuse wire melts (or the circuit breaker trips open), breaking the circuit and cutting off the current. Why this scores One mark for what they protect against (overheating, fire, shock) and one for how: excess current makes the fuse melt or the breaker open. The examiner report warns against the idea that fuses “control” the normal current; they only act when it is too large. 0625/41/M/J/25 Q4(b)(ii) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: The power of the heater is 2.0 kW when it is connected to the mains supply with an e.m.f. of 230 V. The plug connecting the heater to the mains supply is fitted with a fuse. Fuse ratings of 3 A, 5 A, 10 A and 13 A are available. State which fuse is used. Explain your answer. Normal current: I = P ÷ V = 2000 ÷ 230 = 8.7 A Fuse: 10 A 10 A is just above the normal current of 8.7 A, so the fuse does not melt when the heater works normally, but it melts quickly if a fault makes the current rise. A 3 A or 5 A fuse would melt straight away; a 13 A fuse could let a dangerous current flow without melting. Why this scores One mark for 10 A and one for a reason, such as the rating being just above the normal current. The examiner report credited answers that said why the other fuses were unsuitable; weaker answers showed misconceptions about how fuses work. 0625/42/M/J/20 Q7(b) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Another transformer is used in a school laboratory to step down a mains supply with a p.d. of 110 V to 12 V. This transformer is mounted in a metal case. State and explain an essential safety feature required for this arrangement. The metal case must be earthed (connected to the earth wire). If a wire comes loose or the insulation fails so that the live wire touches the case, a large current flows to earth and blows the fuse, so the case does not stay live and nobody touching it gets a shock. Why this scores One mark for “metal case earthed” and one for the fault it guards against: a loose wire or failed insulation making the case live. 0625/41/M/J/22 Q5(c) · May/June 2022 · [3 marks] Source material: Cold water passes over an electric immersion heater inside the tap. The metal tap is earthed and there is a fuse in the cable that connects the heater to the mains. 1. Explain how the earth wire protects the user. 2. Explain how the fuse protects the circuit. 1. If a fault makes the live wire touch the metal tap, the earth wire gives a low-resistance path, so a large current flows to earth instead of through the user. 2. This large current is bigger than the fuse rating, so the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, cutting off the supply before the cable overheats. Why this scores Three marks: the tap becoming live, a current in the earth wire, and the large current making the fuse melt and break the circuit. The examiner report says “electricity is directed to earth” and “the earth wire prevents electric shock” were too vague for credit. 4.5.1 Electromagnetic Induction and the a.c. Generator These questions test electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field, or a conductor cutting field lines, induces an e.m.f. whose size depends on how fast the change happens; examiners reward “cuts the magnetic field”, “induced e.m.f.” and Lenz’s law for the direction. What examiners keep seeing Confusing a generator with a motor: split-ring commutators or “increase the current” score nothing in a generator question. In Lenz’s law questions, copper is not a magnetic material; it is the induced current’s magnetic field that opposes the motion. 0625/42/M/J/25 Q8(a)(ii) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Fig. 8.1 shows a simplified diagram of an a.c. generator. Explain why an electromotive force (e.m.f.) is only induced when the coil is turning. Only when the coil turns do its wires cut the magnetic field lines of the magnet, so the field through the coil changes and an e.m.f. is induced. A stationary coil cuts no field lines. Why this scores One mark for the coil cutting the magnetic field. The examiner report notes answers about “cutting the electromagnetic field” or secondary coils confused generators with motors and transformers. 0625/43/O/N/25 Q7(a)(i) · October/November 2025 · [1 mark] Source material: Fig. 7.1 shows a simple a.c. generator. Explain the function of the slip rings and brushes. The slip rings turn with the coil and the brushes press against them, so there is a continuous connection between the rotating coil and the external circuit without the wires twisting. Why this scores One mark for a continuous connection to the external circuit (or wires not tangling). Do not say they reverse the current: that is the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor. 0625/41/M/J/21 Q7(a)(iii) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: Fig. 7.1 represents an alternating current (a.c.) generator. … A student rotates the handle H, as shown in Fig. 7.1. The student turns the handle more quickly. State two ways in which the e.m.f. between terminals X and Y changes. 1. The peak (maximum) e.m.f. is larger, because the coil cuts the field lines at a faster rate. 2. The e.m.f. changes direction more often: its frequency is higher. Why this scores One mark each for a larger peak e.m.f. and a higher frequency. The examiner report says many candidates gave only the first change; the second must be a different change, not the same idea reworded. 0625/41/M/J/22 Q8(b)(ii) · May/June 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: The magnet is then held at the top of the copper tube and released. As it falls through the copper tube, an electric current is generated in the copper. The current in the copper produces a magnetic field of its own in the tube. The magnet falls much more slowly in the copper tube than in the plastic tube. Explain why the magnet falls more slowly in the copper tube. The magnetic field of the induced current opposes the change that produces it (Lenz’s law), so it opposes the motion of the falling magnet. This gives an upward force on the magnet, which reduces the resultant downward force, so the magnet falls more slowly. Why this scores One mark for an upward (opposing) force on the magnet and one for the induced current’s field opposing the motion. The examiner report says many candidates wrongly called copper a magnetic material. 0625/42/O/N/25 Q8(b)(ii) · October/November 2025 · [3 marks] Source material: The trolley travels back from left to right. It has a lower maximum speed when it travels from left to right. … A magnet is fixed to the trolley. Fig. 8.2 shows a close-up view of the ammeter. As the trolley enters the coil moving from right to left, the ammeter needle deflects to the left and then returns to zero. State and explain any changes to the deflection on the ammeter as the trolley enters the coil when moving back from left to right. The needle still deflects to the left : the trolley now enters the other end of the coil with the other pole leading, and these two reversals cancel, so the induced current is in the same direction. The deflection is smaller , because the trolley moves more slowly, so the magnetic field through the coil changes at a lower rate and a smaller e.m.f. and current are induced. Why this scores Three marks from: no change of direction, a smaller deflection, and the reason (smaller rate of change of field, so smaller induced e.m.f.). Linking “slower” to “smaller rate of change” is the key step. 0625/43/M/J/22 Q9(a)(i) · May/June 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: Fig. 9.1 shows a magnet on the end of a spring and a coil of wire connected to a sensitive centre-zero galvanometer. The magnet can move freely through the coil. The magnet is pulled down and released. Describe and explain what happens to the needle of the sensitive galvanometer. As the magnet moves in and out of the coil, the magnetic field through the coil changes (the coil cuts the field lines). This changing field induces an e.m.f., so a current flows through the galvanometer and the needle deflects. When the magnet moves up the induced current flows one way; when it moves down the current reverses, so the needle swings from side to side about zero as the magnet bounces. The induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the motion of the magnet, so the oscillations, and the deflections, gradually die away. Why this scores Four marks from: the needle oscillates, the field through the coil changes, the changing field induces a current, and the induced current opposes the motion. The examiner report notes some candidates treated the needle as a compass pointing north. 4.5.3 Magnetic Effect of a Current and the Motor Effect These questions test the magnetic field around a current and the force on a current (or moving charges) in a magnetic field; examiners reward precise words such as “the force reverses” and a clear link from current to force to turning effect. What examiners keep seeing Writing that a force or field “changes” is ambiguous: say it reverses, increases or decreases. “Turning effect” means the moment, not how fast the coil spins, so “it spins slower” earns nothing. 0625/43/O/N/23 Q8(a)(iii) · October/November 2023 · [1 mark] Source material: Fig. 8.1 shows the single turn coil of a simple direct current (d.c.) motor. A third coil is identical to the coil in (i) except that its resistance is three times greater. The potential difference (p.d.) across the coil is the same as the p.d. in (i). State how the turning effect compares with the turning effect in (i). The turning effect is smaller (about one third): with the same p.d. and three times the resistance the current is a third as big ( I = V / R ), so the forces on the sides of the coil are smaller. Why this scores One mark for “less”. The examiner report says “slower” or “less current” on its own was not accepted: the question is about the turning effect (moment). 0625/42/F/M/24 Q8(a)(ii) · February/March 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Fig. 8.1 shows a wire carrying a large current. The current in the wire increases and the direction of the current is reversed. State how these changes affect the magnetic field. The magnetic field becomes stronger at each distance from the wire. The direction of the field reverses : the circular field lines point the opposite way round the wire. Why this scores One mark for “stronger” and one for “reverses”. The examiner report notes that “the direction changes” was not enough. 0625/43/O/N/21 Q10(b)(ii) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: The length of the wire between the two supports is in the magnetic field of a horseshoe magnet. … The power supply is switched on and the wire moves down. The power supply is switched off and the wire returns to its original position. The power supply is then switched on so that the current is in the opposite direction. State and explain what happens to the wire. The wire moves upwards . The magnetic field is unchanged but the current is reversed, so by Fleming’s left-hand rule the force on the wire is reversed and now acts upwards. Why this scores One mark for “moves up” and one for “reversing the current reverses the force”. The examiner report says just writing “Fleming’s left-hand rule”, or that the force “changes”, was not enough. 0625/42/O/N/24 Q9(a) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: The coil of wire is part of an electric circuit. … The charging plate is connected to an a.c. power supply. The power supply is turned on. Describe the magnetic field around the charging plate in terms of its magnitude and direction. Magnitude: the field is strongest close to the coil and weaker further away, and it keeps rising and falling because the current is alternating. Direction: the field reverses direction every half-cycle, each time the alternating current changes direction. Why this scores Two marks from: magnitude constantly changing, stronger closer to the coil, and the direction linked to the a.c. Answer both parts the question names (magnitude and direction). 0625/42/F/M/23 Q8(d) · February/March 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: Fig. 8.1 shows a horizontal, flat coil in a magnetic field … The coil is connected to a cell. The coil rotates. To operate as a motor, a split-ring commutator and brushes are added to the parts shown in Fig. 8.1. Explain the effects of the split-ring commutator and the brushes on the action of the motor. The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, as the coil passes the vertical position (at right angles to the field). This reverses the forces on the two sides of the coil, so the turning effect always acts the same way and the coil keeps rotating continuously in one direction. The brushes press on the rotating split ring, so current keeps flowing into the coil from the cell without the wires getting tangled. Why this scores One mark for “reverses the current” plus two from: every half turn, continuous rotation in the same direction, current maintained through the brushes. The examiner report notes weaker answers confused motors with generators. 4.5.6 Transformers Transformer questions mix one explanation (how a changing field in the core induces an e.m.f. in the secondary) with calculations using V p / V s = N p / N s , P = IV and P = I 2 R ; examiners reward the equation written first, then the substitution. What examiners keep seeing Writing “a current in the primary” without saying it is alternating , and thinking high-voltage transmission lowers the cables’ resistance: it lowers the current, which cuts the I 2 R losses. 0625/41/M/J/25 Q8(c)(ii) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: In power stations, transformers are used to step up the voltage of electricity generated before it is transmitted through cables over long distances. A power station generates electricity at 25 000 V. A transformer steps up the voltage to 300 000 V. The primary coil of the step-up transformer has 450 turns. Calculate the number of turns Ns on the secondary coil of the transformer. N s / N p = V s / V p N s = 450 × 300 000 ÷ 25 000 N s = 5400 turns Why this scores One mark for the turns-ratio equation, one for 5400. A step-up transformer must have more turns on the secondary: a quick sense check. 0625/41/M/J/23 Q8(b)(ii) · May/June 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: The transformer steps the supply voltage down from 220 000 V to 33 000 V. The electrical power transferred to the transformer by the high-voltage cable is 77 MW. Calculate the current in the primary coil. P = IV , so I = P ÷ V I = 77 × 10 6 W ÷ 220 000 V I = 350 A Why this scores One mark for P = IV , one for converting 77 MW to 77 × 10 6 W, one for 350 A. The examiner report says the commonest errors were the MW conversion and rearranging the equation; the primary voltage is the 220 000 V side. 0625/42/F/M/24 Q8(b) · February/March 2024 · [3 marks] Electricity is transmitted at high voltage. Explain why a high voltage increases the efficiency of transmission even with thinner wires. For the same power ( P = IV ), a high voltage means a much smaller current in the cables. Thinner wires have a higher resistance, but the power wasted as heat is P = I 2 R , which depends on the square of the current. So the drop in current cuts the losses far more than the extra resistance increases them: less energy is wasted and transmission is more efficient. Why this scores Three marks from: P = I 2 R , high voltage gives low current, thin wires have higher resistance, and the current has the bigger effect. The examiner report says few candidates quoted the power-loss equation or said thin wires have higher resistance. 0625/43/M/J/21 Q9(b) · May/June 2021 · [3 marks] Draw a labelled diagram of a step-down transformer. On the labels, state a suitable material for each of the components. Diagram as shown, with three labels: a closed soft-iron core; a primary coil of insulated copper wire with many turns, connected to the a.c. input; a secondary coil of insulated copper wire with fewer turns than the primary, connected to the output. Figure: a step-down transformer. The secondary has fewer turns than the primary. Why this scores One mark each for a (soft-)iron core, copper coils, and fewer turns on the secondary than the primary. The examiner report says you must label which coil is primary and which is secondary to get the last mark. 0625/41/M/J/23 Q8(a) · May/June 2023 · [4 marks] Source material: A transformer in the town has a soft-iron core. Explain the principle of operation of a simple iron-cored transformer. An alternating current in the primary coil produces a magnetic field that keeps changing in size and direction. The soft-iron core concentrates this changing field and carries it through the secondary coil. So the secondary coil sits in a changing magnetic field (its turns are cut by the changing field lines). This induces an alternating e.m.f. across the secondary coil. Why this scores Four marks, one per step: a.c. in the primary, changing magnetic field, the core transferring the field, and an e.m.f. induced in the secondary. The examiner report says “current in the primary” without “alternating” lost the first mark, and describing step-up and step-down did not answer the question. 0625/43/O/N/20 Q9(b) · October/November 2020 · [5 marks] A computer contains a transformer. The input voltage to the transformer is 240 V. The output voltage from the transformer is 20 V and the output current is 2.3 A. The efficiency of the transformer is 90%. Calculate the input current to the transformer. Output power: P = IV = 2.3 × 20 = 46 W Efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input, so input power = 46 ÷ 0.90 = 51 W Input current: I = P ÷ V = 51 ÷ 240 = 0.21 A Why this scores Five marks: the efficiency equation, P = IV , 46 W output, 51 W input and 0.21 A. The examiner report says weaker candidates mixed up input and output power or treated the transformer as 100% efficient; writing the efficiency equation first protects those marks. Topical Past Papers · Topic 5 Past Paper Questions: Nuclear Physics 18 real Cambridge IGCSE Physics Paper 4 (Extended Theory) questions from 2020–2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0625/42/M/J/24 Q2(b)(ii) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 5.1 The Nuclear Model of the Atom · 5.2.1 Radioactive Emissions and Decay · 5.2.3 Half-life 5.1 The Nuclear Model of the Atom These questions test the structure of the atom, the alpha-scattering evidence for the nucleus, isotopes and how fission and fusion work; examiners reward precise words such as “nucleus” (not “atom”) and links between each observation and its conclusion. What examiners keep seeing Writing “atom” or “element” when the mark needs “nucleus”: examiners only credit fission as a nucleus splitting, and alpha-scattering conclusions must be about the nucleus, not about atoms or electrons. 0625/42/F/M/24 Q9(a)(i) · February/March 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: An experiment directs alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold foil. Most of the alpha particles pass through the thin foil in a straight line. State the conclusion about atoms from this observation. Most of an atom is empty space . Why this scores One mark for “most of the atom is empty space”. The examiner report notes that “lots of empty space between atoms” earns nothing: the space is inside each atom. 0625/43/O/N/22 Q10(b)(i) · October/November 2022 · [2 marks] Describe what is meant by an isotope. Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons in the nucleus (so a different nucleon number). Why this scores One mark for the same number of protons and one for a different number of neutrons. Do not talk about gaining or losing electrons: that describes ions, which the examiners saw confused with isotopes. 0625/42/F/M/23 Q9(a)(i) · February/March 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: A nuclear power station has a reactor where controlled nuclear fission of uranium‑235 takes place. Explain what is meant by nuclear fission. A neutron is absorbed by a large, unstable nucleus such as uranium-235. The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, and two or three neutrons are also released. A large amount of energy is released (as kinetic energy of the products). Why this scores One mark each for the large unstable nucleus / neutron hitting it, the nucleus splitting into smaller nuclei, and the large energy release. The examiner report stresses that it must be a nucleus that splits, not an atom, isotope or element. 0625/41/M/J/22 Q10(b)(i) · May/June 2022 · [3 marks] Source material: In a nuclear fusion reactor, a nucleus of hydrogen-2 fuses with a nucleus of hydrogen-3 at an extremely high temperature. Explain why an extremely high temperature is needed when forcing these two nuclei together. Both nuclei are positively charged, so they repel each other strongly. To fuse, they must get extremely close together despite this repulsion. At an extremely high temperature the nuclei have very high kinetic energy (move very fast), enough to overcome the repulsion and collide. Why this scores Marks for high temperature giving high kinetic energy, the nuclei repelling, and the reason (both positive / must come very close). Many candidates wrongly said the energy was needed to “split” the hydrogen nuclei. 0625/42/F/M/24 Q9(a)(ii) · February/March 2024 · [4 marks] Source material: An experiment directs alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold foil. Some of the alpha particles are deflected through angles less than 90° and a few are deflected through 180°. State and explain two conclusions about the nuclei of atoms from this observation. Conclusion 1: the nucleus is positively charged. Explanation: alpha particles are positively charged, so they are deflected by a repulsive force when they pass close to the nucleus. Conclusion 2: the nucleus is very small. Explanation: only a very few alpha particles pass close enough to a nucleus to be deflected through large angles; most miss it. Why this scores Two marks for two conclusions about the nucleus and two for the matching explanations. Examiners penalised “like charges repel” without stating that alpha particles are positive, and answers about electrons deflecting the particles. 0625/42/O/N/21 Q11(a) · October/November 2021 · [4 marks] Describe the composition and structure of a neutral atom of beryllium-8, which has a proton number of 4 and a nucleon number of 8. The atom has a very small nucleus at its centre, with electrons orbiting around it. The nucleus contains 4 protons and 8 − 4 = 4 neutrons . The atom is neutral, so it has 4 electrons , the same as the number of protons. Why this scores One mark for the structure (small nucleus with orbiting electrons), one for protons and neutrons in the nucleus, and one each for 4 electrons and 4 neutrons. Weaker answers gave the numbers but forgot the structure that the question also asks for. 5.2.1 Radioactive Emissions and Decay These questions test background radiation, the properties of alpha, beta and gamma, how they behave in fields, decay equations and safe handling; examiners reward answers that link each property to the situation in the question. What examiners keep seeing Stating a fact without applying it, e.g. “alpha is stopped by paper” when the question asks about a plastic box, or naming a safety precaution without saying how it reduces the radiation received. 0625/42/M/J/25 Q9(a)(i) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] State what is meant by background radiation. Radiation that is always present in the environment, coming from natural sources such as radon gas, rocks and cosmic rays. Why this scores One mark for radiation that is always present / from natural sources. Examiners saw weaker candidates confuse it with half-life or with cosmic microwave background radiation. 0625/43/M/J/25 Q11(c) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] A different element decays by the emission of an alpha particle (α-particle). Give two reasons why α-particles are more strongly ionising than β-particles. An α-particle has a greater charge (+2) than a β-particle (−1). α-particles have greater kinetic energy than β-particles. Why this scores One mark per comparison. The examiner report says “energy” instead of kinetic energy, or “charge” without a comparison, was not enough. 0625/42/M/J/24 Q9(a)(i) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Radioactive isotopes that emit ionising radiation are used in hospitals. State and explain two safety precautions necessary for the use of these isotopes in medical procedures. 1 Staff stand behind lead or concrete shielding during the procedure, because the shielding absorbs the radiation before it reaches them. 2 Staff keep the time spent near the patient or source as short as possible, so less radiation is absorbed by their bodies. Why this scores Each mark needs a precaution AND its explanation. The examiner report notes that just saying it would “harm humans”, or describing school-laboratory rules, earned nothing. 0625/42/F/M/21 Q10(b) · February/March 2021 · [3 marks] A nucleus of strontium-90 consists of 38 protons and 52 neutrons. Strontium-90 is radioactive and decays by β-emission to an isotope of yttrium. The symbol for strontium is Sr and the symbol for yttrium is Y. Write down the nuclide equation of this decay. 90 38 Sr → 90 39 Y + 0 −1 β Check: top numbers 90 = 90 + 0; bottom numbers 38 = 39 + (−1). Why this scores One mark for nucleon number 90 on both sides, one for Sr 38 and Y 39, one for the β-particle written as 0 over −1. Common errors were using the neutron number (52) as the nucleon number and leaving the numbers off the β. 0625/41/O/N/20 Q7(c) · October/November 2020 · [3 marks] A beam consists of α-particles, β-particles and γ-rays. Explain how a uniform magnetic field may be used to separate the α-particles, the β-particles and the γ-rays. The beam is passed through the magnetic field at right angles to the field lines. α- and β-particles are charged, so they are deflected. They have opposite charges, so they bend in opposite directions ; the α-particles are deflected less because their mass is much greater. γ-rays are uncharged, so they are not deflected and carry straight on. Why this scores Marks for the charged parts of the beam deflecting, α and β deflecting in opposite directions (or α deflecting less), and γ not deflecting. Explaining in terms of penetration instead of charge in a field gets no credit. 0625/42/M/J/21 Q11(b) · May/June 2021 · [3 marks] The substance emits α-particles and γ-rays. The student suggests that it is safe to store the substance in a plastic container of thickness 2 mm. State and explain whether the student’s suggestion is correct. Statement: the suggestion is not correct. Explanation: 2 mm of plastic will absorb the α-particles, but γ-rays are highly penetrating and pass straight through it. The container should be lined with thick lead to reduce the γ-radiation escaping. Why this scores One mark for “incorrect”, one for γ passing through the plastic, one for extra detail (plastic stops α / lead needed). Link every point to the 2 mm plastic box, as the examiner report advises. 5.2.3 Half-life These questions test the definition of half-life, calculations over whole numbers of half-lives (with background correction) and choosing an isotope by its half-life; examiners reward clear step-by-step working. What examiners keep seeing Forgetting to subtract the background count before halving, and to add it back on at the end; also defining half-life as the time for the “mass” or “source” to halve instead of the number of nuclei or the activity. 0625/43/M/J/25 Q11(a) · May/June 2025 · [1 mark] Define the half-life of a radioactive source. The time taken for half of the nuclei in a sample of the isotope to decay. Why this scores One mark for half the nuclei decaying (or the activity halving). “The time for the mass to halve” or “the source to halve” was judged insufficient. 0625/42/F/M/21 Q10(c) · February/March 2021 · [2 marks] The half-life of radon-220 is 56 s. A sample of radon-220 is in a container. After 112 s the mass of radon-220 is 9.2 mg. Calculate the mass of the original sample. number of half-lives = 112 ÷ 56 = 2 original mass = 9.2 × 2 × 2 = 37 mg Why this scores One mark for 2 half-lives, one for 37 mg. The common wrong answer was 18.4 mg (multiplying by 2 only); there is no need to convert to grams. 0625/42/O/N/20 Q11(b)(i) · October/November 2020 · [2 marks] Source material: Radioactive tracers emitting γ-rays can be used in medicine. The half-life of the source of these γ-rays is 6 hours. Explain why a source of γ-rays used in this way should not have a half-life shorter or longer than about 6 hours. If the half-life were much shorter, the activity would fall too much before the tracer had time to spread round the body and the measurements were taken. If it were much longer, the tracer would stay radioactive inside the patient for a long time, increasing the dose and the risk of cell damage. Why this scores One mark for each end: too short gives too little time for the investigation, too long leaves the patient exposed for a long time. Examiners saw answers about therapy rather than tracing. 0625/42/F/M/24 Q9(b)(ii) · February/March 2024 · [3 marks] Source material: A source contains a radioactive isotope of strontium. This isotope decays by emission of β-particles. The half-life of this isotope is 29 years. The initial mass of this isotope of strontium in the source is 25 µg. Calculate the mass of the strontium isotope that decays in 87 years. number of half-lives = 87 ÷ 29 = 3 mass remaining = 25 ÷ 2 3 = 25 ÷ 8 = 3.1 µg mass decayed = 25 − 3.1 = 22 µg Why this scores Marks for 3 half-lives, for 1/8 remaining (3.125 µg) and for the final 22 µg. Read the question: it asks for the mass that has decayed , so subtract from 25. 0625/43/O/N/23 Q9(a)(ii) · October/November 2023 · [3 marks] Source material: For each application of radioactive isotopes, state and explain which type of radioactive emission is suitable and suggest an appropriate half-life for the isotope. measuring the thickness of aluminium strips produced in a factory Type of emission: beta. Explanation: some β-particles pass through the thin aluminium and some are absorbed, and the amount absorbed depends on the thickness, so the count rate changes when the thickness changes. (α would all be stopped; γ would nearly all pass through.) Half-life: several years (e.g. 30 years), so the count rate stays steady and the source does not need replacing often. Why this scores One mark each for beta, absorption depending on thickness, and a half-life in years. The examiner report says “long” or “big” is not enough, and many wrongly gave seconds or days. 0625/42/M/J/23 Q9(c) · May/June 2023 · [4 marks] A radiation detector used in a laboratory detects a background count rate of 30 counts / min. A radioactive source is placed in front of the radiation detector. The initial reading on the detector is 550 counts / min. The half-life of the source is 25 minutes. Calculate the expected reading on the detector after 75 minutes. count rate from the source = 550 − 30 = 520 counts/min number of half-lives = 75 ÷ 25 = 3 source count rate after 75 min = 520 ÷ 2 3 = 520 ÷ 8 = 65 counts/min reading on detector = 65 + 30 = 95 counts/min Why this scores Four marks: subtract background (520), 3 half-lives, 520 ÷ 8 = 65, then add the background back to get 95. Forgetting either the subtraction or the adding back was the most common mistake.
