Use them to see how a precise definition, a developed explanation, a chain of analysis and a balanced discussion each earn their marks.

Past paper (a) · [2 marks] State the formula used to calculate PED. PED = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price. Why this scores One mark for “percentage change in quantity demanded” on top and one for “percentage change in price” underneath. Writing “change in demand” or dropping the word “percentage” loses marks, as does putting the terms the wrong way up. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Past paper (b) · [4 marks] Explain two reasons why the price of sugar may fall. Increase in supply. A good harvest, caused by favourable weather or better fertilisers, raises the quantity of sugar cane produced at every price. The supply curve shifts to the right, so at the old price there is a surplus of sugar. Sellers cut the price to clear the excess stock, so the equilibrium price falls. Decrease in demand. Health campaigns warning about obesity and diabetes, or a sugar tax on soft drinks, change tastes away from sugary products. Demand for sugar falls at every price, shifting the demand curve to the left. This creates a surplus at the original price, and competition between sellers pushes the price down. Why this scores Two separate causes (one supply-side, one demand-side), each identified and then developed by explaining the shift and how the resulting surplus lowers price. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (b) · [4 marks] Explain two causes of a shift to the right in the demand curve for fish. A rise in the price of a substitute such as meat. If beef and chicken become more expensive, fish becomes relatively cheaper. Some consumers switch from meat to fish, so more fish is demanded at every price and the demand curve shifts right. A change in tastes in favour of fish. If reports show that eating oily fish is good for heart health, or consumers switch away from meat for environmental reasons, fish becomes more desirable. People are willing and able to buy more fish at each price, so demand increases and the curve shifts right. (Other creditworthy causes: a rise in incomes, as fish is a normal good; a fall in the price of a complement such as rice or chips; a rise in population; successful advertising.) Why this scores Each cause is a non-price determinant of demand (a change in price would cause a movement along the curve, not a shift) and each is explained in terms of more being demanded at every price. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (b) · [4 marks] Explain what effect more firms producing tyres would have on the PED of individual firms’ tyres. More firms producing tyres would make the demand for each individual firm’s tyres more price elastic. With more producers, consumers have a greater number of close substitutes to choose from. If one firm raises its price, buyers can easily switch to a rival’s similar tyres, so the firm would lose a large proportion of its sales. The percentage change in quantity demanded would be greater than the percentage change in price, so PED would rise (in absolute value) above 1. As a result, each firm has less power to raise prices and would be under pressure to keep prices low or to differentiate its tyres through branding or quality. Why this scores States the direction of change (more elastic), gives the reason (more substitutes), develops it (consumers switch, large fall in quantity demanded) and links it to the PED value and the firm’s pricing power. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (b) · [4 marks] Explain how market forces will eliminate a surplus and a shortage. Surplus. A surplus occurs when the price is above equilibrium, so quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. Sellers are left with unsold stock, so they lower their price. As the price falls, quantity demanded extends and quantity supplied contracts until the two are equal at the equilibrium price and the surplus disappears. Shortage. A shortage occurs when the price is below equilibrium, so quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. Consumers compete for the limited goods and sellers realise they can charge more, so the price rises. The higher price causes quantity demanded to contract and quantity supplied to extend until the market clears at equilibrium. Why this scores Defines each disequilibrium, explains the price movement and uses “extension” and “contraction” correctly to show how equilibrium is restored without government intervention. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (b) · [4 marks] Explain two ways a firm could increase the productivity of its workers. Training. The firm could provide on-the-job or off-the-job training. This improves workers’ skills and knowledge, so they work faster, make fewer mistakes and can operate more advanced equipment. Output per worker per hour therefore rises. Investing in better capital. The firm could buy more advanced machinery or technology, such as automated production lines or faster computers. Each worker then has more and better capital to work with, which allows them to produce more output in the same time, raising labour productivity. (Other valid ways: incentive schemes such as piece rates or bonuses, improving working conditions and motivation, better management and organisation of tasks through division of labour.) Why this scores Two distinct methods, each linked explicitly to higher output per worker, which is the definition of labour productivity. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Past paper (c) · [6 marks] Analyse, using a demand and supply diagram, the effect of an increase in demand for cars on the market for tyres. Figure: An increase in demand for tyres shifts D to D1, raising price from P to P1 and quantity from Q to Q1. Cars and tyres are complements (joint demand): every new car needs tyres, and more cars on the road means more replacement tyres are needed. So an increase in demand for cars leads to an increase in demand for tyres at every price. In the diagram the demand curve for tyres shifts to the right from D to D1. At the original price P there is now a shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Tyre buyers (car manufacturers and motorists) compete for the limited supply, pushing the price up. The higher price gives tyre producers an incentive to produce more, so quantity supplied extends along the supply curve S. A new equilibrium is reached where D1 crosses S, at a higher price P1 and a higher quantity Q1. As a result, tyre producers’ revenue rises (both price and quantity sold increase), which may raise their profits, attract new firms into the industry and increase demand for the rubber and labour used to make tyres. The size of the price rise depends on the PES of tyres: if supply is elastic, most of the effect is on quantity rather than price. Why this scores A fully labelled diagram (axes, S, D, D1, P, P1, Q, Q1), the link between the markets (complements/joint demand), the correct shift, the adjustment process via the shortage, and the outcome with a consequence for firms. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (c) · [6 marks] Analyse why an actor may decide to become a teacher. Workers choose an occupation by weighing up its wage and non-wage factors. Wage factors. Most actors earn low and irregular incomes: they are paid per role and may spend long periods with no work. There is a large supply of people wanting to act relative to demand, which keeps the typical wage low. Teachers, by contrast, usually receive a regular salary on a pay scale, often with annual increments and a pension. An actor who wants a higher and more predictable income may therefore switch to teaching, because the expected lifetime earnings are greater and allow them to plan borrowing, such as a mortgage. Non-wage factors. Teaching offers greater job security, since there is continuous demand for teachers and posts are often permanent contracts, whereas acting jobs are temporary. Teachers usually have long holidays and regular hours rather than evening and weekend performances and touring away from home, which can suit someone with a family. Teaching can also offer job satisfaction from helping young people and clear promotion prospects, for example to head of department. Transferable skills. An actor already has skills in communication, confidence and presenting to an audience, so the cost of retraining (for example, a teaching qualification) may be relatively low, making the move easier. Occupational mobility is higher when skills overlap. Overall, if the combined wage and non-wage benefits of teaching exceed those of acting, the actor will change occupation. Why this scores Uses the economic framework of wage and non-wage factors, compares both jobs rather than describing one, and develops each point into why it would change the actor’s choice, with a link to occupational mobility. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Past paper (d) · [8 marks] Discuss whether or not demand for coffee is likely to rise in the future. Why demand may rise. Incomes are rising in many developing and emerging economies, such as China and India. Coffee, especially café coffee, is a normal good, so as real incomes grow consumers can afford to buy more of it at every price. The demand curve shifts to the right. Tastes are also changing. Coffee-shop culture is spreading, and advertising by large chains and social media promotes coffee as a lifestyle product. Population growth in countries with a young, urban population also adds more potential consumers. Both increase the number of people willing and able to buy coffee. Why demand may not rise. Health concerns about too much caffeine could shift tastes towards substitutes such as herbal tea, fruit juice or water, reducing demand for coffee. If the price of a close substitute such as tea falls, some consumers will switch away from coffee. Climate change may reduce the supply of coffee beans, as coffee plants are sensitive to rising temperatures and droughts. This would raise the price of coffee, causing a contraction in quantity demanded (a movement along the curve). A recession would also reduce incomes and cut spending on non-essential purchases such as café coffee. Conclusion. Demand for coffee is likely to rise overall, because the growth in incomes and population in emerging economies is a long-term trend that outweighs health concerns in most markets. However, it depends on the country: in high-income countries where consumption is already high, demand may be stable or fall as tastes shift, and it also depends on whether a future recession cuts incomes. Why this scores Two developed arguments on each side using determinants of demand, a clear distinction between a shift in demand and a contraction caused by a price rise, and a conclusion that makes a judgement and says what it depends on. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (d) · [8 marks] Discuss whether or not skilled workers are always paid more than unskilled workers. Why skilled workers are usually paid more. The supply of skilled workers is limited. Skills such as those of surgeons or engineers take years of education and training to acquire and require particular abilities, so few people can do the job. The supply of labour is low and inelastic, which pushes the wage up. Skilled workers also tend to have high productivity: they produce more output, or output of greater value, per hour. Firms’ demand for labour is a derived demand, so they are willing to pay a high wage to workers who add a lot of revenue. High demand combined with low supply gives a high equilibrium wage. Why skilled workers are not always paid more. Demand for some skills can be low or falling. A skilled craftworker in a declining industry, or a worker whose skill has been replaced by automation, may earn less than an unskilled worker in a booming sector, because the derived demand for their labour has fallen. Wages also depend on bargaining power and government. Unskilled workers in an industry with a strong trade union may win higher pay than non-unionised skilled workers, and a national minimum wage can raise unskilled pay. In some public-sector jobs, such as nursing or teaching, skilled workers are paid by government pay scales that may be lower than the wages of unskilled workers doing dangerous or unpleasant work, such as offshore oil labourers who receive compensation for poor conditions. Some skilled workers also accept lower pay for non-wage benefits, such as job satisfaction. Conclusion. Skilled workers are usually, but not always, paid more. It depends on the demand for the skill relative to its supply: a skill that is in short supply and highly valued by employers earns a high wage, but where demand for a skill is low, or unskilled workers have strong unions, dangerous conditions or minimum wage protection, the gap can narrow or reverse. Why this scores Uses demand and supply of labour on both sides, brings in trade unions, government, compensating differentials and non-wage factors, and the word “always” is directly challenged in a reasoned conclusion. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (d) · [8 marks] Discuss whether all monopolies have low costs of production. Why monopolies may have low costs. A monopoly is the single or dominant supplier in its market, so it usually produces on a very large scale. This allows it to benefit from economies of scale: for example, bulk-buying discounts on raw materials (purchasing economies), cheaper borrowing because lenders see it as low risk (financial economies) and the use of specialist, efficient machinery (technical economies). Average costs fall as output rises. A monopoly can also earn supernormal profits in the long run because barriers to entry stop new firms entering. It can use these profits to fund research and development, leading to new, more efficient production methods that cut costs further. Natural monopolies, such as water supply networks, have very high fixed costs, so one firm supplying the whole market has the lowest average cost. Why monopolies may not have low costs. Without competition, a monopoly has little incentive to keep costs down. It can survive while being inefficient, for example by overstaffing, paying managers high salaries or using out-of-date equipment, because customers have no alternative supplier. Rising costs can simply be passed on as higher prices. A monopoly may also grow so large that it suffers diseconomies of scale: communication becomes slower, management becomes harder to coordinate and workers feel less motivated, so average costs rise. In addition, a monopoly in a small local market (such as the only shop on an island) may not be large enough to gain significant economies of scale at all. Conclusion. Not all monopolies have low costs. It depends on their size and on whether they face pressure to be efficient: a large monopoly that reinvests profits and faces the threat of regulation or potential competitors is likely to have low costs, whereas a protected monopoly with no competitive pressure, or one that has grown too large, may have high costs. Why this scores Names specific economies and diseconomies of scale, uses monopoly concepts (barriers to entry, supernormal profit, lack of competition) and gives a conclusion that directly answers “all”. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (d) · [8 marks] Discuss whether or not a firm should have growth as its main objective. Why growth should be the main objective. Growth allows a firm to benefit from economies of scale. As output increases, average costs fall through bulk buying, specialist machinery and cheaper finance. Lower costs allow the firm to cut prices, compete more strongly and earn higher profits in the long run. A larger firm also gains market share and becomes more secure. It is less likely to be taken over or forced out of business, it can spread risk by diversifying into different products and markets, and it has more power when negotiating with suppliers. Managers may also gain status and higher salaries from running a larger firm. Why growth should not be the main objective. Chasing growth can reduce profits in the short run. Expanding requires heavy spending on new premises, machinery and marketing, and the firm may cut prices to win sales. Shareholders usually want profit maximisation, so they may be unhappy if dividends fall. If the firm grows too large, it may suffer diseconomies of scale, such as poor communication and low worker motivation, pushing average costs up. Other objectives may be more important depending on the situation. A new firm or one in a recession may need survival as its main aim, keeping costs low and cash available. Some firms aim for social welfare or environmental sustainability, for example reducing carbon emissions, which rapid expansion could undermine. Small firms may deliberately stay small to keep personal control and offer a specialised service. Conclusion. Growth is a sensible main objective for an established, financially strong firm in a growing market where economies of scale are significant. However, it depends on the firm’s stage and circumstances: for a new firm or one facing a downturn, survival or profit should come first, and growth is only worthwhile if it does not lead to diseconomies of scale or conflict with owners’ aims. Why this scores Covers the main alternative objectives from the syllabus (survival, growth, profit maximisation, social welfare), develops each point with a consequence, and reaches a conditional judgement. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Quick Checklist In my answer I use the exact definition or formula, with “percentage change” where needed. In my answer I separate a shift of a curve (non-price factor) from a movement along it (price change). In my answer I fully label every diagram and explain what shifts, why, and the new equilibrium. In my answer I develop each point into a consequence rather than listing several brief points. In my answer I give two developed arguments on each side of a “Discuss” question. In my answer I finish with a judgement that says what the outcome depends on and tackles words like “always” or “all”.

Model Answers · Topic 4 Model Answers: Government & the Macroeconomy Full-mark model answers to typical Paper 2 questions on monetary policy, inflation and deflation, redistribution, supply-side policy, unemployment and poverty. They show how to build a chain of reasoning from a policy change to its effect on the economy, and how to balance a discussion.

Past paper (d) · [4 marks] Explain how government spending on training may increase tax revenue in the long run. Government spending on training improves the skills of the labour force, which raises labour productivity and occupational mobility. Better-trained workers are more attractive to employers, so unemployed people are more likely to find jobs, and existing workers can move into higher-skilled, better-paid occupations. More people in work and higher wages mean higher incomes, so the government collects more income tax. Workers with higher incomes also spend more, which increases revenue from indirect taxes such as VAT or sales tax. In addition, a more productive workforce lowers firms’ costs and raises their profits, increasing corporation tax revenue. Fewer people claiming unemployment benefits also frees up government funds. Because training takes time to have an effect, this increase in tax revenue happens in the long run rather than immediately. Why this scores A clear chain from training to productivity and employment, then to higher incomes, spending and profits, with named taxes that rise, and a reason why the effect is long run. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (b) · [4 marks] Explain two reasons why governments redistribute income. To reduce poverty. In a market economy some people, such as the unemployed, the sick and the elderly, earn little or no income and cannot afford necessities such as food, housing and healthcare. By taxing high earners progressively and paying benefits to low-income households, the government raises the living standards of the poorest. To reduce inequality and increase economic welfare. A large gap between rich and poor can cause social tension and crime and may reduce equality of opportunity, since children in poor households may receive less education. An extra dollar gives more benefit to a poor person than to a rich person, so transferring income from rich to poor can raise total welfare and create a fairer society. (Other creditworthy reasons: to increase spending and aggregate demand, as poorer households spend a higher proportion of their income; to improve health and education and so increase future productivity.) Why this scores Two distinct reasons, each identified and developed with who gains and why, plus a mention of how redistribution works (progressive taxes and benefits). Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Past paper (c) · [6 marks] Analyse how a central bank could reduce inflation. A central bank can use contractionary monetary policy to reduce inflation, mainly by raising the interest rate (and by reducing the money supply). A higher interest rate increases the cost of borrowing. Households take out fewer loans and mortgages to buy houses, cars and other consumer goods, and people with existing variable-rate mortgages have to make higher repayments, leaving them with less disposable income. A higher interest rate also increases the reward for saving, so households save more and spend less. As a result, consumer expenditure falls. Firms also face higher borrowing costs, so some investment projects, such as buying new machinery, become unprofitable and investment falls. In addition, higher interest rates may attract foreign financial capital, raising the exchange rate. This makes imports cheaper, reducing imported cost-push inflation, and makes exports dearer, reducing net exports. With lower consumption, investment and net exports, total (aggregate) demand in the economy falls. Firms face less demand for their products, so they are less able to raise prices and may offer discounts to sell stock. Workers also have less bargaining power for wage rises. This reduces demand-pull inflation, so the general price level rises more slowly and the inflation rate falls. Why this scores Names the tool, then links it logically through borrowing, saving, consumption, investment and the exchange rate to lower aggregate demand and a lower inflation rate, using precise terms throughout. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (c) · [6 marks] Analyse how a central bank could avoid deflation. Deflation is a sustained fall in the general price level, often caused by weak aggregate demand. A central bank can avoid it by using expansionary monetary policy: cutting the interest rate and increasing the money supply. A lower interest rate reduces the cost of borrowing. Households are more willing to take out loans and mortgages to buy houses, cars and furniture, and those with existing mortgages pay less each month, leaving more disposable income. Saving earns a lower return, so people are encouraged to spend rather than save. Consumer expenditure therefore increases. Firms can borrow more cheaply, so more investment projects become profitable and investment rises. Lower interest rates can also cause financial capital to leave the country, lowering the exchange rate. Exports become cheaper abroad and imports become dearer, so net exports rise and imported goods push up the price level. If the central bank increases the money supply, for example by buying government bonds, banks have more funds to lend, reinforcing the rise in spending. Higher consumption, investment and net exports increase aggregate demand. Firms face stronger demand and can raise prices rather than cut them, so the general price level stops falling and inflation returns to a low positive rate, avoiding deflation. Why this scores Defines deflation, identifies expansionary tools and traces them through each component of aggregate demand to a stable or rising price level. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (c) · [6 marks] Analyse the advantages of a low rate of inflation. International competitiveness. If a country’s inflation rate is low compared with its trading partners, its products become relatively cheaper. Demand for its exports rises and domestic consumers buy fewer imports. This improves the current account of the balance of payments and increases output and employment in export industries. Certainty and investment. Low and stable inflation makes it easier for firms to predict future costs, prices and profits. With less uncertainty, firms are more confident to invest in capital goods, which increases productive capacity and leads to economic growth in the long run. Protecting purchasing power. With low inflation, the real value of incomes and savings is not eroded quickly. People on fixed incomes, such as pensioners, keep their standard of living, and savers are not penalised, which encourages saving that banks can lend for investment. There are also fewer menu costs and shoe-leather costs, as firms do not need to change prices frequently. Advantage over zero or negative inflation. A low positive rate, rather than deflation, means consumers do not delay purchases in expectation of lower prices, and firms’ revenues grow steadily. A small rise in prices can encourage firms to produce more, supporting employment. Why this scores Several advantages, each taken through to an outcome for the economy (current account, investment and growth, living standards), showing analysis rather than a list. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Past paper (d) · [8 marks] Discuss whether or not a fall in a country’s unemployment rate will reduce poverty in that country. Why it may reduce poverty. Unemployed people rely on savings or low government benefits, and many live in poverty. When unemployment falls, more people earn a wage, which is usually higher than benefit payments. Their incomes rise, so they can afford necessities such as food, housing and healthcare, and the number of households in poverty falls. Lower unemployment also helps the government. It pays out less in unemployment benefits and collects more income tax and indirect tax revenue. These funds can be spent on education, healthcare and targeted benefits for the poor, reducing poverty further. Workers who gain jobs also develop skills and experience, raising their future earnings. Why it may not reduce poverty. The new jobs may be low-paid, part-time or temporary. Many workers in poverty are already employed (the “working poor”), especially where there is no minimum wage or it is low. If the fall in unemployment is due to more insecure, low-wage jobs, workers may still be unable to afford necessities. Poverty also affects people who are not in the labour force, such as pensioners, the sick and disabled, and children in large families. A fall in unemployment does not raise their incomes. In addition, unemployment may fall because people have given up looking for work or emigrated rather than because they found jobs. If falling unemployment leads to higher inflation as demand rises, the real incomes of the poor may even fall. Conclusion. A fall in unemployment is likely to reduce poverty, especially absolute poverty in countries where most poor people are unemployed. However, it depends on the quality and pay of the new jobs, whether there is an adequate minimum wage, why unemployment fell, and whether the government also supports those outside the labour force. Why this scores Two developed points on each side, including the working poor and groups outside the labour force, and a conclusion that states the conditions under which poverty falls. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (d) · [8 marks] Discuss whether or not supply-side policy measures will encourage firms to operate in an economy. Why supply-side measures may attract firms. Education and training policies raise the skills and productivity of the labour force. Firms can produce more output per worker, lowering their average costs, and they can find the skilled workers they need. A productive, skilled workforce is a strong reason for firms, including multinationals, to locate in a country. Cutting corporation tax and reducing regulation (deregulation) increases firms’ after-tax profits and lowers the cost and time of starting and running a business. Improving infrastructure, such as roads, ports, power supplies and broadband, reduces transport and production costs. Higher expected profits give firms an incentive to set up and expand. Why supply-side measures may not attract firms. Many supply-side measures take a long time to have an effect. A new education programme may take ten years or more to produce skilled workers, and large infrastructure projects take years to build, so firms deciding where to locate now may not be influenced. Firms consider many other factors as well. If demand in the economy is low because of a recession, firms will not operate there even with low taxes, because they cannot sell their output. Political instability, high crime, a volatile exchange rate or better incentives offered by other countries may outweigh the benefits. Some measures may also have side effects: cutting regulations on the environment or workers’ rights may attract firms but cause pollution and damage sustainability, while tax cuts reduce government revenue for infrastructure. Conclusion. Supply-side measures are likely to encourage firms to operate in an economy in the long run, because they reduce costs and raise productivity. However, it depends on which measures are used, how quickly they take effect and whether other conditions, such as strong demand, political stability and competitive policies compared with other countries, are also present. Why this scores Names specific supply-side measures and links each to firms’ costs and profits, then evaluates using time lags, demand conditions and competing locations, ending with a conditional judgement. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (d) · [8 marks] Discuss whether or not the fall in the price of a product is a disadvantage to an economy. Why it may be a disadvantage. If the product is a major export, such as oil or copper for a country that depends on it, a fall in its price reduces export revenue (particularly if demand is price inelastic, so quantity sold rises by proportionally less than price falls). This worsens the current account of the balance of payments, lowers producers’ profits and can cause firms to cut output and make workers redundant, increasing unemployment and reducing economic growth. Government tax revenue from the industry also falls. If the price falls because demand has fallen, for example during a recession, it is a sign of a weak economy. If falling prices spread across many products and become deflation, consumers may delay purchases expecting prices to fall further, reducing aggregate demand, output and employment even more. Why it may not be a disadvantage. Consumers benefit: a lower price increases their real income and purchasing power, allowing them to buy more of this and other products, raising living standards. If the product is a necessity such as food or fuel, low-income households gain the most. If the price falls because supply has increased, for example through new technology or lower costs, output and consumption rise, which is a sign of efficiency. If the product is an important raw material or input, such as oil for an importing country, firms’ costs fall, reducing cost-push inflation, making exports more competitive and encouraging higher output and employment. A fall in the price of a product that causes pollution could, however, increase its consumption and harm the environment. Conclusion. A fall in the price of a product is not necessarily a disadvantage. It depends on why the price fell (higher supply is usually beneficial, lower demand is not), whether the country is mainly a producer or consumer of the product, how important it is to exports, and whether the fall is limited to one product or part of a general deflation. Why this scores Considers producers, consumers, the balance of payments and the government, distinguishes demand-side from supply-side causes of the price fall, and ends with a justified “it depends” judgement. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Quick Checklist In my answer I name the specific policy tool (interest rate, money supply, tax, subsidy, training) before analysing it. In my answer I trace effects through the components of aggregate demand: consumption, investment, government spending and net exports. In my answer I link each step with connectives such as “so”, “therefore” and “as a result”. In my answer I consider different groups: consumers, workers, firms, government and the environment. In my answer I use evaluation points such as time lags, the cause of the change and other factors at work. In my answer I end every “Discuss” question with a conclusion that says what the outcome depends on.

Model Answers · Topics 5–6 Model Answers: Development & Trade Full-mark model answers to past Paper 2 questions on population, development, specialisation, trade restrictions and the current account. These questions reward long chains of reasoning and balanced, well-justified conclusions.

Past paper (c) · [6 marks] Analyse the economic effects of a reduction in a country’s export of services. Exports of services, such as tourism, banking, insurance, transport and education sold to foreigners, bring money into the country and are recorded as credits in the trade in services part of the current account. If these exports fall, for example because foreign tourists stop visiting after a rise in the exchange rate or a global recession, less money flows in. If imports stay the same, the current account moves towards a deficit (or a larger deficit). Exports are also an injection of spending into the economy, so lower exports reduce aggregate (total) demand . Hotels, airlines and banks sell less, so they cut output and need fewer workers. This leads to higher unemployment and slower, or even negative, economic growth . The workers who lose their jobs have lower incomes, so they spend less in other local businesses, spreading the fall in demand further through the economy. With less demand, pressure on prices eases, so inflation may fall . Lower incomes and profits also mean the government collects less tax revenue while paying more in unemployment benefits, which can worsen its budget position. Less demand for the currency from foreigners buying the country’s services may cause the exchange rate to depreciate , which could eventually make exports cheaper and help them recover. Why this scores A clear chain from fewer service exports to the current account, then to aggregate demand, output, jobs and growth, with further effects on inflation, government finances and the exchange rate, all in correct economic terms. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (c) · [6 marks] Analyse how cleaning up pollution could benefit an economy. Pollution is an external cost of production and consumption: it harms third parties who are not part of the transaction. Cleaning it up reduces these external costs and moves the economy towards the socially optimum use of resources, supporting the government aim of environmental sustainability . Cleaner air and water improve people’s health . Fewer people suffer from breathing problems or water-borne diseases, so workers take fewer days off sick and the productivity of the labour force rises. Healthier people also live and work longer. This increases the quality of labour, shifts the economy’s PPC outwards and raises potential economic growth . At the same time, the government and households spend less on treating pollution-related illness, so the government can use the money saved on other services, such as education, and families have more income to spend on other goods. Cleaning up polluted land and rivers also improves the quality of land as a factor of production. Farmland becomes more fertile and fish stocks recover, raising output in agriculture and fishing. A cleaner environment attracts more tourists and can encourage multinational firms and skilled workers to locate in the country, increasing exports of services, employment and incomes. The clean-up work itself creates jobs. Overall, living standards rise, not just through higher real GDP but through a better quality of life. Why this scores Uses the concept of external costs, then develops two full chains (health → productivity → growth; better land and environment → tourism, investment, output) linked to living standards and sustainability. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Past paper (h) · [6 marks] Discuss whether or not an increase in a country’s import tariff on rice would increase the output of its domestic rice farmers. Why output may increase. A tariff is a tax on imports, so a higher tariff raises the price of imported rice in the domestic market. Imported rice becomes less competitive compared with rice grown by domestic farmers, so consumers switch to domestic rice. Higher demand for domestic rice and a higher market price increase the profitability of rice farming, so domestic farmers have an incentive to expand production, for example by planting more land or using more fertiliser, and output rises . New farmers may also be attracted into the industry. Why output may not increase. Domestic farmers may be unable to expand quickly because supply of rice is price inelastic in the short run: it takes a growing season to plant and harvest, and suitable land and water may be limited. Output may also be held back by poor weather or a lack of capital. In addition, other countries may retaliate by putting tariffs on this country’s exports; if the farmers export some of their rice, they lose foreign sales. If demand for rice is price inelastic and the tariff is small, consumers may carry on buying imported rice they prefer, such as a particular variety, so demand for domestic rice rises only slightly. Conclusion. The tariff is likely to increase domestic output over time, but by how much depends on the size of the tariff, how easily domestic farmers can increase supply, and whether imported and domestic rice are close substitutes. Output will rise most in the long run, when farmers have had time to expand. Why this scores A developed argument for (higher import price → switch to domestic rice → higher profits → more output) and developed arguments against (inelastic supply, retaliation, weak substitution), with a conclusion naming what it depends on. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (g) · [6 marks] Discuss whether or not an increase in a country’s population will benefit its economy. Why it may benefit the economy. A larger population, especially one with more people of working age, increases the size of the labour force . More workers raise the economy’s productive capacity, shifting the PPC outwards, and help fill skill shortages. A larger population also means a bigger domestic market , so demand for goods and services rises. Firms can produce on a larger scale and benefit from economies of scale, lowering average costs, and the government collects more tax revenue. Why it may not benefit the economy. If the population grows faster than the economy’s output, real GDP per head falls and living standards decline. The increase may be mainly children, raising the dependency ratio and requiring more government spending on schools and healthcare. Pressure on scarce resources such as housing, water and farmland can cause shortages, higher prices, congestion and pollution, harming environmental sustainability. If there are not enough jobs, unemployment rises. Conclusion. Population growth is more likely to benefit an economy that has spare resources, a shortage of workers and the capital to employ extra people productively, as in some high-income countries with ageing populations. It is less likely to benefit a low-income country where output is already growing slowly. It depends on the age structure and skills of the extra people and on whether output grows faster than population. Why this scores Balanced development of labour force and market-size benefits against lower GDP per head, dependency and resource pressure, with a conclusion that depends on the country’s circumstances and age structure. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Past paper (d) · [8 marks] Discuss whether or not an increase in government subsidies will reduce a deficit on the current account of the balance of payments. Why it may reduce the deficit. A current account deficit occurs when spending on imports of goods and services (plus outflows of income and transfers) exceeds receipts from exports. A subsidy is a payment from the government to producers, which lowers their costs of production. If subsidies are given to exporting firms , they can lower the prices of their products abroad. This makes exports more price competitive, so foreign demand rises and export revenue increases, as long as demand is price elastic. Higher export earnings reduce the current account deficit. Subsidies to domestic firms that compete with imports , such as local food producers, allow them to cut their prices. Domestic consumers then switch from imported goods to cheaper domestically produced goods, so spending on imports falls, again reducing the deficit. In the longer run, subsidies for training, research or new technology can raise productivity and quality, making the country’s firms more internationally competitive. Why it may not reduce the deficit. If demand for the country’s exports is price inelastic , for example because foreign buyers value brand or quality more than price, a small price cut will raise the quantity sold only slightly, and export revenue may even fall. Firms may also keep the subsidy as extra profit rather than lowering prices. Moreover, subsidies must be financed. If the government pays for them by raising taxes or cutting other spending, or by borrowing, other parts of the economy may be harmed. Other countries may regard export subsidies as unfair and retaliate with tariffs on this country’s goods, reducing exports. Also, if subsidised firms expand production, they may need more imported raw materials and components , so imports rise. And if the subsidy increases incomes in the economy, households may spend more on imported goods. The deficit may also be caused by factors subsidies do not address, such as large outflows of profits to foreign-owned firms or a high exchange rate. Conclusion. Subsidies can reduce a current account deficit if they are targeted at exporters and import-competing firms with price elastic demand, and if the price reductions are passed on to buyers. They are less likely to work when demand is inelastic, production relies on imported inputs, or trading partners retaliate. On balance, subsidies are more effective as a long-term supply-side measure that raises productivity than as a quick fix, and the result depends on how they are targeted and financed. Why this scores Two developed arguments for (cheaper exports; switching from imports) and at least two against (inelastic demand, retaliation, imported inputs, opportunity cost of financing), finished with a judgement about targeting, elasticity and time. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Past paper (d) · [8 marks] Discuss whether or not countries specialising benefits consumers. Why specialisation may benefit consumers. When countries specialise, they concentrate on producing the goods and services they are best at, for example because of their climate, natural resources or skilled workforce, and trade for the rest. Producing on a larger scale allows firms to gain economies of scale and to become more efficient, so average costs fall. These lower costs can be passed on to consumers as lower prices , raising their real incomes and allowing them to buy more goods and services. Specialisation and trade also give consumers greater choice and quality . Consumers can buy products their own country cannot make, or cannot make well, such as tropical fruit in a cold country or advanced electronics in a country without the technology. Competition from specialist foreign producers pressures domestic firms to improve quality and innovate, which also benefits consumers. Why specialisation may not benefit consumers. A country that relies on others for key products becomes dependent on imports . If supply is disrupted, for example by war, a natural disaster, a pandemic or export restrictions in the supplying country, consumers may face shortages and sharp price rises, as happened with some food and energy products in recent years. Transport costs and tariffs may also offset the cost advantage. In addition, over-specialisation can harm consumers as workers : if world demand for the country’s main export falls, or a cheaper producer appears abroad, workers in that industry lose their jobs and incomes. Their occupational immobility can lead to long-term unemployment, reducing their ability to buy goods and services. Specialisation may also lead to a few large global firms dominating markets. If they gain monopoly power , they may raise prices and restrict choice rather than passing lower costs on. Transporting goods over long distances also increases pollution and CO 2 emissions, an external cost that consumers bear as members of society. Conclusion. Specialisation generally benefits consumers through lower prices and wider choice, and this is the main reason countries trade. However, the benefit depends on whether cost savings are passed on through competition, how reliable supply chains are, and how diversified the economy is. A country that specialises but keeps several sources of supply and several export industries is most likely to gain without exposing its consumers to excessive risk. Why this scores Developed benefits (economies of scale → lower prices; more choice and quality) balanced against developed drawbacks (dependence and supply disruption, unemployment of consumers as workers, monopoly power), with a conclusion stating the conditions for benefit. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Quick Checklist In my answer I defined the key term first (tariff, subsidy, current account deficit, specialisation, external cost). In my answer I traced each effect through a full chain, e.g. price → competitiveness → demand → output → jobs. In my answer I used price elasticity of demand or supply to judge how large an effect would be. In my answer I considered retaliation, imported inputs and the cost of financing government measures. In my answer I linked outcomes to government aims, including living standards and environmental sustainability. In my answer I gave both sides and ended with a conclusion that says what the outcome depends on.

How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0455/22/M/J/25 Q2(d) means Paper 2, variant 2, May/June 2025, Question 2 part (d). F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 1.1 The nature of the economic problem · 1.2 The factors of production · 1.3 Opportunity cost · 1.4 Production possibility curve (PPC) diagrams 1.1 The nature of the economic problem These questions test whether you can explain scarcity precisely (unlimited wants, finite resources) and the difference between economic and free goods; examiners reward exact economic definitions rather than everyday meanings. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports say weaker candidates use the everyday meaning of a ‘free good’ (something given away at no charge) instead of the economic one: a good that is not scarce, uses no resources and has no opportunity cost. Others explain the economic problem in general terms but never apply it to the group the question names, such as consumers. 0455/22/F/M/25 Q2(a) · February/March 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: South Korea makes use of both economic goods and free goods. Identify a difference between economic goods and free goods. Economic goods are scarce because resources (factors of production) are used up to produce them, so they have an opportunity cost. Free goods are not scarce: they are in unlimited supply, need no resources to produce and so have no opportunity cost. Why this scores One mark for the economic-good half and one for the free-good half of the same difference, so the answer states both. Examples earn nothing here, and the examiner report warns against the everyday meaning of ‘free’: a free newspaper is still an economic good, because resources were used to make it. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/24 Q5(a) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Free goods and economic goods are consumed in Poland. Identify two free goods. 1. Air. 2. Sunlight. Why this scores One mark each. Air, sunlight, water and wind are all accepted. Avoid fish, wood or stone: resources are needed to catch, cut or extract them, so the mark scheme does not accept them. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/22 Q1(c) · October/November 2022 · [2 marks] Source material: Tourism relies on natural resources including sunshine and beaches. State why sunshine has no opportunity cost. Sunshine is a free good: it occurs naturally and is in unlimited supply, so no resources have to be used to produce it. Using sunshine in Ecuador’s tourism industry therefore means nothing has to be given up, so there is no opportunity cost. Why this scores One mark for identifying sunshine as a free good and one for a reason (unlimited supply, not scarce, needs no resources so nothing is sacrificed). The examiner report says vague answers such as ‘sunshine is everywhere’, or answers that only defined opportunity cost, did not score. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/F/M/23 Q5(b) · February/March 2023 · [4 marks] Source material: Consumers experience the economic problem when buying raspberries. Explain how the economic problem results in consumers having to make choices. The economic problem is that people’s wants are unlimited but the resources available to satisfy them are limited (finite). This creates scarcity: there is not enough to produce everything that everyone would like. For consumers, the limited resource is their income. A household in Serbia has only a certain amount of money to spend each week, so it cannot buy everything it wants and has to choose, for example between buying raspberries and buying another fruit or a snack. Choosing one product means giving up the next best alternative, which is the opportunity cost of that choice. Scarcity therefore forces consumers to rank their wants and decide which ones to satisfy. Why this scores Marks for the economic problem itself (unlimited wants, limited resources, scarcity) and then for applying it to consumers: limited income means they cannot buy everything, so each purchase has an opportunity cost. The examiner report says many answers explained the economic problem well but did not relate it to consumers , which limited their marks. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 1.2 The factors of production These questions test the four factors of production, their rewards, and how mobile each factor is; examiners reward precise terms such as ‘resource used to produce goods and services’ and the distinction between occupational and geographical mobility. What examiners keep seeing The examiner report says a high proportion of candidates asked to define a factor of production simply listed land, labour, capital and enterprise, which is not a definition. Rewards are another trap: some candidates matched rewards to the wrong factor or named the factor itself (machinery, farmland) instead of its reward. 0455/22/F/M/25 Q3(a) · February/March 2025 · [2 marks] Define factor of production. A factor of production is a resource, or input, that is used to produce goods and services. Why this scores One mark for ‘resource’ or ‘input’ and one for ‘used to produce goods and services’. The examiner report says many candidates just named the four factors, which is not a definition, and the mark scheme gives no marks for examples. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/M/J/25 Q3(a) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: Since 2008, its capital has increased and its land has not changed significantly, but its labour force and its enterprise have decreased. Identify the rewards to capital and land. Capital: interest. Land: rent. Why this scores One mark each. The examiner report says weaker answers gave the rewards for the wrong factors, or described the factor (machinery, farmland) instead of its reward. Learn the full set: rent for land, wages for labour, interest for capital and profit for enterprise. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/F/M/22 Q5(b) · February/March 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: Ghana uses much of its agricultural land to grow cocoa. Explain whether land is mobile. Most land is geographically immobile. Land is fixed in one place: a cocoa farm in Ghana cannot be moved to another region or country where it might be more productive or where demand is higher. Some natural resources counted as land, such as fish or wild animals, can move from place to place, but they are the exception. Land can be occupationally mobile. The same piece of land can usually be switched to a different use. Ghana’s farmland could change from growing cocoa to growing other crops, or be cleared for housing, factories or roads if those uses become more profitable. How occupationally mobile it is depends on the type of land: flat, fertile land has many possible uses, whereas a mountainside has very few. Why this scores Two marks for each type of mobility: identifying that most land is geographically immobile (1) and explaining that it is fixed in one place (1), then identifying that it is occupationally mobile (1) with an example of a change of use (1). The examiner report credited answers that separated the two kinds of mobility, as this one does. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/25 Q2(c) · May/June 2025 · [6 marks] Source material: Three of the accountancy firms reduced the number of new workers they hired and the other accountancy firm announced job losses. The ability of workers to gain new jobs is influenced by their mobility. Analyse the advantages of an increase in labour mobility. Labour mobility is the ability of workers to change jobs. Occupational mobility is the ability to move from one type of job to another, and geographical mobility is the ability to move from one area to another to work. Lower unemployment. If accountants who lose their jobs are occupationally mobile, for example because their numeracy and IT skills are transferable, they can move quickly into banking, finance or teaching. If they are geographically mobile, they can move to regions or countries where jobs are available. This reduces structural and frictional unemployment, which means the government spends less on unemployment benefits, receives more income tax and fewer households fall into poverty. Higher incomes for workers. Mobile workers can move to the jobs that pay best and make the most of their skills, and changing jobs gives them new experience. As a result their productivity and earning power rise, so their standard of living improves. Fewer labour shortages, so more output. Firms in expanding industries can fill vacancies more easily when workers are able to move to them. This stops shortages of workers pushing up wages and costs, so there is less cost-push inflation, and it allows these firms to expand. The economy’s resources are used more fully, so real GDP and economic growth increase. A more flexible economy. When consumer demand changes, as it did for accountancy services in 2023, workers can move out of declining industries and into growing ones. Resources are reallocated more quickly to the products consumers want, which reduces surpluses and shortages. Why this scores Defines both types of mobility, then builds complete chains for workers (jobs, wages), the government (benefits, tax), firms (shortages, costs) and the economy (output, growth), matching the mark scheme’s points. The examiner report praised answers that distinguished geographical from occupational mobility and analysed the effects on unemployment, firms’ flexibility and output. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/22 Q1(g) · May/June 2022 · [6 marks] Source material: To achieve this, it announced increased spending on some areas including mental health, child poverty and pollution. … It was, however, difficult to predict firms’ future profits. Discuss whether or not enterprise is likely to have increased in New Zealand after 2019. Enterprise is the willingness and ability of entrepreneurs to take risks and organise the other factors of production to set up and run businesses, in return for profit. Why enterprise might have increased. New Zealand has high productivity, partly because of high investment in capital goods and education. A well-educated population has more people with the skills and confidence to start firms, and high productivity keeps costs down, raising the profits that reward entrepreneurs. The government’s extra spending on mental health, child poverty and pollution also raises total demand. Higher demand increases firms’ expected revenue and profits, giving people a stronger incentive to set up or expand businesses. New Zealand’s high GDP per head also attracts net immigration. Some immigrants are likely to be entrepreneurs who set up new firms, and a larger population means more customers. If the government also followed the economists’ advice and cut income tax rates, households would have more disposable income, raising demand and profits further. Why enterprise might not have increased. The source says it was difficult to predict firms’ future profits because of uncertainty about GDP and corporation tax rates. Entrepreneurs bear risk, so if they fear a recession could cut demand, the expected reward for taking that risk falls and fewer people start businesses. The extra government spending also has to be paid for. If the government raised corporation tax, firms would keep less of their profit, reducing the incentive to be an entrepreneur. Measures to reduce pollution may also raise firms’ costs of production, for example by forcing them to use cleaner but more expensive methods, which cuts profits further. Conclusion. Enterprise is likely to have increased in New Zealand after 2019, because an educated, productive labour force and rising demand give entrepreneurs good opportunities. This is most likely if corporation tax was not raised to fund the extra spending and confidence about future GDP stayed high; if taxes on profits rose during a period of uncertainty, enterprise may have stayed the same or fallen. Why this scores Up to 4 marks are available for each side, so the answer gives developed reasons both ways, each linked to the reward for enterprise (profit) or to risk, and uses the source material: education, government spending, immigration, uncertainty and corporation tax. The examiner report picked out exactly these points in strong answers, and the conclusion names the conditions the outcome depends on. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 1.3 Opportunity cost These questions test whether you can identify the next best alternative given up in a real choice and explain how it shapes decisions; examiners reward a specific, relevant alternative rather than a general mention of ‘cost’. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports note that some candidates describe opportunity cost as the option that is chosen rather than the next best alternative that is given up, and others pick an alternative that does not fit the context, such as saying the opportunity cost of exporting is importing (it is selling the products in the home market). 0455/22/F/M/24 Q1(b) · February/March 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: They spend this time in a variety of ways including cycling, jogging and playing golf. Identify two possible opportunity costs of a Danish person using their leisure time to cycle. 1. Jogging. 2. Playing golf. Why this scores One mark each for the two other leisure activities named in the source, because these are the alternative uses of the same leisure time that are given up. “Identify” needs no explanation; the key is to pick alternatives from the source rather than a money cost. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/23 Q5(a) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: In 2019, China’s economic growth rate was 6.1% and Chinese households increased their spending. … China exported more despite a rise in tariffs on some of its products. Identify the opportunity cost of households spending their income and the opportunity cost of Chinese firms exporting goods and services. Households spending their income: the saving they could have done instead. Chinese firms exporting: selling those goods and services to consumers in China’s home market instead. Why this scores One mark for saving and one for selling (consuming) the products at home. The examiner report says many candidates wrongly gave ‘importing’ as the opportunity cost of exporting; ask what else the firm could have done with the same products. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/F/M/25 Q2(b) · February/March 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: The country is building the world’s first floating city, estimated to cost $180m. Explain how opportunity cost will influence a government’s decision on whether to spend tax revenue on a large infrastructure project. Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. A government’s tax revenue is limited, so if it spends $180m on a large infrastructure project such as South Korea’s floating city, that money cannot be used for something else, for example building new hospitals or schools. The government therefore has to compare the benefits of the project with the benefits of the best alternative it would give up. It will go ahead only if it judges that the project gives the greater benefit, for example because protecting people and property from rising sea levels is a higher priority than extra healthcare. If the forgone hospitals would bring greater benefits, the opportunity cost is too high and the government may reject or delay the project. Why this scores Marks for defining opportunity cost (best alternative forgone), for explaining that limited tax revenue spent on the project cannot be spent elsewhere, with an example, and for showing how the government weighs its priorities to decide. The examiner report said strong answers explained that tax revenue is limited and identified which choice would be given up. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/25 Q2(c) · October/November 2025 · [6 marks] Source material: Over this period, its decisions have always been influenced by opportunity cost. Analyse how opportunity cost influences the decisions made by consumers, workers and producers. Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. Consumers, workers and producers all have limited resources, so every decision involves giving something up, and they compare what they would gain with what they would sacrifice. Consumers. Consumers have limited incomes, so they cannot buy everything they want. If a family spends $50 on a meal out, it cannot spend that $50 on new clothes. A rational consumer chooses the option that gives more satisfaction than the alternative given up. If the price of a product rises, such as the 8% rise in the MNC’s food prices, its opportunity cost rises because buying it now means giving up more of other goods, so consumers may switch to cheaper brands. Workers. Workers have limited time. An hour spent at leisure means the wage for that hour is given up, so if wages rise, leisure becomes more expensive and a worker may choose to work more hours. Workers also choose between jobs: accepting one job means giving up the pay and conditions of the next best job, so they compare wages and non-wage factors before deciding. Producers. Firms have limited finance, land, labour and capital, so they must decide what to produce, how to produce it and where to locate. If a food manufacturer uses its factory to make more chocolate, the opportunity cost is the cereal or coffee it could have made instead. The firm therefore puts its resources into the products that earn the highest profit, and switches them when another product becomes more profitable. Why this scores Opens with a definition, then analyses all three groups, each with its limited resource (income, time, finance), a specific choice and the alternative forgone. The mark scheme caps answers at 4 marks if they cover fewer than two of consumers, workers and producers, so covering all three, each with a chain to the decision made, secures full marks. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/M/J/24 Q1(h) · May/June 2024 · [6 marks] Source material: Nicaragua is the world’s twelfth largest producer of coffee. Global coffee consumption continues to increase. Discuss whether or not Nicaragua should devote more of its resources to coffee production. Devoting more resources to coffee means using more of Nicaragua’s land, labour, capital and enterprise to grow and process coffee. Every extra resource used this way has an opportunity cost: the other goods those resources could have produced. Why Nicaragua should. Global coffee consumption continues to increase, so demand for Nicaragua’s coffee is likely to rise. Demand for coffee is price-inelastic (PED of 0.3), so as rising world demand pushes up the price, farmers’ revenue rises. More coffee exports would also improve the current account of the balance of payments, and as agricultural products already make up 60% of exports, Nicaragua has the land, skills and experience to produce coffee efficiently. Expanding coffee production would also create jobs in rural areas, where wages are particularly low and unemployment rose in 2020. More employment would raise incomes, reduce poverty and increase tax revenue. Larger coffee firms could also gain economies of scale, lowering average costs and making Nicaragua more competitive against other producers. Why Nicaragua should not. Coffee output is often affected by droughts and earthquakes. Putting even more resources into one crop makes the economy more vulnerable, because a single natural disaster could wipe out much of its output and export earnings. If world coffee prices fall, for example because other countries expand production, Nicaragua’s income would also fall sharply. There is also a significant opportunity cost. The land and workers used for extra coffee could instead produce food for the domestic market or develop manufacturing and tourism, which may pay higher wages than low-paid coffee farming. Table 1.1 suggests that relying on agriculture keeps GDP per head low: only 3% of the Bahamas’ labour force works in agriculture and its GDP per head is $25 194, compared with 31% and $1905 in Nicaragua. Conclusion. Nicaragua should devote somewhat more resources to coffee, because world demand is growing and it already produces coffee well. The case is strongest if the extra resources come from unemployed workers and are used for drought-resistant farming and high-quality coffee; it is weakest if they are taken from manufacturing or tourism, which would do more to raise GDP per head in the long run. Why this scores Up to 4 marks are available for each side, so the answer develops reasons both ways and uses the source data (rising world demand, PED of 0.3, natural disasters, low rural wages, Table 1.1). The opportunity-cost argument is credited directly by the mark scheme, and the conclusion makes a judgement that depends on where the extra resources come from. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 1.4 Production possibility curve (PPC) diagrams These questions test what a PPC shows and the difference between a point on it, a point inside it and a shift of the whole curve; examiners reward fully labelled diagrams and linking every shift to a change in the quantity or quality of resources. What examiners keep seeing The 2022 examiner report says weaker answers treated a fall in actual output, such as a poor grape harvest, as a shift of the PPC. A PPC shows productive capacity, not actual output: only a change in the quantity or quality of resources shifts it, while unemployed resources put the economy inside the curve. Diagram marks are also lost when the curves do not touch both axes. 0455/22/M/J/22 Q3(a) · May/June 2022 · [2 marks] Define a production possibility curve. A production possibility curve is a diagram showing the maximum combinations of two types of products that an economy can produce with its given resources and technology. Why this scores One mark for ‘maximum output’ or ‘possible combinations’ and one for ‘two products’ or ‘given resources’. The examiner report notes that some candidates just drew a diagram: a diagram is not a definition and earns nothing here. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/25 Q1(c) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: In January 2022, Malawi was hit by Storm Ana. This damaged agricultural crops, factories, forests and power stations. Explain what is likely to have happened to Malawi’s production possibility curve (PPC) in January 2022. Malawi’s PPC is likely to have shifted to the left (inwards). Storm Ana damaged or destroyed resources such as factories, power stations and forests, reducing the quantity of capital and land, so Malawi’s productive capacity fell. Why this scores One mark for the inward shift and one for a reason from the source material (resources destroyed, so productive capacity fell). Naming the damaged resources, rather than just saying ‘output fell’, shows why the whole curve moves. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/25 Q2(b) · October/November 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: The Belgian Government wants the economy to move to a production possibility point beyond its current production possibility curve (PPC). Explain two ways an economy could reach a point outside its current PPC. Increase investment in capital goods. If firms and the government devote more resources to building new machinery, factories and infrastructure, the quantity of capital increases. With more capital the economy can produce more of both types of goods, so the PPC shifts outwards and a point that was outside the old curve becomes attainable. Improve the quality of labour through education and training. Spending on education and training makes workers more skilled, like the highly specialised workers in Belgium’s scientific industry. Their productivity rises, so the same number of workers can produce more output. Productive capacity increases and the PPC shifts outwards. Why this scores One mark for each way identified and one for each explanation of how it raises the quantity or quality of resources and so shifts the PPC outwards. Other creditworthy ways include immigration, land reclamation, new technology and discovering new natural resources. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/23 Q2(c) · October/November 2023 · [6 marks] Source material: In 2019, Mozambique was hit by a serious storm which destroyed bridges, factories, roads and electricity lines. Analyse, using a production possibility curve (PPC) diagram, the effect of a serious storm on an economy. A production possibility curve (PPC) shows the maximum combinations of two types of goods, here capital goods and consumer goods, that an economy can produce with its existing resources and technology. A serious storm, such as the one that hit Mozambique in 2019, destroys factors of production. Bridges, factories, roads and electricity lines are all capital, so the quantity of capital falls. Farmland may be flooded and workers may be injured or forced to leave the area, which reduces the quantity of land and labour as well. With fewer resources, the economy’s productive capacity falls: it can no longer produce as much of either type of good as before. As shown in the diagram, the PPC shifts inwards from PPC to PPC1. A combination on the old curve, such as point A, is no longer attainable, and the most the economy can now produce is a combination on PPC1, such as B. In the short run, damaged roads and power lines may also stop firms that still have their machinery from getting raw materials or electricity, so some resources become unemployed and the economy may produce inside even its new PPC. The economy can only move back out as the damaged capital is rebuilt. Figure: A serious storm destroys capital, land and labour, so the PPC shifts inwards from PPC to PPC1. Combination A on the old curve is no longer attainable; the most the economy can now produce is a combination on PPC1, such as B. Why this scores Up to 4 marks are for the diagram: axes labelled with two types of output, both curves touching both axes, and the inward shift shown with an arrow and labels. The other 2 marks are for explaining that the storm destroys resources and so reduces productive capacity. A new curve that does not reach both axes loses the diagram marks. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/M/J/22 Q1(g) · May/June 2022 · [6 marks] Source material: The interest rate in Cyprus was very low in 2019. … In 2019, two concerns for the future of Cyprus’s economy were that the quality of some of its agricultural land may decline and that some of its top entrepreneurs may emigrate. Discuss whether or not, after 2019, Cyprus’s production possibility curve (PPC) is likely to shift to the right. A PPC shows the maximum output of two types of goods that an economy can produce with its resources. It shifts to the right (outwards) when the quantity or quality of those resources increases, raising productive capacity. Why it might shift to the right. The interest rate in Cyprus was very low in 2019. Cheaper borrowing encourages firms to invest in capital goods, and some firms have already become more capital-intensive. More and better machinery increases the quantity and quality of capital, so productive capacity rises and the PPC shifts outwards. The labour force may also grow. The population rose from 1.1 million in 2015 to 1.2 million in 2019, life expectancy is rising and more workers are working past retirement age. If the retirement age is raised, people will stay in the labour force for longer, increasing the quantity of labour and shifting the PPC to the right. Why it might not shift to the right. The quality of some agricultural land may decline, which would reduce the productivity of land, and some top entrepreneurs may emigrate. Enterprise organises the other factors and takes risks, so losing entrepreneurs means fewer new firms and less efficient use of resources. Both would reduce productive capacity and could shift the PPC to the left. In the longer term, the birth rate fell from 11.0 to 10.2 per 1000, so fewer young people will enter the labour force in future. Unless immigration increases, the quantity of labour may eventually fall, which would also stop the PPC shifting outwards. Conclusion. Cyprus’s PPC is likely to shift to the right in the next few years, because low interest rates and longer working lives should increase the quantity of capital and labour. This depends on how many entrepreneurs actually emigrate and how quickly land quality declines: if those losses are large, they could cancel out the gains and leave the PPC unchanged or shift it to the left. Why this scores Each side links evidence from the source to a change in the quantity or quality of a factor of production, and so to productive capacity, which is what the mark scheme rewards (up to 4 marks per side). The examiner report says weaker answers wrongly used the bad grape harvest, a fall in actual output, as a reason for a shift; this answer avoids that and ends with a conditional judgement.
