x: Topical Past Papers · Topic 2 Past Paper Questions: The Allocation of Resources 48 real Cambridge IGCSE Economics Paper 2 questions from 2020 to 2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0455/22/M/J/25 Q2(d) means Paper 2, variant 2, May/June 2025, Question 2 part (d). F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 2.1 Microeconomics and macroeconomics · 2.2 The role of markets in allocating resources · 2.3 Demand · 2.4 Supply · 2.5 Price determination · 2.6 Price changes · 2.8 Price elasticity of supply (PES) · 2.9 Market economic system · 2.10 Market failure · 2.11 Mixed economic system Price elasticity of demand (2.7) has its own page: Past Paper Questions: Price Elasticity of Demand → 2.1 Microeconomics and macroeconomics These short questions test whether you can say precisely what microeconomics and macroeconomics study and classify examples of each; examiners reward the key phrases ‘individual markets and decision makers’ and ‘the economy as a whole’. What examiners keep seeing The examiner report for October/November 2020 says weak answers described microeconomics as ‘a small part of the economy’ or only ‘how households behave’. Define it as the study of individual markets and decision makers (households, workers and firms), and macroeconomics as the study of the whole economy. 0455/21/M/J/20 Q4(a) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Define macroeconomics. Macroeconomics is the study of the economy as a whole, for example a country’s total output (GDP), unemployment, inflation and balance of payments. Why this scores ‘The study of the whole economy’ earns both marks; adding an example of a macroeconomic topic, such as unemployment, makes the answer secure. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/20 Q2(a) · October/November 2020 · [2 marks] Define microeconomics. Microeconomics is the study of individual markets and the decisions of individual economic agents, such as households, workers and firms, for example how the price of cigarettes is determined in the market for cigarettes. Why this scores Both marks come from ‘individual markets’ or ‘individual economic agents’. The examiner report says ‘how households behave’ on its own was too narrow and ‘a small part of the economy’ was wrong; an example of one market, as here, makes the meaning clear. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/24 Q3(a) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Identify the difference between microeconomics and macroeconomics. Microeconomics studies individual decision makers and individual markets, such as households, firms or the market for housing, whereas macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, such as total output, inflation and unemployment. Why this scores One mark for each side of the difference: individual markets or decision makers for microeconomics (1) and the whole economy for macroeconomics (1). Writing both halves in one comparative sentence makes the difference clear. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/O/N/25 Q1(b) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: Price levels are more stable because of a combination of microeconomic and macroeconomic policy measures. These include maximum prices, subsidies and a contractionary monetary policy. Identify two microeconomic policy measures. 1. Maximum prices. 2. Subsidies (such as those given to solar energy producers). Why this scores One mark each. Both measures act on individual markets, so they are microeconomic; contractionary monetary policy affects the whole economy, so it is a macroeconomic measure and would not score. The mark scheme also accepts organising a merger, which the source mentions. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 2.2 The role of markets in allocating resources These questions test the three key resource allocation questions (what, how and for whom to produce) and how the price mechanism answers them; examiners reward answers that explain price signals and the profit incentive, not just describe demand and supply. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports say this is often poorly answered: in 2021 many candidates wrote about the price mechanism in general without addressing what, how and for whom to produce, and in 2025 many read ‘a market’ as the whole economy and wrote about factors of production or sectors instead of buyers, sellers and prices. 0455/22/M/J/20 Q5(a) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] State two key questions about how resources are allocated. 1. What to produce? 2. How to produce it? Why this scores One mark each for any two of the three questions: what to produce, how to produce it and for whom to produce. State them as the syllabus phrases them; no explanation is needed. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/M/J/24 Q2(b) · May/June 2024 · [4 marks] Source material: This transformation was possible as local villages shared resources to develop their area. Explain two key resource allocation decisions. What to produce. Because resources are scarce, an economy has to decide which goods and services to make and in what quantities, for example whether to use land in Shenzhen for factories or for housing for migrant workers, or whether to produce more capital goods or more consumer goods. Producing more of one product means producing less of another. How to produce. Producers must decide which combination of factors of production to use, for example a capital-intensive method using machinery and robots or a labour-intensive method using many workers. The aim is to choose the most efficient method, which keeps the cost of production as low as possible and wastes the fewest resources. Why this scores One mark for each decision identified and one for each explanation of what it involves, with an example. The third decision, for whom to produce (those who can pay or those who need the product), would also be credited. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/M/J/25 Q5(b) · May/June 2025 · [4 marks] Explain how a market allocates resources. A market is where buyers (demand) and sellers (supply) come together to trade a product. The interaction of demand and supply sets the equilibrium price, and that price acts as a signal and an incentive to producers about how to use their resources. If consumers’ demand for a product increases, its price rises. Producing it becomes more profitable, so firms are encouraged to move more land, labour and capital into making it. If demand falls, its price and profits fall, so firms move resources out of that product and into others. In this way the price mechanism shifts resources towards the products consumers want most, without the government having to decide. Why this scores Marks for explaining that a market is buyers and sellers whose demand and supply create an equilibrium price, that price signals and the profit incentive guide sellers, and that more resources go to products in higher demand and fewer to products in lower demand. The examiner report says many candidates misread ‘a market’ as the economy and wrote about sectors or factors of production, and very few mentioned price at all. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/21 Q2(c) · October/November 2021 · [6 marks] Source material: In Russia, the role of the price mechanism to answer key resource allocation questions is increasing. Analyse how the price mechanism answers the three key resource allocation questions. The price mechanism is the way the forces of demand and supply determine prices in a market economy, and those prices then decide how resources are used. It answers the three key questions without government planning. What to produce. Consumers signal what they want through their spending. If demand for a product rises, its price rises. A higher price means higher profits, so firms have an incentive to produce more and move resources into that industry. If demand for a product falls, its price and profits fall, so firms produce less and resources move elsewhere. Output therefore follows consumer demand. How to produce. Firms aim to maximise profit, so they choose the cheapest combination of factors of production, and the prices of those factors guide the choice. If wages rise relative to the cost of machinery, firms switch to more capital-intensive methods; if labour is cheap, they use more labour-intensive methods. Resources are therefore used efficiently. People’s ability to pay depends on their income, which is also set by the price mechanism: workers whose skills are in high demand and short supply earn high wages, so they can buy the most goods and services. A planned (command) economy is also accepted, but the mark scheme gives no marks for “free market system” or “controlled market system”, so use the syllabus names. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/21 Q5(b) · October/November 2021 · [4 marks] Source material: The US operates a mainly market economic system. Explain two advantages of a market economic system. Consumer sovereignty. In a market economic system, firms aim to make a profit, so they produce the goods and services that consumers are willing to pay for. If consumers want more of a product, its price rises and making it becomes more profitable, so firms move resources into producing it. Consumers therefore decide what is produced. Lower prices and greater efficiency. Private firms compete with each other for customers. To win sales they must keep their costs down, for example by using new technology, and pass this on as lower prices. Firms that are inefficient make losses and leave the market, so resources are used more efficiently. Why this scores Each advantage is identified (1) and explained (1) with a reason linked to the price mechanism, competition or the profit motive. The examiner report says some candidates lost marks by writing about the advantages of a mixed economy, and the mark scheme gives nothing for “no taxes”. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/M/J/20 Q1(h) · May/June 2020 · [6 marks] Source material: The Greek government introduced market-friendly measures, including privatisation and labour market reforms. These measures brought back some investors and moved the Greek economy closer to a market economic system. Discuss whether or not a market economic system improves living standards. A market economic system is one where resources are allocated by the price mechanism, with consumers and private firms deciding what, how and for whom to produce. Why it might improve living standards. Firms compete for consumers’ spending and are motivated by profit, so they have an incentive to cut costs, innovate and produce what people want. Consumers get a wide choice of goods at lower prices, so their incomes buy more and their material living standards rise. In Greece, market-friendly measures such as privatisation brought back some investors, and more investment can increase output, create jobs and raise incomes. Why it might not. A market system will not provide public goods such as street lighting, because firms cannot charge for them, and merit goods such as healthcare and education will be under-consumed by people on low incomes. Income and wealth are likely to be very unequally distributed, so the poor may be left behind. Markets can also be unstable: in a recession many people lose their jobs and incomes, and Greece’s unemployment rate was 24% in 2015. Conclusion. A market system is likely to raise average material living standards through efficiency and choice, but not the living standards of everyone. It is most likely to improve living standards if competition is strong and the government still provides public goods, merit goods and a safety net for the unemployed, which in practice means a mixed economy. Why this scores Up to 4 marks are available for each side, so both are needed for 6. Each point is developed into an effect on living standards (prices, choice, jobs, income), the Greek source is used, and the conclusion makes a judgement with conditions. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/23 Q2(d) · May/June 2023 · [8 marks] Source material: A growing private sector can move an economy towards a market economic system. Discuss whether or not a market economy allocates resources in the best possible way. A market economy is one in which resources are allocated by the price mechanism: private firms decide what to produce in response to consumer demand, with little government intervention. Why it might allocate resources in the best possible way. The price mechanism responds automatically to consumers’ wishes. If demand for electric bikes rises and demand for petrol cars falls, the price of electric bikes rises and the price of petrol cars falls. Making electric bikes becomes more profitable, so firms move land, labour and capital out of car production and into bikes. Resources are therefore used to make what consumers value most, without a government needing to plan it. Competition between private firms also encourages efficiency. Firms that keep costs low and make good-quality products win customers, while inefficient firms make losses and close, releasing their resources to better uses. Wages work in the same way: higher wages attract workers into the jobs where labour is most in demand. As a result, output is produced at low cost and sold at low prices. Why it might not. The market ignores external costs and benefits. A factory that pollutes a river does not pay for the damage, so its product is over-produced, while goods with external benefits, such as vaccinations, are under-produced. In the same way, merit goods such as education are under-consumed because people do not realise their full benefit, demerit goods such as cigarettes are over-consumed, and public goods such as street lighting are not produced at all because firms cannot stop non-payers from benefiting. A market economy may also not stay competitive. A firm may grow into a monopoly, for example through mergers like the one between the two Thai banks, and then restrict output and raise prices. Resources may be slow to move too: if workers are occupationally or geographically immobile, there can be unemployment in declining industries while growing industries are short of labour. Conclusion. A market economy is good at allocating resources to private goods that consumers want, such as clothing or smartphones, when markets are competitive. It does not allocate resources in the best possible way where there are external costs or benefits, merit, demerit or public goods, or monopoly power. How close it comes to the best allocation depends on how competitive its markets are and how important these market failures are, which is why most countries choose a mixed economy. Why this scores This meets Level 3: a definition, two developed arguments on each side (price signals moving resources and competition; externalities, merit, demerit and public goods, monopoly and immobility) and a conclusion that states the conditions. The examiner report says weaker answers confused a market economy with a mixed or planned economy, or just stated points without explaining how resources move. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/24 Q3(d) · October/November 2024 · [8 marks] Source material: However, Madagascar has a largely market economic system. Nearly 70% of Madagascar’s population live in poverty. Discuss whether or not a high level of poverty is likely to exist in a market economic system. A market economic system allocates resources through the price mechanism, with little government intervention. Absolute poverty is when people do not have enough income to meet their basic needs; relative poverty is when people have much less income than the average in their country. Why a high level of poverty is likely. In a market system, people’s incomes depend on the factors of production they own. Workers with few skills earn low wages, while owners of capital and land earn profit and rent, so income and wealth are very unequally distributed. With little or no government welfare, such as unemployment benefits or pensions, people who cannot work or who lose their jobs have no income to fall back on, so they fall into poverty. Merit goods such as education and healthcare are available only to those who can pay for them. Poor families cannot afford them, so their children stay unskilled and unhealthy and earn low wages as adults, which keeps poverty going from one generation to the next. Firms may also grow into monopolies and raise the prices of necessities, reducing what low-income households can buy. Madagascar, with a largely market system, has nearly 70% of its population living in poverty. Why a high level of poverty is not likely. Competition and the profit motive encourage firms to be efficient, which keeps prices low, so people’s incomes buy more. Efficient firms also expand and create jobs; higher employment means more households earn an income and fewer are in absolute poverty. Market economies respond quickly to changes in consumer demand and give entrepreneurs an incentive to invest and innovate, which can lead to high economic growth: Madagascar grew by 6% in 2020. Over time, faster growth raises average incomes, so even if relative poverty remains because incomes are unequal, absolute poverty can fall, as it has in many high-income economies with large private sectors. Conclusion. A market economic system is likely to have a high level of relative poverty because it creates income inequality and provides no safety net. Whether absolute poverty is high depends mainly on how productive and competitive its firms are and how fast the economy grows: a low-income, labour-intensive economy like Madagascar is likely to have high poverty, while a high-income market economy with efficient firms is likely to have low absolute poverty but still some relative poverty. Why this scores This meets Level 3: it defines the key terms, develops two arguments on each side, uses the Madagascar data, and the conclusion separates absolute from relative poverty, which the mark scheme credits as an evaluative point. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 2.10 Market failure These questions test why a free market can produce an inefficient allocation of resources, through external costs and benefits, merit and demerit goods, public goods and monopoly power; examiners reward precise definitions and clear links to over- or under-consumption. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports say candidates often confuse public goods with merit goods, free goods or basic necessities, and give an example of an external cost (such as pollution) without explaining why it is external: it falls on third parties who are not involved in producing or consuming the product. 0455/23/M/J/20 Q5(a) · May/June 2020 · [2 marks] Source material: Part of the change in price may have been the result of UK energy firms abusing their monopoly power. This would be an example of market failure. Define market failure. Market failure is when the market (price) mechanism does not lead to an efficient allocation of resources, for example when firms ignore the external costs of the pollution they cause. Why this scores One mark for the market or price mechanism and one for “does not lead to an efficient allocation of resources”. Both key phrases are needed: a vague answer such as “when a market does not work well” is unlikely to score. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/25 Q1(c) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: However, if rainforests continue to be cut down and soil erosion continues to pollute the coral reefs, killing off marine life, tourism may be discouraged. Explain how tourism causes external costs in St. Kitts and Nevis. External costs are harmful effects on third parties who are not involved in producing or consuming a product, so the tourists and hotels do not pay for them and the social cost of tourism is greater than the private cost. For example, sewage and waste from hotels and tourist boats in St. Kitts and Nevis can pollute the coral reefs and kill marine life, which harms local fishermen who take no part in the tourism. Why this scores One mark for explaining what an external cost is (a cost to third parties, so social cost exceeds private cost) and one for a relevant tourism example. The examiner report says most candidates gave an example such as pollution but did not explain why it was an external cost. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/25 Q3(b) · May/June 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: Its government provides merit goods and public goods. Explain, with an example of each, the difference between a merit good and a public good. Merit good. A merit good is a product that is more beneficial to consumers than they realise, so in a free market it is under-consumed and under-produced. It is rival and excludable, so it can be sold by private firms as well as provided by the government. An example is education. Public good. A public good is non-excludable, because people who do not pay cannot be stopped from using it, and non-rival, because one person’s use does not reduce the amount left for others. Because of the free rider problem, private firms will not supply it, so it is provided by the government and paid for out of taxes. An example is street lighting. Why this scores One mark for each explanation and one for each correct example. The examiner report warns that some candidates compared merit goods with demerit goods, called education or healthcare public goods (they are rival and excludable), or said merit goods are simply “beneficial” rather than more beneficial than people realise. Roads are not accepted as a public good unless qualified. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/22 Q4(b) · October/November 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: However, public goods are not supplied in a market economic system. Explain why public goods would not be supplied in a market economic system. Non-excludability and free riders. Public goods are non-excludable: once a public good such as a flood defence is provided, it is impossible to stop people who have not paid from benefiting. Consumers therefore have an incentive to be free riders and wait for others to pay, so a private firm cannot collect enough revenue to cover its costs. Non-rivalry and the profit motive. Public goods are also non-rival: one more person using street lighting does not reduce the benefit to anyone else and costs the producer nothing extra, so there is no way to charge each extra user a price. Private firms in a market economy are motivated by profit, and because they would make a loss supplying a product they cannot sell, they do not supply public goods at all. Why this scores Each characteristic is identified (1) and linked to why firms cannot earn revenue or profit (1). The mark scheme gives no marks for examples, so the marks come from the explanation. The examiner report notes that some candidates confused public goods with merit goods, free goods or basic necessities. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/O/N/23 Q3(c) · October/November 2023 · [6 marks] Source material: However, there can be market failure due to external costs arising from high energy usage of non‑renewable sources. Analyse the consequences of market failure. Market failure occurs when the free market does not lead to an efficient allocation of resources. Its main consequence is that the wrong quantity of some products is produced and consumed, which reduces society’s welfare. Over-consumption of products with external costs and of demerit goods. Producers and users of digital money do not pay for the pollution caused by the non-renewable energy it uses, so its price is below its full social cost. As a result, more is produced and consumed than is socially efficient, and too many resources are allocated to it. Demerit goods such as cigarettes are over-consumed in the same way because consumers underestimate the harm, leading to ill health and higher healthcare costs for society. Under-consumption of merit goods and products with external benefits. People underestimate the benefits of education and healthcare and ignore the benefits to others, so they buy too little. The economy then has a less skilled and less healthy labour force, which lowers productivity and economic growth. Non-provision of public goods. Because of the free rider problem, private firms will not supply public goods such as defence at all, so society goes without services it values. Abuse of monopoly power. A monopoly can restrict output and charge higher prices, which reduces consumers’ choice and what they can afford, while resources are under-used. Why this scores It defines market failure, then traces each type through to its consequence (over- or under-consumption, misallocation of resources, and effects on health, productivity or prices), using the digital money context. Each link in a chain earns credit; the mark scheme also accepts factor immobility leading to unemployment. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 2.11 Mixed economic system These questions test how and why governments intervene in a mixed economy, through maximum and minimum prices, taxes, subsidies, regulation, privatisation and direct provision; examiners reward answers that trace the effect on price and quantity and then weigh up whether the intervention works. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports say candidates often confuse a minimum price with a maximum price, and on price-control diagrams shift the demand or supply curve instead of drawing a horizontal price line and marking the quantity demanded and quantity supplied at that price. 0455/22/F/M/23 Q3(a) · February/March 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: The Indian government sets a minimum price for sugar cane and subsidises the export of sugar. Define a minimum price. A minimum price is a price floor set by the government above the equilibrium price, below which the product cannot legally be sold, such as the minimum price India sets for sugar cane to protect farmers’ incomes. Why this scores One mark for “set by the government” (or a price floor) and one for “above the equilibrium price”. The examiner report says some candidates confused it with a maximum price or described it as the lowest price a firm can charge and still make a profit. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/F/M/25 Q1(e) · February/March 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: In April 2022, the Romanian Government placed a maximum price on electricity. Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect of setting a maximum price on electricity. The maximum price (Pmax) is set below the equilibrium price (Pe). At this lower price, consumers want to buy Qd of electricity but producers are only willing to supply Qs, so there is a shortage equal to Qd − Qs. The demand and supply curves do not shift. Figure: A maximum price (Pmax) set below the equilibrium price (Pe). At Pmax consumers demand Qd but producers supply only Qs, so there is a shortage of Qd − Qs. Why this scores One mark each for labelled axes, labelled D and S curves, a maximum price drawn below the equilibrium price, and Qd and Qs shown at the maximum price. The examiner report says the strongest diagrams showed both quantities, while some candidates wrongly shifted the demand or supply curve or drew them the wrong way round. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/21 Q1(d) · October/November 2021 · [4 marks] Source material: A successful sale would have raised money for the Indian government and might have increased the airline’s efficiency. Explain two reasons why a government may privatise an industry. To raise revenue. Selling a state-owned firm such as Air India to the private sector brings in a large one-off sum for the government. This money could be spent on education or healthcare, or used to cut taxes or reduce government debt. Air India was also loss-making (its total cost of $2.9bn exceeded its total revenue of $2.2bn in 2018), so privatisation ends the need to use tax revenue to cover its losses. To increase efficiency. Private sector owners are motivated by profit, so they have an incentive to cut waste, lower costs of production and improve the quality of the service. Facing competition from other airlines, a privatised Air India would have to become more efficient to keep its customers, which could lead to lower fares and a better service for passengers. Why this scores One mark for each reason identified and one for each explanation. The examiner report says most candidates picked raising revenue and increasing efficiency from the source; the revenue point is strongest when it says what the money could be used for. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/O/N/25 Q5(c) · October/November 2025 · [6 marks] Analyse how government regulation can reduce market failure. Market failure occurs when the free market leads to an inefficient allocation of resources. Regulation means rules and laws, backed by penalties such as fines, that control what firms and consumers may do. Reducing demerit goods and external costs. Demerit goods such as cigarettes are over-consumed because people underestimate the harm. A law banning smoking in public places, or banning sales to under-18s, directly reduces consumption and protects third parties from passive smoking. Similarly, legal limits on the pollution a factory may emit force firms to cut their external costs, so output moves closer to the socially efficient level. Increasing the consumption of merit goods. Merit goods are under-consumed because people do not realise their full benefits. Making it compulsory to wear seat belts, or for children to attend school until 16, ensures more people consume them, which reduces injuries and raises the skills of the labour force. Controlling monopoly power. A monopoly can restrict output and charge high prices. A regulator can set a maximum price, for example on what a monopoly water company may charge, or block mergers, so consumers pay lower prices and more is produced. Setting minimum standards. Sellers often know more than buyers about a product’s quality. Rules such as hygiene standards for restaurants protect consumers who cannot judge quality for themselves. Why this scores It defines market failure, then builds several chains: the type of market failure, the regulation used, and how it changes consumption or production. The mark scheme rewards only regulation, so taxes and subsidies are deliberately left out. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/O/N/23 Q3(d) · October/November 2023 · [8 marks] Source material: One way of reducing external costs is to tax the product. Discuss whether or not a tax on a product can reduce external costs. External costs are costs imposed on third parties who are not involved in producing or consuming a product, such as pollution from the electricity used to create digital money. A tax on the product is an indirect tax, which raises its cost and price. Why a tax might reduce external costs. A tax increases firms’ costs of production, so the supply curve shifts to the left and the price rises. Consumers respond to the higher price by buying less, so output falls. Since less is produced and consumed, less pollution is created and the market moves closer to the socially efficient output. In effect, the tax makes the polluter pay for some of the external cost it causes. The tax also raises revenue for the government, which can be spent on reducing external costs directly, for example by subsidising renewable energy or cleaning up pollution. It also gives firms an incentive to switch to cleaner methods, such as renewable electricity, if that lets them avoid the tax. Why it might not. If demand for the product is price-inelastic, for example because it is addictive like cigarettes or a necessity with few substitutes like petrol, a rise in price causes only a small fall in quantity demanded. Consumption, and so the external cost, falls very little; the main effect is that consumers pay more. The tax may also be too small compared with the final price of the product to change behaviour, and it is hard for a government to measure external costs in money terms, so it may not know the right rate. If the tax is set high, it may encourage tax evasion and informal markets, where the product is sold untaxed and unregulated, so external costs may not fall at all. Digital money transactions could also simply move to countries with lower taxes. Conclusion. A tax is likely to reduce external costs, but by how much depends mainly on the price elasticity of demand for the product and the size of the tax. It works best when demand is elastic, cleaner substitutes are available and the tax can be enforced. For addictive products or necessities, a tax works better combined with regulation, such as pollution limits, and with the revenue used to fund cleaner alternatives. Why this scores This meets Level 3: it defines external costs, develops two arguments on each side (the effect on supply, price and quantity; revenue and incentives; inelastic demand; evasion and choosing the rate) and reaches a conclusion that names the conditions. Linking the effect to PED, as the mark scheme does, is what lifts the evaluation. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/M/J/24 Q2(d) · May/June 2024 · [8 marks] Source material: However, the supply of housing has not been able to keep up with demand and the government is now setting a maximum price on housing. Discuss whether or not a government should introduce a maximum price on housing. A maximum price is a price ceiling set by the government below the equilibrium price; the product cannot legally be sold for more. A maximum price on housing limits the rent or purchase price that can be charged. Why a government should. In cities like Shenzhen, where the supply of housing has not kept up with demand, prices and rents rise sharply. A maximum price makes housing more affordable for low-income households and migrant workers, so they can afford shelter, a basic necessity. Because they spend less on housing, they have more income left for food, education and healthcare, which raises their living standards and reduces relative poverty and inequality. Affordable housing also helps the wider economy. Firms in the city can attract workers more easily, so labour becomes more geographically mobile and labour shortages fall. Lower housing costs also mean workers press less for wage rises, which helps to control cost-push inflation. Why a government should not. If the maximum price is below the equilibrium price, quantity demanded rises but quantity supplied falls, because building and renting out homes becomes less profitable. This creates a shortage of housing, so many people who want a home at the lower price cannot get one. In the long run, developers may build fewer new homes, making the shortage even worse. A shortage also encourages informal markets, where landlords charge above the legal price or demand extra payments. Landlords trying to protect their profits may spend less on maintenance, so the quality of housing falls. And if the maximum price is set above the equilibrium price, it has no effect at all. Conclusion. A maximum price helps households that already have a home, but it is likely to worsen the shortage of housing, which is Shenzhen’s main problem. It is more likely to be beneficial if it is set only slightly below equilibrium, is enforced to stop informal markets, and is combined with measures to increase supply, such as subsidies for house-building or the government building homes itself. Without extra supply, the government should not rely on a maximum price alone. Why this scores This meets Level 3: a definition, two developed arguments on each side using the Shenzhen context, analysis of the shortage caused by a price below equilibrium, and a conclusion that makes a judgement and names the conditions (the level of the price, enforcement and action on supply). The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0455/22/M/J/25 Q2(d) means Paper 2, variant 2, May/June 2025, Question 2 part (d). F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports note that many candidates confuse commercial banks with central banks, for example saying a commercial bank sets the interest rate or issues the currency. Central banks serve the government and the banking system; commercial banks serve households and firms. 0455/23/O/N/24 Q5(a) · October/November 2024 · [2 marks] Define a central bank. A central bank is a country’s government-owned bank that issues the currency and runs monetary policy, for example by setting the rate of interest. It also acts as the banker to the government and to the commercial banks. Why this scores One mark for “government-owned bank” and one for a correct function, such as operating monetary policy or being the banker to the government and commercial banks. Describing what a commercial bank does, such as taking deposits from the public, scores nothing. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/24 Q4(b) · May/June 2024 · [4 marks] Source material: Its currency, the somoni, has the key characteristics of money. Explain two characteristics of money. Generally acceptable. People must be willing to accept money in exchange for goods and services and in settlement of debts. If sellers trust that they can spend the somoni themselves, they will take it as payment, so it can act as a medium of exchange. Durable. Money has to last a long time without wearing out or losing its physical form. Coins and notes that survive being passed from hand to hand many times can be kept and used later, so they can also be saved as a store of value. Why this scores One mark for each characteristic identified and one for explaining why it lets money do its job. Other creditworthy characteristics are portable, divisible, recognisable, homogeneous and limited in supply. Do not give functions (medium of exchange, store of value) as the characteristics themselves: they belong in the explanation. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/F/M/25 Q5(b) · February/March 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: It has a strong commercial banking sector which has increased its lending in recent years. Explain why commercial banks may increase their lending. To increase profits. Most commercial banks are private-sector firms whose main aim is profit. Every loan earns the bank interest, and the rate it charges borrowers is higher than the rate it pays savers, so lending more increases its revenue and therefore its profits. Greater confidence that loans will be repaid. In a high-income country such as Finland, rising incomes and secure jobs mean households and firms are more likely to keep up their repayments. The risk of bad debts falls, so banks are willing to lend more, and to more customers. Why this scores One mark for each reason identified and one for each explanation. The examiner report says strong answers linked lending to the extra interest earned or to central bank encouragement; weaker answers named reasons without explaining them. The mark scheme gives only one identification mark in total for interest-rate points, so use two different reasons. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/O/N/25 Q3(c) · October/November 2025 · [6 marks] Source material: Japan has faced significant periods of deflation in recent decades. Analyse reasons why central banks are important for an economy. A central bank is the government-owned bank that controls the money supply, runs monetary policy and acts as the banker to the government and to commercial banks. Keeping prices stable. The central bank changes the rate of interest to influence total demand. In a period of deflation, as Japan has experienced, it can cut the interest rate, which makes borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding. Households spend more on credit and firms invest more, so total demand rises and prices stop falling. This matters because deflation encourages people to delay purchases, which cuts output and jobs. When inflation is too high it does the opposite, raising interest rates to protect people’s purchasing power. Maintaining financial stability. The central bank supervises commercial banks, for example by checking they keep enough liquid assets. If a bank runs short of cash it acts as lender of last resort, lending to it so that it does not collapse. This protects savers’ deposits, keeps public confidence in the banking system and makes sure households and firms can still borrow, so spending and investment are not suddenly cut. Managing the exchange rate. The central bank holds the country’s foreign currency reserves and can buy or sell its own currency to stop sharp swings in the exchange rate. A more stable exchange rate reduces uncertainty for exporters and importers, so they can plan and invest with more confidence. Why this scores Each function is linked through to why it matters for the economy, which is what “coherent analysis” needs. The mark scheme credits controlling inflation and deflation through monetary policy, financial stability, lender of last resort and exchange-rate management, and the Japan context shows application. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/22 Q5(d) · October/November 2022 · [8 marks] Source material: In 2019, commercial bank lending to firms and households in Palau increased. Discuss whether or not an increase in commercial bank lending will increase economic growth. Economic growth is an increase in a country’s real GDP, that is, in the output of goods and services. Commercial bank lending is the loans that banks make to households and firms. Why it might increase economic growth. More loans allow households to buy expensive items such as houses, cars and furniture that they could not pay for out of current income. Consumer spending rises, so total demand rises. Firms respond by producing more and employing more workers, so real GDP increases, especially if the economy has spare capacity. Firms can also borrow to invest in capital goods such as machinery, buildings and technology, and new firms can borrow to start up. Investment adds to total demand straight away, but it also increases the economy’s productive capacity, because more and better capital raises productivity. This means output can keep rising in the long run. Why it might not increase economic growth. If the economy is already at or near full employment, firms cannot easily produce more. Higher total demand then pulls up prices rather than output, causing demand-pull inflation instead of growth. The extra spending may also go on imports. Palau is a small island economy that has to import many goods, so loans spent on imported cars or electronics raise output in other countries, not in Palau. In addition, some households and firms may borrow simply to repay old debts, and those who take on more debt must use future income for repayments. If interest rates later rise, their spending and investment will fall, which can reverse any growth. Conclusion. Higher commercial bank lending is likely to give at least a short-term boost to growth. It is most likely to raise growth in the long run if the loans finance investment by firms rather than consumer spending, if the economy has unemployed resources, and if the money is spent on domestically produced goods. In a small, import-dependent economy like Palau, much of the effect of extra household borrowing may leak abroad, so the benefit depends mainly on how much of the lending goes to productive investment. The examiner report gave a Level 1 example that stated points such as “small firms are not as developed” without explaining them, and noted that weaker answers did not distinguish average from total cost. Get it marked → 3.6 Firms and production These questions test what determines a firm’s demand for labour and capital, why firms choose labour-intensive or capital-intensive production, and what raises productivity; examiners reward answers that link each influence to the firm’s costs, output or profit. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports note confusion between productivity (output per worker or per hour) and production (total output). Remember too that the demand for a factor of production is a derived demand : firms want workers and machines because consumers want the products they make. 0455/22/F/M/23 Q4(a) · February/March 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: Over this period, labour productivity increased. Identify two causes of an increase in labour productivity. 1. Better education and training, giving workers higher skills. 2. Advances in technology, giving workers better capital equipment to work with. Why this scores One mark for each correct cause. Other accepted answers include better healthcare, higher pay or bonuses, more experience and specialisation. The mark scheme gives nothing for just “more motivated”, and the examiner report warns against confusing productivity with total production. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/24 Q5(b) · May/June 2024 · [4 marks] Source material: In 2020, demand for both economic goods and factors of production increased in Poland. Explain two influences on demand for factors of production. Demand for the product. Factors of production are a derived demand. When Polish consumers demanded more football shirts, clothing firms needed to increase output, so they demanded more workers, more sewing machines and more factory space. The price of substitute factors. Labour and capital can often replace each other. If the price of machinery falls, or wages rise, firms find it cheaper to use machines instead of workers, so their demand for capital rises and their demand for labour falls. Why this scores Each influence is identified (1) and explained by showing the direction of its effect on demand for the factor (1). The mark scheme wants the price of a substitute or complementary factor, not just “price”. Other valid influences are the price of the factor itself, its productivity and the method of production. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/24 Q3(b) · October/November 2024 · [4 marks] Source material: Most of the country’s industries are labour-intensive. Explain two reasons why a firm may adopt labour-intensive production. Labour is cheap. In a country such as Madagascar, where many people live in poverty, there is a large supply of workers willing to work for low wages. Labour may therefore be cheaper than buying expensive machinery, so using more workers keeps the firm’s costs of production low. The product needs a personal service. Some products, such as hairdressing, tour guiding or handmade crafts, depend on individual attention and skill that machines cannot provide. Consumers value this quality, so the firm uses mainly labour because that is what creates the product customers want to buy. Why this scores One mark for each reason and one for each explanation. The first point uses the context of the stimulus (poverty and a large labour supply). Other accepted reasons include a government subsidy for employing workers and a low-skilled labour force that cannot operate high-technology machinery. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/23 Q4(c) · October/November 2023 · [6 marks] Source material: Recently, US farmers have switched to keeping other livestock and growing crops that changed their demand for labour. Analyse what influences a farmer’s demand for labour. A farmer’s demand for labour is the number of workers the farmer is willing and able to employ at a given wage rate. It is a derived demand, because workers are needed only to produce the food that consumers buy. Demand for the food produced. If demand for the crops or meat the farmer produces rises, the price and the profit from extra output rise. The farmer then expands output and needs more workers, so demand for labour increases. This explains why switching to different livestock or crops changes how many workers farmers need. The wage rate. The lower the wage, the cheaper each worker is to employ, so the farmer can hire more workers and still make a profit. A rise in the national minimum wage would make labour more expensive and reduce the quantity of labour demanded. The productivity and cost of machinery. If the price of farm machinery such as harvesters or drones falls, or it becomes more productive, the farmer can replace workers with machines and production becomes more capital-intensive. Demand for labour falls. If workers become more skilled and productive, each one adds more output, so they become more worth employing and demand for labour rises. Subsidies and the type of farming. A government subsidy for selected foods lowers the farmer’s costs, encouraging higher output and more workers. Some types of farming, such as fruit picking, are labour-intensive, and demand for labour is especially high at harvest time. Why this scores It defines demand for labour and then analyses four separate influences, each with a chain to the number of workers the farmer will hire. Linking to the stimulus (switching crops, subsidies) and to capital as a substitute for labour is exactly what the mark scheme rewards. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/24 Q4(d) · May/June 2024 · [8 marks] Source material: Despite this possibility, some Tajik firms bought new capital equipment. Discuss whether or not consumers would benefit from firms buying new capital equipment. Capital equipment is the man-made machinery, tools and technology that firms use to produce goods and services. Buying new capital equipment is a form of investment. Why consumers might benefit. New machinery usually embodies the latest technology, so it raises productivity: more output is produced with the same workers and materials. This lowers the firm’s average cost of production. If the firm passes these lower costs on, consumers pay lower prices, which raises their purchasing power and allows them to buy more goods and services. Modern equipment also tends to be more accurate, so it reduces mistakes and improves the quality and reliability of products. It may allow the firm to produce entirely new products, and because output increases, goods are more widely available and shortages are less likely. Consumers therefore gain more choice and better products. Why consumers might not benefit. New capital equipment is expensive. In the short run the firm may raise its prices to cover the cost of the purchase or the interest on a loan, so consumers pay more. While workers learn to use the new machines there may be disruption, so output and quality could fall for a time. In addition, the firm may not pass lower costs on at all. A firm with little competition, such as a monopoly, may keep prices the same and take the cost savings as higher profit. Machine-made products can also become more standardised, so consumers who valued handmade or personalised goods lose out. If workers are replaced by machines, some consumers may lose their jobs and their income. Conclusion. Consumers are likely to benefit in the long run, mainly through lower prices and better quality, once the new equipment is working fully. The benefit is smaller, or may not appear, in the short run, or when the firm faces little competition and so has no need to cut its prices. Whether consumers gain therefore depends mainly on how competitive the market is and on the time period being considered. Why this scores Level 3 needs a reasoned discussion of both sides: the answer defines capital, develops two arguments each way (cost and price; quality and choice; short-run price rises; lack of competition and standardisation) and ends with a judgement that depends on competition and time. Each chain goes all the way to the effect on consumers , which is the focus of the question. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 3.7 Firms’ costs, revenue and objectives These questions test the definitions and formulas for costs and revenue, how fixed and average costs behave as output changes, and why firms do not always aim to maximise profit; examiners reward precise formulas and a clear distinction between total and average figures. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports say weaker answers drew total fixed cost rising with output or confused average fixed cost with average variable cost. When asked why a loss-making firm carries on, “to pay its workers” or “to meet customer demand” earns nothing, because these do not stop the losses. 0455/23/O/N/24 Q1(a) · October/November 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: Number of cars produced 32 000 Total cost of cars produced $340.8m Calculate the average cost of producing a car in Belarus in 2021. Average cost = total cost ÷ output = $340 800 000 ÷ 32 000 = $10 650 per car. (On average, each car cost $10 650 to produce in 2021.) Why this scores The single mark is for $10 650 (or $0.01065m). Write the formula first and convert $340.8m into $340 800 000 before dividing, otherwise it is easy to give 0.01065 with no units and lose the mark. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/25 Q3(a) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Define average total cost. Average total cost is total cost divided by the quantity of output, that is, the cost of producing each unit. For example, if a firm’s total cost is $5 000 and it produces 1 000 bottles of perfume, its average total cost is $5 per bottle. Why this scores The mark scheme gives both marks for “total cost divided by output”, and only one for the vaguer “cost per unit”, so state the formula in words. The short example is not required but shows you understand it. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/21 Q5(b) · October/November 2021 · [4 marks] Source material: Many markets are becoming more competitive, causing some firms to make losses. Explain two reasons why a loss-making firm may continue to produce. It expects the loss to be temporary. The firm may be making a loss because of a recession or because it is a new firm still building up its sales. If it expects demand to rise or its costs to fall in the future, it will keep producing because it expects to return to profit in the long run. It can cover the loss. The firm may have large retained profits from earlier, more successful years, which it can use to pay its costs while it is making a loss. Alternatively, the government may subsidise it, for example because it produces a merit good or employs many workers, so the subsidy covers the gap between its revenue and its costs. Why this scores One mark for each reason identified and one for each explanation. The examiner report praised answers based on subsidies and expected future profit, and gave no credit for “to pay its workers” or “to meet customer demand”, which would not solve the losses. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/F/M/22 Q3(c) · February/March 2022 · [6 marks] Analyse, using a diagram, the effect of an increase in output on average fixed cost (AFC) and total fixed cost (TFC). Fixed costs are costs that do not change with the level of output in the short run, such as rent, insurance and loan repayments. They have to be paid even if the firm produces nothing. Total fixed cost. Because fixed costs do not depend on output, an increase in output has no effect on total fixed cost. If a firm pays $10 000 a month in rent, it pays $10 000 whether it makes 100 units or 1 000 units. TFC is therefore shown as a horizontal line in the diagram. Average fixed cost. AFC is total fixed cost divided by output. As output rises, the same total fixed cost is spread over more units, so AFC falls continuously. With rent of $10 000, AFC is $100 per unit at an output of 100 but only $10 per unit at an output of 1 000. In the diagram, an increase in output from Q1 to Q2 causes AFC to fall from AFC1 to AFC2. This is why firms with high fixed costs try to increase output: spreading fixed costs more thinly lowers their average total cost and allows them to charge lower prices or earn more profit on each unit. In the long run, however, all costs can change, for example if the firm moves to bigger premises, which would shift TFC upwards. Figure: Total fixed cost (TFC) stays the same at every level of output, so it is a horizontal line. Average fixed cost (AFC = TFC ÷ output) falls continuously as output rises, from AFC1 at Q1 to AFC2 at Q2. Why this scores The mark scheme gives up to 4 marks for the diagram (axes labelled costs and output, a horizontal TFC, a downward-sloping AFC, both curves labelled) and 2 for the written analysis that TFC does not change and AFC falls because TFC is divided by a larger output. The examiner report says some candidates drew TFC rising, or confused AFC with average variable cost. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/F/M/23 Q2(d) · February/March 2023 · [8 marks] Source material: Some of their firms have grown and now compete with foreign multinational companies (MNCs) and public sector firms. Discuss whether or not private sector firms are likely to charge lower prices than public sector firms. Private sector firms are owned by individuals or shareholders and usually aim to maximise profit. Public sector firms are owned by the government and often aim to provide an affordable service and to increase social welfare. Why private sector firms might charge lower prices. Most private sector firms face competition from rivals. To attract customers and avoid losing market share, they must keep their prices low. They also have a strong incentive to be efficient: if they waste resources their costs rise, they make losses and they may go out of business. Lower costs allow them to charge lower prices than a public sector firm that has no fear of closing down. Large private sector firms, such as MNCs, may also produce on a very large scale and gain economies of scale, such as bulk buying and advanced technology. They may have more funds to invest in new machinery than a government-owned firm, which lowers their average cost and allows them to cut prices. Why private sector firms might not charge lower prices. The main objective of a private sector firm is usually profit, so if it can charge a high price without losing many customers, it will. This is most likely if it is a monopoly with no close rivals, or if demand for its product is price-inelastic, for example water or electricity. Public sector firms, by contrast, may deliberately charge low prices to make essential services affordable for poorer households, for example public transport. They may be subsidised by the government, so they can charge a price below their cost of production. A public sector firm may also be very large, such as a national electricity company, and gain its own economies of scale. Conclusion. Private sector firms are likely to charge lower prices than public sector firms when they face strong competition, because competition forces them to keep costs and prices down. However, where a private firm is a monopoly selling an essential product, it is likely to charge more than a subsidised public sector firm whose objective is affordability rather than profit. The answer therefore depends mainly on the level of competition in the market and on whether the public sector firm is subsidised. Why this scores This reaches Level 3 by explaining how each firm’s objective and situation affects its price, rather than only stating the objectives. The examiner report said many candidates recognised the different motives but did not go on to explain the effect on prices, and that stronger answers explored competition, funds available and the size of firms, as this answer does. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 3.8 Market structure These questions test the features of competitive markets and monopoly and how each affects consumers through price, quality, choice and efficiency; examiners reward explained chains (why a monopoly might have lower costs, or why competition pushes prices down), not bare assertions. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports say weaker answers state that one firm “may charge a lower price” without explaining why (economies of scale), are one-sided against monopolies, or write about perfect competition, which is not on the syllabus. Stay with the idea of a competitive market with many firms and few barriers to entry. 0455/22/O/N/21 Q1(c) · October/November 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: share of India’s international and national air travel market in 1994 100% Explain one characteristic that suggests that Air India was a monopoly in 1994. In 1994 Air India had 100% of India’s air travel market, so it was the only firm supplying air travel in the country, a pure monopoly. With no competing airline for passengers to switch to, Air India faced no effective competition. Why this scores One mark for using the evidence (a 100% market share) and one for explaining what it means: the only firm, with no competition. The examiner report says most candidates found the figure but only some went on to explain it, which the command word “Explain” requires. Being able to set price (a price maker) would also be credited. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/24 Q2(b) · October/November 2024 · [4 marks] Source material: Some of the country’s firms operate in competitive markets but some are monopolies. Explain two characteristics of monopoly. High barriers to entry. A monopoly is protected by barriers that make it difficult for new firms to enter the industry, such as the very high cost of setting up, patents or legal rights granted by the government. As a result, it can keep its position as the single or dominant supplier and continue to earn high profits in the long run. It is a price maker. Because consumers have no close substitutes to switch to, the monopoly controls the supply of the product and can set its own price. It can restrict output to push the price up, and consumers have little choice but to pay it, so demand for its product is relatively price-inelastic. Why this scores One mark for each characteristic identified and one for each explanation. Other creditworthy characteristics include being the only firm or having a dominant market share, a unique product with no close substitutes, and large size giving economies of scale. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/24 Q5(c) · October/November 2024 · [6 marks] Source material: There are many firms in the Peruvian tourism industry. Analyse the benefits consumers may gain from a competitive market. A competitive market is one with many firms selling similar products and low barriers to entry, so consumers have many close substitutes to choose from. Lower prices. Because consumers can easily switch to a rival, each firm must keep its prices low to attract customers and win market share. If one Peruvian tour operator raised its prices, its customers would go to another. Lower prices increase consumers’ purchasing power, so they can buy more with the same income. Higher quality and innovation. To stand out from rivals, firms try to improve their products, for example better hotels, guides or booking websites. Competition also pressures firms to be efficient and to cut waste, because inefficient firms with high costs are driven out of the market. Consumers therefore receive better products at lower cost. More choice. With many firms, consumers can choose between a wide variety of products, from budget backpacker tours to luxury holidays, so they are more likely to find one that matches their tastes and income. Responsiveness to consumers. Firms in a competitive market must respond quickly to changes in what consumers want, or lose sales to rivals that do. Resources are therefore allocated according to consumer demand, which is known as consumer sovereignty. Why this scores Defines a competitive market, then analyses four separate benefits, each with a chain from many firms → firm behaviour → gain for consumers, applied to the tourism context. The mark scheme credits exactly these: low prices, quality and innovation, choice and responsiveness to demand. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/25 Q3(d) · May/June 2025 · [8 marks] Source material: There are several firms in the industry, but the number is declining. There is a possibility that soon there may be just one firm in the industry. Discuss whether or not consumers would benefit from only one firm producing shampoo. If only one firm produced shampoo, it would be a monopoly: the single supplier of a product, protected by barriers to entry. Why consumers might benefit. A single firm would supply the whole market, so it would produce on a very large scale. It could buy ingredients and bottles in bulk at a discount and use the most advanced, automated production lines. These economies of scale would lower its average cost. If the firm passed some of these savings on, consumers could pay a lower price than when several smaller firms each had higher costs. A monopoly may also earn high profits and feel secure that rivals cannot copy its ideas. It can therefore afford to spend heavily on research and development, producing better shampoos, for example for different hair types, and maintaining a high quality. Consumers would also save time, as they would not need to compare many brands. Why consumers might not benefit. With no competition, consumers cannot switch to another supplier, so demand for the firm’s shampoo becomes more price-inelastic. A profit-maximising monopoly can restrict supply and raise its price without losing many sales, so consumers pay more and lose purchasing power. Consumers would also have less choice: the firm may offer only a few types of shampoo. With no rivals to fear, it has less incentive to keep quality high or to be efficient, and if its quality falls, consumers have no alternative. A very large firm may also suffer diseconomies of scale, such as poor communication, which raise its average cost and its prices. Conclusion. Consumers are more likely to lose than gain from only one shampoo producer, because without competition the firm has the power and the incentive to raise prices and reduce choice. They could benefit if the firm gains large economies of scale and passes them on as lower prices, but that is most likely only if the government regulates its prices or if the threat of imported shampoo keeps it efficient. Why this scores This is a Level 3 answer: it defines monopoly and then explains why a single firm might have lower costs or higher prices, using economies of scale, R&D and price elasticity. The examiner report criticised answers that claimed one firm would charge a lower price without explaining why, and those that said pollution would fall, since pollution depends on total output and methods, not the number of firms. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/20 Q3(d) · October/November 2020 · [8 marks] Source material: Privatisation can reduce monopoly power in a market. Discuss whether or not a government should allow monopolies. A monopoly is a single firm that supplies the whole of a market, or has a dominant share of it, and is protected by barriers to entry. Why a government should allow monopolies. A monopoly produces on a very large scale, so it can gain economies of scale, such as bulk-buying discounts and specialised machinery. Its average cost may therefore be lower than if many small firms shared the market, and it can charge lower prices. In industries such as water supply or railways, having several firms each building their own pipes or tracks would waste resources, so one firm is more efficient. Monopolies often earn high profits, which they can reinvest in research and development. This can lead to new, better-quality products and more efficient methods of production. A large monopoly may also be able to compete with big foreign firms in international markets, increasing the country’s exports. A state-owned monopoly may even have social welfare objectives and keep its prices low. Why a government should not allow monopolies. A private monopoly with no rivals can abuse its market power. Since consumers have no alternative, it can restrict output and raise its price to maximise profit, so consumers pay more and buy less. This is a form of market failure because resources are not allocated in the way consumers would choose. Without the pressure of competition, a monopoly may also become complacent. It has little incentive to cut costs, improve quality or offer choice, so costs may rise and products may be poorer. The high profits go to the owners at the expense of consumers, which can widen income inequality, especially if the product is a necessity such as electricity. Conclusion. A government should allow monopolies in industries where large-scale production gives major economies of scale or where competition would waste resources, such as water supply, but only if it regulates their prices and quality. Where a monopoly is likely to raise prices and become inefficient, the government should prevent it or open the market to competition, for example through privatisation and allowing new firms to enter. The decision depends on whether the cost savings from size are large enough to outweigh the risk of abuse of market power. Why this scores Level 3 requires both sides to be developed; the examiner report noted that weaker answers were stronger on not allowing monopolies, while strong answers also evaluated the benefits (better quality, funds for research and development, competing with foreign firms). This answer gives both sides equal depth and ends with a conditional judgement about regulation and economies of scale. Written your own answer?
