x: Topical Past Papers · Topic 6 Past Paper Questions: International Trade and Globalisation 23 real Cambridge IGCSE Economics Paper 2 questions from 2020 to 2025, sorted by sub-topic, each with its exact paper reference and a full-mark exemplar answer. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0455/22/M/J/25 Q2(d) means Paper 2, variant 2, May/June 2025, Question 2 part (d). F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 6.1 International specialisation · 6.2 Globalisation, free trade and protection · 6.3 Foreign exchange rates · 6.4 Current account of balance of payments 6.1 International specialisation These questions test why whole countries concentrate on producing particular goods and services and what they gain and risk by doing so; examiners reward answers that stay at the level of the country and link specialisation to efficiency, trade, growth and dependence. What examiners keep seeing The 2021 and 2022 examiner reports both note candidates writing about workers specialising (division of labour, boredom on a production line) when the question was about a country specialising. Keep every point about national output, exports, imports and reliance on a few industries. 0455/22/M/J/21 Q1(b) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Source material: Producing just a few products can be risky for a country. Identify two disadvantages of a country specialising. 1. World demand for the country’s main export may fall, for example if new competitor countries start producing it. 2. Output of the main product may be cut by bad weather, disease or a natural disaster, as can happen with an agricultural crop such as cherries. Why this scores One mark for each of two disadvantages. The mark scheme says that simply writing “it relies on a small number of industries” is not enough: say what could go wrong. Other creditworthy answers are non-renewable resources running out, structural unemployment and over-dependence on imports. The examiner report notes that some candidates wrote about workers specialising instead of countries. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/23 Q1(c) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Source material: Honduras used to concentrate on growing bananas and coffee, gaining skills and a good reputation in those industries. Explain one advantage of an economy specialising. By concentrating on bananas and coffee, Honduran farmers and workers gained skills in those industries. More skilled workers are more productive, so Honduras could produce more output at a lower cost per unit and of a higher quality, making its exports more competitive on world markets. Why this scores One mark for an advantage taken from the source material (gaining skills, or gaining a good reputation) and one for explaining it (higher productivity and lower costs, or a good reputation raising demand). The mark scheme says the identification mark must come directly from the source, so quote its idea rather than a textbook advantage. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/O/N/23 Q4(b) · October/November 2023 · [4 marks] Source material: However, despite still being in the top 5 of natural rubber exporters in the world, Malaysia has moved towards producing manufactured goods that use natural rubber instead of just producing and exporting this primary product. Explain two reasons why a country may change its specialisation. A change in costs of production. Natural rubber is labour-intensive, so as a country develops and its wages rise, producing it becomes more expensive. Countries with cheaper labour can then produce it at a lower cost, so the country loses its cost advantage and moves its resources into products where it is now relatively more efficient, such as manufactured rubber goods. A change in demand. If world demand shifts towards higher-value products, for example rubber gloves and tyres rather than raw rubber, firms can earn more revenue and profit by making those products. Resources move to the goods that buyers now want, so the country’s pattern of specialisation changes. Why this scores Each reason is identified (1) and then explained (1) by showing why producing the old product became less attractive. Other reasons the mark scheme credits include the discovery of new resources, new technology and other countries’ producers gaining a competitive advantage. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/M/J/25 Q5(c) · May/June 2025 · [6 marks] Source material: This agency also aims to coordinate trade between African countries to help technological development. Analyse the benefits a country may gain from exporting to and importing from other countries. International trade is the buying and selling of goods and services across national borders: exports are sold abroad and imports are bought from abroad. Benefits of exporting. Exporting lets a country specialise in what it is best at producing. Its workers build up skills and its firms become more efficient, so output rises. Selling abroad also gives firms a much larger market than the home country alone, so they can grow and gain economies of scale, which lowers their average cost and lets them charge more competitive prices. Exports are also a component of total (aggregate) demand. When foreign buyers spend more on a country’s products, domestic firms raise output and take on more workers, which causes economic growth and reduces unemployment. The export revenue also brings foreign currency into the country, which helps the current account of the balance of payments. Benefits of importing. Imports give consumers a wider choice of goods and services, often at lower prices than domestic firms could offer, which raises living standards. Firms can import raw materials and capital goods that the country cannot produce, or cannot produce cheaply, which lowers their costs of production. Imports also bring competition, which puts pressure on domestic firms to cut costs and improve quality. Trading with other countries spreads ideas and technology, as the African Space Agency hopes, which raises productivity and allows the economy to produce more in the future. Why this scores It defines international trade, then analyses exports and imports separately, as the examiner report advised, linking each to a macroeconomic outcome (growth, employment, living standards, costs). Each paragraph is a chain worth several marks. The report warns against treating this as a “Discuss”: no disadvantages are needed. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/M/J/22 Q1(g) · May/June 2022 · [6 marks] Source material: However, to ensure growth is sustainable, the government sees the importance of economic diversification and does not want the economy to overspecialise. Discuss whether or not specialisation at a national level is harmful to an economy. Get it marked → 0455/21/O/N/20 Q4(d) · October/November 2020 · [8 marks] Source material: The intention is to raise economic growth through more international trade. Discuss whether or not increased international trade can promote economic growth. Economic growth is an increase in a country’s real GDP, its output of goods and services. International trade is the exchange of goods and services between countries, through exports and imports. Why it might promote economic growth. Lower trade barriers give domestic firms access to a much larger market. Small and medium-sized firms in ASEAN countries can sell to millions more customers, so exports rise. Exports are an injection into total (aggregate) demand, so firms increase output and employ more workers, and real GDP rises. Selling to a larger market also lets firms specialise and gain economies of scale, which lowers their average costs. Imports of cheaper raw materials and capital goods reduce costs further, while foreign competition pushes domestic firms to become more efficient. Lower costs and higher productivity increase the economy’s productive capacity, so growth can be sustained in the long run. Why it might not promote economic growth. More trade also means more imports. If consumers switch from domestic products to cheaper foreign ones, spending leaks out of the economy, total demand for domestic output falls and real GDP may fall rather than rise. Increased international trade is likely to promote growth when the country’s firms are competitive enough for exports to rise faster than imports and can use the larger market to gain economies of scale. The mark scheme’s Level 2 example was marked down for being limited on one side. Written your own answer? Discuss whether or not high tariffs can reduce unemployment. A tariff is a tax on imports. Unemployment is when people who are willing and able to work cannot find a job. Why high tariffs might reduce unemployment. A high tariff, such as India’s 90% tariff on coffee, raises the price of imports. Consumers switch to domestically produced substitutes, so demand for Indian coffee rises. Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/25 Q4(d) · October/November 2025 · [8 marks] Source material: Some economists suggest that the Chadian Government should impose import quotas to reduce its trade in goods deficit. Discuss whether or not imposing import quotas will reduce a trade in goods deficit. An import quota is a limit on the quantity or value of a product that can be imported over a period. A trade in goods deficit occurs when spending on imports of goods is greater than revenue from exports of goods. Why quotas might reduce the deficit. A quota directly restricts the quantity of goods coming into the country. With fewer imports allowed in, the amount spent on imports falls, so the gap between import spending and export revenue narrows. Because imports are scarcer, their price rises. Consumers and firms then switch to domestically produced substitutes. Domestic firms sell more and may expand, which further reduces the need for imports and could, in time, allow them to export. Why quotas might not reduce the deficit. If the quota is set above the quantity currently imported, it has no effect. If it only covers a few goods, total import spending changes little. Trading partners may retaliate by restricting Chad’s exports, which reduces export revenue and can leave the deficit just as large. Quotas may also encourage smuggling. If imported raw materials and capital goods are restricted, Chad’s own producers face higher costs, which makes its exports less competitive. Conclusion. Import quotas can reduce a trade in goods deficit in the short run if they cover a wide range of products for which domestic substitutes exist and trading partners do not retaliate. Why this scores Level 3: both key terms are defined (the mark scheme gives Level 1 credit for understanding quotas), each side has two developed arguments, and the conclusion is applied to Chad and names the conditions: breadth of the quota, domestic substitutes and retaliation. Written your own answer? Write the price effect out each time: a fall in the currency makes exports cheaper abroad and imports more expensive at home. 0455/21/M/J/22 Q2(a) · May/June 2022 · [2 marks] Define foreign exchange rate. A foreign exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another currency, for example A$1 = US$0.65. Why this scores One mark for “price” (or value) of a currency and one for “in terms of another currency”. The examiner report notes that weaker answers mentioned another currency but left out the word price or value, and very weak ones confused it with the balance between exports and imports. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/23 Q4(b) · May/June 2023 · [4 marks] Source material: The year saw an increase in the value of the country’s floating foreign exchange rate. Explain two causes of an increase in the value of a country’s floating foreign exchange rate. A floating exchange rate is set by the demand for and supply of the currency, so its value rises when demand for it increases or supply of it falls. Higher demand for the country’s exports. If incomes rise abroad, or the country’s products become cheaper or better quality than rivals’, foreigners buy more of its exports. To pay for them they must buy the country’s currency, so demand for the currency rises and its value increases. A rise in the rate of interest. Higher interest rates make it more rewarding to save money in the country’s banks. Why this scores Each cause is identified (1) and explained through the demand for the currency (1). The mark scheme also credits causes on the supply side, such as a fall in imports, but credits “higher demand” only once, so the two causes here are clearly different. The examiner report notes that some candidates explained a fall instead of a rise. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/F/M/25 Q4(c) · February/March 2025 · [6 marks] Source material: Its high inflation rate of 22% had several effects on the country’s firms. In 2022 and the start of 2023, Nigerians increased their demand for foreign currency. Analyse the causes of an increase in the demand for foreign currency. People and firms demand foreign currency when they need to pay for goods, services or assets priced in another country’s currency. Several changes can increase that demand. Buying more imports. With inflation at 22%, Nigerian goods were rising in price faster than many foreign goods, so imports became relatively cheaper and more attractive. Nigerian households and firms switched to imports, and to pay foreign suppliers they had to buy more US dollars and other currencies. Rising incomes, more foreign travel and more students studying abroad have the same effect. Higher interest rates abroad. If interest rates in other countries rise above those at home, savers earn a higher return by moving their money abroad. To deposit funds in foreign banks they must first buy foreign currency, so these hot money flows increase demand for it. Speculation and loss of confidence. If people expect their own currency to fall in value, perhaps because of high inflation, they buy foreign currency to protect the value of their savings and to make a profit when they later sell it. Expectations can therefore raise demand for foreign currency quickly. Investment abroad and profit flows. Firms that want to set up branches or buy assets in other countries need foreign currency to do so. Foreign MNCs operating in the country also buy their home currency when they send profits back, which adds to demand for foreign currency. Why this scores It explains why foreign currency is demanded, then analyses four separate causes, each linked to a reason for buying the currency, and uses Nigeria’s 22% inflation from the stimulus. The examiner report praised the strong analysis of interest rates and foreign direct investment on this question. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/O/N/25 Q1(h) · October/November 2025 · [6 marks] Source material: Malawi’s foreign exchange rate fell in 2022. The country’s currency, the kwacha, bought fewer US dollars. Discuss whether or not a government should try to stop its country’s foreign exchange rate falling in value. A fall in the foreign exchange rate (depreciation) means the currency buys fewer units of other currencies, so exports become cheaper abroad and imports more expensive at home. Why the government should try to stop the fall. Imports become more expensive. Malawi imports fuel, and many firms rely on imported raw materials and capital goods, so their costs of production rise. They pass these on as higher prices, causing cost-push inflation, which hits the poor hardest and can slow economic growth. A falling currency can also damage confidence. Foreign investors may expect further falls and hold back investment, and any debts owed in US dollars become more expensive to repay in kwacha. Why the government should allow the fall. Malawi’s exports, such as tea and sugar, become cheaper for foreign buyers, so demand for them rises, while imports fall. This could help reduce its current account deficit of 12.9% of GDP and raise output and employment in export industries. Stopping the fall is also costly. The central bank would have to use its foreign currency reserves to buy kwacha or raise interest rates, which would reduce investment and spending, and money used this way has an opportunity cost in lower spending on education or healthcare. Conclusion. Malawi should allow a gradual fall, because it needs more competitive exports to reduce its large current account deficit. It should intervene only if the fall becomes rapid enough to cause high inflation through fuel and other import prices, since a poor country with low reserves cannot afford to defend its currency for long. Why this scores Up to 4 marks are available for each side, with a maximum of 3 if reasons are not developed. Each reason here is a developed chain applied to Malawi (imported fuel, tea and sugar exports, the 12.9% deficit). The mark scheme warns that many candidates get the effects the wrong way round, so the opening sentence fixes the direction before the argument starts. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/21/M/J/25 Q5(d) · May/June 2025 · [8 marks] Source material: The Australian Government imposes relatively low import tariffs and the country has a floating exchange rate. Discuss whether or not having a floating exchange rate benefits an economy. A floating exchange rate is one whose value is determined by the market forces of demand for and supply of the currency, without the government or central bank fixing it. Why it might benefit an economy. A floating rate can correct a current account imbalance automatically. If a country has a deficit, it is supplying more of its currency to buy imports than foreigners demand to buy its exports, so the exchange rate falls. Its exports become cheaper and its imports more expensive, so exports rise, imports fall and the deficit shrinks without the government having to act. The government and central bank do not have to keep large reserves of foreign currency to defend a fixed value, and they do not need to change interest rates to protect the exchange rate. This leaves interest rates free to be used for other macroeconomic aims, such as controlling inflation or reducing unemployment. Why it might not benefit an economy. A floating rate can change frequently and unpredictably. Firms do not know how much they will earn from exports or pay for imports, which makes planning difficult and can discourage trade and investment, including investment by foreign MNCs. Speculation can make the swings larger. If traders expect the currency to fall, they sell it, which makes it fall further than the economy’s trade position would justify. A sharp fall raises import prices and can cause cost-push inflation, while a sharp rise makes exports uncompetitive and can cause unemployment in export industries. Conclusion. A floating exchange rate is likely to benefit a large, diversified economy with well-developed financial markets, such as Australia, where firms can protect themselves against currency changes and the automatic adjustment of the current account is valuable. It is less beneficial for a small economy that relies on one export or on imported essentials, where large swings in the currency cause damaging uncertainty and inflation. Why this scores Level 3: a definition, then developed arguments that are about the floating system itself (automatic correction, no reserves needed, freedom for interest rates; uncertainty, speculation) rather than just a strong or weak currency, which the examiner report says limited many answers. The report singled out automatic correction of the current account as the mark of the best responses. Written your own answer? What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports note candidates confusing a current account deficit with a government budget deficit, and many forgetting that the current account includes primary and secondary income as well as trade in goods and services. Name the component you are talking about. 0455/22/M/J/24 Q1(a) · May/June 2024 · [1 mark] Source material: Trade in goods and services balance – $3bn Primary and secondary income balance $0.6bn Calculate Tunisia’s balance on the current account of its balance of payments. Current account balance = trade in goods and services balance + primary and secondary income balance = −$3bn + $0.6bn = −$2.4bn (Tunisia has a current account deficit of $2.4bn: its surplus on income only partly offsets its trade deficit.) Why this scores The mark is for −$2.4bn; the minus sign or the word deficit is needed to show which way the balance goes. Add the two balances: subtracting the $0.6bn instead of adding it gives −$3.6bn and scores zero. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/M/J/24 Q4(a) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: In 2021, the US had a trade in goods deficit on the current account of its balance of payments. Define a trade in goods deficit. A trade in goods deficit is when a country’s expenditure on imports of goods is greater than its revenue from exports of goods over a period of time. Why this scores Two marks for saying that import expenditure on goods exceeds export revenue from goods. “Imports exceed exports” on its own scores only 1, so use the words expenditure and revenue (or value). Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/23/M/J/22 Q4(b) · May/June 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: Despite having more imports of goods than exports of goods, it still records a surplus on the current account of its balance of payments. Explain how a country with more imports of goods than exports of goods can still record a surplus on the current account of its balance of payments. The current account has four parts: trade in goods, trade in services, primary income and secondary income. Importing more goods than it exports gives a country a deficit on trade in goods, but the overall current account can still be in surplus if the other three parts together have a larger surplus. For example, the country may export more services than it imports, such as tourism or financial services. It may also receive a large primary income from abroad, such as interest, profits and dividends on investments its citizens own in other countries, and a large secondary income, such as foreign aid and money sent home by its nationals working abroad. If these credits outweigh the trade in goods deficit, the current account is in surplus. The examiner report says very few candidates saw this; answers about high export prices and low import prices got only partial credit. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/F/M/22 Q2(c) · February/March 2022 · [6 marks] Source material: South Africa’s foreign exchange rate fell from 1 SA rand = US$0.08 in 2018 to 1 SA rand = US$0.06 in 2019. Analyse how a fall in a country’s foreign exchange rate could reduce a deficit on the current account of its balance of payments. A current account deficit occurs when the money flowing out of a country for imports and other debit items is greater than the money flowing in from exports and other credit items. Exports become cheaper. When the rand falls from US$0.08 to US$0.06, a South African product priced at R100 falls in price for American buyers from $8 to $6. South African exports become more price-competitive, so foreign demand for them rises and South Africa’s export revenue increases. Imports become more expensive. A product costing $10 now costs South Africans about R167 instead of R125. Households and firms buy fewer imports and switch to domestically produced substitutes, so spending on imports falls and less money flows out of the country. With export revenue rising and import expenditure falling, net exports increase and the deficit on the current account narrows. This is most likely if demand for exports and imports is price-elastic, so that the changes in quantity are larger than the changes in price. In addition, money sent home by South Africans working abroad is worth more in rand, which raises the value of secondary income and further helps reduce the deficit. Why this scores It defines a current account deficit (1), then follows both chains from price to demand to revenue or expenditure, which the examiner report praised in strong answers. Using the stimulus exchange rates to work out new prices shows clear understanding, and the price-elasticity condition and remittances are extra points the mark scheme credits. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/M/J/23 Q5(d) · May/June 2023 · [8 marks] Source material: In 2019, China’s economic growth rate was 6.1% and Chinese households increased their spending. Discuss whether or not a country with a high economic growth rate will have a deficit on the current account of its balance of payments. Economic growth is an increase in real GDP. A deficit on the current account occurs when a country’s spending on imports and other debit items exceeds its earnings from exports and other credit items. Why it might have a deficit. Higher growth raises incomes, so households are both able and more willing to spend more, including on imported goods and on services such as foreign holidays. As spending on imports rises faster than export earnings, more money flows out than in. Firms expanding production also import more raw materials and capital goods. A fast-growing home market can also draw goods away from exports, as firms find it easier to sell at home. If total demand grows faster than the economy’s ability to produce, prices rise and the country’s products become less price-competitive abroad, so exports fall and imports rise. Why it might not have a deficit. The growth may be export-led. If the economy is growing because foreign demand for its products is rising, as with China, export revenue increases along with output, so the current account may move into surplus. Growth also encourages firms to invest in new capital and technology, which raises productivity, lowers costs and improves quality. Higher tax revenue from growth can fund education and healthcare, raising labour productivity. Both make domestic products more competitive, so exports rise and consumers switch away from imports. Conclusion. A country with a high growth rate is likely to have a current account deficit when growth is driven by household spending and it relies on imported consumer goods and inputs. It is unlikely to have a deficit when growth is export-led and accompanied by rising productivity, as in China, where strong export earnings outweigh the extra imports that higher incomes bring. Why this scores Level 3: definitions, two developed arguments on each side with clear links to imports and exports, and a conclusion that depends on what is driving the growth. The examiner report criticised answers that said exports would rise without explaining why, and those that confused a current account deficit with a budget deficit. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0455/22/O/N/25 Q5(d) · October/November 2025 · [8 marks] Source material: The country has one of the world’s largest deficits on the current account of its balance of payments (as a percentage of GDP). Some economists suggest cutting taxes would reduce this deficit. Discuss whether or not cuts in taxes will reduce a deficit on the current account of a country’s balance of payments. A current account deficit is when a country’s spending on imports and other debit items is greater than its earnings from exports and other credit items. Tax cuts could be cuts in income tax, corporation tax, indirect taxes or tariffs. Why tax cuts might reduce the deficit. A cut in corporation tax leaves firms with more profit after tax, so they are more able and willing to invest in new machinery and technology. This raises productivity and quality and lowers costs, so their products become more competitive. Exports rise and consumers buy domestic products instead of imports, which reduces the deficit. Lower corporation tax may also attract export-oriented MNCs to the country. A cut in income tax increases the reward from working, which may motivate workers to work harder, raising productivity and lowering costs. Cutting tariffs on imported raw materials and components lowers firms’ costs too, so they can cut the prices of their exports. Why tax cuts might not reduce the deficit. A cut in income tax raises disposable income, and some of this extra income is spent on imports, so import spending may rise and the deficit may widen. Higher spending also increases total demand, which may cause demand-pull inflation and make the country’s products less price-competitive abroad. Tax cuts also reduce government revenue, so the government may have to spend less on education, healthcare and transport, which harms productivity in the long run. In addition, if foreign MNCs are attracted, they send their profits home, which is a debit on primary income and adds to the current account deficit. Conclusion. Tax cuts are more likely to reduce the deficit if they are targeted at firms, such as lower corporation tax linked to investment or cheaper imported inputs for exporters, because these raise competitiveness. Cuts in income tax are likely to make the deficit worse in the short run, since much of the extra spending will go on imports. The overall effect depends on which taxes are cut and on whether higher investment raises productivity quickly enough to outweigh the extra spending on imports. Why this scores Level 3: definitions, developed arguments on both sides that distinguish between types of tax, and a conclusion that judges which tax cuts would work and why. The mark scheme rewards recognising that different taxes have different effects, and the MNC profit point links to primary income. Written your own answer? Salt is very cheap and is bought infrequently, so a price change is hardly noticed and has very little effect on the quantity bought. Demand is price-elastic when a change in price causes a greater percentage change in quantity demanded, so PED is greater than 1. Why demand may be price-elastic. There are many close substitutes for chocolate, both other chocolate brands and other snacks such as biscuits or sweets. If one firm raises the price of its chocolate bars, consumers can easily switch to a rival brand, so quantity demanded falls by a larger percentage than the price rise. Nobody needs it to live, so if the price rises, especially for premium chocolate, consumers can cut back, buy it less often or postpone the purchase. Over a longer time period, consumers also have more opportunity to find alternatives and change their habits, so demand becomes more elastic over time. Why demand may be price-inelastic. A chocolate bar is cheap and takes up only a small proportion of most people’s income, particularly in high-income countries. A 10% rise in the price of a bar is hardly noticed, so consumers keep buying roughly the same amount and quantity demanded falls by a smaller percentage than the price. In addition, chocolate contains sugar and many people buy it out of habit, so for regular consumers it can be habit-forming. Strong brand loyalty, built up by advertising, also means consumers may stick with their favourite brand even when its price rises. Both make demand less responsive to price. Conclusion. Demand for one particular brand of chocolate is likely to be price-elastic, because so many close substitutes exist. However, demand for chocolate as a whole is likely to be price-inelastic in high-income countries, because it is cheap relative to incomes and habit-forming. The answer depends on how widely the product is defined, the income of consumers, whether it is an everyday bar or an expensive luxury box, and the time period being considered. Discuss whether or not demand for cars will become more price-elastic in the future. Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price. Demand would become more price-elastic if a change in the price of cars caused a bigger percentage change in the quantity of cars demanded than it does now. Why demand may become more price-elastic. If these alternatives become cheaper and more convenient, consumers can more easily choose not to buy a car when car prices rise, so quantity demanded will fall by a larger percentage. There may also be more car producers and models to choose from, for example new firms making electric cars. Habit also matters: people who are used to the convenience of driving are reluctant to give it up. Demand for cars is likely to become more price-elastic in large cities, where public transport and ride-sharing provide closer substitutes, and for individual brands as competition grows. It may become less elastic in rural areas or where incomes are rising quickly. h: Command words: what each one needs
x: The command word tells you the type of answer and how far to take it. Matching the command word is the fastest way to stop losing marks you actually know. Command word What the examiner wants How to write it State / Name / Identify A short, precise fact or term One word, phrase or sentence. No explanation needed; extra writing earns nothing. Define The exact meaning of a term A complete, textbook-style sentence, e.g. “Capital is the amount the owner has invested in the business.” Explain A point plus the reason or effect behind it Make the point, then develop it with “because…”, “this means that…”. One point developed well usually beats two bare points. Calculate A numerical answer Show the formula, the figures substituted and the answer with units ($, %, times, days). Workings earn method marks. Prepare / Complete A ledger account, journal, cash book or financial statement Use the correct layout: full heading, dates, details, b/d and c/d balances, totals ruled off, sub-totals labelled. Advise / Evaluate / Discuss A balanced, reasoned judgement Give points for and against, use figures from the question, then a clear decision with a justification. No decision = capped marks. Compare Similarities or differences between two items Write about both items in each point, e.g. “Year 2’s margin of 25% is higher than Year 1’s 20%…” Model answer Explain why a business owner might want to know the profit for the year. [3] The profit shows whether the business is earning more revenue than the expenses it incurs (1). If profit is high, the owner can decide whether to withdraw more drawings or reinvest to expand (1). If profit is falling, the owner can investigate which costs have risen and take action before the business makes a loss (1). Model answer Advise Priya whether she should accept a bank loan of $20 000 to buy a delivery vehicle. Justify your answer. [5] For: the vehicle would allow Priya to deliver to customers further away, which could increase revenue and profit. A loan means she does not need to use her own savings or reduce working capital. Against: interest will be charged, which reduces profit for the year, and the loan must be repaid even if sales do not rise. Her current ratio is only 1.1 : 1, so repayments may cause cash flow problems. Decision: Priya should accept the loan only if forecast extra profit is greater than the interest cost; based on her low liquidity, she should first consider a smaller loan or leasing the vehicle.

t: Exam Technique: How to Score Full Marks
x: 1 Full headings Every statement needs the business name, the statement title and the period or date, e.g. “Lee Traders – Income statement for the year ended 31 December 2026” or “Statement of financial position at 31 December 2026”. An income statement covers a period (“for the year ended”); a statement of financial position is at a single date (“at”). 2 Dates in ledgers and journals Every entry needs a date. Balances carried down use the last day of the period; balances brought down use the first day of the next period. 3 Details column names the other account In a ledger account the details column shows the name of the account where the double entry is completed (e.g. “Bank”, “Sales”, “R Lee”), never a vague description like “money in”. 4 Balance c/d and Balance b/d Balance carried down goes on the smaller side to make totals equal; the same figure is brought down on the opposite side below the totals. Totals must be level and ruled. 5 Label every sub-total Write “Gross profit”, “Profit for the year”, “Net current assets”, “Total assets”. An unlabelled figure often scores nothing even if it is correct. 6 Show workings Put workings next to the answer or below the statement, clearly labelled (W1, W2). For ratios write the formula, the figures, then the answer to the decimal places asked. 7 Journal narratives Each general journal entry needs a short narrative explaining the transaction, unless the question says narratives are not required.
