Calculate the change in profit between 2024 and 2025. Show your working. Profit 2024 = 52.0 − 48.4 = RM3.6 million Profit 2025 = 54.5 − 53.9 = RM0.6 million Change = 0.6 − 3.6 = −RM3.0 million (profit fell by RM3.0 million) Common Mistake Subtracting the wrong way round and writing “3.0 million” as if profit had risen. Change = new − old ; a negative answer means a fall, so show the minus sign or say “fell by”. Keep the units: “million” and the currency. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [2 marks] Arjun will pay his new technician RM700 a week. Each repair uses RM15 of parts and customers pay RM50 per repair. Calculate how many repairs a week are needed to cover the cost of employing the technician. Show your working. Contribution per repair = RM50 − RM15 = RM35 Repairs needed = RM700 ÷ RM35 = 20 repairs a week Common Mistake Dividing by the price: 700 ÷ 50 = 14 repairs. That ignores the RM15 of parts used in every repair, so 14 repairs would only bring in 14 × RM35 = RM490 towards the wage, leaving RM210 uncovered. Use contribution , and round up if the answer is not a whole number. Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [4 marks] A business has current assets of RM45,000, of which RM25,000 is inventory, and current liabilities of RM30,000. Calculate the current ratio and the acid test ratio, and comment on its liquidity. Current ratio = 45,000 ÷ 30,000 = 1.5 Acid test ratio = (45,000 − 25,000) ÷ 30,000 = 20,000 ÷ 30,000 = 0.67 The current ratio looks acceptable, but the acid test ratio is well below 1. More than half of the current assets are inventory, so if the business cannot sell its inventory quickly it may struggle to pay its short-term debts on time. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Exam-style · [2 marks] Explain why demand for some products might rise if consumers’ incomes fall. When incomes fall, consumers can no longer afford their usual, more expensive choices, so they switch to cheaper substitutes . For example, they buy supermarket own-brand rice instead of a premium brand, or take the bus instead of driving, so demand for these cheaper products rises even though people are poorer. Why this scores The key idea is switching from expensive products to cheaper alternatives, with an example. Saying that people “still need” cheap products only explains why demand doesn’t fall; it does not explain why it rises . Written your own answer? Get it marked → Exam-style · [4 marks] Explain two ways a rise in interest rates could affect a car dealership. Lower sales. Most customers buy cars with a loan. Higher interest rates make monthly repayments more expensive, so some customers delay buying or choose a cheaper model, reducing the dealership’s revenue. Higher costs. If the dealership has an overdraft or loan to pay for the cars in its showroom, it must now pay more interest. This raises its costs and reduces profit, and it may postpone plans to open a new branch. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

Case reminder Siti sells hand-made batik scarves, mainly through Instagram, at RM45 each. Some customers are tourists and overseas buyers. Exam-style · [6 marks] Analyse how changes in the external environment could affect the profit Siti’s business makes in the future. Changes in consumer incomes. Silk batik scarves at RM45 are a luxury, not a necessity. If the economy enters a recession and incomes fall, customers are likely to cut back on luxuries first, so demand for Siti’s scarves could fall sharply. Because her rent and loan repayments must still be paid, lower revenue would reduce her profit and could push her towards a loss. In contrast, during economic growth, rising incomes would increase demand and profit. Exchange rates. Some of Siti’s buyers are overseas. If the ringgit depreciates, her RM45 scarves become cheaper in other currencies, for example in US dollars, so overseas demand is likely to rise, increasing her revenue. However, if she imports silk, a weaker ringgit makes it more expensive, raising her variable cost per scarf. The overall effect on profit depends on whether she sells more abroad than she spends on imported materials. Why this scores Each external change is followed through a chain to profit, using details of Siti’s product and customers. A point such as “e-commerce is growing” is fine only if it is linked to her profit (she already sells online, so more online shopping raises her potential market). The final sentence of each paragraph adds a small piece of evaluation. Written your own answer? Get it marked →

These are typical first-draft answers (shortened). Each one has the right idea but loses marks. See what changes. Draft answer says… Why it loses marks Full-mark fix “Profit 2018 = 3, profit 2019 = 0.3, so 3 − 0.3 = 2.7 million.” The answer doesn’t say profit fell and has no currency. “Change = 0.3 − 3.0 = −$2.7 million: profit fell by $2.7 million.” “800 ÷ 30 = 26.67, so 27 repairs.” Divides by the price, ignoring the materials cost of each repair. Use contribution: 800 ÷ (30 − 10) = 40 repairs. “Recruiters review the resumes and look at experience, skills and qualifications.” Describes the stage vaguely; doesn’t say what they compare against or why. Name the stage (shortlisting) and link it to the person specification and the purpose (only interview the best). “Setting objectives will motivate the staff so they work harder.” (for a sole trader working alone) Not applied: the case has no staff. Use the owner’s actual objectives: e.g. the 5-day delivery target guides decisions about production. “TQM will help because the new manager has announced plans and staff will see changes happening.” Doesn’t explain what TQM is or how it improves quality. Explain zero defects, self-checking at every stage and quality circles, then link to the fault and return figures. “I recommend delayering because it’s easier to communicate with fewer people.” Repeats one advantage; doesn’t weigh it against the drawbacks or the case’s main problem. Decide, explain why the deciding factor outweighs the main drawback for this firm, and say what it depends on. A 12-mark answer with two recommendation paragraphs saying the same thing. The second conclusion adds nothing new; time is wasted. One conclusion, with a new comparative reason and an “it depends on”. Quick Checklist I write formula → working → answer with units and direction of change. I use contribution, not price, in every break-even style calculation. I interpret ratios rather than just calculating them. I follow each external change through to revenue, costs and profit for this business. My conclusions decide, compare and say what the decision depends on.

How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0450/12/M/J/24 Q2(b) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. Jump to: 1.1 Business Activity · 1.2 Classification of Businesses · 1.3 Enterprise, Business Growth and Size · 1.4 Types of Business Organisation (sole traders, partnerships, private/public limited companies, franchises, joint ventures, limited liability, public sector corporations) · 1.5 Business Objectives and Stakeholder Objectives (objectives, stakeholder groups, their objectives, conflicts between stakeholders, social enterprises) 1.1 Business Activity These questions test needs and scarcity, opportunity cost, specialisation and added value; examiners reward precise definitions and, above all, explaining how a change widens the gap between the selling price and the cost of bought-in materials. What examiners keep seeing On added value, most students name a way (“raise prices”, “branding”) but never explain how it increases the gap between price and material cost, so they lose the analysis marks. On opportunity cost, many describe the option chosen instead of the one given up. 0450/11/O/N/22 Q2(a) · October/November 2022 · [2 marks] Define ‘opportunity cost’. Opportunity cost is the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made about how to use scarce resources. Why this scores Two marks for the full idea of the next best alternative given up ; “what you give up” alone earns one. The examiner report notes that many students lost marks by describing the option that was chosen rather than the one given up. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/13/O/N/23 Q1(a) · October/November 2023 · [2 marks] Identify two benefits to a business of specialisation. Benefit 1: Workers become expert at one task, so productivity (output per worker) increases. Benefit 2: Fewer mistakes are made, so less material is wasted. Why this scores One mark for each distinct benefit; only the first two are marked. The examiner report warns against giving the same point twice in different words, and effects on sales or reputation were not credited because they are not direct benefits of specialisation. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/11/M/J/25 Q1(d) · May/June 2025 · [6 marks] Source material: Brendan wants to be a successful entrepreneur. He plans to start up a flower shop using government support. Explain two ways Brendan could increase added value for his business. Way 1: Improve presentation so he can charge a higher price. Brendan could turn loose flowers into ready-made bouquets with attractive wrapping, ribbon and a message card for birthdays and weddings. Customers see these as a gift worth more than a plain bunch, so he can charge a higher price while the cost of the flowers he buys in stays almost the same. This widens the gap between the selling price and the cost of materials, so the added value on each bouquet rises. Way 2: Lower the cost of bought-in materials. Brendan could buy his flowers directly from growers or at a wholesale flower market instead of through a middleman. As a new business, his flower shop can keep the same prices as rivals, but each stem now costs him less. Because the cost of materials falls while the price stays the same, the difference between the two, his added value, increases, as long as the flowers are still fresh enough to keep customers coming back. Why this scores Each way earns K (the way), App (flowers, the new shop) and An (how it widens the gap between price and material cost). The examiner report says even strong answers lost the analysis marks by not explaining how branding or design increases added value: always finish with the price–cost gap. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/O/N/24 Q1(e) · October/November 2024 · [6 marks] Explain two ways a business can increase added value. Which is likely to be the best way for a business to use? Justify your answer. Improve quality and branding to raise the price. If a business uses better design, packaging or service, customers believe the product is worth more and are prepared to pay a higher price. If the cost of materials stays the same, the gap between price and material cost widens, so added value per item rises. However, in a competitive market some customers may switch to cheaper rivals, so sales could fall. Buy cheaper raw materials. A business could find a cheaper supplier or cut waste in production. This lowers the cost of materials in each item, so even with no change in price, added value increases. However, cheaper materials may be lower quality, leading to faulty products and complaints. Decision. Improving quality and branding is likely to be the best way, because it gives customers a reason to pay more and can attract new customers, so both added value and sales can grow. Using cheaper materials is riskier: if quality falls, the damage to the firm’s reputation can lose more sales than the cost saving is worth, and there is a limit to how far costs can be cut. This depends on the market: if customers buy mainly on price, cutting waste may be the safer choice. Why this scores This is a general question, so there are no application marks: 2 marks for two ways, 2 for developing them, 2 for a justified decision. The second evaluation mark needs a comparison, here explaining why cheaper materials could cost more in lost reputation than they save. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/21/O/N/21 Q1(a) · October/November 2021 · [8 marks] Explain two benefits and two drawbacks of specialisation within a manufacturing process. Benefit 1: Higher productivity. Each worker repeats one task until they are very skilled and fast at it, and no time is lost moving between jobs. More is produced per worker per hour, so the cost of each unit falls. Benefit 2: Quicker, cheaper training. A new production worker only needs to learn one task, so training takes less time and costs less, and they become productive sooner. Drawback 1: Boredom. Doing the same task all day is monotonous, so workers lose interest and motivation. They may work more slowly or carelessly, and some may leave, raising recruitment costs. Drawback 2: Production can stop when someone is absent. Other workers are not trained to do that task, so if one worker is ill the whole production line may slow down or halt, and orders may be delayed. Why this scores One mark for each benefit or drawback, plus one for explaining why it matters (4 × 2). The examiner report notes this was the one generic question on the paper, so no case application was needed, and that weaker answers confused specialisation with flow production. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/21/M/J/24 Q1(b) · May/June 2024 · [12 marks] Source material: EP has a reputation for producing high-quality products. … Raw materials are currently purchased locally as imported raw materials are of a lower-quality. EP operates in a very competitive market. Many of EP’s competitors sell lower quality products at lower prices. There are many substitutes for pottery products, including products made from plastic or bamboo. Consider the following two ways EP could use to increase added value. Which way should EP use? Justify your answer. • Increasing prices • Reducing raw material costs Increasing prices – advantage. EP has a reputation for high-quality pottery made from local materials, so some customers will accept a higher price for its plates, cups and bowls. If prices rise while the cost of the local raw materials stays the same, every item sold carries more added value. EP could support the rise by stressing quality and local materials in its newspaper and magazine adverts, so profit per item rises without producing any more. Increasing prices – disadvantage. EP operates in a very competitive market where rivals already sell at lower prices, and buyers can switch to plastic or bamboo substitutes. Demand is therefore likely to be price elastic, and sales are already affected by changing consumer spending. A price rise could make retail shops order fewer items, so EP’s total revenue and total added value could fall even though each item is worth more. Reducing raw material costs – advantage. EP could negotiate bulk discounts from its local suppliers or cut wasted clay in the factory. This widens the gap between price and cost without changing the price customers see, so EP stays competitive against its cheaper rivals and does not risk losing sales. Reducing raw material costs – disadvantage. The obvious way to cut costs is to switch to imported raw materials, but these are lower quality. Pottery that chips or breaks would damage the high-quality reputation EP has built over 40 years, which is the main reason customers choose it over cheaper rivals. EP would also lose the “made using materials from local suppliers” message in its advert, so sales could fall sharply. Recommendation. I recommend that EP increases prices , by a small amount and backed by stronger branding of its quality. Quality is EP’s unique selling point, and loyal customers who buy for quality are less sensitive to price than customers who buy cheap pottery. Reducing raw material costs is less suitable because the main saving comes from cheaper imported materials, which would destroy the very reputation that lets EP compete; once lost, it would be forced to compete on price against firms that already undercut it. Only cutting waste would be safe, and that saving is likely to be small. This decision depends on how sensitive EP’s customers are to price: if consumer spending keeps falling, even a small rise could lose many sales, and EP should then focus on cutting waste instead. Why this scores Level 3 needs detailed, applied discussion of both ways and a well-justified recommendation that explains why the other way was rejected. Every point uses EP’s facts (local materials, 40-year quality reputation, cheaper rivals, plastic and bamboo substitutes), and the recommendation names what it depends on. Written your own answer? If Ramon decides not to use crowdfunding, he can show his business plan to a bank as evidence that his home tutoring service has been carefully thought through, making a loan more likely. Way 2: Setting targets. The plan sets objectives, such as how many maths students he wants each month, so Ramon can compare actual bookings with the targets and act early if his start-up is falling behind. Why this scores One mark for each way (K) and one for linking it to Ramon’s business (App): crowdfunding in the first, the maths tutoring start-up in the second. An outline needs no further analysis. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/M/J/25 Q3(d) · May/June 2025 · [6 marks] Source material: Hal wants to be a successful entrepreneur. He plans to leave his job to start up a bakery. Explain two characteristics Hal will need to become a successful entrepreneur. Characteristic 1: Willing to take risks. Hal is giving up the regular salary from his job, and he will probably put his own savings into ovens, ingredients and premises for the bakery. If not enough customers buy his bread and cakes, he could lose both his income and the money he invested, so he must be prepared to accept that risk to start the business at all. Characteristic 2: Hard-working. In a new bakery Hal will have to start very early to bake fresh products each morning, then serve customers, order ingredients and keep the accounts himself. He needs to work long hours, because he cannot yet afford many employees, and the bakery must be stocked and open on time every day or customers will go elsewhere. Why this scores Each characteristic earns K (a recognised characteristic), App (leaving his job, the bakery) and An (why it matters for success). The examiner report notes students lost marks by giving manager functions such as planning instead of characteristics, or by repeating the characteristic’s name instead of explaining it. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/11/M/J/24 Q2(e) · May/June 2024 · [6 marks] Do you think it is better for a business to use internal growth or external growth when planning to expand? Justify your answer. Internal growth. Growing by opening new branches or launching new products lets managers expand at a pace they can control, so communication and quality are less likely to suffer. It also usually needs less finance at once, so the business does not have to borrow large sums and pay high interest. External growth. Merging with or taking over another business is much quicker, so the firm can take advantage of a market opportunity before rivals do. If it takes over a competitor, it removes that rival and gains its customers, increasing market share and giving it more power to set prices. Decision. I think internal growth is usually better because it carries less risk. A takeover needs a large amount of finance up front, and if the two firms’ cultures clash, the expected gains in market share may never arrive while the debt still has to be repaid. Internal growth is slower, but the business only expands when it can afford to and keeps control of its quality. However, this depends on the market: if competitors are expanding fast, the speed of external growth may matter more than the lower risk. Why this scores General question, so no application marks: 2 K, 2 An and 2 for a justified decision that compares the two methods. The mark scheme does not reward points such as economies of scale that apply to both methods, or the same point mirrored (“internal is slow” and “external is fast”) twice. Written your own answer? New businesses need employees, so they create jobs, which lowers unemployment and the cost of unemployment benefits. Reason 2: To increase competition. Why this scores One mark for each reason and one for its explanation (4 × 2); there are no application marks for this question, so the answer stays general. Each reason is different: repeating “jobs” and “unemployment” as two reasons would score only once. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/23/M/J/21 Q1(b) · May/June 2021 · [12 marks] Source material: After he left school he worked in a fast food takeaway serving customers. Ruben has inherited $50 000 from his grandparents and wants to start a new business (RB). … If he chooses to buy a franchise this will cost $50 000 and Ruben will have to decide on a suitable source of finance. Explain how the following three factors could cause Ruben’s new business to fail: • Lack of management experience • Insufficient working capital • Poor planning Which factor do you think is most important to Ruben? Justify your answer. Lack of management experience. Ruben has only served customers in a takeaway; he has never recruited staff, ordered stock or kept accounts. He must now manage 4 full-time or 8 part-time employees, and plans to pay only the minimum wage when other takeaways pay more, so he may struggle to keep good staff. Untrained or demotivated staff mean slow service, yet his customers want food prepared quickly, so they may go to rivals and RB’s revenue could fall until it can no longer cover its costs. Insufficient working capital. Working capital is the cash available for day-to-day costs. If Ruben spends his whole $50 000 inheritance on the franchise, he has nothing left to pay wages, local suppliers for ingredients, or electricity while sales build up. If he cannot pay his suppliers, they may stop deliveries, so he cannot make burgers and fried chicken and sales stop completely. A business can fail from a shortage of cash even if it would eventually be profitable. Poor planning. At certain times of the day more food needs to be ready to serve. If Ruben does not plan staff rotas and stock for these peak times, customers face long waits, while at quiet times food is wasted. Poor planning of his marketing campaign aimed at children could also waste money if it is not based on the market research in Appendix 1. Both raise costs and lose customers, reducing profit. Conclusion. Insufficient working capital is the most important factor for Ruben. The franchise costs exactly $50 000, the whole of his inheritance, so unless he borrows, he will open with no cash at all to cover wages and ingredients: this is a certain problem from the first day, not just a possible one. Lack of management experience is less important because buying a franchise reduces it: the franchisor provides the menu and a known brand, and usually training and support. Poor planning can be reduced by writing a business plan before opening. This depends on how he finances the franchise: if he uses a bank loan and keeps part of his inheritance as cash, his working capital problem becomes much smaller and lack of experience would then be the biggest risk. Why this scores Level 3 needs all three factors discussed in detail and in context, with a conclusion that says why the other factors are less important. The examiner report says many answers were too general and confused working capital (short-term cash) with capital; the conclusion here uses Ruben’s own figures and the franchise to rank the factors. Written your own answer? What examiners keep seeing Defining a partnership as people who “run” or “manage” a business (the key idea is ownership ), confusing a partnership or joint venture with a merger, and claiming that limited liability means shareholders “do not pay any debts”: the money they invested can be lost; only their personal assets are protected. 0450/11/M/J/25 Q1(a) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Define ‘business partnership’. Why this scores Two marks need both ideas: the business is owned by the partners, and there are at least two of them. The examiner report says many students lost a mark by writing “run” or “managed” instead of “owned”, and some described a merger, which scored nothing. Written your own answer? In 2023 SNT produced 300 000 bottles of soft drinks each week. … SNT’s directors are planning to expand the business into new markets in other countries by forming a joint venture. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to SNT of forming a joint venture when entering new markets in other countries. Advantage: shared costs and local knowledge. In a joint venture SNT and a business already based in the new country would both put money into the project, and the partner already understands local tastes in soft drinks, the retailers and the laws. This means SNT spends less of its own capital and less on market research, so if the drinks do not sell abroad, its losses are much smaller. Disadvantage: disagreements and shared reputation. The partner may not share SNT’s ethical approach; for example, it may want cheaper, less sustainable ingredients or packaging to raise profit. Get it marked → 0450/13/M/J/25 Q2(e) · May/June 2025 · [6 marks] Do you think the advantages of operating as a sole trader business are greater than the disadvantages? Justify your answer. Advantages. A sole trader keeps all the profit, so they have a strong incentive to work hard and keep costs down. They also make every decision alone, so they can react quickly, for example cutting a price the same day a rival does, and there are no arguments with other owners. Their accounts do not have to be published, so competitors cannot see how well the business is doing. Disadvantages. The owner has unlimited liability, so if the business fails owing money, they could lose personal possessions such as their house or car. Finance is also hard to raise because there are no shareholders and banks see a one-person business as risky, so the owner may face cash-flow problems or be unable to expand. If the owner is ill, nobody may be able to run the business, so sales are lost. Judgement. I think the advantages are greater for a business that plans to stay small and needs little capital, such as a local shop. For that owner, control and the profit incentive matter every day, while unlimited liability is only a serious danger when the business borrows heavily, so it can be managed by avoiding large loans. However, if the owner wants to grow quickly, the disadvantages become greater, because the lack of finance and the personal risk would hold the business back, and a private limited company would then be more suitable. Why this scores Up to 2 marks for relevant points, 2 for developing them (each point is followed by “so…” and a consequence) and 2 for a justified decision that explains when the main advantage outweighs the main disadvantage. The examiner report found most students added new points instead of developing them, and decisions were rarely justified. This is a general question, so no case is needed. Written your own answer? Explain two advantages and two disadvantages to Philip of changing PF from a sole trader business to a private limited company. Advantage 1: limited liability. PF is now a separate legal body, so Philip can lose no more than the money he has put into the company, such as his original $100 000. If the shoes from the new factory do not sell and the bank loan cannot be repaid, his house and other personal possessions are safe. Advantage 2: easier to raise capital. PF can now sell shares privately, for example to Philip’s sister, a successful entrepreneur who is thinking of investing. Her money could help pay for the new factory without a larger bank loan, so PF has lower interest costs while it grows. Disadvantage 1: profits must be shared. If his sister buys shares, part of the profit from the rubber shoes will be paid to her as dividends. Philip no longer keeps all the profit from a business he has built up over 10 years. Disadvantage 2: legal requirements and less privacy. Philip has to complete legal documents to register the company and prepare formal accounts each year, which adds accountancy costs. Some financial information, such as PF’s statement of financial position, becomes available to others, so rivals in this very competitive market may learn how well PF is doing. Why this scores Each of the four points earns 1 mark for the advantage or disadvantage and 1 for an explanation applied to PF (the $100 000, the factory loan, the sister’s investment, the competitive market). Each paragraph uses a different case detail, so no application mark is repeated. The examiner report says half the marks were for application, and the strongest answers linked limited liability to the $100 000 and dividends to the sister. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/23/O/N/25 Q1(b) · October/November 2025 · [12 marks] Source material: Tim plans to take out a bank loan to help fund the expansion. His two brothers will also invest in the business. One of his brothers has experience of financial management and the other is skilled in IT. Consider the advantages and disadvantages of the following two types of business organisation that Tim could use when his brothers join the business. Which would be the best type for Tim to choose? Justify your answer. • Partnership • Private limited company Partnership – advantage. A partnership is quick and cheap to set up: Tim and his brothers only need a partnership agreement, with few legal requirements and no formal accounts to file. This saves legal and accountancy costs, so more of the money the brothers invest can go into selling ES’s boats abroad, and ES’s financial details stay private from larger boat builders. Partnership – disadvantage. The partners would usually have unlimited liability. Tim is taking out a bank loan to expand into other countries, where ES has no reputation yet and now faces foreign competition because tariffs and quotas have been removed. If the exports fail and ES cannot repay the loan, all three brothers could lose personal assets such as their homes, even because of a decision made by one of the others. Private limited company – advantage. The shareholders have limited liability, so each brother can lose only the money he invests. This makes the brothers more willing to put in capital, and as a separate legal body with continuity, ES may find it easier to borrow from the bank. The well-known brand and its 12 skilled employees would also continue if one brother left. Private limited company – disadvantage. Setting up costs more and takes longer, because ES must be registered and must file accounts every year, which competitors can see. Shares can only be sold privately, so if ES needs more capital later, it cannot raise it from the public, and Tim will have to share profits as dividends and share control of decisions with his brothers. Recommendation. I recommend that ES becomes a private limited company . The expansion combines a bank loan with selling in new, more competitive markets, so the risk of debts is much higher than when Tim sold only in country X. Limited liability protects three families’ homes, which matters far more than the set-up costs and paperwork. A partnership is less suitable because its main advantage, being cheap and simple, is small compared with the danger that all three brothers lose their personal assets if exports fail; the brothers also gain the financial and IT skills under either form, so a partnership offers no extra benefit there. This depends on the size of the loan: if Tim delayed exporting and borrowed only a small amount, a partnership could be a sensible first step. Why this scores Level 3 (9–12): both forms get a developed advantage and disadvantage applied to ES (the bank loan, the brothers, exporting after tariffs were removed, the brand and 12 employees), and the recommendation explains why the partnership was rejected and what the choice depends on. The mark scheme reserves the top of the band for answers that say why the alternative was rejected. Written your own answer? What examiners keep seeing Answering a slightly different question: listing objectives when asked why objectives have changed, or naming stakeholder objectives without explaining the reason behind them or how they conflict. Examiner reports also note answers that discuss disagreements within one group when the question asks about conflict between groups. 0450/11/M/J/24 Q4(a) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Define ‘social enterprise’. A business that has social or environmental objectives as well as aiming to make a profit, and that reinvests most of its profit in the business or in its cause rather than paying it out to its owners. Why this scores Two marks need both parts: social (or environmental) objectives and a profit or surplus that is reinvested. “A business that helps society” on its own would earn at most 1 mark, and “a charity” misses the point that a social enterprise trades to make a profit. Get it marked → 0450/13/O/N/25 Q3(e) · October/November 2025 · [6 marks] Do you think employees are the most important stakeholder group for a manufacturing business? Justify your answer. Employees are very important. In a manufacturing business, employees physically make the products. If they are poorly trained or demotivated, output falls and quality suffers, so orders are late and faulty goods damage the firm’s reputation. Skilled workers are also hard to replace, so high labour turnover raises recruitment and training costs. Other groups matter too. Customers buy the products, so without them there is no revenue at all, however well the goods are made. Shareholders provide the capital for factories and machinery; if they are unhappy with their dividends, they may sell their shares or refuse to fund expansion. Judgement. I think customers are the most important group, because employees’ work only creates value if someone pays for the product: a factory full of motivated workers will still close if demand disappears. Employees come a close second, since they decide whether the firm can give customers the quality and delivery times they want, so the two groups depend on each other. The answer depends on the type of production: in a highly automated factory employees matter less, while in a business that relies on skilled workers they may be the deciding factor. Justify your answer. • Shareholders • Employees • Customers Shareholders. Since AD became a public limited company, its shareholders are no longer only the family; most have invested to earn a return. They want high profits, high dividends and a rising share price, because they could have put their money elsewhere. The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0450/12/M/J/24 Q2(b) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 2.1 Motivating Employees · 2.2 Organisation and Management · 2.3 Recruitment, Selection and Training of Employees · 2.4 Internal and External Communication 2.1 Motivating Employees These questions test whether you can tell Herzberg’s motivators from hygiene factors, match a method of motivation to the workers in the case, and explain what better motivation does for output, costs and labour turnover. What examiners keep seeing The examiner reports repeatedly see pay or working conditions given as Herzberg “motivators” (they are hygiene factors), or Maslow’s levels given instead. In method questions, “it increases motivation” is not analysis: say how the method motivates and what that does for the business. 0450/12/F/M/25 Q1(a) · February/March 2025 · [2 marks] Identify two motivators from Herzberg’s theory of motivation. Motivator 1: Recognition. Motivator 2: Achievement. Why this scores One mark for each correct motivator; only the first two are marked. The examiner report says many students gave hygiene factors such as pay or working conditions, or levels of Maslow’s hierarchy, which score nothing. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/11/M/J/22 Q4(c) · May/June 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: It controls 5 hospitals and has 5600 employees including 440 doctors. … The business has a tall organisational structure and a long chain of command. Outline two ways MBH can use ideas from Herzberg’s theory to motivate its employees. Way 1: Give more responsibility. Experienced doctors could be put in charge of running a ward or training junior doctors in their hospital, so they feel trusted and gain a sense of achievement, which Herzberg says is a true motivator. Way 2: Offer chances for promotion. MBH has a tall organisational structure with many levels, so it can set out clear promotion steps (for example from nurse to senior nurse to ward manager) and promote staff who perform well, giving them recognition and a goal to work towards. Why this scores One mark for each Herzberg motivator (responsibility, promotion) and one for linking each to MBH (doctors, hospitals, tall structure). The examiner report called this the hardest question on the paper: answers about higher pay or better conditions scored zero because these are hygiene factors. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/M/J/25 Q2(e) · May/June 2025 · [6 marks] Do you think job rotation is the best method for a large business to use to motivate its employees? Justify your answer. For job rotation: Moving employees between tasks at the same level, such as from the till to stock control to customer service, makes the work less repetitive. Workers who are less bored are less likely to be absent or to leave, so absenteeism and labour turnover fall. In a large business with thousands of staff, even a small fall in labour turnover saves a lot in recruitment and training costs. Rotation also creates multi-skilled workers who can cover for absent colleagues, so work is not held up. Against job rotation: The tasks are often just as routine as each other, so the boredom simply moves from one job to the next and any rise in motivation may not last. Workers must be trained for each task and are slower while they learn, which raises costs and can lead to more mistakes. Alternative: job enrichment. Giving employees more challenging work and responsibility, such as letting an experienced worker organise a team’s schedule, meets Herzberg’s motivators of responsibility and achievement. This gives longer-lasting motivation, although it also needs training and not every worker wants extra responsibility. Decision: I do not think job rotation is the best method. It reduces boredom but does not make the work any more challenging, so its effect tends to be short-lived. Job enrichment is better for a large business because genuine responsibility motivates staff over the long term, raising productivity and lowering labour turnover. Job rotation is still useful alongside it where tasks are simple and the business needs workers who can cover absences. Why this scores Two knowledge marks (less boredom, multi-skilling; training needed), two analysis marks (lower absenteeism and turnover costs; slower work and mistakes) and two for a decision justified by comparing with job enrichment. This is a general question, so there are no application marks. The examiner report warns that “it increases motivation” repeats the question, and that some students confused job rotation with job enrichment or thought it meant extra rest breaks. Written your own answer? Explain two benefits to RF of having a well-motivated workforce. Benefit 1: Higher productivity. Motivated workers work harder and waste less time, so each of RF’s employees repairs more tables and chairs each day. This means Santhosh can meet demand without recruiting extra workers, so the labour cost of each piece of furniture falls. Motivated employees are loyal and less likely to leave. This matters for RF because Santhosh and the 3 skilled carpenters have to spend time training the 6 unskilled school leavers. If the trained school leavers stay, RF does not have to pay to recruit and train replacements, and the carpenters can spend their time repairing furniture instead of teaching new staff, so output and RF’s limited start-up capital are protected. Justify your answer. • Paying bonuses • Piece-rate • Job rotation Paying bonuses. Advantage: A bonus for reaching a monthly target gives PF’s 20 workers an extra reward on top of their hourly wage. This narrows the gap with other local businesses that pay more, so fewer workers leave and Philip spends less time and money recruiting new production workers. Disadvantage: Bonuses add to PF’s wage bill just as it is taking on a bank loan to build a new factory, raising the cost of each pair of shoes in a very competitive market. If the bonus goes only to the fastest workers, the others may feel it is unfair and still leave. Piece-rate. Advantage: Paying workers for each pair of shoes they make links pay directly to output. Fast workers could earn more than the current hourly wage, possibly more than at other local businesses, which would help PF keep its staff. Labour cost per pair is fixed, so Philip can control costs as output grows. Disadvantage: Workers paid per pair may rush, so the quality of the rubber shoes falls and more faulty pairs are returned. That would damage a brand that tells customers they “will never buy a different brand again”. Piece-rate also does nothing to make the boring job more interesting. Job rotation. Advantage: It tackles the reason given in the case, that the jobs are boring. Moving workers between stages such as cutting, moulding and packing adds variety and creates multi-skilled workers who can cover absences, which will be useful when the new factory opens. It costs little apart from some training. Disadvantage: All the stages of making rubber shoes are fairly repetitive, so the boredom may soon return. It also does not fix the lower pay, so workers may still leave for the higher wages paid by other local businesses. Recommendation. PF should pay bonuses, based on team targets for both output and quality. The main reason workers leave is that other local businesses pay more, and Herzberg shows that pay below what others receive causes dissatisfaction that variety alone cannot remove; a bonus deals with this directly. Piece-rate is rejected because the risk to quality is too high for a brand that relies on customer loyalty, and job rotation is rejected as the main method because it does not close the pay gap, although it could be added later at little cost. This depends on PF being able to afford the bonuses alongside its loan repayments; if profit falls, Philip could start with job rotation and introduce bonuses once the new factory is earning revenue. Why this scores Level 3 (9–12): all three methods are discussed in context with a developed advantage and disadvantage, and the recommendation explains why the other two are rejected and what the decision depends on. Justify your answer. • Joint venture • Franchising Joint venture – benefit: VP would work with a business that already operates in the new country, so it gains local knowledge of tastes, competitors and good locations. VP could adapt its vegetarian menu to local dishes without paying for expensive market research. The partner would also share the cost of opening restaurants, so VP needs to raise less capital and loses less if the expansion fails. Joint venture – limitation: profits from the new restaurants must be shared, reducing the return for VP’s shareholders. The two businesses may also disagree, for example if the partner wants to add meat dishes to attract more customers, which would clash with VP’s vegetarian-only brand. Disagreements slow down decisions and make the venture less efficient, and finding the right partner in the first place could delay the expansion. Franchising – benefit: franchisees in the new country would pay for the premises and kitchen equipment and run the restaurants themselves, so VP can expand quickly without raising large amounts of finance. VP receives a fee and a share of revenue from each franchise, earning a return on very little investment. Because franchisees own their restaurants, they are motivated to make them succeed. Franchising – limitation: VP has much less control over how each restaurant is run. VP’s advertising guarantees a meal in under 5 minutes; if a franchisee is slow or uses poor ingredients, customers blame the VP brand, and the reputation built over 10 years in country Z could suffer. Franchisees also learn VP’s recipes and could use them to open competing restaurants when the agreement ends. Recommendation. I recommend a joint venture. VP has never operated outside country Z, and its success depends on vegetarian food suiting local tastes, so a partner’s local knowledge is the most valuable thing it can gain. As a public limited company with 500 restaurants, VP can afford its share of the investment, and it keeps far more control over its brand and its 5-minute promise than it would with franchising. Franchising is less suitable because VP would be relying on franchisees it does not know, in a market it does not understand, to protect its reputation. This depends on finding a partner who accepts VP’s vegetarian values and agreeing clearly how profits and decisions are shared; if no such partner can be found quickly, franchising with strict rules and regular inspections would be the fallback. Why this scores Level 3: both methods discussed in detail with a benefit and a limitation each, applied to VP (vegetarian brand, 500 restaurants, the 5-minute promise), and a recommendation that rejects franchising with a reason and says what it depends on. The examiner report notes that some students wrongly assumed VP would become a franchisee, which made their arguments contradict each other: VP would be the franchisor. Written your own answer? What examiners keep seeing Examiners repeatedly report weak knowledge of kaizen: students define lean production or kaizen instead of explaining its effect, or confuse it with quality assurance. In definitions, never repeat the word being defined (“batch production is producing in batches”). 0450/12/M/J/25 Q1(a) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Define ‘batch production’. Batch production is where a quantity of one identical product is made as a group, and the whole group moves through each stage of production together before the equipment is changed to make a group of a different product. Why this scores Two marks need both elements: a group of identical items made together, and the group moving through the stages of production together before another product is made. The examiner report says students often missed one element, used the word “batch” in the definition or defined flow production by mistake. Written your own answer? Outline two advantages to GAE of introducing new technology. Advantage 1: Higher productivity. Two different pieces of application are used (its factories in 4 countries; making steel): the examiner report says the best answers did this, and the mark scheme allows “lower cost” only once. Get it marked → 0450/12/M/J/24 Q4(e) · May/June 2024 · [6 marks] Do you think the advantages for a manufacturing business of using flow production are greater than the disadvantages? Justify your answer. Advantages: flow production makes very large quantities of identical products continuously, so the business gains economies of scale, such as discounts for buying raw materials in bulk. This lowers the average cost of each unit, so the business can cut its price to win customers or keep the price and earn a higher profit margin. Production lines are often automated and can run 24 hours a day, so labour costs per unit are low. Disadvantages: every product is the same, so the business cannot easily customise its products or respond to changing tastes, and it may lose sales to competitors who offer more variety. The work is repetitive and boring, which can demotivate employees and raise absenteeism and labour turnover. If one machine breaks down, the whole line stops, so output is lost while costs continue. Decision: I think the advantages are greater for a manufacturer of everyday products with high, steady demand, such as soft drinks or paper cups. Lower unit costs let it charge competitive prices, and customers for these products do not expect variety, so the lack of flexibility matters little. The disadvantages only outweigh the advantages when demand is small or customers want individual designs; then an expensive line would stand idle and batch or job production would be better. The risk of breakdowns can be reduced with regular maintenance, so it is less important than the cost advantage. Why this scores Two marks for valid points (economies of scale, inflexibility), two for developing them (lower unit costs; customer needs not met) and two for a justified decision that weighs one against the other and says when it would change. There are no application marks on this general question, and the mark scheme credits economies of scale only when it is developed to lower unit or average costs, not just “lower costs”. Benefit 2: able to reward and motivate workers. ES’s production workers do boring, repetitive jobs and receive no financial rewards apart from their time-rate wage. If output per worker rises, ES could afford to share some of the gain, for example with a bonus linked to output. This would make the workers more motivated, so fewer of them leave, reducing ES’s recruitment and training costs at a time when it already has to recruit 100 extra production workers. Why this scores Each benefit is identified (1 mark) and explained in three linked steps, with application to ES (time-rate pay, no financial rewards, exporting, 100 new workers). The mark scheme also accepts more scooters available to export; don’t write two versions of the same lower-cost point as your two benefits. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/21/M/J/22 Q2(b) · May/June 2022 · [12 marks] Source material: MB’s bread is freshly-made every day in the bakery, which is located at the back of MB’s small shop. Yasin has 2 employees to help him produce the bread and 1 employee to serve customers in the shop. Yasin also buys the cheapest ingredients, most of which are imported. Consider the following two ways MB could achieve lean production. Which is the best way for Yasin to choose? Justify your answer. • Kaizen. • Just-in-time inventory control. Kaizen – advantage: Yasin’s 2 bakery employees make bread every day, so they know where time and ingredients are wasted, for example walking between the mixer and the oven, or dough waiting to be shaped. Yasin uses a democratic leadership style, so they are used to sharing ideas. Many small improvements to the layout and order of tasks mean bread is made faster with less waste, so productivity rises and the cost of each loaf falls, helping MB keep its costs low and stay competitive. Kaizen – disadvantage: MB is very small, with only 2 production workers in a small space behind the shop, so there may be few improvements to find and the gains could be small. Reorganising the bakery could also disrupt the daily baking, and if Yasin lacks the know-how he may have to pay someone to plan the new layout, adding costs for a business that is only 6 months old. Just-in-time – advantage: Yasin would order flour and other ingredients only when they are needed, so he holds very little inventory. This frees storage space in the small bakery and means ingredients do not go stale or out of date. Less cash is tied up in inventory, which matters for a new business that needed government help to start, because the cash can be used to pay rent and wages instead. Just-in-time – disadvantage: most of MB’s ingredients are imported, so deliveries take longer and are more likely to be held up by shipping or customs problems. If flour arrives late, MB cannot bake that day’s bread and has nothing to sell, losing revenue and possibly customers to its competitors. If demand suddenly rises, there may not be enough ingredients to bake extra bread. Recommendation. I recommend kaizen. It costs very little to introduce, which suits a new business that must keep costs low, and Yasin’s democratic style means his employees are likely to put forward ideas. JIT is less suitable because MB relies on imported ingredients: one late delivery would stop the production of bread that has to be sold fresh the same day, so the risk of lost sales outweighs the saving on storage. JIT would become the better choice if Yasin switched to local suppliers, which 85% of those in his survey said they want, because local deliveries are quicker and more reliable. So the decision depends on where MB buys its ingredients. Why this scores Level 3: both methods developed with an advantage and a disadvantage applied to MB (2 employees, small bakery, imported ingredients, bread sold fresh), and a recommendation that rejects JIT for a case-specific reason and says what would change the decision. The examiner report found lean production, especially kaizen, poorly known; for JIT, write about ingredients, not storing finished bread. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/22/M/J/25 Q2(b) · May/June 2025 · [12 marks] Source material: Most of TSE’s production employees are skilled and all work full time. Some of TSE’s factories use new technology and have an automated flow production line. However, to remain competitive TSE needs to make sure all of its factories are as efficient as possible. Consider the following two ways TSE could use to increase efficiency. Which way should TSE use? Justify your answer. • Improving labour skills • Increasing automation and technology Improving labour skills – advantage: training would teach TSE’s production employees quicker and more accurate ways of working. Skilled workers make fewer mistakes, so less plastic and rubber is wasted and fewer rackets and balls are rejected. Output per worker rises, which lowers the cost of each item and protects TSE’s reputation for high-quality sports equipment. Workers who feel valued are also more motivated, supporting the HR Director’s aim of low absenteeism and labour turnover. Improving labour skills – disadvantage: training is expensive and output falls while workers are being trained, especially if it is off-the-job. Most of TSE’s production employees are already skilled, so the extra gain in efficiency may be small compared with the cost. Highly trained workers may also be attracted away by rival manufacturers, so the money spent on training them would be wasted. Increasing automation and technology – advantage: some TSE factories already use an automated flow production line, so TSE knows it works. Machines can run 24 hours a day and make identical, high-quality items much faster than people, which greatly lowers unit costs. Lower costs would let TSE cut prices or raise its profit margin, helping it stay competitive in its 30 markets and gain market share in country P. Increasing automation and technology – disadvantage: new machinery needs a large amount of capital, plus maintenance and training costs. Fewer workers would be needed, so TSE may have to make redundancy payments, and with country P moving into recession and unemployment rising (Appendix 2), job losses could damage morale and TSE’s reputation. Investing heavily just as a recession starts is risky if demand for sports equipment falls. Recommendation. I recommend increasing automation and technology. TSE’s workers are already skilled, so more training would bring only a small improvement, whereas automation is already proven in TSE’s own factories and would cut unit costs in every factory for years to come. As a large multinational, TSE can afford the capital cost far more easily than a small firm. Improving labour skills is less suitable as the main way because it cannot match the speed and consistency of machines. However, this depends on demand during the recession: if sales fall sharply, TSE should automate one factory at a time and retrain workers to operate and maintain the new machines rather than making them redundant. Why this scores Level 3: both ways developed with an advantage and a disadvantage applied to TSE (already-skilled workers, existing automated lines, the recession in Appendix 2), and a recommendation that compares them and rejects labour skills with a case reason. The examiner report says most answers stayed in Level 1 with simple, undeveloped statements and unsupported recommendations; stronger answers noticed that TSE’s workers were already skilled. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 4.2 Costs, Scale of Production and Break-even Analysis These questions test whether you can use cost formulas accurately (average cost, break-even, margin of safety) and explain why average cost falls or rises as a business grows; examiners reward a clear formula → working → answer, and break-even figures that are interpreted, not just calculated. What examiners keep seeing Examiners report that many students mix up economies and diseconomies of scale, inventing “managerial diseconomies” by flipping the economies list; diseconomies are real problems of size such as poor communication, low morale and weak co-ordination. In calculations, dividing fixed costs by the price instead of the contribution is the most common error. 0450/11/M/J/24 Q1(a) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Define ‘diseconomies of scale’. Diseconomies of scale are the factors that cause a business’s average cost (cost per unit) to rise when it grows beyond a certain size. Why this scores Two marks need both ideas: the business is growing and its average or unit cost rises. “Costs go up as a business grows” is only a partial definition (1 mark), and giving an example such as poor communication does not define the term. Average cost = total costs ÷ total output = $595 000 ÷ 85 000 Average cost = $7 per unit per week Why this scores Two marks for $7 as the final answer; the formula or $595 000 ÷ 85 000 earns one mark if the arithmetic slips. Using fixed costs ($400 000 ÷ 85 000 = $4.71) gives average fixed cost, not average cost, and writing “7 units” loses a mark. Written your own answer? Contribution per house = $11 − $1 = $10 Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution = $1250 ÷ $10 = 125 houses per month Margin of safety = actual output − break-even output = 225 − 125 Margin of safety = 100 houses per month Why this scores One mark for the method (actual output minus break-even output) and one for 100. It has 27 000 employees. … Some of PKN’s directors are concerned about possible diseconomies of scale as the business grows. Explain two diseconomies of scale which might affect PKN as it grows. Diseconomy 1: Poor communication. With factories in 30 countries, instructions from head office have to pass through many layers of managers, and across different languages and time zones, before they reach the workers making the glass. Messages arrive late or are misunderstood, for example about a change to a product’s thickness, so mistakes are made and batches of glass have to be scrapped. This waste of materials and time pushes up the cost of each unit produced. Diseconomy 2: Low morale and motivation. In a business with 27 000 employees, an individual worker may feel like a small, unimportant part of a huge organisation and never meet senior managers. Labour turnover rises and productivity falls, which reduces PKN’s profit as it expands. Why this scores Each paragraph has a named diseconomy (K), a different case fact (30 countries, then 27 000 employees) (App) and its own consequence (scrapped glass and higher unit costs; labour turnover and recruitment costs) (An). The mark scheme credits “higher average cost” only once, which is why the second chain ends in a different effect. The examiner report says weaker answers invented “managerial diseconomies” by reversing the economies of scale. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/22/M/J/24 Q1(b) · May/June 2024 · [12 marks] Source material: JJ’s jewellery is beautiful but not expensive and therefore affordable for many people. The business has many competitors. … Type of product Bracelet Ring Fixed cost for each product per week $50 000 $50 000 Selling price per product $50 $120 Variable cost per product $25 $40 Forecast sales per week 2500 750 … Unemployment is forecast to increase from 3% to 6% by the end of the year. Using Appendix 1 and other information, consider the two new products JJ could produce. Which product should JJ choose? Justify your answer using break-even calculations. • Product A • Product B Product A (bracelet). Contribution = $50 − $25 = $25 per bracelet. Break-even = $50 000 ÷ $25 = 2000 bracelets a week. Margin of safety = 2500 − 2000 = 500 bracelets. Forecast profit = 500 × $25 = $12 500 a week. Advantage: Product A gives the higher forecast profit, $12 500 a week, which fits JJ’s objective of increasing profit every year. Its margin of safety is 500 bracelets, so sales could be 20% below forecast before JJ makes a loss. At $50, the bracelet also matches JJ’s image of jewellery that is beautiful but affordable, so existing customers are likely to buy it. Disadvantage: JJ must sell 2000 bracelets every week just to cover its costs, a high volume in a market with many competitors. Each bracelet only contributes $25, so JJ depends on selling large numbers. Making 2500 extra items a week may also stretch its 60 full-time and 25 part-time workers, raising costs if overtime is needed. Product B (ring). Contribution = $120 − $40 = $80 per ring. Break-even = $50 000 ÷ $80 = 625 rings a week. Margin of safety = 750 − 625 = 125 rings. Forecast profit = 125 × $80 = $10 000 a week. Advantage: JJ only needs to sell 625 rings to break even, far fewer than 2000 bracelets, and each ring adds $80 towards fixed costs and profit. Producing 750 rings a week is easier for JJ’s skilled workforce than 2500 bracelets, so quality can be kept high. Disadvantage: the margin of safety is only 125 rings, so if sales are just 17% below forecast JJ makes a loss. Unemployment is forecast to double from 3% to 6%, and a $120 ring is more of a luxury than a $50 bracelet, so demand for it is more likely to fall below 625. Each unsold ring has also cost $40 to make. Recommendation. JJ should choose Product A, the bracelet. It earns $2 500 a week more profit than the ring, which directly meets JJ’s objective of increasing profit, and its larger margin of safety gives more protection. The ring needs fewer sales to break even, but this advantage is outweighed by the rising unemployment: customers with falling incomes are more likely to keep buying a $50 bracelet than a $120 ring, so the ring’s small margin of safety could easily disappear. The bracelet also fits JJ’s affordable brand, while the ring does not. This depends on the forecast of 2500 bracelets a week being accurate; the forecasts were made before the rise in unemployment, so JJ should check the forecast and make sure its factory can produce the extra volume before launching. Why this scores Top level: both products are discussed in detail, the break-even, margin of safety and profit calculations are used as evidence inside the argument, and every point is applied to JJ (its profit objective, affordable brand, workforce and the unemployment forecast). The recommendation explains why the ring’s lower break-even is outweighed, which is what the mark scheme rewards with the top marks in Level 3. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/11/O/N/24 Q4(e) · October/November 2024 · [6 marks] Do you think quality assurance is the best way for a business to achieve quality production? Justify your answer. Quality assurance. Workers check quality at every stage of production, so a fault is found where it happens instead of after the product is finished. This means less money is wasted reworking or scrapping finished goods. Giving workers responsibility for their own quality can also increase their motivation, leading to higher output. However, every worker has to be trained, which raises costs, and checking at each stage can slow production down so productivity falls. Quality control. Inspectors check finished products, so production does not stop while checks are made and only the inspectors need training. However, faults are found only at the end, so the materials and labour used on a faulty product are already wasted, and the business still does not know where in the process the fault started. Inspectors add to labour costs, and as not every product can be checked, some faulty items may still reach customers and damage the business’s reputation. Decision. I think quality assurance is the best way, because it prevents faults rather than just finding them. Quality control only stops faulty goods being sold; it does nothing to stop the same fault happening again tomorrow, so waste continues. The training cost of quality assurance is paid once, while the waste from quality control carries on. However, this depends on the workforce: if workers are unskilled or labour turnover is high, they may not check their work properly, and a business would need some final inspection as well. Why this scores This is a general question, so there are no application marks: the answer develops points for and against quality assurance (K, An) and uses quality control as the comparison, then makes a decision that explains why the alternative is weaker (E).
