Get it marked → 0450/21/O/N/23 Q1(b) · October/November 2023 · [12 marks] Source material: PH produces a range of protective hats for employees working on construction sites, in factories or mines. It has a reputation for producing high-quality products and sells its hats around the world. … They work on a flow production line and carry out the same tasks every day. … Existing employees would also benefit from additional training as there have been issues with motivation. Consider the following two ways PH could ensure quality production. Which way should PH choose? Justify your answer. • Quality control • Quality assurance Quality control — advantage: inspectors check the protective hats at the end of the flow production line, so a cracked or weak hat is removed before it reaches a construction or mining company. Because a faulty safety hat could lead to a worker being injured, catching faults before sale protects PH’s reputation for high quality and its sales around the world. Only the inspectors need specialist training, not all 100 production employees. Quality control — disadvantage: faults are found only after the hat is finished, so on a flow line many faulty hats may be made before the problem is noticed, and all of them must be scrapped or reworked. Inspectors must also be recruited and paid, raising costs at a time when PH’s profit margin has already fallen from 20% to 16%. It also takes responsibility away from production workers, which could make their low motivation worse. Quality assurance — advantage: each of the 100 production workers checks the hats at their stage of the line, so a fault is spotted and corrected as soon as it happens and less material is wasted. Being trusted with quality gives workers who repeat the same tasks every day more responsibility, which could improve their motivation and reduce complaints about working conditions. Quality assurance — disadvantage: all production workers must be trained to check their own work, which is costly, and the Human Resources Director already says current training is not enough. Workers who are paid the minimum wage and are unhappy may not take the checks seriously, so faults could still get through, and stopping to check at each stage may slow the flow line and reduce output. Recommendation. PH should choose quality assurance. As a market leader selling safety equipment worldwide, it needs to prevent faults from happening, not just find them at the end, and quality assurance also cuts the waste that is squeezing its profit margin. Quality control is less suitable because it adds the cost of inspectors and does nothing to fix PH’s motivation problem; on a fast flow line it could also mean large numbers of hats are scrapped before a fault is traced. The training cost of quality assurance fits with the HR Director’s plan to increase training anyway. This depends on PH actually investing in that training and improving working conditions; if workers stay demotivated, PH would need to keep some final inspection of samples to protect its reputation. Why this scores Level 3: both methods are discussed with an applied advantage and disadvantage (flow line, safety hats, 100 minimum-wage workers, the HR Director’s email, the fall in profit margin), and the recommendation explains why quality control is rejected and what the decision depends on. The examiner report says many students mixed up the two methods; it also suggested the strongest recommendations linked quality assurance to the workers feeling more trusted and motivated. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 4.4 Location Decisions These questions test whether you can choose the location factors that fit the type of business (manufacturing or service) and explain how each affects costs, sales or production; examiners reward factors that are explained, not just named, and a conclusion that says why one factor matters more than the others. What examiners keep seeing Examiner reports often note that students give manufacturing factors (such as access to raw materials) for a service business, use single words like “transport” that are too vague to credit, or name a law instead of explaining how legal controls affect the business. 0450/13/M/J/25 Q3(b) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Source material: GAE’s directors are planning to build a new factory and want to know how legal controls over location might affect this decision. Identify two ways legal controls over location might affect a business. Way 1: they may stop the business building in certain areas, such as residential or protected land, so it has to choose another site. Way 2: they may force the business to change how it produces, for example to cut pollution, which increases its costs. Why this scores One mark for each way (only the first two are marked). The examiner report says a common mistake was naming the law itself rather than its effect on the business, and some students gave employment or marketing laws, which are not about location. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/F/M/22 Q2(c) · February/March 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: Nancy wants to be an entrepreneur. She has analysed market research data and decided to start up a book shop. Identify four factors a service business should consider when deciding on a suitable location. The number of potential customers passing the site (footfall). The cost of rent for the premises. How close it is to competitors offering a similar service. How easy it is for customers to reach, for example parking and public transport. Why this scores One mark for each relevant factor; only the first four are marked. The examiner report says single words such as “transport” or “access” were too vague to credit, and manufacturing factors such as access to raw materials were not accepted for a service business. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/13/O/N/23 Q4(d) · October/November 2023 · [6 marks] Source material: FXN manufactures mobile phones. It is a multinational company. FXN plans to build a new factory in country Y. One reason for this is the decision by the government of country Y to introduce import quotas. The Managing Director said: ‘The new factory will create 1200 jobs Explain two factors FXN should consider when deciding on a suitable location for the new factory. Factor 1: Availability of suitable employees. The new factory will need 1200 workers, many of them with the skills to assemble mobile phones accurately. If FXN chooses a site where enough suitable people live nearby, it can fill the jobs quickly and spend less on training. Production can then start on time and phones can be made efficiently, without the delays and errors that an untrained workforce would cause. Factor 2: Access to suppliers of components. Country Y has introduced import quotas, which could limit how many parts FXN can bring into the country. Locating near local suppliers of components such as screens and batteries means FXN can rely on a steady supply that the quotas do not restrict. Shorter journeys also cut transport costs and delivery times, keeping the cost of each phone down. Why this scores Each factor (K) is linked to a different case fact (1200 jobs; import quotas) (App) and explained in terms of its effect on FXN’s production or costs (An). The examiner report says most students named good factors but repeated the knowledge point instead of developing it, and some wrote about benefits to employees or suppliers rather than the business. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/O/N/22 Q4(e) · October/November 2022 · [6 marks] Do you think legal controls are the most important factor for a manufacturing business to consider when deciding which country to locate its operations in? Justify your answer. Legal controls. Planning laws may prevent a factory being built in certain areas, or in some countries at all, so the business could not produce anything there. Strict environmental laws may also force it to change its production methods or fit equipment to cut pollution, which raises costs. Some countries limit imports and exports, which could stop the business sending its products to other markets and reduce potential sales. Cost and availability of labour. Wages are often a large part of a manufacturer’s costs. Locating in a country with lower wages would lower the cost of each unit, so the business could cut prices or increase its profit margin. However, if workers lack the right skills, training costs rise and productivity may be lower, which reduces the saving. Decision. I think legal controls are the most important factor, because they decide whether the factory can operate at all: if the law forbids it, there is no output, however cheap the labour is. Problems with labour can be managed, for example by training workers or using more machinery, which may raise costs but still allows production to take place. However, once several countries all allow the factory legally, legal controls no longer separate them, and then the cost of labour or access to raw materials would become the deciding factor. Why this scores A general question, so no application marks: the answer develops legal controls and one alternative factor (K, An), then justifies why legal controls come first and what would change the decision (E). The examiner report says some answers wasted time on the scenario, and that competition and demand are not significant factors for a manufacturing business. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/23/M/J/21 Q1(a) · May/June 2021 · [8 marks] Explain four factors that may influence the location of a tertiary sector business. Factor 1: Access to customers. A tertiary business, such as a restaurant or a hairdresser, sells its service face to face, so it needs to be where many potential customers live, work or pass by. A busy location increases the number of customers and therefore its revenue. Factor 2: Cost of the site. Rent in a busy town centre is usually much higher than in a quieter area. The business must be able to afford the rent from its expected sales, otherwise high fixed costs could turn a profit into a loss. Factor 3: Availability of employees. Service businesses rely on staff to serve customers, often at evenings and weekends. Locating where enough suitable workers live makes recruitment easier and keeps wage costs reasonable, so the service is not short-staffed. Factor 4: Security. A business that handles cash or keeps valuable stock should avoid areas with high crime. A safer location reduces the risk of theft and lowers insurance costs, and customers are more willing to visit. Why this scores One mark for each of four different factors and one for each explanation. This question carried no application marks: the examiner report says answers that stayed generic found it easier to gain the explanation marks, and that access to raw materials was not appropriate for a tertiary business. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/21/M/J/25 Q2(b) · May/June 2025 · [12 marks] Source material: PF makes shoes out of natural rubber. … Philip often has to recruit new production workers as the jobs are boring. … PF’s products will still be made from natural rubber which is grown in the local area. … We use sustainable sources of raw materials unlike our competitors which use imported artificial rubber. Consider the following three factors that may influence the location of PF’s new factory. Which factor is likely to be the most important when deciding on the location? Justify your answer. • Availability of raw materials • Transport links • Government influence Availability of raw materials. PF’s shoes are made only from natural rubber grown in the local area, and its advert uses this to stand out from competitors that use imported artificial rubber. Building the new factory close to the rubber forests keeps transport costs low and means extra rubber can be delivered quickly if a large order arrives, so production does not stop. Being near its suppliers may also help PF build a good relationship with them and gain trade credit. However, if the best sites near the forests are far from towns, PF may find it harder to recruit workers, which is already a problem because the jobs are boring. Transport links. Good roads would let PF deliver finished shoes to shops quickly and cheaply, which matters in a very competitive mass market where late deliveries could lose orders. Good public transport would also let PF attract workers from a wider area, helping to solve its recruitment problem. However, sites with the best transport links are usually more expensive, which adds to fixed costs at a time when PF is already taking on a large bank loan for the factory. Government influence. The government may offer grants to businesses that locate in areas of high unemployment, which would reduce the cost of building the new factory and could provide many people looking for work. However, government controls on land use or on emissions could restrict where PF can build or how it operates, and grant areas may be far from the rubber forests, raising transport costs. Conclusion. Availability of raw materials is the most important factor. Without a reliable supply of local natural rubber, PF cannot make any shoes, and its whole brand is built on using sustainable local rubber, so it cannot simply switch to imported materials. Transport links are less important because they mainly affect the cost and speed of deliveries, which PF can manage if the factory is near the forests, and they could be improved over time. Government influence is the least important, as grants are a one-off saving and are not certain to be available near the rubber. This depends on whether there is a site close to the forests that is also within reach of enough workers; if not, PF may need to accept slightly higher transport costs to solve its recruitment problem. Why this scores Level 3: each factor gets a developed positive and negative point applied to PF (local natural rubber, the competitive market, recruitment problems, the bank loan), and the conclusion explains why the chosen factor matters most and why each of the other two matters less. The examiner report says knowledge of government influence was weak, and the best conclusions avoided repeating earlier points and compared the factors directly. Written your own answer? The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0450/12/M/J/24 Q2(b) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 5.1 Business Finance: Needs and Sources · 5.2 Cash-flow Forecasting and Working Capital · 5.3 Income Statements · 5.4 Statement of Financial Position · 5.5 Analysis of Accounts 5.1 Business Finance: Needs and Sources These questions test whether you can explain why a business needs finance and match a source to its situation; examiners reward answers that use the case (its age, size, legal form, existing debt and the purpose of the money) to say why a source does or does not fit. What examiners keep seeing Describing a source in general, or mentioning “debts” without a clear reason for the finance, instead of linking it to the business in the case. In the 12-mark choice, the top level needs every source discussed in context and a conclusion explaining why the other sources were rejected. 0450/12/O/N/20 Q3(a) · October/November 2020 · [2 marks] Define ‘micro-finance’. Micro-finance is the provision of small loans and other financial services to poor people and small entrepreneurs who are not served by traditional banks, usually because they have no security or credit history. Why this scores Two marks need both parts: small loans / financial services and for poor people who cannot borrow from traditional banks . The examiner report notes that “small loans” or “money for start-ups” on its own was too vague and earned only one mark. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/11/O/N/24 Q2(c) · October/November 2024 · [4 marks] Source material: Mitchell is an entrepreneur. He wants to start up a business selling books. … Mitchell will use microfinance as a source of finance. Outline one advantage and one disadvantage to Mitchell of using microfinance as a source of finance. Advantage: Microfinance providers do not usually ask for security (collateral) or a long credit history, so Mitchell can still borrow even though his book business is a brand-new start-up with no trading record and possibly no assets. Disadvantage: Microfinance loans are only for small amounts, so Mitchell may not be able to borrow enough to buy a wide range of books to stock, which could limit his sales when the business opens. Why this scores One mark for each correct advantage and disadvantage (K) and one for linking each to Mitchell’s new book-selling business (App). “Only small amounts” is knowledge; “so he cannot buy many books” is what earns the application mark. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/13/O/N/24 Q2(e) · October/November 2024 · [6 marks] Do you think crowdfunding is the best source of finance for a start-up business to use? Justify your answer. For crowdfunding: A start-up has no trading record and often no assets to offer as security, so a bank may refuse it a loan. Crowdfunding raises money online from a large number of people who each put in a small amount, and there is no interest to pay. This means the new business has no loan repayments taking cash out every month at the very time its cash flow is weakest. A successful campaign also acts as free promotion and market research: if many people back the idea, the owner knows there is demand and may already have the first customers. Against crowdfunding: There is no guarantee the target will be reached. If too few people back the project, the entrepreneur may raise only part of the money and has spent weeks on a campaign that has delayed the launch, so another source must be found anyway. The idea also has to be shown publicly before the business opens, so a competitor could copy it and take sales. A bank loan, if it is approved, gives the full amount quickly. Decision: I think crowdfunding is the best source for most start-ups, because a new business is risky and may not get a bank loan at all, and even if it did, fixed monthly repayments with interest could cause a cash-flow crisis in the first months when revenue is still low. However, it depends on the idea appealing to the public: for a business that is hard to explain online, or one that needs money urgently, the owner’s savings or a loan would be a safer choice. Why this scores This is a general question, so no case is needed: two points of knowledge, each developed to an effect on cash flow or sales (analysis), then a justified decision that compares crowdfunding with a bank loan and says what the choice depends on (evaluation). Evaluation that simply repeats an earlier point earns nothing extra. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/13/M/J/24 Q1(d) · May/June 2024 · [6 marks] Source material: WFT has 30 employees and uses a lot of technology to process the timber. … WFT often needs finance. … Current assets 120 000 Current liabilities 150 000 Non-current liabilities 320 000 Explain two factors WFT should consider when deciding on a source of finance. Factor 1: The amount of finance needed. WFT uses a lot of technology to process its timber, and new saws or processing machinery cost a great deal. With only $120 000 of current assets, it is unlikely to have enough internal finance for a large purchase, so it would need a long-term external source such as a bank loan or a share issue. An overdraft would be unsuitable because it is meant for small, short-term amounts and has high interest. Factor 2: Its existing level of debt. WFT already has non-current liabilities of $320 000, and its current liabilities ($150 000) are higher than its current assets. A bank may therefore see it as a high risk and refuse more borrowing or charge a higher interest rate, which would increase WFT’s cash outflows. This means WFT might be better using a source that does not add to its debt, such as issuing shares if it is a limited company. Why this scores Each factor earns one mark for knowledge (amount needed, existing debt), one for applying it to WFT (its technology, the $320 000 of non-current liabilities) and one for analysis (the effect on which source is possible, or on cash outflows). Using the figures from Table 1.1 is the quickest way to secure the application marks. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/21/M/J/23 Q4(a) · May/June 2023 · [8 marks] Source material: VP has a chain of 500 fast-food restaurants that operate across country Z. … Each VP restaurant has a Manager, an Assistant Manager and 50 employees who cook and serve the meals. … VP wants to expand into another country. Explain, using an example, one reason why VP might need: • short-term finance • long-term finance. Short-term finance: to pay day-to-day costs (working capital). Each of VP’s 500 restaurants has to buy vegetarian ingredients and pay wages to its 50 cooks and serving staff every week, even in a quiet month when fewer meals are sold. If cash from diners comes in more slowly than these payments go out, VP could be short of cash. A bank overdraft would be a suitable example: VP only borrows what it needs, for the days it needs it, so interest is kept low and suppliers and staff are still paid on time. Long-term finance: to fund the expansion into another country. Opening new VP restaurants abroad needs a very large sum for premises, kitchen equipment and staff training, and the new restaurants will take several years to pay for themselves. As VP is a public limited company, it could issue new shares as an example of long-term finance. Shares never have to be repaid and carry no interest, so VP’s cash flow is not drained by repayments while the new restaurants are still building up sales. Why this scores For each type: one mark for a valid reason, and up to three more for explaining it, which must include VP’s context (500 restaurants, staff wages, expansion abroad) and a named example of finance (overdraft, share issue). The examiner report says weak answers mentioned “debts” without a specific reason and did not link the answer to VP. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/21/O/N/22 Q2(b) · October/November 2022 · [12 marks] Source material: Tokumbo is a sole trader. He started SA 2 years ago in country X. … New vehicles will be needed whichever option you choose for the future growth of your business. … Interest rates on bank loans have fallen to 2% whilst interest rates on savings are 3%. Consider the following three sources of finance Tokumbo could use for the new vehicles. Which source should he choose? Justify your answer. • Leasing • Bank loan • Retained profit Leasing – advantage: SA can use new safari vehicles straight away without paying a large lump sum. As SA is only 2 years old, Tokumbo may not have that much capital, so leasing lets him pay monthly out of the money tourists pay for their tours. The leasing company usually maintains the vehicles too, so breakdowns on the game reserve and cancelled tours become less likely. Leasing – disadvantage: Over the whole lease SA pays more than the price of buying the vehicles, and it never owns them. At the end of the lease the vehicles must be returned, so SA has no asset to sell or to use as security, and Tokumbo must arrange (and pay for) replacements again. Bank loan – advantage: Interest rates on bank loans have fallen to just 2%, so borrowing is cheap. The loan can be repaid over several years, keeping each monthly repayment small, and SA owns the vehicles, which will be used for many 7-day tours. Bank loan – disadvantage: The repayments and interest must be paid every month even if bookings fall, for example if the 4% inflation in country X makes tours less affordable. As a sole trader Tokumbo has unlimited liability, and the bank may ask for security, so his own house could be at risk if SA cannot repay. A small, young business may also be charged more than the 2% headline rate. Retained profit – advantage: It does not have to be repaid and has no interest, and no security is needed, so it adds nothing to SA’s monthly cash outflows and puts none of Tokumbo’s personal assets at risk. Retained profit – disadvantage: SA has only traded for 2 years, so it may not have built up enough retained profit to pay for several new vehicles. Using it all would leave no reserve for emergencies such as a vehicle repair. There is also an opportunity cost: money kept in savings earns 3%, which is more than the 2% a loan costs. Recommendation. I recommend a bank loan. With loan interest at 2% and savings earning 3%, it is actually cheaper for Tokumbo to borrow and keep any profit in the bank as a safety reserve, and SA will own vehicles it can use for years. Retained profit is less suitable because a 2-year-old business is unlikely to have enough, and spending it would remove SA’s emergency cash. Leasing is less suitable because it costs more in total and SA would end up with no assets. However, this depends on the bank actually offering a small sole trader a rate close to 2%; if it refuses or wants Tokumbo’s house as security, leasing would be the safer choice because it needs no lump sum and no security. Why this scores Level 3 (9–12): all three sources are discussed with an advantage and a disadvantage applied to SA (2 years old, sole trader, 2% loan rate vs 3% savings), and the recommendation explains why the other two were rejected and what the decision depends on. The examiner report says candidates were least confident about leasing, and that top conclusions avoided repeating earlier points. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 5.2 Cash-flow Forecasting and Working Capital These questions test why cash matters, how a cash-flow forecast and working capital help a business survive, and how cash-flow problems can be solved; examiners reward answers that trace each point to its effect on cash inflows or outflows. What examiners keep seeing Confusing cash with profit, the commonest error in the examiner reports, and writing “revenue” or “money” where the answer needs cash inflows and cash outflows. Two examples of the same reason (paying wages, then paying suppliers) earn only one mark. 0450/12/O/N/25 Q2(a) · October/November 2025 · [2 marks] Define ‘cash flow forecast’. A cash-flow forecast is an estimate of the cash a business expects to flow in and out in the future, usually set out month by month, showing the net cash flow and closing balance for each month. Why this scores One mark for cash inflows and outflows, one for the idea that it is an estimate of the future . “Shows the cash coming in and going out of a business” misses the forecast idea and is only a partial definition. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/11/M/J/24 Q3(b) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Table 3.1 Extract from IDT’s statement of financial position ($ million) 2022 2023 Current assets 380 420 Current liabilities 250 280 Calculate IDT’s working capital in 2023. Working capital = current assets − current liabilities = $420 million − $280 million = $140 million Why this scores One mark for the correct method, two for $140 million with the unit “million”. Using the 2022 column by mistake ($380m − $250m = $130 million) earns only the method mark, so check which year the question asks for. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/M/J/23 Q4(c) · May/June 2023 · [4 marks] Source material: CPF is a clothing retailer. It is a private limited company. It has 4 shops and 30 employees. … CPF’s directors are planning to expand the business by opening a new shop. Outline two possible reasons why working capital is important for CPF. To pay day-to-day expenses. CPF needs enough working capital to pay the wages of its 30 employees and the running costs of its 4 shops on time each month, even when clothes sales are slow, so it can keep trading. To cover unexpected costs. As CPF expands by opening a new shop, unplanned costs may arise, such as repairs to the new premises or delays before the shop reaches its expected sales; working capital lets CPF pay these without running out of cash, which matters because its retained profit is low. Why this scores One mark for each reason (K) and one for linking each to CPF (30 employees, 4 shops, the new shop). The examiner report warns that paying wages and paying suppliers are two examples of the same reason and score only once, and that many candidates confused working capital with profit. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/O/N/25 Q2(d) · October/November 2025 · [6 marks] Source material: OTK is a small jewellery shop in the centre of Main City. … OTK buys its jewellery from local suppliers. It pays for the jewellery 30 days later. … She is concerned that the business might have a short-term cash flow problem. Explain two ways OTK could overcome a short-term cash flow problem. Way 1: Arrange a bank overdraft. OTK could agree an overdraft with its bank to cover the weeks when its balance is likely to be negative, for example after buying new jewellery stock before a busy festival period. This lets the shop spend more than it has in its account, so it can still pay the rent on its city-centre premises and its staff on time. Because the problem is only short-term, OTK pays interest only on the amount it actually uses, for as long as it is overdrawn. Way 2: Ask suppliers for longer to pay. OTK currently pays its local suppliers 30 days after delivery. If it negotiates 60 days, the cash outflow for each delivery of jewellery is delayed by a month, so OTK has more time to sell the pieces and receive cash from customers before it has to pay. This would improve its closing cash balance in the months the manager is worried about. Why this scores Each way earns one mark for knowledge, one for applying it to OTK (jewellery shop, city centre, local suppliers, 30 days) and one for analysis, which the mark scheme says must show the effect on cash inflows or outflows. “An overdraft gives the business money” is not enough; explain how it keeps payments flowing. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/22/M/J/23 Q3(a) · May/June 2023 · [8 marks] Source material: They plan to start up a theatre in a low-income area of Main City. … Zane is planning to prepare a cash-flow forecast for the first year. … ET will have 24 part-time employees as shown in the organisational chart in Appendix 1. Explain four reasons why it is important that Zane prepares a cash-flow forecast before starting ET. 1. To identify when ET might run short of cash. Before the theatre opens, Zane and Zaara must pay for costumes, scenery and the wages of 24 part-time employees, but ticket sales only start once performances begin. The forecast shows in advance any months with a negative closing balance, so they can arrange an overdraft before the shortage happens. 2. To help obtain a bank loan. ET is a new business with no trading record, so a bank will want evidence that it can afford repayments. A forecast of expected cash inflows from selling the 100 seats each evening, set against planned outflows, shows the bank how the loan would be repaid. 3. To make sure day-to-day costs can be paid. The forecast shows whether ET will have enough working capital to pay its part-time actors and ticket-office staff every week. Without this cash, performances might have to be cancelled, damaging the new theatre’s reputation. 4. To help plan and make decisions. Zane can test what happens to cash inflows at different ticket prices. As the theatre is in a low-income area, a high price could leave seats empty, so the forecast helps them choose a price and a first performance they can afford. Why this scores One mark for each reason (K) and one for applying it to ET (24 part-time staff, 100 seats, costumes, low-income area). The examiner report says the commonest error was confusing cash flow with profit, and that many answers used “revenue” or “money” instead of cash inflows and outflows, or forgot this is a forecast for the future. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/22/F/M/22 Q4(b) · February/March 2022 · [12 marks] Source material: The total revenue from these 50 rooms is $3000 per night. … We do not have any savings. … Other hotels in the area require a 30% deposit. Consider the following three ways Sadiq could improve MH’s cash flow. • Arrange a bank loan. • Ask customers to pay a deposit of 20% when they book a room. • Ask for trade credit from food suppliers. Which would be the most effective way for MH to improve its cash flow? Justify your answer. Bank loan – advantage: A loan gives MH a large cash inflow straight away. As the hotel has no savings at all, this would give it a cash buffer to pay wages to its 40 employees and other bills during a quiet period. Bank loan – disadvantage: The loan has to be repaid with interest, so every month for years there is an extra cash outflow. In the long run this makes MH’s cash flow worse, not better, and it does nothing about the causes of the problem. The bank may also want detailed financial documents, which could take time as Sadiq has few financial skills. 20% deposit – advantage: Cash arrives when a room is booked, before the guest stays. The average room earns $60 a night ($3000 ÷ 50), so each booking brings in $12 early; across 50 rooms that is around $600 of cash received in advance for each night that is booked. A deposit also makes guests less likely to cancel, and at 20% it is still lower than the 30% that other local hotels charge. 20% deposit – disadvantage: Many guests return every year and have never paid a deposit, so some may be annoyed and book elsewhere, reducing future inflows. It also only brings cash forward; it does not increase the total amount guests pay. Trade credit – advantage: If food suppliers allow, say, 30 days to pay, MH’s cash outflows for ingredients are delayed. Guests pay for restaurant meals straight away, so the hotel holds the cash before it has to pay suppliers. Trade credit – disadvantage: Suppliers may refuse because MH has no savings, or offer smaller discounts, which raises the cost of food. Food is also only one part of the hotel’s costs, so the improvement in cash flow is limited, and Sadiq, who already works 60–90 hours a week, may not have time to negotiate with each supplier. Recommendation. The 20% deposit is the most effective way. It increases cash inflows immediately on every booking, costs MH nothing in interest, and because it is below the 30% competitors charge, few guests should be put off. A bank loan is less effective because the repayments and interest will drain cash every month after the first inflow, so it is only a short-term fix. Trade credit is weaker because it only delays the food bill, a small share of MH’s costs, and suppliers may not agree. This depends on how loyal regular guests are: if many of them stop booking because of the deposit, Sadiq should combine a lower deposit with trade credit. Why this scores Level 3 needs all three ways discussed in context with their effect on cash inflows or outflows, plus a conclusion that explains why the other two were rejected. The examiner report says many answers discussed the three ways without linking them to cash flow, which kept them in Level 1, and that trade credit was the least understood option. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 5.3 Income Statements These questions test whether you can read an income statement, say what each profit figure means and explain why profit matters; examiners reward precise definitions and reasons that are developed with the business’s own figures. What examiners keep seeing Treating revenue, profit and cash as the same thing, and saying profit is used to pay day-to-day costs. Examiner reports also note many answers say profit is important “to expand” without explaining how: it is a source of finance with no interest to pay. 0450/12/M/J/23 Q4(a) · May/June 2023 · [2 marks] Define ‘retained profit’. Retained profit is the profit left over after all costs, tax and dividends to shareholders have been paid, which the business keeps and reinvests in itself. Why this scores One mark for “profit left after tax and dividends”, one for “kept and reinvested in the business”. The examiner report says many candidates defined profit instead, or just reordered the words of the term. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/M/J/25 Q2(c) · May/June 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: FLD is a furniture retailer. It has 460 shops and 20 000 employees. The manufacturers that supply FLD may have raised the prices it pays for the furniture it resells. Get it marked → 0450/12/F/M/22 Q3(c) · February/March 2022 · [4 marks] Source material: D2G is a driving school. Mattan wants to understand the difference between profit and cash. Revenue 20 000 Gross profit 12 000 Profit for the year 2000 Outline, with reference to D2G, the difference between profit and cash. Profit is D2G’s revenue minus all its costs over the year, which was $2000 in 2021. Cash is the actual money D2G holds at any moment to pay bills such as fuel for its cars and the instructor’s wages. The two differ because of timing. If a learner pays in December for a block of ten lessons taught in January, D2G receives the cash now, but the revenue and profit only count when the lessons are given. And when Mattan buys the new vehicle, a large amount of cash leaves the business at once, yet the car is a non-current asset, so its whole cost is not taken off this year’s profit. D2G could therefore report a profit of $2000 and still be short of cash. Why this scores One mark for knowing what profit or cash is, one for showing the difference (when money is received or paid versus when profit is earned), and two for links to D2G (lessons, the new car, the $2000 profit). The examiner report says only the strongest answers explained the difference, and many wrongly assumed revenue is the same as cash. Written your own answer? Extract from TJM’s financial statements for 2021 ($m) … Profit for the year 200 Explain two possible reasons why profit might be important to TJM. Source of finance. TJM can keep part of its $200m profit as retained profit and use it to fit out the 20 new shops. This means it does not need a large bank loan, so there is no interest to pay and no repayments, which keeps its costs down while it expands. It also avoids bringing in new shareholders, so the existing owners keep control of the company. Reward for the owners. The shareholders of this private limited company invested their money and could have lost it if the food shops had failed. A profit of $200m allows TJM to pay them dividends, giving a better return than they could earn by investing elsewhere. As a result, they are more willing to keep their money in TJM and to put in more if the expansion needs it. Why this scores Each paragraph earns one mark for the reason, one for a link to TJM ($200m, 20 new shops, private limited company) and one for the consequence. The examiner report says this was poorly answered: many simply wrote “to expand” without saying how profit helps, and some wrongly said profit pays day-to-day expenses. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/13/O/N/25 Q1(e) · October/November 2025 · [6 marks] Explain two reasons why profit is important for a business. Which reason is likely to be the most important? Justify your answer. Reward for risk-taking. Owners put their own money into a business and could lose all of it. Profit gives them a return, for example as dividends, that should be higher than they could earn from a bank. Without that reward, owners would have no reason to keep their money in the business, and few people would start new ones. Source of finance. Profit that is retained can be reinvested in new machinery, more stock or a new branch. It does not have to be repaid and carries no interest, so it is the cheapest source of finance. This lets the business grow and stay competitive without adding to its costs or its debts. Decision. I think being a source of finance is the most important reason. Retained profit pays for the investment that keeps a business ahead of its rivals, and that investment creates more profit, and so a bigger reward for the owners, in the future. The reward for risk-taking matters, but owners of a growing business will often accept low dividends for a few years if the business is getting bigger; a business that cannot fund investment may fall behind and fail, and then there is no reward at all. Why this scores Two marks for two reasons, two for developing each with a consequence, and two for a decision that explains why the chosen reason outweighs the other. It is a general question, so there are no application marks; to reach the evaluation marks you must discuss both reasons first. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/23/O/N/23 Q4(b) · October/November 2023 · [12 marks] Source material: He plans to invite his father and sister to invest in the business partnership. All three of them will each invest $30 000 to start BB. However, Benjy thinks BB may need more investment as it expands. Consider the following three reasons why profit will be important to BB. Which reason is likely to be the most important? Justify your answer. • Reward for risk-taking • Source of finance • Way to measure the success of the business Reward for risk-taking. Benjy, his father and his sister are putting $90 000 in total into a brand-new business, building houses for people with disabilities, a market where Benjy does not yet know the demand. If BB fails they could lose all of it. Profit is their reward for taking that risk. This matters most for the father and sister, who will not run BB, so their share of the profit is the only return they get. If BB makes a good profit they are likely to leave their money in and invest more when BB expands. However, BB uses job production with high-quality materials for each customer, so profit may be low in the first years, and if they judge BB only on early profit they may lose patience and take their money out. Source of finance. Retained profit can pay for growth, such as more equipment, more timber or extra skilled workers, without a bank loan. BB pays no interest and has no repayments, which keeps its costs low and leaves the partners in full control. However, profit from each house is small compared with the cost of building it: from Appendix 2, House B costs $100 000 to build and sells for $110 000, giving a profit of only $10 000. It would take many houses before retained profit could fund a big expansion, and the partners may want the profit paid out to them, so BB will probably still need a loan. Measure of success. Profit shows whether specialising in houses for people with disabilities is working. Benjy can compare the two options: House A makes $7000 profit on $70 000 (10%), House B $10 000 on $110 000 (about 9%). This helps him decide which houses to build and whether BB is doing better than other building firms, so the partners know whether to expand. However, for a new business, profit is not the only measure: in the first year the number of orders, customer satisfaction and BB’s reputation may show its success better, because start-up costs keep early profit low even when the business is going well. Recommendation. I think the reward for risk-taking is the most important reason. BB is funded entirely by three family members’ $90 000, and two of them are only investors, so profit is the whole reason they are involved. Benjy already expects to need more investment as BB grows, and the easiest place to get it is from his father and sister; they will only agree if BB has rewarded them. Profit as a source of finance is less important because one house earns only $7000 to $10 000, so BB will need loans or extra partners anyway. Profit as a measure of success is less important early on because BB can judge its progress by orders and reputation. This depends on how much demand Benjy’s market research finds: if demand is high and steady, BB could expand quickly and retained profit as finance would become more important. Why this scores Level 3 (9–12): all three reasons discussed in detail with BB’s facts (the $30 000 each, the father and sister as investors, the Appendix 2 house costs) and a conclusion explaining why the other two were rejected. The examiner report says few candidates got past Level 1: they repeated the question (“they took a risk so they deserve a reward”), thought the reward went to employees, or said profit pays operating costs rather than funding investment. Written your own answer? A statement of financial position is an accounting statement that shows the value of what a business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owners’ equity, at one particular date. Why this scores One mark for assets and liabilities (what it owns and owes), the second for “at a particular point in time”. The examiner report says most answers left out the date, and some confused it with an income statement or cash flow forecast. Written your own answer? Why this scores One mark for “debts owed by the business” and one for “repaid within one year”. The examiner report says “short-term” on its own was too vague: you need the 12-month limit. Get it marked → 0450/11/M/J/24 Q3(d) · May/June 2024 · [6 marks] Source material: IDT manufactures clothes for the mass market. It is a multinational company with factories in 4 countries. Extract from IDT’s statement of financial position ($ million) 2022 2023 … Non-current liabilities 300 400 Explain two ways an increase in non-current liabilities might affect IDT. Higher interest costs. IDT’s non-current liabilities, such as long-term loans, rose from $300 million to $400 million. Interest must be paid on the extra $100 million every year, which increases IDT’s expenses and cash outflows. As a result, the profit from its clothing factories falls unless sales rise at the same time. Harder to borrow more. With $400 million already owed long-term, lenders may see IDT as a riskier borrower. If it wants another loan, for example to open a factory in a fifth country, banks may refuse, demand more collateral or charge a higher interest rate, which could delay or stop its expansion. Why this scores Each way earns one mark for the point (interest to pay, harder or dearer to borrow), one for a link to IDT ($400 million, its factories and clothes) and one for the consequence (higher expenses and lower profit, delayed expansion). Get it marked → 5.5 Analysis of Accounts These questions test whether you know what profitability and liquidity ratios measure, can calculate them, and can explain who uses accounts and why; examiners reward answers that say what a ratio shows for this business, not just the number. What examiners keep seeing Confusing profit with profitability, and liquidity with profit: liquidity is about paying short-term debts on time. Examiner reports also note many candidates describe profit or cash flow when the question asks about ratios. 0450/12/O/N/20 Q4(b) · October/November 2020 · [2 marks] Define ‘Return on Capital Employed’. Return on capital employed is profit expressed as a percentage of the capital employed (invested) in the business: profit ÷ capital employed × 100. Why this scores Two marks for profit as a percentage of capital employed (the correct formula alone also earns both). The examiner report says many candidates did not know the term, defined profit margin instead, or simply reordered the words. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/13/M/J/24 Q1(b) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Source material: Extract from WFT’s statement of financial position at 30 April 2024 $ Non-current assets 600 000 Current assets 120 000 Current liabilities 150 000 Non-current liabilities 320 000 Calculate WFT’s current ratio in 2024. Show your working. Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = 120 000 ÷ 150 000 = 0.8 (0.8 : 1) WFT has only $0.80 of current assets for every $1 of current liabilities, so it may struggle to pay its short-term debts. Why this scores Two marks for 0.8 or 0.8 : 1; one mark for the correct method if the arithmetic slips. Use only the current figures, and do not turn the ratio into a percentage. Extract from AHG’s statement of financial position at 30 March 2022 ($000) Non-current assets 800 Current assets 660 Current liabilities 600 Outline two possible reasons why liquidity is important to AHG. To pay short-term debts on time. AHG needs enough cash and other current assets to pay the suppliers of its plants and flowers and its 34 staff. Its current ratio is only 660 ÷ 600 = 1.1, so it has little to spare if sales are slow. To be able to borrow. Banks check liquidity before lending. If this established business can show it covers its short-term debts comfortably, it will find it easier to arrange an overdraft, for example to buy extra garden stock before its busy season. Why this scores One mark for each reason (paying short-term debts; arranging finance) and one for each different link to AHG (the current ratio of 1.1, plants and flowers, an established business). The examiner report warns that “pay wages” and “pay suppliers” count as the same reason, and some wrongly thought liquidity measures profit. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/11/M/J/21 Q2(d) · May/June 2021 · [6 marks] Source material: PJA make fashion clothing for 16-25 year olds. Many of its competitors are multinational companies. Extract from PJA’s financial statements for 2020 Revenue ($m) 7 400 Gross profit ($m) 3 330 Profit ($m) 1 100 Current ratio 1.5 Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) 8% Explain two ways PJA’s managers can use ratio analysis. Compare performance over time. PJA’s managers can compare this year’s ratios with last year’s. For example, if ROCE was 10% in 2019, the fall to 8% shows the capital invested in its clothing factory is earning less profit. This warns managers to act, for example by cutting costs or dropping fashion lines that young customers no longer buy, before profitability falls further. Compare with competitors. Managers can compare PJA’s ratios with those of its multinational rivals. PJA’s gross profit margin is 3 330 ÷ 7 400 × 100 = 45%. If rivals achieve 55%, PJA knows its cost of sales is too high, so it could look for cheaper fabric or raise prices on its most popular styles to stay competitive. Why this scores Each way earns one mark for knowledge (trends over time; comparison with competitors), one for application (PJA’s ROCE of 8%, its gross margin, its multinational rivals) and one for analysis (what managers then do). The examiner report says even strong candidates did not develop their points, and many described profit or cash flow instead of profitability and liquidity. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/M/J/24 Q2(e) · May/June 2024 · [6 marks] Do you think banks are the main external users of the accounts of a business? Justify your answer. Banks. Before lending, a bank studies a business’s accounts to see whether it makes enough profit, and has enough liquidity, to repay a loan with interest. The accounts help the bank decide whether to lend, how much, and at what interest rate, since a riskier business is charged more. Suppliers. Suppliers that sell on credit look at the current and acid test ratios to judge whether the business can pay its trade payables on time. If liquidity is poor, they may refuse credit or ask for cash on delivery, which protects them from bad debts. Decision. I think banks are usually the main external users, because a bank loan is often far larger than the credit any one supplier gives, so the bank has more to lose and studies the accounts in more detail. Its decision also has the biggest effect on the business, as refusing a loan can stop an expansion. However, it depends on the business: a firm with no loans that buys most of its materials on credit from one supplier would find that supplier is its main external user. Why this scores Two marks for identifying users and what they look for, two for developing why, and two for a judgement that compares banks with another user. This mirrors the mark scheme’s reasoning that banks often lend large sums, while suppliers may care less if orders are small; an answer about banks alone cannot reach the evaluation marks. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/23/M/J/25 Q3(b) · May/June 2025 · [12 marks] Source material: The restaurant will serve a wide range of vegan meals and Jemi will purchase ingredients, including fruit and vegetables, directly from local suppliers. Jemi is going to use her own capital of $50 000 to buy the franchise, but she will also need a source of external finance to help set up the business. Consider why the profitability and liquidity ratios for her restaurant will be important to Jemi. Which is likely to be the most important for the success of Jemi’s restaurant? Justify your answer. Profitability ratios. The gross profit margin shows whether Jemi is controlling the cost of her ingredients. Appendix 3 says reliable fruit and vegetable suppliers are getting harder to find and restaurants are buying from further away, so her cost of sales may rise; a falling gross margin would warn her to change suppliers or raise menu prices. The profit margin shows whether expenses such as the chef’s wages and the other 11 staff are under control. ROCE compares her profit with the $50 000 she has invested: if it is lower than she could earn by saving the money, the restaurant is not worth the risk. However, these ratios use past figures, and a new restaurant has no previous year to compare with, so in the first year they may simply show low profit while the business builds up customers. Liquidity ratios. The current ratio and acid test ratio show whether the restaurant can pay its short-term debts: fresh ingredients from local suppliers, wages for 12 employees and repayments on her external finance. Fresh fruit and vegetables cannot be kept for long, so the acid test ratio, which leaves out inventory, is a useful check. A current ratio of about 1.5 to 2 would show she can pay comfortably, and the lender of her external finance will look at these ratios before and after lending. If the ratios fall below 1, suppliers may stop delivering and the restaurant could be forced to close even if it is popular. However, liquidity ratios only show the position on one date, and very high liquidity can mean cash is lying idle instead of being used to grow the business. Recommendation. I think liquidity ratios are the most important for the success of Jemi’s restaurant, at least in its first year. She has put all $50 000 of her own money into the franchise and must also repay external finance, so cash will be tight while she has daily bills for ingredients and wages. A new restaurant can survive a year of low profit, but not a month in which it cannot pay its suppliers, especially when reliable suppliers are already scarce. Profitability ratios are less important at the start because new businesses often make little profit while they build a customer base, and the rising trend in vegan eating (10% to 25%) suggests profit should follow. This depends on how large her external finance and repayments are; once the restaurant is established, ROCE becomes more important in deciding whether the franchise is a good use of her $50 000. Why this scores Level 3 (9–12) needs detailed discussion of both types of ratio applied to Jemi (her $50 000, external finance, fresh ingredients from local suppliers, a new restaurant) and a conclusion that explains why the other was rejected. The examiner report says this was the lowest-scoring question on the paper: most candidates confused profit with profitability, and only said liquidity is “about paying debts” without developing it. Written your own answer? The questions are quoted exactly; the model answers are my own, written to the published mark schemes and the advice in the examiner reports. How to use this page Cover the answer, write your own in timed conditions (about 1½ minutes per mark), then compare. 0450/12/M/J/24 Q2(b) is the paper reference: syllabus/component/session/year, then question and part. F/M = February/March, M/J = May/June, O/N = October/November. Jump to: 6.1 Economic Issues · 6.2 Environmental and Ethical Issues · 6.3 Business and the International Economy 6.1 Economic Issues These questions test whether you can trace an economic change (interest rates, inflation, taxes, the business cycle, unemployment) through to a named business’s sales, costs and profit; examiners reward the full chain, not a list of effects. What examiners keep seeing Stating effects in general (“costs will rise”) without saying which costs, for which product, and what happens to revenue or profit. Examiners also report candidates misreading economy-wide changes: the unemployment question was often answered as if it were about the business recruiting more staff. 0450/12/M/J/21 Q4(b) · May/June 2021 · [2 marks] Identify two government economic objectives. Objective 1: Low unemployment. Objective 2: Low and stable inflation. Why this scores One mark for each correct objective (economic growth and a stable balance of payments would also score). The examiner report notes a common error: giving a way to achieve an objective, such as “cut taxes”, instead of the objective itself. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/O/N/25 Q4(c) · October/November 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: DJU manufactures clothing including jeans and trousers. There are 90 employees working in its factory. … DJU’s directors are considering different ways a business could grow including taking over a competitor. Outline two ways lower interest rates might affect DJU. Way 1: Cheaper borrowing for growth. Lower interest rates reduce the cost of a loan, so it becomes cheaper for DJU to finance taking over a competitor and grow the business. Way 2: Higher demand. Consumers pay less interest on their own loans and credit cards, so they have more income to spend on non-essentials such as new jeans and trousers, increasing DJU’s sales. Why this scores One mark for each way (cheaper borrowing, higher consumer spending) and one for each application. The two points use different case details (the takeover plan, and jeans and trousers), so both application marks are earned. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/O/N/24 Q1(d) · October/November 2024 · [6 marks] Source material: Avtar owns a car repair business which operates in the private sector. It is a small business with 2 full-time employees. Explain two ways an economic recession might affect Avtar’s business. Way 1: Lower demand for repairs. In a recession incomes fall and unemployment rises, so car owners put off non-urgent servicing and repairs. Avtar’s car repair business will therefore have fewer jobs each week, so its revenue falls. With only 2 full-time employees, a fall in work could force him to make one of them redundant to cut his costs. Way 2: Cash-flow problems. Customers who are short of money may ask to pay later or fail to pay at all, so Avtar’s cash inflows fall while he still has to pay his 2 employees’ wages and buy spare parts. He may need an overdraft to cover the gap, and because banks lend more cautiously in a recession, the finance his business needs may be harder or more expensive to obtain. Why this scores Each way earns three marks: the effect (lower demand; cash-flow problems), a link to Avtar’s car repairs and 2 full-time employees, and development to a consequence such as lower revenue, redundancy or needing an overdraft. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/M/J/22 Q2(e) · May/June 2022 · [6 marks] Do you think a reduction in the level of unemployment always benefits businesses? Justify your answer. Yes, it can benefit businesses. When unemployment falls, more people have a regular income, so household spending rises. Businesses such as shops and restaurants see higher demand for their products, so their revenue and profit can increase. No, it can create problems. With fewer people looking for work, it becomes harder for a business to recruit, especially skilled workers. Vacancies may stay empty, so output cannot rise to meet the extra demand and orders may be lost. To attract and keep staff, firms may also have to offer higher wages, which raises labour costs and squeezes profit margins. Decision. I do not think it always benefits businesses. A retailer selling to consumers is likely to gain, because the rise in spending directly increases its revenue while it needs few extra staff. But a labour-intensive manufacturer that needs many skilled workers to expand may find that staff shortages and a higher wage bill outweigh the extra sales. It depends on how much the business relies on recruiting new workers. Why this scores Two marks for identifying both sides (higher sales; recruitment difficulty and higher wages), two for developing them to revenue and costs, and two for a decision that explains when the benefit outweighs the drawback. The examiner report says many candidates misread this as the business itself hiring more staff; the question is about unemployment in the whole economy. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/21/O/N/22 Q4(a) · October/November 2022 · [8 marks] Source material: SA organises safari tours which take tourists to view wild animals on a game reserve. Most of SA’s customers are tourists from other countries. … The inflation rate in country X has increased to 4% which may affect some of our local safari businesses. Explain two possible effects on SA of the increase in the rate of inflation in country X. Effect 1: Higher costs. With inflation in country X now at 4%, the prices SA pays for its inputs will rise: fuel for its 4 safari vehicles and the rooms it books in small local hotels for each 7 day tour. Tokumbo’s cost per tour therefore increases. If he cannot pass all of this on in higher prices, the profit margin on each safari shrinks; if he does raise prices, he must keep re-pricing the tours he advertises to tourists. Effect 2: Lower demand from foreign tourists. Most of SA’s customers come from other countries. If SA raises its prices to cover higher costs, a safari in country X becomes more expensive compared with holidays elsewhere. Price-sensitive tourists, such as the younger travellers looking for cheaper holidays, may choose another destination, so bookings fall. Lower sales would reduce SA’s revenue just as its costs are rising, so profit could fall sharply for a business that has only been operating for 2 years. Why this scores One mark for each effect plus up to three for explaining it, at least one point applied to SA: here the 4% rate, safari vehicles, local hotels and foreign tourists. The examiner report praised answers that linked rising fuel and accommodation costs to higher prices and then to lower demand and profit, and criticised brief effects that were not linked to SA. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/21/O/N/24 Q2(b) · October/November 2024 · [12 marks] Source material: Sam’s cookies are high-quality and often purchased by customers for special occasions such as birthdays or weddings. … The government has announced that interest rates will decrease from 1st November 2024. … Taxes will also change and will increase from 1st April 2025. Consider how a decrease in interest rates and an increase in taxes in country P could affect CC. Which is likely to have the biggest effect on CC’s profit? Justify your answer. Decrease in interest rates: positive effect. Sam is considering taking out a bank loan. Lower interest rates reduce the interest he pays on it, so CC’s expenses are lower and profit is higher. Cheaper borrowing also makes it more affordable to buy extra specialised baking equipment for the new cookies he plans to sell to other retail shops, raising output and possibly lowering average costs. Decrease in interest rates: limited effect. CC is a small business with one shop, so if Sam borrows only a modest amount the saving in interest will be small compared with his total costs. CC’s cookies are bought for birthdays and weddings, which customers do not usually pay for with loans, so cheaper borrowing may do little to increase demand. The cut in interest rates may therefore change profit only slightly. Increase in taxes: negative effect. If income taxes rise, consumers have less disposable income. High-quality cookies bought for special occasions are a treat rather than a necessity, so customers may buy fewer, choose cheaper cookies or drop the personalised messages. Sales in CC’s city-centre shop would fall, reducing revenue and profit. If taxes on sales rise instead, Sam may have to raise his prices, which could reduce demand further. Increase in taxes: possible benefit. The government plans to use some of the extra tax revenue to increase payments to people on the lowest incomes. Some of these people may now be able to afford a cookie to celebrate a birthday, which could partly offset the lost sales. A cookie is also a small purchase, so a modest tax rise may not stop customers buying one for a wedding. Recommendation. I think the increase in taxes is likely to have the biggest effect on CC’s profit. It affects every customer who buys from CC’s shop, and because Sam’s cookies are high-quality treats, demand will fall when after-tax incomes fall, cutting revenue directly. The interest rate cut matters less because it only lowers the cost of a loan Sam has not yet taken out, so the saving is small for a business of CC’s size. However, this depends on how much Sam borrows: if he takes a large loan to buy new equipment and supply other retail shops, the lower interest rate could have the bigger effect. Why this scores Level 3 (9–12 marks) needs detailed, applied discussion of both changes and a well-justified conclusion that explains why the other change is rejected. Each change is analysed both ways using CC’s facts (bank loan, special-occasion cookies, city-centre shop, payments to people on low incomes), and the conclusion weighs them and says what would change the decision. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 6.2 Environmental and Ethical Issues These questions test external costs and benefits, sustainable development, pressure groups and ethics; examiners reward precise definitions and effects traced to a named business’s costs, sales and reputation. What examiners keep seeing Confusing external costs and benefits with the business’s own costs and benefits (its wages or its sales), and confusing sustainable development with “sustainable production”, business growth or ethical behaviour, which the examiner reports highlight. 0450/13/M/J/25 Q3(a) · May/June 2025 · [2 marks] Define ‘external benefits’. External benefits are the gains from a business’s activity that are enjoyed by third parties in the rest of society, not by the business itself. Why this scores Two marks for a full definition: gains to the rest of society (third parties) that result from business activity. The examiner report says most candidates lost a mark by describing benefits to the business, giving only examples, or making vague references to “people”. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/11/M/J/25 Q4(c) · May/June 2025 · [4 marks] Source material: PKN manufactures glass. Contributing to sustainable development is important to the business. PKN has factories in 30 countries. Outline two ways PKN could contribute to sustainable development. Way 1: PKN could power its glass furnaces with renewable energy, such as solar or wind power, in its factories in all 30 countries, cutting the fossil fuels it burns. Way 2: PKN could collect broken and waste glass and recycle it into new glass, so it uses fewer raw materials such as sand. Why this scores One mark for each way (renewable energy; recycling) and one for each link to PKN (its factories in 30 countries; making glass). The examiner report notes that answers about “sustainable production” or growing the business, or that confused sustainability with ethics, did not score. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/12/M/J/24 Q3(e) · May/June 2024 · [6 marks] Explain two ways a pressure group might try to influence business decisions. Which way do you think is likely to be the most effective? Justify your answer. Way 1: Organise a boycott. A pressure group can persuade consumers to stop buying a business’s products, for example through a social media campaign. If many customers join in, the business’s sales fall, so its revenue and profit fall directly. Way 2: Lobby the government. A pressure group can lobby politicians to pass new laws, such as stricter limits on pollution. If the law changes, the business must change its methods, which may raise its costs. However, getting a law passed can take years and may not succeed. Most effective. I think a boycott is likely to be the most effective, because it hits the business’s revenue quickly and the business can only end it by changing its decision, whereas lobbying depends on the government agreeing and may achieve little more than publicity. However, a boycott works only if consumers can easily switch to a substitute and the campaign gets wide public support; against a business that sells to other firms rather than to consumers, lobbying for a new law may be more effective. Why this scores Two marks for two ways, two for developing each to sales, revenue or costs, and two for a justified choice. As this is a general question, no application is needed; the evaluation marks need a comparison explaining why the other way is less effective. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/11/M/J/24 Q4(e) · May/June 2024 · [6 marks] Do you think being ethical will always lead to lower profit for a business? Justify your answer. Yes, it can lower profit. An ethical business may pay its suppliers a fair price for materials and pay its workers a fair wage. This raises its variable and labour costs. Unless it can raise its price by the same amount, its profit margin on each item falls, so profit is likely to be lower, at least in the short run. No, it can raise profit. Being ethical gives the business a good reputation. Customers who care how products are made may become loyal and be willing to pay a higher price, so revenue can rise. A good reputation also helps attract and keep motivated workers, lowering recruitment costs and raising productivity. Decision. I do not think being ethical will always lower profit. Costs rise straight away, but if the business promotes its ethical image well, the higher prices and extra loyal customers can outweigh those costs, so profit may even rise in the long run. It depends on the customers: in a price-sensitive market where buyers only want the cheapest product, the extra costs are unlikely to be recovered and profit is more likely to fall. Why this scores Two marks for knowledge on both sides (higher costs; better reputation and higher prices), two for developing them to costs, margins and revenue, and two for a decision justified with a condition (whether customers will pay more). Arguing that being unethical raises profit does not answer the question and is not credited. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/22/F/M/23 Q4(a) · February/March 2023 · [8 marks] Source material: RW produces paint which is used for all types of wood products, including wooden furniture. … Waste from the production of paint is put into local rivers and pollutes the water. … The new factory will need 100 production employees. Explain two external benefits and two external costs from RW’s factories. External benefit 1: Jobs for local people. The new factory will need 100 production employees, so local people who were out of work gain jobs and an income, which they then spend in other local businesses. External benefit 2: Higher tax revenue. As RW expands to 2 million tins of paint a year, it should earn more profit and pay more tax, which the government can spend on schools, hospitals or roads for the whole community. External cost 1: Water pollution. Waste from making paint is put into local rivers, which harms fish and makes the water unsafe for people and farms downstream. A second factory could double this pollution. External cost 2: Traffic and noise. More lorries delivering imported raw materials and carrying tins of paint to specialist shops and furniture makers will cause congestion, noise and fumes for residents living near the factories. Why this scores One mark for each correct external benefit and cost, plus one for explaining each in RW’s context (100 production employees, 2 million tins, waste in local rivers, imported raw materials). The examiner report notes that weaker answers gave the business’s own gains, such as more sales and wages, which are not external. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 0450/22/M/J/24 Q4(b) · May/June 2024 · [12 marks] Source material: We use coal for fuel in our factory which we know contributes to global warming. … We know the price of coal is increasing and will continue to increase in the future. However, the government in country X is encouraging businesses to invest in solar panels and is providing a 25% grant. … These mines are further away from our factory. Using Appendix 3 and other information, consider the following two environmental issues when JJ manufactures its products. Which issue should JJ choose to solve first? Justify your answer. • Using coal for fuel in its factory • Buying from suppliers that damage the environment Using coal: why solve it first. The price of coal is increasing and will keep rising, so the cost of powering JJ’s factory goes up every year, raising the cost of making each bracelet and ring. Switching to solar panels would stop this rising cost, and the government’s 25% grant reduces the investment JJ must fund itself. Because other jewellery manufacturers also use coal, JJ could become the greener choice in a market with many competitors, improving its image and easing the pressure from pressure groups. Using coal: drawbacks of solving it first. Solar panels are still a large upfront cost even with the grant, as JJ must pay the other 75%, which reduces the cash available for its objective to expand. As all its competitors also use coal, customers may not see coal as a reason to avoid JJ, so solving this issue may not increase sales in the short run. Buying from damaging suppliers: why solve it first. JJ’s gem stones come from local mines that leave land unusable for farming. If pressure groups publicise this, customers may link JJ’s jewellery with environmental damage and switch to one of its many competitors, cutting sales in country X and to its online customers abroad. Changing to suppliers that use alternative mining methods protects JJ’s reputation and its objective of increasing profit each year. Buying from damaging suppliers: drawbacks of solving it first. The alternative mines are further away, so transport costs and delivery times rise, increasing the cost of each piece of jewellery. JJ’s jewellery is beautiful but not expensive, so it may not be able to raise prices without losing price-conscious customers, and its profit margin would fall. Many buyers may not even know where the gems come from, so the benefit to sales is uncertain. Recommendation. I recommend that JJ solves the coal issue first. It is the only issue that is already raising JJ’s costs and will keep doing so, and the 25% grant makes the switch to solar affordable now; over time the savings on coal should increase profit, matching JJ’s objective. Changing suppliers is less urgent because the damage happens away from JJ and many customers are unaware of it, while the change would raise costs on jewellery that must stay affordable. However, this depends on the pressure groups: if they launch a public campaign about the mines, the threat to JJ’s reputation and sales would become the bigger problem and should be solved first. Why this scores Level 3 needs both issues discussed in detail with JJ’s facts and a well-justified decision. Each issue gets a case for and against using Appendix 3 (rising coal price, 25% grant, mines further away), and the recommendation explains why the other issue is less urgent and what would change the decision. Written your own answer? Get it marked → 6.3 Business and the International Economy These questions test globalisation, protectionism, multinationals and exchange rates; examiners reward answers that say exactly which prices change (imports or exports) and follow that through to the business’s costs, sales and profit. What examiners keep seeing Getting the direction of an exchange-rate change wrong: examiners report many candidates thinking an appreciation makes imports dearer, or a depreciation makes imports cheaper. Many also confuse quotas (limits on quantity) with tariffs (taxes on imports). 0450/12/M/J/24 Q4(a) · May/June 2024 · [2 marks] Define ‘import quota’. An import quota is a limit set by the government on the quantity of a product that can be imported into a country. Why this scores Two marks for a full definition: a physical limit on the quantity (number or amount) of goods allowed into a country. Describing it as a tax confuses it with an import tariff and is not credited. Written your own answer?
